title: In progress, 2026-10-14
text:
Notes on the chord-change lessons built in this session. Nothing here is committed unless git log says so.


Twelve lessons now share one look: numbered steps, each a chord chart (TuneChart) with a staff under it and the Backing Track band, then usually a builder and an ear test.








Lesson
File
Notes




Blues changes
lessons/blues-changes.qmd
Existing. Now has a grand staff under every chart. Hand-written script.


C, Am, F, G
lessons/pop-changes.qmd
Hand-written script, same shape as the blues one.


Four-chord loops
lessons/four-chord-loops.qmd
Hand-written script. Eight loops, builder, ear test.


Cadences
lessons/cadences.qmd
Engine. Plagal taught as the “fake” cadence (the argument is in section 4).


Guide tones
lessons/guide-tones.qmd
Engine. Staff shows a single line; the band’s piano plays it.


Minor changes
lessons/minor-changes.qmd
Engine. Written in A minor (tonic 9).


Borrowed chords
lessons/borrowed-chords.qmd
Engine.


Turnarounds
lessons/turnarounds.qmd
Engine.


Reharmonizing
lessons/reharmonize.qmd
Engine. Ode to Joy with four sets of chords, melody played by the band.


Pop changes for guitar / piano / bass
lessons/pop-changes-guitar.qmd, -piano, -bass
Engine, with fretboard, keyboard or bass diagrams.



The nine newest .qmd files were generated by a script (not kept in the repo) that pasted the same style block, bottom strip and script tags into each, then a ChordLesson.init({...}) config. To change the shared page furniture, edit each .qmd or write the generator again. To change behaviour, edit the engine.




apps/shared/lessons/chord-staff.js (LessonChordStaff): the staff under a chart. Modes: chords (grand staff, block chords and bass note), third, seventh, guide (one line), bass (bass clef). Also describe(sym, transpose, flats) for the diagrams.
apps/shared/lessons/chord-lesson.js (ChordLesson): steps, builder, ear tests, key strip, diagrams (guitar, piano, bass), and a tune’s melody above the chart. Config is documented in its header.
apps/shared/lessons/tunes.js: added BluesTunes.ode (key C), and inKey now uses a tune’s own key instead of assuming F.
apps/shared/tune-chart.js: bars with a chord under a third of the bar wide are drawn smaller (tc-tight), which fixed the cramped numerals in ~/Desktop/cramped.png. Script version is ?v=31 in the lessons that load it.




tests/band/lessons/loops.cdp.js (“CHORD LESSONS OK”): every new page has the right number of staves, the key menu respells them, the sounding bar lights on chart and staff, the ear tests give a verdict and reveal the chart, the guide-tone staff has one note per chord, the guitar lesson draws four diagrams, tight bars get tc-tight. tests/band/lessons/blues.cdp.js still passes. Setup is in tests/band/README.md (render the pages into tests/band/lead/site/lessons, serve on port 8500).



All of it. I checked layout in screenshots and that the pages run without errors, but not how it sounds. In particular:

the guide-tone lines played by the band’s piano (does the melody sit well over the comping?);
the “busy” setting in the reharmonizing lesson, and whether the chords really fit Ode to Joy note for note;
the minor, borrowed and turnaround lessons in each feel (Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Motown, Medium swing, Bossa nova);
the staff lighting during playback on a phone-width screen.





Song names in four-chord-loops.qmd: Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry, Don’t Stop Believin’, Zombie, Despacito, Stand by Me, I Got Rhythm, Louie Louie, Wild Thing, Sweet Home Alabama, Hit the Road Jack were written from memory.
The cadences lesson states a position (plagal is not a cadence) and cites William Caplin’s Classical Form for it. Please check the citation against the book before it is relied on.
Guitar diagrams come from the band’s open-shape library, which ignores the note after a slash. G/B shows the G shape. The lesson says so.
“Mario cadence” in borrowed-chords.qmd (♭VI–♭VII–I) is a popular name, not a textbook one.
Prose in the nine newer lessons was written in one pass and read only by me.





No lesson links yet from the blues lessons to the new ones.
The instrument lessons stop at secondary dominants. No two-fives or builder.
The guitar and bass lesson pages are long (a diagram per chord per step); they may want a “show one chord at a time” control.
The generator script should be kept in scripts/ if the nine pages are going to be edited in bulk.
Quiz questions pick answers at random, and the second cadence question uses my own wording for how each ending “feels”. Rewrite it in your own words.





Generator kept: scripts/chord-lessons.mjs holds the shared furniture (front matter, style block, bottom strip, script tags with versions); each lesson is scripts/chord-lessons/<name>.json (title, body prose, init config). --check compares with lessons/<name>.qmd, --write [name] writes, --extract rebuilds the JSON from the .qmd files. Eight of nine reproduced the existing files byte for byte; guide-tones differed only in key order (JS puts the integer-like key "251" first), same content at runtime. To bump a script version for all nine, edit SCRIPTS and --write. If you hand-edit a .qmd, run --extract first or the next --write overwrites it.
Links from the blues lessons (one bullet or line each): changes -> cadences/turnarounds/guide tones/borrowed chords; guitar, piano, bass -> their pop-changes page; melody -> guide tones and reharmonizing; improvising -> guide tones. blues-drums.qmd untouched.
“Show one chord at a time” (chord-lesson.js?v=2, all nine pages regenerated with the new version): a button above the diagrams on guitar and bass pages (not piano, which is one card). Off by default; on, only the sounding bar’s chords are shown (the first bar’s when stopped), and it follows the band. Test added in loops.cdp.js; loops.cdp.js and blues.cdp.js pass. Not looked at on a phone.
Still not done: two-fives/builder in the instrument lessons, rewriting the quiz wording.




reading-swing.qmd, changes-now.md, the tests/abc folder and many changes to the band and tools files were in the tree when this was written and are not part of this work. _quarto.yml and lessons/index.qmd have both sets of edits in them.



Committed (in the commits up to e4f1887): the seven blues lessons (lessons/blues-*.qmd, apps/shared/lessons/blues-kit.js, diagrams.js, score.js, tunes.js, drumkit.js), the Lessons landing page, scale charts in every .bl-scale panel and .bl-notes, the play row beside each chord grid, staff margins (no first-line indent, nothing cut off, two bars a line under 600 px), drum-note tooltips and the clickable kit picture. Tests: tests/band/lessons/{blues,instruments,more,tune,layout}.cdp.js, t_drumstaff.js, t_tune.js; setup in tests/band/README.md; history in apps/shared/band/NOTES.org.
Uncommitted blues-lesson edits now in the tree (step 8 “Grabbing the crash” in blues-drums.qmd, chokeBars in blues-kit.js, tunes.js, _blues-kit.qmd versions) are another session’s, not this one’s.
Open for this thread: - Nobody has listened: the kit picture’s sounds (cross-stick uses the rim sample), the swung ▶ Play, the arp bass line. - A player should check: piano fingerings (modes take the fingering of the major scale with the same notes, so C Mixolydian’s left hand starts on 1); the violin first-position chart; the Oscar Pettiford credit on Blues in the Closet (X:1009). - Saxophone charts: not started, on purpose (the user has a plan for them). - Offered, never answered: guitar and piano steps show chords as whole notes, not the comping rhythm. - The tune’s pickup is not played at the top of each chorus; the melody is played by the band’s chord instrument. - tests/band/pat/t_tunes.js expected 10 built-in setups and there were 12 (failed before this work). - The lyrics site’s copy of the engine (bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh) was not rebuilt.

title: In progress, 2026-10-14
text:
Done

Backing Track → melody entry. tools/_backing-track.qmd: a button “Open in the melody entry tool” (#bt-mel-entry) in the Melody panel. It opens chord-entry.html#from=tune&d=… the way the lyrics site’s Band panel does, with the changes, tempo, style, title and the melody so far (gridMelody). A pickup in front of bar 1 is not sent; the panel says so.
Pickups between sections (tools/_chord-entry.qmd):

On loading a .cho, the words before a section’s first chord (“Gone a[Eb]way”) become its pickup (lyr[k].lead), if the last bar of the section before has notes to spare (pickOf, choSections records pick). Before this, the pickup count was lost on every reload.
If there are no notes for those words, the load note says so (“…has no notes for it: record Verse 3 with the pickup played in the count-in”).
mergeTake: a take to the end of a section keeps the next section’s pickup notes at the end of its last bar, unless the take played into them. (Re-recording the Bridge used to wipe Verse 3’s “Lat-er”.)

Syllables in the words box. The first lyric box (“The words, by syllable”) shows the words hyphenated once the dictionary has loaded (splitWords, once per section, lyr[k].split). Hyphens there drive the drafts. The Split into syllables button (#ce-words-split) splits typed or pasted words that have no hyphen yet. Words split only by their vowels are listed in the warning line.
Count-off menu (#ce-countin beside Hear it in the Check panel: 1, 2 or 4 bars, default 1, kept in localStorage ceCountIn). It sets the band player’s countIn (player clamp raised from 2 to 4) for Hear it and band takes, and the page’s own click for click takes (sess.count = bars x one bar’s beats, accent on every bar of the count-off). The take engine is unchanged: only the last count-off bar is read (pickup notes), earlier ones are dropped as before. 4 bars are “1 2 3 4” bars; only a count-off of 2 keeps the half-speed first bar. chord-entry.js tag is now ?v=10 (its content did not change; the page and player.js?v=122 did). Test: tests/band/entry/countin.cdp.js (“COUNT-IN OK”).

title: In progress, 2026-10-14
section: One shared ABC parser, toward a notation system with MIDI and audio entry (a separate session)
text:
One shared ABC parser, toward a notation system with MIDI and audio entry (a separate session)
The goal, agreed in chat: one notation system built from the tune, tonal and rhythm assessments, Song Builder and Chord/Melody Entry. You set the parameters first (key, meter, allowed rhythm cells, strictness), then enter by MIDI, tapping or microphone, and a decoder ranks what you might have meant (an extended MelodyDwim). Microphone input is built last, but the design allows for it from the start: every event carries a confidence, and noisy MIDI stands in for the microphone in tests.
Done, not committed (the tests/abc entry under “Other people’s changes” above is this): - apps/shared/abc-core.js (AbcCore): tokenizer, header fields, key signatures, note→MIDI, chord symbols. - apps/assessment/abc-pitch.js, apps/rhythm-assessment/abc-rhythm.js, apps/tune-assessment/abc-tune.js are now thin wrappers over it, with exactly the old output. Each throws a clear error if abc-core.js was not loaded first. - <script src="/apps/shared/abc-core.js?v=1"> before the parser in 13 .qmd pages (seven practice pages, tools/_backing-track, tools/_chord-entry, lessons/_blues-kit, blues-changes, four-chord-loops, pop-changes). tests/band/tune/t_score.js and t_oracle.js load it too. One pointer line was added to CLAUDE.md. - Tests: node tests/abc/compare.js → “ABC SAME” (frozen old parsers in tests/abc/baseline/ against the new ones, on every tune, pattern, rhythm and benchmark plus edge cases; also checks every page loads the core first). The test was checked by planting five errors in the core; it catches all of them. SITE=<rendered pages> node tests/abc/pages.cdp.js → “PAGES SAME” (13 pages in headless Chrome, old parsers against new). quarto preview copied everything into _site, and every _site page that loads a parser has the core tag. - Later: re-rendered tools/backing-track.qmd into tests/band/lead/site (its copy predated the core tag); entry/melody-bt, side, entry pass again. Every lesson page in the test site loads the core.
Found, deliberately not fixed (it changes grades): - The tonal assessment grades 53 of the 148 live patterns (pattern-set.js) on the wrong pitches. abc-pitch.js knows only C major and C minor. Any key starting with a letter then “m” (Dm, also Gmix) is read as C minor, and other keys as C major. The staff shows the right key, but grading expects e.g. F where the staff shows F♯ in D. apps/assessment/app.js also assumes C for the key menu names and the resting-tone target (60 + transpose). Fix: grade with AbcCore.keyAccidentals, then rework those two places. Students’ past results were scored the old way.
Next, in order: 1. (Recommended first) fix the tonal key bug above. 2. The event model: { t_on, t_off, pitch candidates, confidence, source }, built on AbcCore.tokens. Keep written events (one per notehead, which the rhythm assessment’s notehead colouring needs) separate from sounding notes (ties merged). 3. The profile schema (key/mode, allowed degrees, meter, subdivision, swing, triplets, RhythmCells vocabulary, strictness). 4. A decoder on MIDI that wraps Chord Entry’s quantizer, plus a noisy-MIDI test helper (jitter, cents drift, merged and split notes). 5. MelodyDwim ranking by profile. 6. Presets (Assess, Dictate, Build, Chart). 7. Tap entry. 8. Microphone note segmenter (YIN + onsets).
Watch: swing should come from the one shared setting the swing worktree (changes-now.md) is building, not a new copy.
Update (agent, 2026-10-14 afternoon) — Next steps 1 and 2 done, not committed. - Tonal key bug fixed. apps/assessment/abc-pitch.js grades with AbcCore.keyAccidentals (new exports keySignature, tonicPc). apps/assessment/app.js: key menu names come from the pattern’s own key (“D”, “E dor”, “A mix”, …; keyNameAt); the resting-tone target, the tonality cadence and the “no response” reference use writtenTonicMidi + transpose (tonic of the written key, C4..B4, not 60); the sung-response staff is written in the pattern’s key and spelled against its signature (midiToAbcToken(midi, ksig); with no signature it spells exactly as before); currentMinor now means “minor third” (minor, dorian, …), so Gmix is no longer treated as minor and Ddor is. - tests/abc/compare.js still verifies everything else identical and now reports the intended difference: 53 of 148 pattern-set patterns grade on different pitches, and for them the test checks the change is only the key-signature shift per note. title: everything-music-site
text:
everything-music-site

Adding or changing a Backing Track style, bass line, comping rhythm or drum groove: read apps/shared/band/ADDING-STYLES.md first.
The band’s history, open questions and what nobody has listened to yet: apps/shared/band/NOTES.org.
Tests and headless page drivers: tests/band/README.md.
The tonewheel organ (tonebars, swell pedal, Leslie, and the rules the band’s organist follows, with sources): apps/shared/band/ORGAN.md.
The Notation page (tools/_notation.qmd, model apps/shared/notation-doc.js): chunks, sections, voices, chords, words, takes. At its top, Play it in: takes from a MIDI keyboard (Space / sustain pedal; Shift+R redo, Shift+Backspace drop), each a chunk of its own; notes in the count-in of the first take make a Pickup chunk (chunk.pickup, a short first bar, up to a bar less one eighth). The other ways in (letters, rhythm bank, chords, words, the older Play it in time) are in the right sidebar. Keys act on the active note (red: the selection, else the first note without a pitch): letters, z rest, T tie to the note before (t: to the next), U unpitch, u undo, Space play from the active note to the chunk’s end (Play through ticked: to the piece’s end, from that bar’s start), j/k or a click on a chunk make its first note active, r record a take (new chunk below), I insert at the start, yy / DD copy / cut the chunk (the first DD asks y/n: Caps Lock), p / P put it after / before, Backspace delete, h/l notes, H/L bars (inside the chunk), i Insert mode (a caret), s split the chunk at the caret / before the active note (a cut inside a bar gives the second part a lead), o/O new chunk, v/V show/hide this chunk / the others (chunk.off), J Join (D.merge), M Merge (D.combine: rhythm-only + pitch-only chunk, or two the same length as two voices); J/M ask y/n to show hidden chunks first. Only a chunk with no rhythm collects pitches (stemless, | = part.breaks); in a chunk with rhythm | sets chunk.lead (a pickup). Every chunk starts on beat 1, or its lead before a barline, whatever ends the chunk before (D.offsets; invisible rest in the ABC, Join writes it in as rest). Tempo: written Q: (90 when unset; abcjs would play 180), and [Q:] in every voice where it changes. Keys are an ABC key with a mode (Ddor), or hm for harmonic minor (Dhm: written K:Dm, letters raise the 7th; D.keyName, D.majorOf); the menus are tonic + tonality + an enharmonic switch. Tempo: doc.tempo / chunk.tempo (D.at, Q:). Meter menus have Other… (two number boxes). Words follow ABC’s w: rules (- syllables, _ hold over the next note, * skip). The ChordPro ends with the notes as a {start_of_abc} block: with it, editing the ChordPro edits the piece (D.fromChordPro takes notes from the ABC, words from the ChordPro, keeping each word’s syllables). Line breaks: doc.lineEvery (bars a line, a pickup bar not counted) and RET’s own breaks chunk.nl (barline times from the chunk’s start, drawn ↴; click or RET removes); with either, toAbc breaks lines there and at every chunk (lines in its result) and the score draws each line on its own. S starts a section at the active chunk (a heading row in Chunks, its name input focused, TsLabels names as a datalist; repeated words numbered); J / M refuse to cross a section start. Words: Paragraphs to sections (each paragraph a chunk heading Verse n). Play: the sounding note lit (nt-playing, abcjs TimingCallbacks mapped through the play map to the drawn lines); with chords the band plays the chords AND the notes (bar.melody on the parsed chart, so nothing drifts; band scripts loaded on first use, makeBand: D.bandChart, doc.band.style else “pop”, tempo per bar, a Pickup chunk = the chart’s short first bar after one bar of count-in; playhead from onBar/onBeat; 12 s without samples: the abcjs piano). Rhythm bank keys: 2 3 4 8 are always half, dotted half, quarter, eighth (shown when the ticked boxes give that note); patterns take 1 5 6 7 9. Play it in’s Tempo shows the piece’s tempo at the chunk; one typed there is the take’s and goes on its chunk (Q.bpmOwn). The score draws each shown chunk on its own line (drawChunks: bars a fixed width, a mid-bar start padded so barlines line up). Test: node tests/abc/notation-quick.cdp.js. DWIM there (re-reading a take, kept with the chunk) is documented in apps/shared/NOTATION-DWIM.md, as are phrase seams (the bar shared by a phrase’s end and the next one’s pickup; apps/shared/phrase-seam.js, NotationDoc.writeLeadIn; after Timestamp Notes’ nt-goto a Play it in take goes into that phrase, count-in notes into the bar before; node tests/abc/phrase-seam.test.js). It opens the Backing Track as a remote window (bt-load, bt-focus, and bt-setup reports back). Tests: node tests/abc/notation-doc.test.js, node tests/abc/notation.cdp.js.
Non-harmonic tones (passing, neighbour, suspension 4-3, …) of a melody against its chord symbols: apps/shared/abc-nht.js, over abc-events.js; not on any page yet. Tests: node tests/abc/nht.test.js.
ABC reading for the assessments (apps/shared/abc-core.js, and abc-pitch.js, abc-rhythm.js, abc-tune.js over it): a page loads abc-core.js before any of them. After changing them run node tests/abc/compare.js (old vs new on every tune and pattern; how to run the browser check is at the top of tests/abc/pages.cdp.js).
The tune collection (apps/tunes/tunes-object.js): after importing or editing tunes run node scripts/clean-tunes.mjs --write. It normalises the ABC, bakes %%id, and tags tunes that still fail a parse/bar-length check needs-repair; the Tune Library hides those unless the Tags filter asks for them.
The sound-design lessons (lessons/sound-*.qmd, 25 of them: harmonics to chiptune, in the order of _quarto.yml) are widgets from apps/shared/lessons/synth-kit.js (kinds and attributes documented at its top), included via lessons/_synth-kit.qmd. Plain Web Audio, nothing shared with the band. Tests: node tests/lessons/sound.cdp.js (after rendering).
The Vocal Warm-up (tools/vocal-warmup.qmd, apps/shared/vocal-warmup.js): a routine built from the Set up form (stretches, breathing, piano-led patterns, two band grooves). Tests: node tests/lessons/warmup.cdp.js (after sh scripts/render-test-page.sh tools/vocal-warmup.qmd; the band check skips when no samples can load).
Timestamp Notes (tools/timestamp-notes.qmd, was the Big Timestamp Player; apps/shared/timestamp-player/): audio (YouTube link or file), S a section stamp with a label menu (section-labels.js, TsLabels: words, solos, letters A A′ B …, Other; repeats numbered, choruses per soloist; lesson lessons/section-labels.qmd; test node tests/lessons/section-labels.test.js, node tests/lessons/section-stamps.cdp.js) in the same list as C notes; the MIDI keyboard connects in the right sidebar; words and chords pasted from Ultimate Guitar and turned into ChordPro (apps/shared/ug-chordpro.js), S stamps the next section from the words, B taps each downbeat, then Send on: the Notation page (?remote=1, nt-ready / nt-chordpro) or the Backing Track (bt-load), each section’s chords spread over its tapped bars at the tapped tempo. C stamps, Shift+L loops, Space plays, arrows / h l go 5 s; a bar’s own Beats (meter change) goes out as a {time:} that fromChordPro reads mid-song. Fill from the tempo (bar-map.js extrapolate): bars after / between the taps from the tapped tempo, spread evenly between section stamps, heads and solos snapped to whole choruses; guessed bars kept apart (guessed), a B tap among them re-anchors. Halve / Double bars rescale the taps (warning first about irregular bars; Undo). Chord timing (live.js): N, or MIDI all at once (left hand one note = bar, two = section; right hand = chord hits, matched to the ChordPro’s chords in order), placed per bar and rounded; sent as nt-doc (a whole doc). The stage shows the current section’s words large (drag its grip taller) and the next section’s first line; the chord grid (tune-chart.js, as on the Backing Track) shows each chord as it is hit (the rest once confirmed). At each pause timed sections are written into the ChordPro as {start_of_grid} blocks (UgChordPro.grids/gridBlock); a grid edited there is the section’s timing until its hits change. Now playing sits in the right column (Float / Pin, A− A+). Correct chords (MIDI): a bar played in is rewritten with the chord named from its notes (ChordEntry.analyse); bars played through keep theirs. A meter change inside a section splits it (_cont pieces) so charts show it. The Backing Track’s Melody tab opens the Notation page (nt-abc); its Show bar has Side by side (notation beside the grid). Sent to the Notation page every named part is a section, chunks labelled by NotationDoc.chunkLabels (I1a, V1a, PC2b, A3a). The Notation page’s score has a Show menu (whole piece or one section). Every part folds, with a jump sidebar (page-nav.js). One song file (.json: stamps, bar map, words, chord hits, the link) saves everything; older .txt / bar-map .json still open. Phrases (phrases.js, TsPhrases): each section cut into 2/4/8-bar phrases, each looped from its lead-in (pickup, up to 2 bars, the phrase before keeps a beat; P, , ., - =); T / Notate sends nt-goto (the Notation page answers nt-need-doc when it lacks the section, then gets nt-doc), its Back button nt-back loops the next phrase. Test: node tests/lessons/phrases.test.js. “Follow in a tab” when YouTube refuses. The site’s search has no keyboard shortcut (_quarto.yml), so letters stay free. Tests: node tests/abc/ug-chordpro.test.js, node tests/lessons/timestamp.cdp.js (after quarto render tools/timestamp-notes.qmd and tools/notation.qmd into _site).
Pitch from the microphone (YIN, a mic helper, the strobe bank, target pitches in 12-ET / just / 31-ET / cents): apps/shared/pitch-detect.js (window.PitchDetect; the Tune Assessment uses it). The tuner (strobe) and bendboard widgets are synth-kit kinds (documented at the top of synth-kit.js); LessonDiagrams.bendboard is in diagrams.js. A page with its own fixed bottom bar sets window.SK_NO_BAR = true before _synth-kit.qmd (guitar-bends does). Tests: node tests/lessons/tuner.test.js (no browser), node tests/lessons/tuner.cdp.js (after rendering lessons/tuning-systems, lessons/guitar-bends, practice/assessment-tune). The strobe drawing and target text are apps/shared/strobe-view.js (shared by the tuner widget and the navbar panel). The navbar Strobe tuner (apps/shared/tuner-panel.js, loaded on first open by practice-widgets.js) listens to the microphone, to this page’s sound, to a page video/audio, or to another tab (getDisplayMedia, Chrome). Sound sources hand their master to window.AudioTap.register(ctx, node, label) (apps/shared/audio-tap.js, in the head of every page; drone, synth-kit, audio.js, the band do); the tuner analyses inside the source’s own AudioContext, so no bridge is needed. Lesson: lessons/strobe-tuner.qmd. Tests: node tests/lessons/tuner-panel.cdp.js (after rendering index and lessons/strobe-tuner).
Audio pre-flight (apps/shared/audio-check.js, window.AudioCheck.run()): Chrome note, a soft test sound (capped at -24 dBFS, steps up from -48) that tells speakers from headphones and measures latency, then a mic level meter; returns getUserMedia constraints; ensure() reuses it for the tab (sessionStorage audio-check-v1). Used by pitch-detect, synth-kit, the assessments, the Backing Track and tools/webcam-demo.html. Page tests that open the mic seed that key so the dialog stays shut. Tests: node tests/lessons/audiocheck.cdp.js (after rendering practice/assessment-tune).
Dictation (practice/dictation.qmd, grader apps/shared/dictation.js): plays a Reading Benchmarks line, opens the Notation page as a remote window (?dictation=1: a scratch doc kept apart from the user’s own; dict-load, dict-replay, dict-submit), grades the handed-in ABC note by note (pitch, rhythm, extra notes). Tests: node tests/abc/dictation.test.js, node tests/lessons/dictation.cdp.js (after rendering both pages).
Write an Ending (lessons/write-an-ending.qmd): every tune in the library with %%id unfinished-song-* (chords as real chord symbols, the last two bars x rests over V and I/i), with the Notation page framed in it (?ending=1: pared down, no site chrome, its own store ntEndingDoc; end-ready, end-load {abc,title}, end-change {abc}). Each song’s ending is kept in localStorage ending:<id>. Tests: node tests/lessons/ending.cdp.js (after rendering it and tools/notation.qmd). In ?ending=1 the Notation page shows only Rhythm and Notes: rhythm fills the open bars in order and stops when they’re full (no bar is added); letters fill the first empty note.
Sing and Notate (lessons/sing-and-notate.qmd, matcher apps/shared/sing-notate.js; not in the sidebar yet): plays Unfinished Song #1 (read from the tune library; it sets key, tonality, meter) three times in a row, records its empty last two bars each time, matches the takes to the familiar rhythm / tonal pattern banks (lenient; warns when nothing fits), then grades what is written into those bars in the framed Notation page. Tests: node tests/lessons/sing-notate.test.js, node tests/lessons/sing-notate.cdp.js (after rendering it and tools/notation.qmd).
The IPA chart (tools/ipa-chart.qmd, apps/shared/ipa/): its vowel trapezoid is draggable through ipa-synth.js (window.IpaSynth, a four-formant voice; API at its top). The lesson lessons/vowel-formants.qmd (F1, F2, F3, singer’s formant, formant tuning) uses the same synth. Tests: node tests/ipa/ipa-chart.cdp.js, node tests/lessons/formants.cdp.js (after rendering both pages).
The Lessons read like a book: the lessons sidebar in _quarto.yml groups them by topic (parts), with Previous / Next. The Lessons index (lessons/index.qmd) is a Quarto listing (its contents: list, in order; template lessons/_lessons-listing.ejs), filtered by text, instrument, topic and Has. Each lesson’s front matter carries description, instruments, topics and has (band, notation, fingering, interactive, svg, images; not categories:, which would print chips). A new lesson: add those fields, add it to the listing’s contents: and to a sidebar section. has: is written by node scripts/lesson-features.cjs (headless Chrome over the rendered _site lessons; --dry only prints): rerun it after adding a lesson or changing what one shows, then render lessons/index.qmd.
The large tools’ page design (Timestamp Notes, the Notation page): two columns of folding parts plus a sidebar column of its own (jump links, staying put as the page scrolls). Every part moves between the columns (its header’s ⇄, or drag its grip), kept in localStorage (ts-columns, ntColumns; Reset columns in the sidebar): apps/shared/panel-columns.js / .css. A part moved out of a group goes into a .pc-shell with the group’s classes; scripts look inside their group with PanelColumns.q(root, sel) and find the group itself as .group:not(.pc-shell).
Tap Along (tools/tap-along.qmd, apps/shared/tap-along/): Timestamp Notes cut down for a phone, against a song playing in any other app. Its own clock; Mark taps 1 Bar / 2 Chord / 3 Section (the n-th chord tap is the sheet’s n-th chord), Play’s Sync puts the clock on the first tapped bar. Each tap has its button’s lag taken off (localStorage tap-latency-v1), measured on Tap Latency (tools/tap-latency.qmd: metronome, four to count in, twelve taps per button). Song file .tap-along.json, not Timestamp Notes’. Test: node tests/lessons/tap-along.cdp.js (after rendering both pages).
Long instruction paragraphs (class *hint* / *-note, 160+ characters, not *warn* / aria-live) start folded behind an lower-case i in a circle button: apps/shared/help-eye.js, in _includes/head.html. data-help-eye="off" keeps one open.
Notation lessons (lessons/notation-steps.qmd, not in the sidebar yet): steps that frame the Notation page as ?stage=1 (st-ready, st-load {show, doc, rhythm}, st-change {doc, abc}; store ntStageDoc): only the panels a step lists are shown, keys for hidden parts do nothing, and the step’s target (rhythm slots, want) unlocks the next. Add steps to its STEPS list. The page also has Save to file / Open file (.notation.json: { kind: "notation-doc", version: 1, doc }, or ABC).
The DAW lessons (lessons/daw-*.qmd, eight, in _quarto.yml after the Recording lessons; include lessons/_daw-kit.qmd): a small DAW, apps/shared/daw/mini-daw.js (MiniDaw; <div class="mdaw" data-id data-preset data-show>, documented at its top), playing the band’s sounds (BandSounds) with its parts written by BandMidi.generate (“Session players”). Timeline, loop, click, step sequencer, piano roll, record from computer keys / MIDI, audio tracks from the mic (DAW 6: bleed, headphones, latency), quantize, clips, mixer, MIDI export, bounce to WAV, undo. Each lesson ends with an “In other DAWs” table (BandLab, Ableton Live, Logic Pro); DAW 8 (daw-real.qmd, no DAW on it) is a tabbed first-session checklist for each, every step linked to its manual page. Checked Oct 2026 against BandLab Help Center, Live 12 manual, Logic 12.3 guide. Test: node tests/lessons/daw.cdp.js (after rendering them).
The Sampling and DJ lessons (lessons/sampling-*.qmd, six: what a sample is to the law; lessons/dj-*.qmd, seven: gear to a set; sidebar parts Sampling, DJing; include lessons/_dj-kit.qmd): apps/shared/dj/turntables.js (Turntables; <div class="dj-tt" data-a data-b   data-decks data-show>, documented at its top): two decks (an AudioWorklet each: platter drag = scratch, rim = nudge, motor spin-up, pitch ±8/±16 % moving the key, cue, waveform, BPM / Tap, key + Camelot) and a mixer (gain, 3-band EQ with kill, filter, cue, faders, crossfader with curve, phones mix / split cue / Listen). apps/shared/dj/sampler-pads.js (SamplerPads; <div class="sp-pads" data-loop data-slice>): 16 pads from a loop (equal / beats / at the hits, chops draggable), keys ZXCV…1234 and MIDI 36–51, repitch or OLA stretch per pad, a recorded, quantized pattern. Built-in loops are synthesised offline (Turntables.DEMOS, demo:<id>). Songs from elsewhere (the R2 hook): Turntables.TRACK_SOURCES; a manifest JSON named by window.DJ_CONFIG.manifest, <meta name="dj-manifest">, data-manifest or Turntables.addManifest(url) lists tracks (url relative to it), fetched CORS (the bucket needs a GET CORS rule); Turntables.load(deck,   src) takes those, URLs, files, buffers. Both register with AudioTap. Test: node tests/lessons/dj.cdp.js (after rendering them).
Sources: every cited source is in scripts/works-cited.py (MLA 9, with the pages that use it). python3 scripts/works-cited.py rewrites each page’s Works Cited block (between <!-- works-cited markers) and writes bibliography.qmd (every source, with links to the lessons using it). Add a source there, not on the page. bibliography.qmd is not in _quarto.yml yet.
Chord shapes taught in lessons: node scripts/chord-taught.cjs (after rendering the lessons into _site) records every chord diagram a lesson draws (LessonDiagrams) into apps/shared/chord-taught-data.js; the Chord Library shows “Taught in …” on matching cards, links to the lesson section in a card’s details, and filters on it (Taught in a lesson, search word taught). Rerun it after adding or changing a lesson’s diagrams. A lesson can draw library-checked shapes with <div class="sc-shapes"> (apps/shared/lessons/shape-cards.js, documented at its top); each links to the library with #…&shape= (that card first, outlined). Test: node tests/band/lessons/first-rock-song.cdp.js.
Lesson drawings (SVG): the house style is apps/shared/lessons/DIAGRAMS.md (schematic, site tokens, a colour = one role, labels and <title>s on the parts, placed by a tag, drawn by a script). Gear figures: apps/shared/lessons/gear-diagrams.js (<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="connectors | jack-wiring | xlr-pins | balanced | signal-flow | keyboard-panel | midi-chain">, documented at its top); used in gear-cables and gear-keyboards.
Gear 3 (lessons/gear-amps.qmd) has two synth-kit kinds: amp (guitar or bass amp: Gain, tone stack with a Mid frequency, Master, power amp, Presence, Resonance, a Cabinet menu (CABS); sources guitar / bass are the band’s samples via BandSounds, loaded on first use; “Vintage” = one Volume) and pa (one mixer channel: gain + peak, high-pass, EQ, monitor send into a wedge that can feed back, pan, mute, fader). Both have a View menu, Sliders / Knobs (w.knobView() in synth-kit; localStorage sk-view). Test: node tests/lessons/amp.cdp.js (after rendering it).
Any slider’s shown number can be clicked and typed into (apps/shared/num-edit.js, in _includes/head.html; a slider whose number is not its raw value sets range.numEdit = {get, set}, as synth-kit does; data-num-edit="off" opts out).
Interactive tools catalogue: node scripts/tool-catalog.cjs scans lessons/*.qmd for widgets (synth-kit / recording-kit data-w kinds, kit classes in its CLS map, the Mini DAW, the framed Notation page) into apps/shared/lessons/tool-catalog-data.js. lessons/tools.qmd draws it (filterable, by family); apps/shared/lessons/tool-links.js (loaded on /lessons/ pages from _includes/head.html) adds a “Same tools in” box to each lesson’s foot. Rerun after adding a lesson or widget; a new kit class goes in CLS.
Guitar Tuning (tools/guitar-tuning.qmd, apps/shared/guitar-tuning.js): ear-first tuning, six methods (reference, drone, fifth-fret, harmonics, octaves, tuner with guess-before-you-see), any tuning incl. Custom (GuitarTuning.parseTuning), a fretboard to click, the mic via PitchDetect. Setup Check (tools/guitar-setup-check.qmd, apps/shared/setup-check.js): guitar/bass relief, buzz map, action, nut, 12th-fret intonation (mic) -> what to adjust and who (you / teacher / tech). Lessons lessons/guitar-tuning-{ear,methods,tuners}.qmd, lessons/guitar-harmonics.qmd. Pages’ window.TEST_MIC_SOURCE replaces the mic. Test: node tests/lessons/guitar-tuning.cdp.js (after rendering both tools).
Hand drums and mic figures: gear-diagrams.js also draws congas, bongos, djembe, tabla (Gear 9, congas-basics) and polar-patterns, mic-response, proximity, off-axis, cupping (Recording 2 and 3). rec-kit-mic.js kinds proximity (distance -> bass) and offaxis (drag round the mic, Cup the grille). Every drum / conga step of blues-kit draws the kit or congas from above, lit as the band plays (apps/shared/lessons/groove-anim.js, LessonGrooveAnim). title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
“Do what I mean”: select some music, press DWIM, and the page shows the other ways that music could have been written, best first, each with a small score and a Use this button. The Notation page (tools/notation.qmd) offers it; the engine is Chord Entry’s (ChordEntry.alternatives) and the panel is MelodyDwim (apps/shared/melody-dwim.js), shared with the Chord Entry page.
This file is the plan and the record: what works now, how it stays working long after a take, and what is still to build. Keep it up to date when DWIM changes.











Kind
Needs
Examples
Status




Re-reading a take
the take’s log (every key down/up with its time, and the settings)
staccato vs note + rest, triplets or not, swing or straight, eighth vs sixteenth grid, plainest vs as-released note ends, grace notes, pickup
built


Re-writing what is written
only the notes on the page
enharmonic spelling (F♯ / G♭), a chord’s other names (C6 / Am7), tie vs dotted note, octave of a passage, meter (6/8 vs 3/4), key
planned, below



Re-reading is the stronger kind: it goes back to how the music was played and reads it again, so it can recover things the first reading threw away (a note too short to keep, a triplet read as eighths). It can only work where the page still has the playing.



On the Chord Entry page a take’s log lives only until the next take. Here it is kept with the chunk:
chunk.takes = [{ voice, log, from, bars, sig: [per-bar signature], lb }]

log is ChordEntry.take(...).log(): { v, cfg, events }. It is small (a few kilobytes for a page of music) and is saved with the piece (localStorage), so DWIM works after a reload, tomorrow, next month.
voice is the voice the take was written into (a take for voice 2 does not answer for voice 1).
from is the chunk bar where the take’s first bar sits (0 when it was recorded into the chunk; it moves when a split or merge moves the take), and bars is how many bars the take wrote.
sig[b] is a signature of what the take wrote in bar b (its rhythm and pitches, NotationDoc.barSig).
lb is the bar of the log that is the take’s first bar (0 if missing). A take from Play it in with a pickup is kept twice: by the Pickup chunk (lb 0, one bar: the log’s pickup bar, re-read at the chunk’s own length) and by the chunk after it (lb 1). The page’s bars are turned into the log’s in toLog, and back in apply.

When it still applies. DWIM compares each selected bar’s signature now with the one recorded. A bar that is unchanged is fully “the take’s”. A bar that was edited (a note moved, a rhythm pattern added) is reported: “Bar 3 was changed after the take: using a reading replaces your changes in that bar.” Using a reading is still allowed: it is your call. Bars outside the take (added later) cannot be re-read.
What survives what.







Operation
What happens to the take




editing notes elsewhere in the chunk
nothing; only the edited bars report a change


splitting the chunk on a bar line
each half keeps the take, with its bars counted from where the half starts (from)


splitting inside a bar
the take is kept by the first half only for its whole bars; the bar that was cut is reported as changed


merging two chunks
both takes are kept, the second one’s bars shifted by the first chunk’s length


duplicating a chunk or a section
the copy keeps the take: DWIM works on the copy too


a new take into the same bars and voice
replaces the old one there


reading ABC or ChordPro in
takes are not in ABC: they are dropped (the page says so)



Using a reading replaces only the selected bars of that voice (NotationDoc.replaceBars) and puts the new signatures in the take, so those bars count as “the take’s” again. The take’s own settings are not changed: the next DWIM still lists every reading, and its “As first written” card is the take’s original reading, not the one you chose.




Select on the staff: click a note (that bar), or shift-click a second note (all the bars between).
DWIM is enabled when the selection lies in one chunk and that chunk has a take for that voice.
The DWIM panel opens with those bars; its own From / To boxes can widen or narrow the range.
Each card: what the reading changes, why someone would mean it, its cost (lower is plainer; notes left out cost most), and Use this.

Takes come from Play it in time. Chords from a take have their own DWIM (below) and are not touched by melody readings.



These work on any music on the page, typed, pasted or played. Each is a list of candidates with a cost, in the same panel, so the user sees one DWIM, not several tools.

Chords. Every chord played in (one a bar, or in a take) keeps the notes that were played (chord.midis). ChordEntry.analyse(midis, { all: true }) already returns every reading that fits (C6 / Am7, slash or not); DWIM on a chord lists them. Typed chords have no notes; for those, offer enharmonic names only (C♯m / D♭m).
Spelling. A selected note or span: the other spelling of each note out of the key (F♯ / G♭), using ChordEntry.spellNotes with the chord of the bar, which is what Chord Entry does for takes. Needs a spelling override on the note (pitches hold MIDI numbers; add spell: { k: "Gb" } beside them).
Rhythm, plainer. Without the playing, the written durations can still be re-read: a note and rest pair as one staccato note, a dotted note vs a tie, sixteenth pairs as eighths when the meter allows.
Meter. A chunk’s rhythm read in another meter with the same length of bar (6/8 vs 3/4, 2/2 vs 4/4), scored by how many notes cross beats; useful after a take recorded in the wrong meter.
Octave. A passage that sits far from the voice’s clef: one octave up or down.
Key. The key guess (NotationDoc.guessKey) with its runners-up and their scores, so a doubtful key can be compared and chosen; still confirmed by the user.

Order of work: 1 (data is already there), 2, then 3–6 as they are wanted.



Transcribing a recording a phrase at a time (Timestamp Notes loops a phrase, the Notation page takes it), the bar where phrase A ends and phrase B’s pickup begins is written by both. That bar is the seam bar.
Lead-in. A phrase’s lead-in (how far before its first downbeat the melody starts) may be up to 2 bars, but never earlier than the previous phrase’s last note; reaching further means A ends earlier, so A’s end moves. The first phrase of a piece: whole bars before its last lead-in bar become a chunk of their own, and the part in the last bar is chunk.pickup (a short first bar, under a bar). Mid-piece the lead-in is written in the closing bar(s) of the chunk before; whole bars of it belong to B, only the last one is a seam.
Where the line goes (PhraseSeam.suggest, best first, each with its reasons; the user can drag it, snapped to eighths): the rest before it and a held note ending A; B’s onsets matching a familiar pickup shape (PhraseSeam.PICKUPS; later the rhythm pattern bank); A ending on a tone of its chord and B starting on a tone of the next chord or a step from its downbeat; where the user’s loop for B started. In a run of even notes with no rest the other hints decide.
Stitching (PhraseSeam.stitch): A owns the bar before the line, B after it; the bar is written once, the other side shown greyed out while one side is edited. - An A note held over the line is cut at B’s first note (not a conflict). - The same note at the same time on both sides is one note, elided (the end of A and the start of B). - Both sides sounding at once is a conflict: “A’s D or B’s E?”, the later transcription kept by default. - A side’s stray note where the other side has nothing is kept; gaps become rests (PhraseSeam.toSlots). - Beaming, accidentals and chord symbols need nothing: the bar is written as one bar by toAbc.
Written by NotationDoc.writeLeadIn(doc, ci, v, bar, lead, { prefer }): the lead-in’s notes (quarters before the phrase’s downbeat) go into the bar before, stitched with what is there, the line at the lead-in’s first note; a bar further back is all the lead-in’s. At the top of the piece the lead-in becomes a Pickup chunk (a short first bar), or a Pickup chunk and a whole Lead-in bar when it is longer than a bar; a Pickup already there is rebuilt with it. Nothing extra is stored: the seam is in the bars themselves, so re-recording either phrase stitches again. (leadIn / tailEnd on chunks, planned earlier, turned out not to be needed.)
On the Notation page, after nt-goto the page is in that phrase: Play it in writes the take into the phrase’s bars (no new chunk; the count-in is lengthened to hold the lead-in) and notes started in the count-in are the lead-in (phraseApply). Shift+R redoes it in place, Shift+Backspace drops it. Where both sounded, the lead-in wins and Keep the earlier notes swaps to the other stitching.
Status: built. Engine apps/shared/phrase-seam.js; phrases in Timestamp Notes (apps/shared/timestamp-player/phrases.js, nt-goto { section, nth, bar, bars, leadIn, label }, nt-need-doc, nt-back); writeLeadIn in notation-doc.js; phraseApply on the Notation page. Not yet: the draggable line (the line is always the lead-in’s first note), suggest() used for a bar typed by hand, the old Play it in time deck in a phrase (only Play it in is).




node tests/abc/notation-doc.test.js: takes kept through split, merge, duplicate; bar signatures; replaceBars.
node tests/abc/notation.cdp.js: a take recorded (synthetic events), saved, the page reloaded, DWIM run on a bar, a reading used.
node tests/abc/phrase-seam.test.js: seam line suggestions, stitching (trim, elision, conflicts), slots.
node tests/abc/notation-doc.test.js (writeLeadIn) and node tests/abc/notation-quick.cdp.js (a take into a phrase, its pickup in the chunk before, redo and drop, a first phrase making a Pickup chunk).

text:
On the Chord Entry page a take’s log lives only until the next take. Here it is kept with the chunk:
chunk.takes = [{ voice, log, from, bars, sig: [per-bar signature], lb }]

log is ChordEntry.take(...).log(): { v, cfg, events }. It is small (a few kilobytes for a page of music) and is saved with the piece (localStorage), so DWIM works after a reload, tomorrow, next month.
voice is the voice the take was written into (a take for voice 2 does not answer for voice 1).
from is the chunk bar where the take’s first bar sits (0 when it was recorded into the chunk; it moves when a split or merge moves the take), and bars is how many bars the take wrote.
sig[b] is a signature of what the take wrote in bar b (its rhythm and pitches, NotationDoc.barSig).
lb is the bar of the log that is the take’s first bar (0 if missing). A take from Play it in with a pickup is kept twice: by the Pickup chunk (lb 0, one bar: the log’s pickup bar, re-read at the chunk’s own length) and by the chunk after it (lb 1). The page’s bars are turned into the log’s in toLog, and back in apply.

When it still applies. DWIM compares each selected bar’s signature now with the one recorded. A bar that is unchanged is fully “the take’s”. A bar that was edited (a note moved, a rhythm pattern added) is reported: “Bar 3 was changed after the take: using a reading replaces your changes in that bar.” Using a reading is still allowed: it is your call. Bars outside the take (added later) cannot be re-read.
What survives what.







Operation
What happens to the take




editing notes elsewhere in the chunk
nothing; only the edited bars report a change


splitting the chunk on a bar line
each half keeps the take, with its bars counted from where the half starts (from)


splitting inside a bar
the take is kept by the first half only for its whole bars; the bar that was cut is reported as changed


merging two chunks
both takes are kept, the second one’s bars shifted by the first chunk’s length


duplicating a chunk or a section
the copy keeps the take: DWIM works on the copy too


a new take into the same bars and voice
replaces the old one there


reading ABC or ChordPro in
takes are not in ABC: they are dropped (the page says so)



Using a reading replaces only the selected bars of that voice (NotationDoc.replaceBars) and puts the new signatures in the take, so those bars count as “the take’s” again. The take’s own settings are not changed: the next DWIM still lists every reading, and its “As first written” card is the take’s original reading, not the one you chose.

title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
Select on the staff: click a note (that bar), or shift-click a second note (all the bars between).
DWIM is enabled when the selection lies in one chunk and that chunk has a take for that voice.
The DWIM panel opens with those bars; its own From / To boxes can widen or narrow the range.
Each card: what the reading changes, why someone would mean it, its cost (lower is plainer; notes left out cost most), and Use this.

Takes come from Play it in time. Chords from a take have their own DWIM (below) and are not touched by melody readings.

title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
These work on any music on the page, typed, pasted or played. Each is a list of candidates with a cost, in the same panel, so the user sees one DWIM, not several tools.

Chords. Every chord played in (one a bar, or in a take) keeps the notes that were played (chord.midis). ChordEntry.analyse(midis, { all: true }) already returns every reading that fits (C6 / Am7, slash or not); DWIM on a chord lists them. Typed chords have no notes; for those, offer enharmonic names only (C♯m / D♭m).
Spelling. A selected note or span: the other spelling of each note out of the key (F♯ / G♭), using ChordEntry.spellNotes with the chord of the bar, which is what Chord Entry does for takes. Needs a spelling override on the note (pitches hold MIDI numbers; add spell: { k: "Gb" } beside them).
Rhythm, plainer. Without the playing, the written durations can still be re-read: a note and rest pair as one staccato note, a dotted note vs a tie, sixteenth pairs as eighths when the meter allows.
Meter. A chunk’s rhythm read in another meter with the same length of bar (6/8 vs 3/4, 2/2 vs 4/4), scored by how many notes cross beats; useful after a take recorded in the wrong meter.
Octave. A passage that sits far from the voice’s clef: one octave up or down.
Key. The key guess (NotationDoc.guessKey) with its runners-up and their scores, so a doubtful key can be compared and chosen; still confirmed by the user.

Order of work: 1 (data is already there), 2, then 3–6 as they are wanted.

title: DWIM on the Notation page
text:
Transcribing a recording a phrase at a time (Timestamp Notes loops a phrase, the Notation page takes it), the bar where phrase A ends and phrase B’s pickup begins is written by both. That bar is the seam bar.
Lead-in. A phrase’s lead-in (how far before its first downbeat the melody starts) may be up to 2 bars, but never earlier than the previous phrase’s last note; reaching further means A ends earlier, so A’s end moves. The first phrase of a piece: whole bars before its last lead-in bar become a chunk of their own, and the part in the last bar is chunk.pickup (a short first bar, under a bar). Mid-piece the lead-in is written in the closing bar(s) of the chunk before; whole bars of it belong to B, only the last one is a seam.
Where the line goes (PhraseSeam.suggest, best first, each with its reasons; the user can drag it, snapped to eighths): the rest before it and a held note ending A; B’s onsets matching a familiar pickup shape (PhraseSeam.PICKUPS; later the rhythm pattern bank); A ending on a tone of its chord and B starting on a tone of the next chord or a step from its downbeat; where the user’s loop for B started. In a run of even notes with no rest the other hints decide.
Stitching (PhraseSeam.stitch): A owns the bar before the line, B after it; the bar is written once, the other side shown greyed out while one side is edited. - An A note held over the line is cut at B’s first note (not a conflict). - The same note at the same time on both sides is one note, elided (the end of A and the start of B). - Both sides sounding at once is a conflict: “A’s D or B’s E?”, the later transcription kept by default. - A side’s stray note where the other side has nothing is kept; gaps become rests (PhraseSeam.toSlots). - Beaming, accidentals and chord symbols need nothing: the bar is written as one bar by toAbc.
Written by NotationDoc.writeLeadIn(doc, ci, v, bar, lead, { prefer }): the lead-in’s notes (quarters before the phrase’s downbeat) go into the bar before, stitched with what is there, the line at the lead-in’s first note; a bar further back is all the lead-in’s. At the top of the piece the lead-in becomes a Pickup chunk (a short first bar), or a Pickup chunk and a whole Lead-in bar when it is longer than a bar; a Pickup already there is rebuilt with it. Nothing extra is stored: the seam is in the bars themselves, so re-recording either phrase stitches again. (leadIn / tailEnd on chunks, planned earlier, turned out not to be needed.)
On the Notation page, after nt-goto the page is in that phrase: Play it in writes the take into the phrase’s bars (no new chunk; the count-in is lengthened to hold the lead-in) and notes started in the count-in are the lead-in (phraseApply). Shift+R redoes it in place, Shift+Backspace drops it. Where both sounded, the lead-in wins and Keep the earlier notes swaps to the other stitching.
Status: built. Engine apps/shared/phrase-seam.js; phrases in Timestamp Notes (apps/shared/timestamp-player/phrases.js, nt-goto { section, nth, bar, bars, leadIn, label }, nt-need-doc, nt-back); writeLeadIn in notation-doc.js; phraseApply on the Notation page. Not yet: the draggable line (the line is always the lead-in’s first note), suggest() used for a bar typed by hand, the old Play it in time deck in a phrase (only Play it in is).

title: The tonewheel organ
text:
The band’s hammond sound (sounds.js), the organist’s pedal and switch (organist in comp.js), and the panel on the Backing Track page. Written 2026-10-10. Nobody has listened to it. Every level and rule below is either taken from a source (linked) or is a first guess, and the two are kept apart so the guesses are easy to find and change.
What was asked for: all nine tonebars, the upper manual only, the C3 chorus, and a band that works the swell pedal and the Leslie speed by itself. Not built: percussion, the lower manual, bass pedals, the other vibrato settings.


Three kinds, in falling order: technical write-ups read in full (Electric Druid, Scott Healy’s playing tips, Wikipedia); documents quoted in search results but not opened (the Hammond service text, Stefan Vorkoetter); and forum posts quoted in search results, where the link is to the thread the search named and the exact post was not checked (Keyboard Corner, Cantabile, Nord, Fractal). Anything resting only on the third kind is one player’s word.



Nothing is sampled. Each note is three oscillators, a few milliseconds of noise, and then one chain shared by all the notes.



Part
What it does
Where the numbers come from




Tonebars
Nine pitches for a key: 16′, 5⅓′, 8′, 4′, 2⅔′, 2′, 1⅗′, 1⅓′, 1′, at 0.5, 1.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 times the note
Electric Druid


Tonebar steps
0 is silent; each step from 8 down is 3 dB quieter
A clone’s description of the real instrument (Hammy 91); widely repeated, not from a Hammond document


Tempering
The fifths and the third are tempered wheels, not pure harmonics: 1.4988, 2.9976, 5.0409 and 5.9953 times the note. So a note is one oscillator for the octaves, one for the three fifths, one for the third
Electric Druid


Foldback
91 wheels. Key 1 (C2) takes its 8′ from wheel 13. A pitch above wheel 91 is taken an octave lower; the bottom octave’s 16′ an octave higher
Electric Druid (its table did not survive being read by machine; the rule here reproduces its wheel ranges)


Leakage
A closed tonebar still lets a trace through (−48 dB, octaves only)
That it exists: Electric Druid. The amount: a guess


Key click
A key’s nine contacts do not close together. Here: 22 ms of filtered noise as a note starts, with its own slider
The cause: Electric Druid. The sound of it: a guess


Touch
None. A note is the same level however it is played
Scott Healy: “the organ isn’t velocity-sensitive”


C3 chorus
A delay swept up and back 6.87 times a second (412 turns a minute), about 0.9 ms from end to end, mixed half and half with the straight sound
Rate and that the scanner runs up the line and back: Hammond service text. About 50 µs a stage over 18 stages: Stefan Vorkoetter (an M-100, not a B-3). The half-and-half mix: a guess; no source gives the real ratio


Swell pedal
Never silent: 24 dB down at its quietest. Keeps the bass up as it closes. Sits before the tube stage, so opening it also adds growl
That it never closes, lifts bass and treble as it comes down, and drives the amp harder as it opens: Nord forum, quoting a Hammond manual. The 24 dB and the 7 dB of bass: guesses; no source gives figures


Tube drive
The amp-chain drive already in the band, set low
A guess


Rotary speaker
Split at 800 Hz into a horn and a drum. Horn 48 turns a minute slow, 400 fast; drum 85% of that. Two microphones on opposite sides
Crossover and speeds: Wikipedia; 48 / 400 and 40 / 342 measured on a 147: Fractal forum


Speed changes
The horn gets most of the way in about 1.5 s, the drum in about 5 s
“Less than two seconds” and “4 to 10 seconds, depending on belt tension”: one forum post, found by search. No measured figure exists that I could find, so treat it as anecdote



Measured in tests/band/pat/organ.cdp.js: with every tonebar out, all nine pitches of A4 come out within 0.2 dB of each other; the 1⅗′ sits at 2218 Hz, not the pure 2200; C7’s 1′ sounds at 4186 Hz (two octaves folded back); two steps of a tonebar are 6.0 dB; the pedal closed is 24 dB down; the speaker moves the level 0.8 times a second slow and 6.67 fast, and summed to mono the swing all but cancels.



None of these is sourced. The searches named famous registrations (Jimmy Smith, Charles Earland, Groove Holmes, Erroll Garner, “full organ”) but gave no digits, so the menu describes each sound and attributes it to nobody. The default is 88 8000 000.



BandComp.organist decides, bar by bar, where the pedal sits and when the speaker changes speed. It uses no random numbers. Each rule, and what it rests on:
Swell pedal



Rule
Why




It follows how hard the band is playing: about half open when the band plays down, nearly open at full, a little more in a chorus
The organ has no touch, so the pedal is its only dynamics (Healy: “vary the dynamics using the expression pedal”)


The last bar of each four-bar phrase opens through the bar into the next one; more so going into a chorus
“Start with the expression pedal at minimum, then increase the pedal slowly”; a crescendo into the build (Healy)


The first bar of a phrase settles back a little
“Back off the pedal as the speaker slows down” (Healy)


A stop bar is hit and then pulled back sharply
“Pull the expression pedal back suddenly for a sforzando effect” (Healy)


The last chord swells and is let go
A guess



Leslie



Rule
Why




Slow is home
Rock and blues players “lean on that chorale mostly” (a forum post: Keyboard Corner or Cantabile)


Fast through the last bar of a phrase that leads into a chorus or back to the top, or that the band is playing hard; slow again as the next phrase starts
“As your single note starts to build, pop your Leslie or rotary switch to fast, and depress the pedal” (Healy). A forum player describes speeding up at the end of a phrase (Cantabile)


On a chord held two bars or more, a flick to fast for the second half of the phrase’s last bar and straight back
“Flip the Leslie to fast, then immediately flip it back to slow” under pads (Healy)


In swing the speaker stays slow, until the last two bars of the last chorus
Jazz players mostly leave the speaker alone and rely on the chorus (a forum post, Keyboard Corner or Cantabile: they “stop the horn entirely for the vast majority of work”). Slow, not stopped, is my choice


Fast on the final chord
A guess; a common ending



Thresholds that are mine: “playing hard” is an intensity of 0.66 or more; the flick lasts a beat and a half; the pedal’s range is 0.48 to 0.90 of its travel across the band’s intensity.
Nothing was found for gospel. The searches turned up no description of gospel pedal or Leslie habits, so the straight-eighth rules above are rock and blues habits applied to everything that is not swing.



Mixer → Organ: tonebars, swell and Leslie, shown while the organ is the comping instrument or the second one: nine tonebars, a registration menu, Leslie (Automatic / Slow / Fast / Stopped), Swell pedal (Automatic / By hand), key click. The chorus, the pedal’s range, the drive and the speaker’s own numbers are in Mixer → Tone (EQ), in the organ’s amp. Settings are kept in the browser (localStorage.btOrgan, and btAmp for the amp).




Percussion, the lower manual, pedals, V1 to V3 and C1, C2.
Tapering (each wheel’s own level across the keyboard), which a commenter on Electric Druid calls the main reason for the instrument’s scream.
Leakage between neighbouring wheels at other pitches; contact bounce note by note.
The cabinet: no reflections, no horn tone, one tube stage for both rotors.
Tonebar moves, chorus on and off, and registration changes are not played by the band: only the pedal and the speed.
The comping is the piano’s voicings. An organist’s held chords with a moving finger under a held top note (Healy, Ex. 2) are not written.





When do you reach for fast: into every chorus, or only the last one? On held chords? At endings?
In jazz, do you leave the speaker slow, stopped, or off altogether with the chorus doing the work?
Where does your foot sit when comping: about half, or lower? How far do you open into a chorus?
Your comping registration, and whether you change it between verse and chorus.
Chorus C3 always on, or only for some styles?

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
This lesson is for a bass player. The bass is the instrument that plays the lowest note of every chord, so on the changes of C, Am, F, G it is the part that decides which passing chords are heard. Each step has the line in bass clef, a fretboard for it and the chart.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
C, Am, F, G. One note for each chord, the root. The bass-clef staff shows the line and the fretboard shows where to play it, on a four-string bass in the lowest position that has the note.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. The roots are the same. The extensions are for the chord instruments, so the bass line does not change.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
3. The walking line
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. Now the bass is the part that carries the passing chords: C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G. Every note is one step from the last. This is the line to learn.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line
text:
4. Leading into the next chord
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. The bass plays the root of the dominant, which is a fifth above the note that follows. E, then A. C, then F. D, then G.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
A song in C major is not limited to the chords of C major. It may borrow chords from the parallel minor (C minor) or from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat 7). The borrowed chord has a note that is not in the key, and it sounds like a colour change. This lesson adds those chords one at a time to a plain I, IV, V, I.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
1. The plain version
C, F, G, C. Every chord is in the key of C major.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
2. The minor iv
C, F, Fm, C. Replace the IV with the iv. F minor has A♭, a note that is not in C major and that falls to G, the 5th of C. It is the sound of a major song turning wistful for one bar.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
3. The ♭VII
C, F, B♭, C. B♭ is the chord of the flat seventh (the 7th of the mixolydian mode). It falls a step to C. It sounds natural after F because the two roots are a whole step apart and the chords share the note F.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
4. The ♭VI and ♭VII together
C, A♭, B♭, C. Two borrowed chords, each a whole step above the last, rising to C. A♭ has A♭, C and E♭ (a minor-key chord), and B♭ has B♭, D and F. It sounds big and triumphant, and is sometimes called the “Mario cadence”.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
5. All three together
C, Fm, A♭ B♭, C. The minor iv in bar 2, then the ♭VI and ♭VII together in bar 3.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
Build your own
Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the versions above.

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:
Test your ear
The band plays a four-bar phrase. Name its borrowed chord (or the lack of one).

title: Lesson: Borrowed Chords
text:

The ♭VII to I ending also appears in the lesson on cadences.

title: Playing Brushes
text: Brushes are fans of thin wire (or nylon) fixed in a handle. On a snare drum they make two kinds of sound: a tap (a short, soft hit, like a quiet stick) and a sweep (the wires dragged across the head, a steady “shhh”). Brush playing is mostly about the sweeps, which no stick can make. They’re standard in jazz ballads, quiet swing, country, folk, and any acoustic gig where sticks are too loud.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
The brush and the drum

Wire brushes on a coated snare head (the white, slightly rough kind). A clear smooth head gives almost no sweep sound. A coated head is the one thing brushes really need.
Retractable brushes pull back into the handle to protect the wires; pull them out until they fan to about the width of your palm. Wider is softer and darker.
Nylon brushes are louder and brighter, and closer to sticks, popular in pop and on cajón.
Turn the snares on for a buzzy sweep, off for a smooth one.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Holding them
Hold a brush like a stick, in matched or traditional grip (see Stick Grips), but lighter, with the wires lying nearly flat on the head. The movement comes from the forearm and wrist, not the fingers. Keep the wires on the head for sweeps; lift them only for taps and accents.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
The basic swing pattern
The classic pattern for a right-handed player:

Left hand: sweeping. In a medium swing, the left hand sweeps back and forth across the head, left to right on beat 1, right to left on beat 2, and so on: one sweep per beat. In a ballad it can draw a full circle (clockwise as seen from above) over two beats, or one a beat.
Right hand: the ride pattern. The right hand taps the swing ride rhythm (“ding, ding-a ding”) on the right side of the head, as it would on a ride cymbal.
Accent 2 and 4. Finish the left-hand sweep with a little push, or tap it, on 2 and 4: the backbeat that a hi-hat would play. The hi-hat foot often plays 2 and 4 as well.
Feathering the bass drum: very soft quarter notes, felt more than heard.

Start slowly: first the left hand alone for a minute without a break, then the right hand alone, then both together. The sweep should sound continuous; any gaps sound like hiccups.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Other patterns








Pattern
What it does
Used for

The patterns are a starting point. Drummers such as Philly Joe Jones, Ed Thigpen and Clayton Cameron made brush playing a language of its own, and listening to them teaches more than any page.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
When to use brushes

When a stick is too loud for the room, the singer, or an acoustic band.
A ballad, or the soft opening of a tune that gets louder (switch to sticks at the change).
Play the ride cymbal with brushes too: a soft, washy sound. Don’t push the wires hard against a cymbal edge; they bend.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Looking after them
Keep retractable brushes closed when not in use. Bent wires can be straightened gently with fingers. A brush spread by the case too much won’t come back: replace it.

title: Playing Brushes
text:
Practice

Left-hand sweeps for two minutes with a metronome at 80, one sweep a beat, without a gap.
Add the right-hand ride rhythm; count “1 2 3 4” aloud.
Add the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
Play the same groove at 60 as circles, then at 140 as half-moons.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
Sing ee and then ah on the same note. The pitch stays the same, yet anyone can hear which vowel is which. Your vocal folds make the same buzz both times; what changes is the shape of the tube above them, and that tube boosts some frequencies and damps others. The boosted regions are the formants, numbered from the bottom: F1, F2, F3 and so on. Two of them, F1 and F2, are enough to tell most vowels apart, and they line up closely with the vowel chart singers already use. This lesson takes you through them with a synthesised voice. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. Each widget has a ▶ button that starts a sustained voice and ■ to stop it (only one plays at a time; start with your volume low). The pictures are spectra: frequency runs left to right up to 4 kHz, each vertical line is one harmonic of the voice, and the curve is the filter the vocal tract puts on top. The same synthesiser drives the vowel chart on the IPA chart, where you can drag through the vowel space.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
1. Source and filter
The voice is two things in a row. The source is the vocal folds: they open and shut at the pitch you sing, so they make a buzz at that pitch plus every whole-number multiple of it (the harmonic series), each one a little quieter than the one below. The filter is the throat, mouth and lips: a tube about 17 cm long in an adult, and like any tube it resonates at certain frequencies. Where it resonates, the harmonics come through strongly; between resonances they are damped.
The pitch belongs to the source and the vowel belongs to the filter, which is why you can sing any vowel on any note. Play the buzz on its own, then put a vowel’s filter on it.



The buzz is rich but has no vowel. With the filter on, the harmonics near each peak of the curve stand out, and that pattern of peaks is what your ear reads as a vowel. Change the pitch: the harmonic lines get closer or further apart, but the curve, and the vowel, stays where it is.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
2. F1: tongue height and jaw
The first formant, F1, is the lowest peak, between about 250 Hz and 850 Hz. It follows how open the vocal tract is: a close vowel like [i] or [u] has a low F1, an open vowel like [a] a high one. Dropping the jaw and lowering the tongue raises F1.



Slide F1 up with F2 high and you go from [i] through [e] and [ɛ] towards [a]. With F2 low you go from [u] through [o] towards [ɔ] and [ɑ]. On the vowel chart, F1 is the vertical axis: close at the top, open at the bottom.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
3. F2: front and back
The second formant, F2, runs from about 700 Hz to 2400 Hz. It follows where the tongue is bunched: forward in the mouth gives a high F2 ([i], [e]), back gives a low F2 ([u], [o]). Rounding the lips lengthens the tube and pulls F2 (and F3) down, so a rounded front vowel like [y] sits between [i] and [u].



On the vowel chart, F2 is the horizontal axis, with high F2 (front) on the left. Try holding F1 low and sweeping F2: [i] to [y] to [ɨ] to [u] is the whole top row of the chart.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
section: 4. The F1–F2 plane is the vowel chart
text:
4. The F1–F2 plane is the vowel chart
Put F1 down the page and F2 across it, high on the left, and the vowels fall into a shape that is close to the IPA trapezoid. The phonetics chart started as a map of the tongue; formant measurements in the twentieth century showed that it is just as much a map of sound. Drag anywhere in the plane.



The trapezoid shape comes from acoustics: front vowels can spread across a wide range of F2, while back vowels are squeezed into a narrow one, so the chart is wider at the top than at the bottom. The values here are averages for an adult male voice; a higher, shorter vocal tract (women, children) moves everything up by roughly 15–20 %, but the shape stays the same, which is how we hear the same vowel from different speakers.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
5. F3, r-colouring and lip rounding
The third formant, F3 (around 2200–3000 Hz), changes less from vowel to vowel, but it carries two things. Lip rounding lowers it along with F2. And an r-coloured vowel, like the General American nurse [ɝ] or butter [ɚ], has a strikingly low F3, down near 1600 Hz, sitting just above F2. Drag F3 down on [ə] and listen to it turn into an American er.



F4 and above vary even less and mostly reflect the size of the singer’s head and throat: they are part of what makes a voice sound like that person.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
6. The singer’s formant
Trained classical singers, especially men, make a strong peak around 2.5–3.2 kHz by clustering F3, F4 and F5 together, mostly by lowering the larynx and narrowing the tube just above the vocal folds. This singer’s formant is the “ring” or squillo that lets an unamplified voice carry over an orchestra: the orchestra is loudest below 1 kHz, and the ear is most sensitive near 3 kHz. Turn it on and off on the same vowel.



The vowel does not change, because F1 and F2 do not move. What changes is the brightness and the carrying power. Pop and musical theatre singers use the same region with a more speech-like vowel; a microphone means they need less of it.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
section: 7. High notes: when the pitch outruns the formants
text:
7. High notes: when the pitch outruns the formants
The harmonics sample the filter curve only at multiples of the pitch. At a speaking pitch they are close together and trace the curve well. A soprano at 880 Hz has harmonics only at 880, 1760, 2640 Hz and so on, so F1 for [i] (about 300 Hz) is below the lowest note she can produce. No harmonic falls near it, and the vowel can’t be heard as [i] any more.



Raise the pitch on [i] and listen to the vowels blur together above about 600 Hz. Then turn on Tune F1 to the pitch: this raises F1 to just above the fundamental, which is what sopranos do by opening the jaw on high notes. It is called formant tuning, and it is the acoustic reason for vowel modification: a high [i] is sung towards [ɪ] or [e], and a high [u] towards [ʊ] or [o], so that F1 stays with the fundamental and the note keeps its power. The cost is that the vowel is less clear, and on the very highest notes listeners cannot tell vowels apart at all.

For singers: if a high note feels thin or hard on a closed vowel, open the jaw and let the vowel drift towards its open neighbour ([i]→[ɪ]→[e], [u]→[ʊ]→[o]). In the words, keep the consonants clear; they carry more of the meaning than the vowels do up there.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
text:
Things to try

In section 4, find your own vowels: say a word, hold the vowel, and hunt for it in the plane. Vowels in your accent may sit between the symbols.
In section 1, play [a] and drag the pitch slowly: the vowel stays put while the harmonics slide under the curve.
On the IPA chart, switch on Hold and click from [i] to [y] to [u]: one formant moves at a time.
In section 7, find the pitch where [i] and [e] stop sounding different without formant tuning.

title: Formants: What Makes a Vowel
