The vocoder: a machine that copies one sound’s formants onto another.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text: Mixing is making the recorded tracks into one piece of music: each part heard, each in its own place, the song coming across. Most of a good mix is done with the plainest tools: level, pan, EQ, compression, and space, in about that order.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Prepare

Name and colour the tracks, group them (drums, bass, guitars, keys, vocals, effects).
Clean up: cut silence and noise between phrases, fade every edit, check for clicks.
Gain-stage: trim each track to an average around −18 dBFS (see gain staging), so faders start near 0.
Listen to a reference: a finished song you love in the same style, at the same level as your mix.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Balance
Faders first, with nothing else. Start with the most important element (usually the vocal, or the kick and bass), bring everything else in around it. A good balance with no plug-ins already sounds like a song; no plug-in will rescue a bad one. Mix quietly: if the balance works quietly it works loud.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Practise a balance
Press ▶, start from “A bad mix” and fix it with faders only, then pan, high-pass and a little reverb. Check it with Mono on, and press B to compare with a reference.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Pan
Spread things across the stereo picture so they don’t sit on top of each other.

Centre: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal: the foundation.
Off centre: guitars, keys, backing vocals, percussion. Two similar guitars hard left and hard right.
Drums panned as the audience sees them (or the drummer does; pick one).
Check in mono: everything should still be heard. Why, and what goes wrong: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
EQ
EQ gives every part its own range of frequencies.

High-pass everything that doesn’t need deep bass (vocals, guitars, keys, overheads), around 80–150 Hz. It clears room for kick and bass and removes rumble.
Cut before boost. Find what’s ugly (boxiness 300–600 Hz, honk around 1 kHz, harshness 2–5 kHz) with a narrow boost swept around, then cut it.
When two parts fight (kick and bass, guitar and vocal), cut a little of one where the other lives.
Judge EQ in the mix, not soloed.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Compression
A compressor evens out the level so a part stays in place.

Vocals: almost always, 3–6 dB of reduction on the loud phrases. Often two compressors gently, rather than one hard.
Bass: steadies the notes. Drums: punch (slow attack lets the hit through) or sustain.
Too much makes it lifeless and pumps. Match the level with it on and off before deciding it helps.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Space
Reverb and delay put the parts in a room and in front or behind.

Put them on sends (aux buses): one or two reverbs and a delay that many tracks share, so they all sound like one place.
Drier and brighter sounds close; more reverb, darker and quieter sounds far.
Pre-delay (20–80 ms) keeps a vocal up front while still giving it a room.
High-pass and low-pass the reverb return so it doesn’t muddy the bass or hiss.

title: Recording 5: Mixing
text:
Automation and finishing

Automate fader moves: the vocal up a little in the busy chorus, a guitar up for its fill, the reverb up on the last word.
Take breaks. Listen on other speakers, earbuds, a phone, a car (monitoring).
Leave the master peaking around −6 dBFS, no limiter on it, ready for mastering.
Export a 24-bit WAV at the session’s sample rate.

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Classical singing fills a room without a microphone. It does that through resonance, not force: a steady breath, tall and pure vowels, and a seamless legato line that carries from the bottom of the voice to the top. Most of its training comes from the Italian bel canto (“beautiful singing”) tradition. This lesson follows that tradition’s order: breath, onset, vowels, registers, agility and the long note.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; tenors and basses read treble-clef notes an octave lower. Step up exercises climb a half step at a time, as in a teacher’s warm-up. Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Posture and the appoggio breath
Stand tall but not stiff: feet hip-width apart, weight forward slightly, sternum comfortably high, shoulders down, head balanced. Breathe in low and wide, so the lower ribs, belly and back expand.
As you sing, keep the ribs open and let the belly come in slowly. Singers call this balance appoggio (“leaning”): the breath is supported rather than pushed out, so the tone stays steady.
Exercise: breathe in for 4 counts, then hiss out on “sss” for 12 counts, keeping the ribs wide. Next time, go for 16 counts, then 20.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Onset and legato
Begin each phrase with a clean, balanced onset: air and tone together, with no click and no rush of air first. Then join the notes so the sound never breaks between them. That’s legato, the basis of classical singing.
Sing this five-note scale on a single “ah”, sliding nothing and dropping nothing between notes.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Pure vowels: i e a o u
text:
Pure vowels: i e a o u
Italian has five pure vowels: [i] as in si, [e] as in che, [a] as in la, [o] as in no, [u] as in tu. Unlike English vowels, they don’t glide into a second sound: Italian no is [nɔ], never “no-oo”. Classical singers learn to sing every language on these clean vowel shapes.
Sing them on one pitch, keeping the same space at the back of the mouth as the lips change shape.



Then sing them on a scale.



The IPA chart shows these and the other sounds singers meet in Italian, German, French and English.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Resonance and the tall vowel
A classical tone rings because the throat stays open and the soft palate is lifted. That’s the feeling at the start of a yawn, or of a pleasant surprise. Singers call the ring squillo, and the warmth that comes with it chiaroscuro (light and dark).
Exercise: sing an easy “ng” (as in sing) on a middle note, then open slowly to “ah” without moving the pitch. Keep the buzz you felt in the “ng”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Registers and the passaggio
Every voice has a lower register (chest) and a higher one (head), with a transition zone called the passaggio. Classical training aims for one even sound across it. To do that, singers modify vowels slightly as they go up: “ah” darkens a little toward “aw”, and “ee” toward “ih”. That keeps the throat open and the tone even.
The arpeggio below climbs through the voice. Step it up a half step at a time, and as you near the top of your comfortable range, round the vowel and lighten the sound rather than push.




If the voice cracks around the passaggio, that’s normal at first. Sing the same arpeggio more quietly, on “oo”, where the voice blends most easily, then return to “ah”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Agility: the nine-note scale
Quick runs (coloratura) need a light, flexible voice with the breath still steady. This scale of nine notes up and down is a classic warm-up. Sing it slowly and clean at first, keeping each note distinct, never “ha-ha-ha”.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: The long note: messa di voce
text:
The long note: messa di voce
Messa di voce means “placing the voice”: one long note that grows from soft to loud and back to soft, with the pitch and the vowel unchanged. It’s the most demanding exercise in breath control, and a lifelong one.



Practice: start on a comfortable middle note, and make the swell only as big as you can keep steady.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Vibrato
A trained classical voice has a natural vibrato: a regular, even pulse in pitch, about five to seven times a second. It isn’t made deliberately. It appears when the breath is steady and the throat is free. If yours wobbles slowly or flutters fast, the cause is usually in breath or tension, and is best fixed with a teacher, not by trying to control the vibrato itself.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
section: Words: diction in Italian, German and French
text:
Words: diction in Italian, German and French
Classical singers sing in many languages, and each has its rules:

Italian: pure vowels; double consonants held longer (nòtte, “night”); a flipped or rolled R.
German: long and short vowels clearly different; final consonants crisp; the “ich” sound [ç] and the “ach” sound [x]; ü [y] and ö [ø] with rounded lips.
French: nasal vowels ([ɑ̃] in chant, [ɔ̃] in mon); the rounded [y] of tu; a smooth line with every syllable even.

The IPA chart gives each of these sounds with examples. Singers write IPA under the words of a song to learn its pronunciation before they sing it.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Reading and solfège
Classical singers read music. Tonal do re mi introduces solfège, which names the notes by their place in the key, so a singer can hear a line before singing it. Sing this phrase on solfège.
crumbs: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

title: Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato
text:
Where to go next

Pop singing: speech-level singing, mix, belt and runs.
Jazz singing: swing, scat and the changes.
The IPA chart for diction in other languages.

title: How to Play Cajón
text: A cajón (“big box” in Spanish) is a wooden box you sit on and play with your hands. It came from Afro-Peruvian music in the 1800s; in the 1970s Paco de Lucía’s band took it into flamenco, and today it’s the drum of choice for acoustic pop and coffee-shop gigs. Most modern cajóns have snare wires or guitar strings inside behind the front face, which make the high notes buzz like a snare drum.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Parts of the cajón

The front plate (tapa): the thin face you strike, facing forward between your legs.
The sound hole: at the back. The low note comes out here, so keep it a little away from a wall, or put a microphone there.
Snares or strings: inside, against the top of the front plate. Many have a knob or key to tighten them or turn them off.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Sitting
Sit on top of the cajón, near the back edge, feet flat on the floor and apart. Tilt the box back a little on its back edge so the front plate is free and you can reach it; grip it with your calves. Play with the hands loose and the fingers together. Take off rings and watches. Keep your back straight: don’t hunch forward over the box.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
The two main sounds









Sound
Where
How
Like a kit’s




Bass (B)
Middle of the plate, about a hand’s width below the top
Flat palm and fingers, let the hand bounce off
Bass drum


Slap (S)
Top corner, the top 5 cm or so
Fingers only, relaxed, the fingertips snap against the edge
Snare drum



Add a ghost note (g): a very soft finger tap near the top, felt more than heard, to fill gaps. A tone (T) between them, struck with the fingers in the middle, gives a round sound in between.
Practise the bass and the slap separately until each sounds clean: the bass low and boomy, without a buzz; the slap bright and cracking, without a thud.

Bass on 1 and 3 (and the “&” of 3), slap on 2 and 4: the backbeat. When it’s steady, add ghost notes on the empty eighths with the other hand, softly, to keep the hands moving: R L R L throughout.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
More grooves

Sixteenths: keep the hands alternating R L R L in sixteenths with ghost notes; bring out the bass on 1 and 3 and the slap on 2 and 4. A busy pop and funk feel.
6/8 ballad: count “1 2 3 4 5 6”: bass on 1, slap on 4, ghost notes between.
Rumba flamenca: bass on 1, slap on 2 and 4, with quick ghost-note “rolls” of the fingers between.
Landó (Afro-Peruvian, in 12/8 or 6/8): the cajón’s own tradition. Listen to Peruvian groups such as Perú Negro before trying it; the accents sit between the beats in a way that’s hard to write down.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Extras

Brushes on the front plate, or a cajón brush on the side, give soft sweeps and a snare-like backbeat (see Playing Brushes).
A foot shaker or a jingle on the heel adds a constant eighth pulse.
A cajón pedal lets a drummer play the box with a kit bass-drum pedal.

title: How to Play Cajón
text:
Practice

Bass and slap alternately for a minute at 70 bpm: B S B S, right hand bass, left hand slap.
The first beat at 80, then at 100.
Play the first beat along with a song you know. Leave out the ghost notes until it’s steady.
Try the 6/8 groove against a slow song in 6/8 or 12/8.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text: Most “the sound isn’t working” moments are cables: the wrong one, the wrong socket, or one that’s broken. Learn the connectors, the two kinds of signal level, and how to coil a cable so it lasts.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
The connectors

1/4” (6.35 mm) jack, two kinds that look almost the same:

TS (tip, sleeve: one black ring): unbalanced. Guitar and instrument cables. Also speaker cables for some amps, which are a different, thicker cable: never use a guitar cable between an amp head and a cabinet.
TRS (tip, ring, sleeve: two rings): balanced mono (keyboards to a mixer, studio monitors) or stereo (headphones, insert cables).

XLR: three pins, locks in place. Microphones, balanced line outputs, DI to mixer. Male end points toward the mixer (the signal flows out of the pins).
3.5 mm mini jack: phones, laptops, small headphones.
RCA (phono): home audio, DJ gear, older keyboards.
speakON: locking speaker connector for PA speakers and amp cabs; can’t be confused with a signal cable.
MIDI (5-pin DIN) and USB (A, B, C, Micro): control data, not audio (except USB audio interfaces).
IEC / kettle lead: the detachable power cable on most gear.


The two you will plug most, opened up:

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Balanced and unbalanced
An unbalanced cable has a signal wire and a shield. It picks up hum and noise, and longer than about 5–6 m (guitar cables) it also loses treble.
A balanced cable carries the signal twice, once upside down. Any noise picked up along the way is the same on both, and the input flips one and adds them, so the noise cancels. Balanced lines can run 50 m or more.
Both ends must be balanced to get the benefit: TRS to TRS, XLR to XLR, or TRS to XLR.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Levels: mic, instrument, line, speaker








Level
Example
Goes into




Mic
microphones (very quiet)
mic input (XLR), with preamp gain


Instrument (Hi-Z)
electric guitar, bass pickups
instrument input, “Hi-Z” or “Inst” switch, or a DI


Line
keyboards, phones, mixers, interfaces
line input


Speaker
amplifier output to a passive speaker
only a speaker. Never into anything else



A DI box turns an instrument or line signal into a balanced mic-level signal for a long run to the mixer. Use one for bass, acoustic guitar with a pickup, and keyboards on stage.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Signal flow
Follow the signal from the source to your ears: instrument → cable → (pedals) → amp or DI → mixer → amplifier → speakers. When there’s no sound, check each step in order: is it on, is the volume up, is the cable in the right socket, does a different cable fix it, is the channel muted. Most problems are found in the first three.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Coil it right: over-under
Wrapping a cable round your elbow twists it; twisted cables kink and break inside. Use over-under: one loop coiled normally, the next with a twist the other way. The cable lies flat, and thrown out it uncoils with no knots. Close it with a velcro tie.

title: Gear 2: Cables and Connectors
text:
Care and spares

Pull by the plug, never the cable.
Don’t walk on, roll over, or bend cables sharply at the plug.
Mark broken cables (tape: “BAD”) and take them out of the box; don’t coil them back in.
Gig bag spares: two instrument cables, two XLRs, a patch cable, a 3.5 mm-to-two-1/4” lead, a DI, and spare batteries.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text: Every microphone turns air pressure into voltage, but the three main types do it differently, and that changes how they sound, how loud a source they can take and how fragile they are.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Dynamic
A thin diaphragm glued to a coil of wire, sitting in a magnet. Sound moves the coil, the magnet makes a current. The Shure SM57 and SM58 are the classic examples.

Tough: dropped, rained on, shouted into, they keep working.
Handles very loud sources: snare, kick, guitar amps, brass close up.
Less detail in the highs and less sensitive, so it picks up less of the room and less bleed. That is why it is the default for live sound and for recording in an untreated bedroom.
Needs a lot of preamp gain (often 50–60 dB on a quiet voice). Some very low-output ones (the Shure SM7B) are used with an inline booster.
No phantom power needed.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Condenser
A very thin, electrically charged diaphragm close to a metal back plate: a capacitor whose value changes as the diaphragm moves. It needs power to hold the charge and to run its small internal amplifier.

Detailed and sensitive: the air on a voice, the pick on an acoustic guitar, cymbals, overheads, a piano, a choir or a room.
Large-diaphragm (an inch or so; the studio vocal mic) sounds warm and flattering; small-diaphragm (“pencil” mics) is more accurate and even off-axis, good for acoustic instruments and stereo pairs.
Picks up everything: the fridge, the computer fan, the reflections off the walls. In a bare room a condenser can sound worse than a dynamic.
More fragile. Keep it out of the damp and away from kick drums unless it is built for it.
Needs phantom power (or its own power supply, for valve/tube condensers).

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Ribbon
A strip of very thin corrugated aluminium hung in a magnetic field.

Smooth, dark, natural highs; loved on guitar amps, brass, strings and drum rooms.
Almost always figure-8 (picks up front and back equally).
Fragile: a blast of air (a kick drum, a puff into it, being carried quickly) can stretch the ribbon. Keep it covered when not in use.
Classic passive ribbons do not want phantom power, and old ones can be damaged by a faulty cable with it on. Active ribbons (they say so) need it.

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Phantom power (+48 V)
Phantom power sends 48 volts DC down the same balanced XLR cable that brings the signal back. It is “phantom” because a dynamic mic, wired the usual way, doesn’t see it at all.

Turn it on for condensers (and active ribbons, and some DI boxes).
Plug in first, then switch on. Switch off and wait a few seconds before unplugging. Plugging in with 48 V live makes a loud pop through the speakers and can, rarely, harm gear.
Monitors down when switching it on or off.
On many cheap interfaces one 48 V button powers two or all inputs at once. Fine for dynamics; check before plugging an old ribbon into any of them.
If a condenser makes no sound: is 48 V on? Is it an XLR cable (not a jack)?


Never patch an XLR in or out with phantom power on, and keep vintage ribbon mics on a channel with 48 V off.

Try the order yourself. Press Monitors on (speakers low), choose a mic, then plug in and switch +48 V in the right and the wrong order:

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Polar patterns
The polar pattern is how sensitive a mic is from each direction.

Cardioid (heart-shaped): picks up the front, rejects the back. The default for almost everything. Point the back at what you don’t want (the drums, the monitor, the window).
Supercardioid / hypercardioid: narrower in front, with a small lobe at the back. Common on live vocal mics. Point the side (not the back) at the monitor.
Omni: everything equally. Natural, no proximity effect (see placement), but hears the whole room.
Figure-8: front and back, nothing from the sides. Ribbons; two singers facing each other; the side mic of a mid/side pair (Sound 23: Stereo).

Many large-diaphragm condensers have a switch for several of these.



Drag the singer and the drums, turn the mic, and compare patterns and mic types. Watch the voice against the drum bleed in dB:




Off axis
A pattern drawing is for the middle frequencies. Off to the side, a mic doesn’t just get quieter: the treble drops first, because a diaphragm stops hearing high sounds that arrive from the side. So a singer who wanders off the mic sounds further away and duller.



Walk the singer round the mic and listen:





Don’t cup the mic
A cardioid is directional because of the rear ports, slots behind the capsule: sound reaching them from behind arrives at the back of the diaphragm too, and cancels. Wrap a hand round the grille and the ports are covered. The mic becomes almost omni, hears the wedge monitor it was meant to ignore, and feeds back. The hollow of the hand also makes a little chamber: the voice goes boxy and honky, and the sound engineer can’t EQ it back. Hold the handle.



Press Cup the grille to hear (and see) it:

title: Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power
text:
Which mic for what
No mic is flat on purpose. A handheld vocal dynamic trims the bass (you’ll be close, and proximity effect puts it back) and lifts 4–6 kHz, where words are clear; a studio condenser stays near flat.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
A compressor turns a sound down when that sound gets loud. A sidechain lets a different sound decide. The music is turned down when the kick drum hits, or when the DJ talks. The sound that decides is called the key.
How to use the page. The source (what gets turned down) starts as chords. The key is a kick drum playing four to the floor. The strip draws the chords’ volume.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Ducking under the kick



Start with Depth at 0 and raise it. Each kick pushes the chords down, and they swell back up between kicks.

Depth: how far the music is pushed down.
Attack: how fast it goes down when the kick hits. Fast, so the kick’s start is clear.
Release: how fast the music comes back. This sets the rhythm of the effect.

Turn Hear the key off: the kick is gone but you can still hear where it was, because the chords breathe in its rhythm. Producers often key the sidechain from a kick nobody hears.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Glue or pump?

Glue: a little ducking, quick release. You barely hear it, but the kick cuts through and the mix sounds tighter. Almost every mix with a bass line and a kick does this: the bass ducks for a moment under each kick so the two don’t fight over the low end.
Pumping: deep ducking and a release that lasts most of a beat. The chords swell up after every kick: whoom, whoom, whoom. This is the sound of French house (Daft Punk’s “One More Time”, Eric Prydz’s “Call on Me”) and most EDM since. Try it at different tempos: the release has to fit the gap between kicks.

title: Sound 14: Sidechain
text:
Ducking a voice
Choose Radio voice-over: the key is now a voice. Whenever it talks, the music dips under it, and comes back slowly when it stops. Radio stations, podcasts, sat-navs talking over the car stereo and announcements at a station all do this automatically.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
text: Most beats in pop, hip-hop and dance music are not played: they are programmed, one hit at a time, in a step sequencer. A bar of 4/4 is cut into 16 steps (sixteenth notes). Each row is one drum; each square is a step. Light a square and that drum hits there.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
section: The parts of a drum row
text:
The parts of a drum row
Count a bar of sixteenths as 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a. The thick lines are beats, the thin ones sixteenths.

Kick (bass drum): the low thump, usually on 1 and somewhere around 3.
Snare: the crack on 2 and 4, the backbeat. Move it and it stops sounding like pop music.
Hi-hat: the ticking that keeps time, in eighths (every other step) or sixteenths.

title: DAW 2: Programming a Beat
text:
Try it
The beat below is one bar, looping. The clip is selected, so its steps show under the tracks.

Press Play. Click squares on and off while it plays: a DAW lets you edit as it goes round.
Fill the closed hi-hat on every step, then only every other step. Which is busier?
Add a kick on the a of 2 (step 8). Then one on the & of 3 (step 11). This is the difference between a stiff beat and one that moves.
Velocity is how hard a hit is (0 to 127 in MIDI). Shift+click a hi-hat to make it an accent, Alt+click for a quiet ghost note. Accent every hi-hat on the beat, ghost a snare just before beat 4. Brightness shows velocity.
Try the Grid menu: at 1/8 there are 8 squares a bar; at 1/8 triplet 12, for a shuffle.
When you like it, make it longer: select the clip and press Duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D) three times. Now there are four bars; change the last one into a fill (snare and toms on the last few steps).
Switch on ⌨ Keys and play the kit from your computer keyboard: A kick, S snare, D closed hat, F open hat, G H toms, J crash, K ride.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
Travis picking is a fingerpicking pattern in which the thumb plays a steady bass on every beat and the fingers play the melody or the chord notes on the strings above it, between the thumb notes. It is named for Merle Travis, from Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, and was spread by Chet Atkins and, later, by folk and country guitarists everywhere. The thumb is a bass player, and the fingers are a rhythm section that plays off it. This lesson builds it a step at a time, from the thumb alone to the band, with hammer-ons and pull-offs added at the end.
The Backing Track band plays the pattern as the comping rhythm Fingerpicking: Travis pattern. There is a lesson on that pattern in the band’s own terms, Comping rhythm: Travis pattern, and one on the simpler pattern before it, John Prine fingerpicking. This lesson is the hands.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, with the high E on top and a number for the fret. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it, and ↻ Loop to repeat it. The strings are numbered 6 (low E) to 1 (high E). The right hand uses p for the thumb, and i, m and a for the index, middle and ring fingers.
Here is what you are working toward, played by the band. Switch the other players off to hear the guitar alone, and slow the tempo with the slider at the bottom of the page.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
1. The thumb alone
Start with the thumb, and only the thumb. On a chord, the thumb plays four bass notes in a bar, one on every beat: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, and the inner string again. For C the root is the 5th string, the alternate bass is the 6th string (fret 3, which is a G), and the inner string is the 4th string, fret 2 (an E). Hold the C shape and play 5, 4, 6, 4.






The alternate bass is the string on the other side of the root, so the thumb swings between a low note and a higher one. That is where the oom-pah comes from, and this pattern is the same as the band’s bass line in its folk and country styles.

Easy because: one finger plays one note on every beat, and your fretting hand holds a chord you already know.
Hard because: the thumb has to find three strings without looking, and keep going in time.
What goes wrong:

The thumb plays the wrong string, usually the next one over.
The beat is uneven because the 5-to-6 jump takes longer than 5-to-4.
The strings ring into each other. Rest the side of the right hand lightly on the bridge to damp the bass, and the notes come out shorter and cleaner.


Practice: play it with a metronome at 60, with your eyes closed, for a minute. Then do the same on G, Am and D (section 4 has the strings).

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
2. Pinches on beat 1
Now add a note on beat 1 only. Pick a treble string with a finger at the same moment as the thumb plays the root: that is a pinch. For C, use the B string (fret 1) with the middle finger. The other beats stay the same, thumb alone.




Easy because: the thumb pattern is unchanged, and only one other note arrives, always on the same beat.
Hard because: the thumb and the finger have to start the note at the same instant. If they drift apart it sounds like a clumsy strum, not a pinch.
What goes wrong: the finger plays first or late. The pinch is louder than the thumb notes that follow.

Practice: play only the pinches, with the thumb and finger leaving the strings together, then add the other three beats.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
3. Fingers between the thumb notes
Now give the fingers their place. On each beat the thumb plays its note on the beat, and a finger plays a note on the “and” after beats 2, 3 and 4. Beat 1 stays a pinch, so there is nothing on its “and”. Count it “1 2-and 3-and 4-and”. The fingers play the treble strings: the middle finger on the B string and the ring finger on the high E string work, or the index finger on the G string. Use whichever fingers you prefer, and keep them the same from bar to bar.



This is the Travis pattern. The thumb and the fingers alternate, so each one has a note, then a gap, then a note, and your hand feels like two people taking turns. Listen to the band play it in the demo above, and look at the staff to see how it matches.

Easy because: the thumb part is the same one from section 2, and the fingers play only three notes in a bar.
Hard because: the thumb and the fingers have to be independent. The thumb keeps its beat while the fingers play off it, and the thumb wants to follow the fingers.
What goes wrong:

The thumb stops or stumbles when the fingers come in.
The finger notes land on the beat instead of after it.
The treble notes are as loud as the bass notes. Play the thumb a little louder and the fingers more lightly.


Practice: count out loud, “one, two-and, three-and, four-and”. Slow it down until it is steady, then bring it up in small steps. Spend a week on this step before the next.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 4. On C, G, Am and D
text:
4. On C, G, Am and D
The same pattern needs a root, an inner string and an alternate bass for each chord. The thumb always plays the root of the chord on beat 1.




C: root on string 5, inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (fret 3). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
G: root on string 6 (fret 3), inner string 4 (open), alternate bass on string 5 (fret 2). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
Am: root on string 5 (open), inner string 4 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 6 (open). Treble: strings 2 and 1.
D: root on string 4 (open), inner string 3 (fret 2), alternate bass on string 5 (open). The strings below the root, 6, stay silent. Treble: strings 2 and 1.





Easy because: the pattern is the same each time, and the four chords are open shapes you know.
Hard because: the thumb has to learn a new set of strings for each chord. D, with only four strings in use, is the one that trips people up.
What goes wrong: the thumb plays a string that is not in the chord, and the bass sounds wrong. The alternate bass on D should be the open 5th string, not the low E.

Practice: one chord for four bars, until the thumb finds the strings by feel. Then the next chord. For the chord shapes and the fretting hand see guitar chord shapes by hand.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
5. Changing chords
Now move from one chord to the next without breaking the thumb’s beat. The thumb keeps going while the fretting hand moves. The change lands on beat 1 of the next bar, on the root. The thumb notes on beats 3 and 4 are the time you have to move: let go of the old shape on beat 4 and have the new one down for beat 1.




Easy because: you can think of a bar at a time, and a bar of a chord you have already played is a bar you know.
Hard because: the picking hand cannot slow down while the fretting hand moves, and the roots of the chords move around on strings 4 to 6.
What goes wrong:

The pattern stops dead at the change, because the picking hand waits for the fretting hand.
The thumb plays the old chord’s root on the new chord.
The last beat of a bar is rushed.


Practice: play C and G, two bars each, with a metronome. Do not stop. If the change is late, drop one beat of the picking (rest the fingers) and keep the thumb going. Then play it with the band.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
section: 6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
text:
6. Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs
Hammer-ons and pull-offs make the pattern sound like Chet Atkins instead of a practice exercise. The hand technique is in Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar; you should be comfortable with sections 1 to 4 of that lesson first.
Hammer onto the 3rd of the chord, on beat 1. The 3rd of a major chord is the note that makes it major, and in an open chord the string next to the root is often an open string a hammer-on away from it. On G, the thumb picks the open 5th string (A) and hammers to fret 2 (B, the 3rd). On C, it picks the open 4th string (D) and hammers to fret 2 (E, the 3rd). The hammered note takes the place of the pinch on beat 1, and then the pattern goes on.



Pull-offs in the treble, between the thumb notes. The “and” after beat 2 can be two quick notes instead of one: pick the higher note, then pull off to the lower. On C the high E string is picked at fret 3 and pulled off to the open string. On Am the B string is picked at fret 1 and pulled off to the open B string.




Easy because: the thumb never changes. The hammer-ons and pull-offs are all in the fingers, and each one fits in one place in the pattern.
Hard because: the fretting hand has to do something while it is also holding the chord, and the picking hand has to stay steady while it waits for the hammer or the pull.
What goes wrong: the decorated beat gets rushed, or the thumb loses its place. The hammer-on is too soft to hear. A pull-off is not loud enough to match the picked notes.

Practice: put one decoration in a four-bar phrase, in the same place each time, until you do not have to think about it. Then try a second one.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
7. With the band
Now play the part with the band. The chart is G, C, D, G. The band’s guitarist plays the pattern in section 3, and its bass plays the root and alternate bass with the thumb. Take the guitar off (the Chords button) and play the part yourself. Start at 70 beats a minute and speed up when it is steady.



The second button is the simpler pattern the band calls thumb, pinch-and. Use it to rehearse the thumb with fewer finger notes, and then play the Travis pattern.

title: Travis Picking on Guitar
text:
8. A neighbour: chicken pickin’
Chicken pickin’ is a cousin of Travis picking that sounds very different. It is a country guitar technique played with a flat pick and the middle and ring fingers (hybrid picking). The pick plays a bass or chord note, and the fingers snap the treble strings, pulling each one up and letting it slap against the frets. Notes are also muted by the picking hand, and the short, dry, clucking sound that results gives it the name. It began in the Telecaster-based country playing of the 1950s and 1960s, and you can hear it in the work of James Burton, Albert Lee and, more recently, Brad Paisley. This lesson does not teach it. If you can play the Travis pattern, you already have the independence of thumb and fingers that it takes.
Unlocks: the band’s other fingerpicking pattern, Prine; Hammer-ons and Pull-offs.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Take a few seconds of recorded sound and cut it into hundreds of tiny pieces, each a few hundredths of a second long, each faded in and out so it doesn’t click. These are grains. Play them back overlapping, dozens a second, and you can do things a tape never could: hold one moment of a sound forever, stretch a sound to ten times its length without making it lower, or scatter it into a glittering cloud. That’s granular synthesis. The idea goes back to the composer Iannis Xenakis in the 1950s, who cut tape into tiny pieces with scissors.
How to use the page. Pick a sound to cut up (or record three seconds of your own voice), press ▶, and move the Position. The strip shows the sound; each flash is one grain being read.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
The grain cloud




Position: where in the sound the grains are read from.
Scan speed: how fast the position moves on its own. At ×1 it plays the sound at normal speed; at ×0.2 it plays it five times slower, but at the same pitch, because each grain still plays at the normal speed. At 0 the sound is frozen.
Grain size: under about 20 ms each grain is a click, and you hear the rate of the clicks as a buzz. From 50 to 200 ms you hear the sound itself, smeared.
Grains per second: few grains give a crackle; many give a smooth cloud.
Spray: each grain is read from a slightly random place near the position. More spray, more blur.
Pitch and Random pitch: each grain can be played faster or slower. With random pitch the grains turn into a shimmering chord.
Backwards grains and Stereo spread make the cloud stranger and wider.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Try this

Freeze on Vowels. Move the position slowly through the sound: you can stop on any vowel and hold it.
Stretch (slow motion) on the Synth riff: the riff, five times slower, at its normal pitch. Video editors and DJs use this to fit a sound to a length without changing the key.
Shimmer: the grains an octave up and spread wide. Ambient music lives here.
Record your own voice and choose Scatter.
Play the keys: the whole cloud moves to the note you play, a melody made from your voice.

title: Sound 10: Granular Synthesis
text:
Where you’ve heard it
Time-stretching in every DAW (Ableton’s warp modes, Melodyne) is granular underneath. So are the “frozen” pads of ambient music, the shimmering textures of film scores, and many synths: Ableton’s Granulator, Mutable Instruments’ Clouds, the Tasty Chips GR-1. The glitch effects and the freeze button on the reverb page use grains too.

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
This is how a pianist plays chords on a 12-bar blues, built up from one finger. You need to be able to find notes on the keyboard by name. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has a keyboard diagram, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. Above the keys there is one coloured lane for each chord, with a square over every key that chord uses, so you can compare chords by looking straight up and down. Middle C is marked in green. Click a chord’s name at the left of its lane to hear it. Under the keyboard the same notes are written on a grand staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its pianist plays exactly the notes shown, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the piano to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the squares show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of C7 is C. A blues has three chords and so three roots. Play them with the left hand, low on the keyboard, one long note per bar.



Count the form as you play: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes. Starting on the root, take every other note of the scale: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Here are all four notes of each chord in the right hand, root at the bottom. The 5th is dashed because it is the first note to leave out. Click a chord name to hear the notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
3. Guide tones over a root
Now play only the 3rd and 7th in the right hand, with the root in the left. Look down the lanes: the right hand’s two notes hardly move. Going from I7 to IV7, each note drops a half step, and they swap jobs: the 3rd becomes the ♭7th and the ♭7th becomes the 3rd. For V7 both notes sit a half step above the I chord’s.
To keep the hand still, the two notes are not always in the same order. Sometimes the 3rd is on the bottom and sometimes the 7th. Switch the labels to chord tones to see which.



The band’s pianist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm once the changes are comfortable.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
4. Shells in the left hand
Put root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone and the right hand is free for a melody. A three-note chord with the 5th left out is a shell voicing. To keep the hand in one place the notes are rearranged from chord to chord, so the root is not always on the bottom.



Play a chorus of shells with the left hand only. Then add one note of your own in the right hand per bar. Any chord tone will do.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
5. Rootless voicings
When there is a bass player, the root is taken care of, and the left hand can spend its fingers on colour instead. A rootless voicing is the two guide tones plus two notes from higher up the chord: the 9th (a whole step above the root) and the 13th (the same note as the 6th). There are two forms, one with the 3rd on the bottom and one with the 7th on the bottom, and they alternate so the hand barely moves. This is the standard left-hand sound of jazz piano since the late 1950s.



The dashed square is the root, shown only so you can see where the voicing sits in relation to it. Leave it to the bass.
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is a half step lower than a dominant chord’s. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide tones take turns to fall by a step: the 7th of each chord drops to become the 3rd of the next.



The same chorus with rootless voicings in the left hand:
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
section: 7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is over guide tones and a root.



The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a half step to become the ♭7th of IV, the same move your right hand makes. Once the guide tones are secure, play the riff in the right hand and rootless voicings in the left:
crumbs: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

title: Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and work the same steps there. Start with F, B♭ and G.
Loop a chorus with the piano left out and comp for yourself.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and find the guide tones of each new chord.
The Chord Sheet tool (Tools menu) draws these and other voicings for any chords you type in, one at a time or superimposed.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text: A mono signal is one channel: one microphone, one cable, one speaker or many speakers all playing the same thing. A stereo signal is two channels, left and right, that differ a little, and the differences are what put sounds somewhere between the speakers (Sound 23: Stereo). Most music is recorded largely in mono, mixed into stereo, and then heard, quite often, back in mono. Each step has its traps.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Recording: mostly mono

One source, one mic is a mono track: vocal, bass DI, kick, snare, guitar amp. That isn’t a weakness: the mix places each mono track in the stereo picture with the pan knob. A “stereo” vocal is almost never wanted.
Two mics on one source is not automatically stereo. Two mics at different distances on a guitar amp hear the same sound at slightly different times; mixed together they comb-filter (cancel some frequencies, boost others). Check the polarity button and nudge the far track in time until the low end is fullest. The 3:1 rule helps: the second mic at least three times as far from the first as the first is from its source.
Stereo pairs record space on purpose (Recording 2: Microphones):

XY: two cardioids, capsules touching at 90–135°. Only level differences, no time differences, so it sums to mono cleanly. Narrower image.
ORTF / spaced pair (AB): capsules apart. Time differences give a wide, airy image, but in mono the delays comb-filter: the more spaced, the more it can go hollow.
Mid/side: a forward mic (mid) and a sideways figure-8 (side), decoded to L = M + S, R = M − S. In mono the side cancels exactly and you get the mid mic, perfectly. Width is adjustable after the fact.

Stereo sources: keyboards, synths and drum machines often come out stereo (L/R outputs). Record both if the patch is really stereo (a chorus, a Leslie, a stereo piano sample); record one if the two sides are identical.
Room and overhead mics are where stereo recording matters most: the drum kit, the choir, the piano, the hall.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Mixing: building the stereo picture
The mixing rules all serve two listeners at once, the one on stereo speakers and the one in mono:

Centre the things that carry the song: kick, snare, bass, lead vocal. A centred (mono) sound is equal in both channels, so it survives every playback system, and its bass energy is shared by both speakers.
Pan the rest. Pan is a level difference; it sums to mono without cancelling.
Pan law: a sound panned centre plays in both speakers; to sound as loud as when it’s hard to one side, the centre is turned down 3 dB (or 4.5 or 6, the DAW decides). When the mix folds to mono, centre sounds come up relative to hard-panned ones, so a balance can shift a little.
Wideners (Haas delays, phase tricks, stereo chorus, some “stereo enhancer” plug-ins) make width out of time and phase differences, and those are exactly what cancel in mono.
Double-tracking (playing the part twice, panned left and right) is the safe way to wide: the two takes differ naturally, so in mono they just sound like two players, not a comb filter.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
section: One earbud: what happens when stereo is summed to mono
text:
One earbud: what happens when stereo is summed to mono
Take one earbud out and the other still plays one channel only: you’d hear the left side of the mix, missing whatever was panned hard right (the second guitar, half the drum kit, a backing vocal). That’s why phones and operating systems have a Mono Audio setting (iOS: Accessibility → Audio & Visual; Android, macOS and Windows have one too), and many earbuds switch to mono by themselves when only one is in. A single Bluetooth speaker, a phone’s speaker, a smart speaker, a shop’s ceiling speakers and many club and church PAs do the same thing: they play L + R (usually scaled by ½, or −3 dB, to keep it from clipping).
What summing does to a mix:

Anything equal in both channels (the centred vocal, kick, bass) adds up and comes through solid. In fact it gets louder relative to the sides (up to 6 dB on a plain L + R, 3 dB with a pan-law sum), so a mono mix sounds more vocal-and-bass heavy.
Hard-panned parts stay, at their own level. Nothing is lost, but they drop back relative to the centre.
Anything that’s different in the two channels only by timing or phase cancels partly or completely:

A Haas widener (the same part a few ms late on one side) becomes a comb filter: hollow, thin, phasey.
Out-of-polarity content (one side inverted, often from a miswired mic, a cable, or an overenthusiastic widener) disappears entirely. Instruments or reverb vanish.
Spaced-pair overheads and room mics go hollow; the cymbals can swish.
Stereo reverb loses much of its tail (a reverb’s two sides are deliberately decorrelated), so a mono mix sounds drier than you meant.
Very wide synths and pads (detuned unison spread across the field, stereo chorus) shrink, thin out, and sometimes almost vanish behind the vocal.
The side of a mid/side signal is gone: at 200% width you were only turning up what mono throws away.

Bass is the worst place for any of this: a bass note slightly out of phase between the sides loses its weight in mono, and a mono subwoofer (see below) gets exactly that cancelled version.

How to check it: press the DAW’s Mono button (or put a utility plug-in on the master set to mono) several times while mixing, and watch a correlation meter or vectorscope. +1 is mono, 0 is wide and unrelated, anything heading toward −1 is trouble. Try it on the widget in Sound 23: Haas delay at 1, 3, 5, 10 ms with Mono on. If a part disappears in mono, fix the source: narrow the widener, use a real double, flip a polarity, or keep the low end (below about 120–150 Hz) mono with a mid/side EQ or a “mono bass” utility.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Live sound
Most of a live audience doesn’t hear stereo. Stereo needs you to sit between the speakers, roughly as far from each, and on a festival field or in a bar almost everyone is much nearer one stack than the other: they hear that side, plus a late copy of the other. So:

Many live mixes are mono, or nearly: both sides of the PA play the same mix, and nothing important is panned. If a hard-left guitar plays only from the left stack, the people on the right don’t get the guitar.
Stereo is used lightly: reverbs and delays, a little spread on keyboards and overheads, panning a few degrees.
Front fills, delay towers and side fills cover the parts of the room the main speakers miss. Delay speakers are delayed to arrive just after the main PA (Haas again, 5–20 ms) so the sound still seems to come from the stage.
Monitors (wedges and in-ears) are separate mixes for each player (Recording 4). In-ears are often stereo, for comfort and a sense of the band; wedges are mono.
Feedback: a mic in front of a speaker playing it howls. Keep mics behind the main PA, wedges in the mic’s dead zone (behind a cardioid, at the sides of a supercardioid).

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Studio listening and speaker placement
In the studio you’re the one listener in the right seat, so stereo works fully, if the room and speakers allow it:

Equilateral triangle: the two speakers and your head at its three corners, 1–2 m on a side, tweeters at ear height, speakers angled to point at (or just behind) your head. The phantom centre (a centred vocal floating between them) is the test: if it’s blurred or pulled to one side, the triangle is off.
Symmetry: the same distance from each side wall, so both sides reflect alike. Put the desk along the short wall, firing down the room’s long dimension.
Off the walls: a speaker near the wall behind it gets extra bass (and a dip where its reflection cancels). Either keep it a metre or more out, or push it nearly flush and use the speaker’s “boundary” EQ switch. Avoid the room’s exact centre (between front and back walls): bass standing waves are worst there.
Decouple: stands or isolation pads, not a resonant desk; the desk surface also reflects into your ears.
First reflections: absorbers on the side walls (where a mirror would show you the speaker) and above.
Level: moderate, ~75–85 dB SPL, then checked quiet.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Laptops, phones and small speakers

Laptop speakers are tiny and a few centimetres apart: almost no stereo width (some laptops fake it with processing), and almost nothing below 150–200 Hz. Phones are often one speaker, or two that sum to near-mono.
Your bass line has to be heard through its harmonics: a bass with some upper-mid character (pick attack, a little saturation, 700 Hz–1.5 kHz) stays audible; a pure sub-bass sine disappears.
Check mixes on the laptop and a phone, in mono. If the vocal is clear, the bass line can be followed and nothing has vanished, the mix translates.
Laptop headphone outputs are usually fine; built-in microphones are mono, noisy, and processed (noise suppression, echo cancellation): not for recording music if anything else is available.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Subwoofers, and why two
A subwoofer plays only the deep bass (below a crossover, often 80 Hz). Low frequencies are hard to locate by ear, so one subwoofer is usually fed a mono sum of L + R. That’s another mono fold: any bass that cancels in mono cancels in the sub.

Why two? Not mainly for stereo bass (below about 80 Hz you can hardly tell where it comes from). The reason is the room. Bass wavelengths (4 m at 80 Hz, 17 m at 20 Hz) are the size of the room, so the room sets up standing waves: at some seats a note booms, at others it nearly vanishes. Two subs in different places excite those modes differently and fill in each other’s holes, so the bass is even across more seats (and each sub works less hard, with more headroom).
Placement: studies (Todd Welti and Allan Devantier at Harman) found two subs at the midpoints of opposite walls, or four at the midpoints of all four, smooth the bass best across a listening area. A corner gives the most level and the most uneven bass.
Phase and time: two subs must arrive together at the listener. Use each sub’s phase (0/180° or a dial) and delay so the bass gets louder at the crossover, not thinner; a sub out of phase with the mains causes the same cancellation as an out-of-phase stereo pair.
Live, subs are often in a cardioid arrangement (one turned backward and delayed) to keep bass off the stage, or spread across the front in an end-fire or arc. Two stacks far apart, left and right, with the same signal, make a bass power alley down the middle and dead spots in between: the same comb filter as a Haas delay, but a room-sized one.
Studio: the sub level is set so it continues the mains smoothly, not as an effect. A mix made with a loud sub will be bass-light everywhere else.

title: Recording 7: Mono and Stereo
text:
Checklist

Kick, bass, snare, lead vocal centred; low end (below ~120 Hz) mono.
Mono button pressed often; correlation meter mostly positive.
No part disappears in mono; wideners and polarity checked.
Checked on speakers, headphones, one earbud, a laptop and a phone.
Speakers in a symmetrical triangle; sub(s) in phase with the mains.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
An oscillator is the part of a synthesizer that makes a repeating wave. Its two settings are the shape of the wave and how fast it repeats (the frequency, heard as pitch). This lesson plays the classic shapes from the harmonic series lesson on a real oscillator, then makes the pulse wave move.
How to use the page. Press ▶, or play the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard; the widget sounds while a key is held. Keep the volume in the bottom bar low to start with. The bright waves are loud.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Four shapes



Play the same note with each Wave and watch both pictures:

Sine: one spike in the spectrum.
Triangle: a few odd harmonics that die away fast. Softer than you’d guess from the pointed shape.
Sawtooth: a comb of every harmonic. The brightest and the most useful, because a filter can carve almost anything out of it.
Square: only every other spike. Listen for the hollow, woody tone.

Move Pitch up and down. On the spectrum the whole comb slides along together, keeping its pattern. That pattern (the timbre) is independent of the pitch.

Frequency and pitch. Each octave doubles the frequency: A2 is 110 Hz, A3 220 Hz, A4 440 Hz. That’s why the spectrum’s frequency axis is drawn with every octave the same width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
Pulse width
A pulse wave is up for part of each cycle and down for the rest. The fraction of the cycle it spends up is the pulse width (or duty cycle). At 50% it is a square wave.



Drag Pulse width slowly from 50% down to 5%. The sound goes from hollow to nasal to thin and reedy. On the spectrum, gaps appear and move: at width 1/k, every kth harmonic is missing. Widths of 30% and 70% sound the same: one is the other upside down.
Inside the browser there is no pulse oscillator, so the widget makes one the way some analogue synths did: it takes a sawtooth and subtracts a delayed copy of the same sawtooth. The delay, as a fraction of the cycle, is the pulse width.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:
PWM: pulse-width modulation
Now let something move the width for you. PWM rate is how many times a second the width swings, and PWM depth is how far.



A slowly swinging pulse width gives the rich, chorus-like shimmer of 1980s string machines and synth pads: the gaps in the spectrum sweep up and down, a little like a phaser. Turn the rate up to 5 Hz or so for a wobble. The thing doing the moving is an LFO, a low-frequency oscillator, which gets its own lesson.

title: Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation
text:

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
You have two ears, and you can tell where a sound is coming from with them: from which ear hears it louder, and which ear hears it first. A stereo recording has two channels, left and right, and mixing engineers use both of those clues to place each sound somewhere between the speakers. Headphones on for this page.
How to use the page. The square is a vectorscope. A sound that’s the same in both ears (mono) is a vertical line. One that’s only on the left leans left; only on the right, leans right. A wide stereo sound is a fuzzy blob. Press Mono to fold left and right together, as a phone speaker or a club sound system does.

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
Pan, Haas and width



Pan (the first tool) uses loudness: more in one ear than the other. Move it and watch the line lean. It’s how most sounds are placed in a mix: bass, kick and lead vocal in the middle, the rest spread around them.
Haas delay uses time. Choose it: the right channel is the same sound, a few milliseconds late.

Under about 1 ms the sound just moves toward the left, the side that arrives first.
From about 5 to 35 ms you don’t hear an echo. The sound seems to come from the earlier side, but much wider. Helmut Haas measured this in 1951 (the precedence effect); it’s how your ears ignore the reflections in a room.
Above about 40 ms it breaks apart into a slapback echo.

Width (mid / side) makes a stereo sound narrower or wider. Any stereo sound can be split into the mid (left + right: what’s the same in both) and the side (left − right: what’s different). Width turns the side up or down. At 0% the sound is mono; at 200% it’s wider than the speakers. Watch the blob.

title: Sound 23: Stereo
text:
The mono check
Set Haas delay to about 1 ms and press Mono. Then try 3, 5 and 10 ms. When the two channels are added back together, the delay cancels some frequencies and reinforces others: a comb filter, the hollow, phasey sound of a flanger standing still. A trick that sounds wide on headphones can sound thin and odd on a phone, a Bluetooth speaker, or a club PA, all of which are often mono. That’s why engineers press their mono button all the time. Now try Width at 200% in mono: the side cancels out completely and the extra width simply disappears.

title: Sound 23: Stereo

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
text:
Play a piano note and hold it: it starts with a hard knock and then fades, even while you hold the key. Bow a violin note: it swells in gently and stays as long as the bow moves. Same pitch, same harmonics perhaps, but they don’t sound like the same instrument. The difference is the envelope: how the loudness of a note changes from the moment it starts to the moment it is gone.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo, or play the computer keys (a w s e d f t g y h u j k), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Hold some notes down and let go of others quickly: the envelope only makes sense when you hear the difference between pressing and letting go.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
text:
The four stages: ADSR



A synth describes an envelope with four numbers, A D S R:

Attack: how long the note takes to reach full volume after you press the key. Short for a drum or a pluck; long for strings swelling in.
Decay: how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level.
Sustain: a level, not a time: how loud the note stays while you hold the key. 100% means no decay at all (an organ); 0% means the note dies away even if you hold it (a piano, a guitar).
Release: how long the note takes to fade to silence after you let go.

The strip draws the shape: rising for the attack, falling for the decay, flat while you hold, falling after you let go. The part that is flat lasts as long as your finger is down; the other three are times.

Click shows why attack and release are never quite zero: switching a wave on or off instantly makes a click, because a sudden jump has every frequency in it (look at the spectrum as a note starts).
Now play fast notes with the Pad preset: the notes never get loud before you let go. A long attack and fast playing don’t mix. That’s why string sections can’t play very fast passages loudly.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
section: The VCA, and envelopes on other things
text:
The VCA, and envelopes on other things
In a synth the envelope drives an amplifier (on analog synths a VCA, voltage-controlled amplifier). But an envelope is just a shape that rises and falls with each note, so it can move anything. In subtractive synthesis a second envelope opens and closes the filter, so a note can start bright and turn dull, which is how most synth basses and brass work. On a drum synth an envelope bends the pitch: the “boom” of a kick drum is a sine wave whose pitch drops fast.

title: Sound 5: Envelopes
text:
Next

Sound 6: LFOs: a shape that repeats instead of following each note.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text: Two full tracks at full volume together are loud and muddy: two kicks, two basslines, two sets of hi-hats. EQ mixing gives each track its own space during a blend. The golden rule: only one bassline at a time.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
The bass swap

Beatmatched and phrased, bring the incoming track in with its Lo cut right down. You hear its hats and mids over the outgoing track’s full sound.
On the first beat of a phrase, swap: incoming Lo up, outgoing Lo down, at the same moment (one hand on each knob).
Over the next 8 or 16 bars take the outgoing track’s Mid and Hi down, then its fader.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
Other transitions

Long blend: both tracks play together for 32 bars or more, EQs moving slowly. House and techno.
Filter mix: sweep the outgoing track’s filter to a high-pass (it thins out to nothing but hats) while the incoming one comes in, or bring the new track in through a low-pass that opens up.
Cut: on the first beat of a phrase, flick the crossfader across. Hip-hop and open-format DJs cut; it’s quick and clean if the phrase is right.
Echo out: an echo or delay effect on the last beat of the outgoing track, then cut it; the echo trails off under the new one.
Gain first: before any of these, set both channels’ gain so the tracks are equally loud. A transition that jumps in volume sounds like a mistake.

title: DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions
text:
Practise




Beatmatch B to A (B: about −1.6 %). With B’s Lo at the bottom (−26 dB, a near kill), start B on a phrase and bring its fader up.
On the next phrase, swap the Lo knobs. Then fade A out over 8 bars, Hi first.
Do it again with the Filter instead: B in at full EQ but low fader; sweep A’s filter to the right (high-pass) over 8 bars while B’s fader rises.
Try a cut: both decks matched, faders up, crossfader full A. On the 1 of a phrase, throw the crossfader to B. Set the Curve towards “cut” and try again: in the middle both channels are now at full, and the change happens only at the very ends.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
FM (frequency modulation) synthesis makes harmonics by a different route from subtractive synthesis. Instead of starting rich and filtering, it starts with two plain sine waves and uses one to wobble the pitch of the other so fast that the wobble becomes new frequencies. John Chowning found this at Stanford in 1967; Yamaha built it into the DX7 in 1983, and its electric piano, bells and slap bass are all over the music of the 1980s.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Choose a preset, then change one control at a time. The dashed lines on the spectrum mark where FM puts its new frequencies.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Carrier and modulator




The carrier is the sine wave you hear. Its frequency is the note you play.
The modulator is a second sine wave that you don’t hear directly. It moves the carrier’s pitch up and down.
The ratio is the modulator’s frequency divided by the carrier’s.
The index is how far the modulator pushes the pitch. At 0 there’s no modulation: a plain sine.

This is the vibrato from the LFO lesson, sped up into the audio range. Below about 20 Hz you hear a wobble; above it you hear a new timbre.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Sidebands
With the preset Steady (to study) loaded, hold a note and slowly raise the index from 0. New spikes appear on the spectrum on both sides of the carrier, spaced by the modulator’s frequency: carrier ± 1 × modulator, ± 2 ×, ± 3 × and so on. These are sidebands. The higher the index, the more sidebands, and the brighter the sound.
Now change the ratio:

Whole-number ratios (1, 2, 3…) put every sideband on a harmonic of the note. The sound is pitched and “musical”. Ratio 1 gives every harmonic, like a sawtooth; ratio 2 gives only odd harmonics, like a square or a clarinet.
Other ratios (1.41, 3.5…) put the sidebands between harmonics. The sound is inharmonic: metallic, bell-like, clangorous. That’s how FM makes bells and gongs so easily, which subtractive synths find hard.
Modulator fine tune detunes the modulator a few cents: the sidebands beat against each other and the sound shimmers.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
text:
Envelopes make FM come alive
In FM the index does the job of the filter in a subtractive synth: it sets the brightness. Give the index its own envelope and the brightness changes during each note, the way real instruments do.

Bell: index starts high and dies away, the volume dies away more slowly. The clang at the start fades into a pure hum.
Electric piano: ratio 1, a quick index decay: a bright “tine” attack and a mellow body.
Brass: the index rises with the attack, so the note gets brighter as it swells.
Bass: a short burst of index gives the slap at the start of each note.

Try the Bell preset and change only the ratio: 3.5, 1.4, 2.76, 5.19. Each is a different metal.

title: Sound 8: FM Synthesis
section: FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
text:
FM and the spectrum, in one sentence
Subtractive starts with all the harmonics and removes some; additive (Sound 1) sets each harmonic by hand; FM makes a whole family of frequencies from two sine waves, controlled by just two numbers: the ratio decides where they go and the index decides how many.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
A compressor is an automatic hand on the volume knob. When the sound gets louder than a set level, it turns it down; when it gets quieter, it lets it back up. The loud parts and the quiet parts end up closer together. Almost every vocal, bass line and drum track on a record goes through one.
How to use the page. The source starts as an uneven riff (some notes loud, some barely there). The graph shows input level across and output level up. The red dot is the sound right now, and the red bar on the right is the gain reduction: how many decibels the compressor is turning the sound down at this moment.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
The controls




Threshold: the level where the compressor starts working. Anything quieter passes through unchanged; on the graph the line follows the dashed diagonal until the threshold.
Ratio: how hard it turns down what goes over. At 4 : 1, a sound 8 dB over the threshold comes out only 2 dB over. At 20 : 1 almost nothing gets over: that’s a limiter.
Knee: how gently it starts. A soft knee bends into compression gradually.
Attack: how fast it reacts when the sound goes over. Slow attack lets the very start of each note through before clamping down, which keeps drums punchy.
Release: how fast it lets go when the sound drops back.
Make-up gain: compression makes everything quieter, so you turn the whole thing back up. Now the quiet notes are louder than before.

Press Bypass on and off with the uneven riff: compressed, the quiet notes come forward and the loud ones stop jumping out.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Hearing attack and release
Switch the source to the drum loop, set the ratio to 8 : 1 and the threshold to about −30 dB.

Attack 1 ms: the snare’s crack is flattened; the drums sound small and thick.
Attack 30 ms: the crack gets through before the compressor reacts; the drums punch.
Release 30 ms with a fast attack: the sound “pumps”, rising between hits. Dance music uses this on purpose.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Parallel compression
Turn Mix down to 50%. Now you hear the untouched drums and a heavily squashed copy together. The natural hits stay sharp and the squashed copy fills in between them. Engineers call it “New York” compression.

title: Sound 13: The Compressor
text:
Your own playing
Choose Microphone (headphones on) and play or sing from very soft to loud. With a threshold of −40 dB and a ratio of 6 : 1, watch the gain reduction bar follow you. The site’s backing band runs through a compressor too (threshold −12 dB, ratio 4 : 1, attack 3 ms), and these sound pages end in a limiter so that nothing comes out too loud.
