title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
This is a first lesson for someone who has never played congas. You will learn five ways to strike the drum, how they are written, and the most common conga part there is, the tumbao. You need one drum. If you have no drum yet you can still follow the notation and listen to the band play each step.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to play them yourself. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.
About the sounds. The sounds on this page are General MIDI stand-ins. The computer has only an open tone, a muted tone and a low drum, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones you hear here are approximations. Listen to a real player for the sound.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The drums
The conga is the higher drum of a pair, and the one this lesson uses. The tumba is the lower drum. A conga player often has both, and step 6 uses the tumba for a moment; everything else on this page is played on one drum.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Sitting and hands
This is ordinary advice, not a method. Sit upright, near the front of the chair, with the drum between your knees. Tilt it slightly away from you, or put it on a stand, so the bottom is open and the sound can come out. Keep your wrists and hands loose: a tight hand makes a dead sound and tires quickly. Take rings off. If anything hurts, stop and rest; a drum head is hard, and a beginner’s hands need time.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
The five strokes
The names and the first description of each stroke are from the teacher’s handout. Each button plays the stroke.
Bass tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand. It is the lowest sound the drum makes.
Open tone ▶ Hear it Strike near the edge of the head with the base of your fingers. Use the first four fingers at the edge and let them bounce off, so that the drum rings.
Muted tone ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand, creating a deep tone. Teachers differ on this name. Some say “muffled”, and some mean a tone where the fingers stay on the head after the strike. The handout’s description is the one used on this page.
Slap tone ▶ Hear it Strike the edge of the head with flat fingertips to create a high, pinging sound. The slap is the hardest stroke to learn and takes time. Do not expect it to ring on the first day.
Heel-toe ▶ Hear it Strike the center of the head with the heel of the palm, then rock forward to slap with the fingers. It is a rocking motion of the hand: first the heel, then the fingertips. It is a quiet stroke, used as filler between the louder ones. On this page the two halves are written as two notes, heel and toe.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Reading a conga part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space of the staff. The head says how it is struck: a plain head for the open tone and the bass tone, an ✕ for the slap, a triangle for the heel and the toe, and a diamond for the muted tone. The open tone and the bass tone look the same, so read the letter.



In a part, two lines of words sit under the notes. The first line is the stroke: H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass. The second line is the hand: L left and R right. A left-handed player can reverse the hands. A low drum, when there is one, is written on a lower space.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
1. The two notes everyone hears
The tumbao is built up from the end of the bar. Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” and play only on the last two. Use the right hand for both, one after the other.



These are the two notes a listener notices. When they come in the right place, the rest of the part has somewhere to go.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
2. The right hand
Now add the slap on 2. The right hand plays all of it: the slap on 2, then the two open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Between them the right hand rests, and you keep counting.



If the slap will not come, play it as an open tone for now and come back to it. Take it slowly.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
3. The left hand
Put the right hand away and play the other half. The left hand plays heel on 1, toe on the and of 1, toe on the and of 2, heel on 3 and toe on the and of 3. It is the rocking heel-toe stroke, quiet. The gaps left in the bar are where the right hand will go.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
4. Both hands, slowly
Put the two hands together. The strokes in order are Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, and the hands are L L R L L L R R. The left hand plays every quiet heel and toe; the right hand plays the slap and the two open tones. This is the tumbao, as the handout writes it: a pattern of heel-toe-slap-toe figures and a pair of open tones. The sticking is the one given for the tumbao by Rebeca Mauleón in Salsa Guidebook, as quoted in the Wikipedia article on the tumbao.



This step is slow, and the band has no drummer, so the congas are easy to hear. Loop it and play along until your hands do not argue.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
5. With a band
The same part in the Cha-cha, at a moderate tempo, with the drummer in. The tumbao is the most common pattern on congas and bongos, and it fits cha-cha, son and boogaloo. The Feel menu at the bottom plays it in the other two.



Listen for the clave in the other instruments: a rhythm of five notes over two bars, three in one bar and two in the other, that the whole band is built around. You do not need to play it to play the tumbao, but it explains the next step.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
6. Two drums
Players who have two drums use the second one in the tumbao. Here, in Son montuno, every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. It is the bar with three clave notes (the second bar of a 2-3 clave, as Mauleón’s book has it, again via the Wikipedia article). Look at the two bars written large: the second has the notes on a lower space.



Stay on one drum until step 5 is easy. The two-drum bar is an extra, not a part of the basic tumbao.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao
text:
Where to go next

Play step 5 with Leave out the congas ticked for ten choruses without losing the beat.
Take the tumbao to a tune: Watermelon Man for Congas plays it in a 16-bar blues.
Tools → Backing Track has a Congas menu that works in any style: put a tumbao under a tune you know.
Listen to a real conga player and copy what you hear. A page cannot give you the sound of the hands.
crumbs: How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
The twelve-bar blues is three four-bar phrases on three chords. Almost everything players have done to it since is one of a small number of moves: go to a chord sooner, approach a chord with its own dominant, split a dominant into a two-five, or replace a dominant with the one a tritone away. This lesson adds those moves one at a time. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays two choruses after a one-bar count-in. Section 8 has a tune written in notation, where the note that is sounding lights up. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
1. The three-chord blues
Four bars of I, two of IV and two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Every chord is a dominant seventh, including the home chord. That is the sound of the blues: a tonic that carries a flat seventh and does not need to resolve.



Listen for the two places the form turns. Bar 5 is the first move away from home. Bar 9 is the highest point of tension, and the last four bars walk it back down.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 2. The quick change and the turnaround
text:
2. The quick change and the turnaround
Two small changes, both very common. In bar 2 the band goes to IV for one bar and comes straight back (the quick change), which breaks up four bars of the same chord. In bar 12 the band plays V instead of resting on I, so the end of the chorus pulls into the top of the next one (a turnaround).



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
text:
3. The jazz blues: a two-five in the last line
Swing and bebop players turned the last line round. Instead of V then IV, they play ii7 then V7: the bass now moves by fifths (G, C, F in the key of F) all the way home. To set up the ii chord, bar 8 becomes VI7, the dominant of ii. The turnaround in bars 11 and 12 is the same idea at twice the speed: I, VI7, ii7, V7, two beats each.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 4. Getting to IV, and getting back
text:
4. Getting to IV, and getting back
Three more moves, each of them a way to make an arrival stronger.

Bar 4: a two-five into IV. The I7 chord in bar 4 is already the dominant of IV, so put its ii chord in front of it (v7 I7, two beats each).
Bar 6: the bass climbs a half step from IV to ♯iv°7, and that chord pulls back to I in bar 7. This one is as old as the blues on the piano.
Bar 8: split VI7 into its own two-five, iii7 VI7.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
5. Tritone substitution
A dominant seventh chord and the dominant seventh a tritone away share the same third and seventh (swapped). So either can stand in for the other, and the substitute’s root arrives by a half step from above instead of by a fifth. Here it is in four places: the end of bar 4 (♯IV7 falling to IV), the end of bar 8 (♭III7 falling to ii), bar 10 (♭II7 falling to I), and a turnaround built entirely of substitutes: I, ♭III7, ♭VI7, ♭II7.



Listen to the bass. Wherever a substitute is used, the line slides down by half step.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
6. The Bird blues
Charlie Parker’s “Blues for Alice” keeps only three landmarks of the form: I in bar 1, IV in bar 5 and the two-five in bars 9 and 10. Everything between is a chain of two-fives. Bars 2 to 4 descend by step to reach IV. Bars 6 to 9 descend by half step to reach ii. The home chord is a major seventh, not a dominant.



Compare it with the jazz blues of section 3. The shaded bars show how little is left.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
text:
7. The minor blues
The same twelve bars with minor i and iv chords. The last line is usually ♭VI7 to V7: a dominant a half step above the dominant (the tritone substitute of V’s own dominant). The turnaround uses a half-diminished ii chord. “Mr. P.C.” and “Equinox” are both built this way.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues
section: 8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. A tune on these changes: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet is a good first tune because its changes are the three-chord blues with just two of the moves above.

Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five, ii7 then V7, as in the jazz blues of section 3.
Bar 12 is V7, the turnaround of section 2.

Everything else is plain. There is no quick change in bar 2 (four full bars of I), bars 5 and 6 are IV, bars 7 and 8 stay on I with no VI7, and bar 11 is one bar of I. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the three-chord blues of section 1.



The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and the note that is sounding lights up as it plays. Listen to bars 5 and 6: one note of the riff is a half step lower there than in bars 1 and 2, because the 3rd of the I chord has become the ♭7th of the IV chord. The changes are in the melody. In bars 9 and 10 the riff does not change at all, even though the chords under it are new: every note of it belongs to both the ii chord and the V chord.
To build this chorus yourself in the next section, choose Stay on I, Stay on I, Stay on IV, Stay on I, Two-five and V in the last bar. Open in the Backing Track puts the tune on that page in a new tab, where the bass line, comping and drums can each be chosen. The instrument lessons each end with this tune, and the improvising lesson is built on it.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Subtractive synthesis starts with a wave full of harmonics and takes some away with a filter. It was the design of the Moog, the ARP, the Prophet-5 and the Minimoog that defined synth bass and synth lead, and most software synths still start from it. It is three parts in a row, each with a helper:
Oscillators (the raw tone) → filter (the brightness) → amplifier (the loudness). Envelopes shape the filter and the amplifier over the length of each note, and an LFO adds movement.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo to hear the synth play, or play it from the computer keys (a w s e d…), the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. It plays chords. Start with the presets, then change one control at a time.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text: The synth

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
1. Oscillators
Two oscillators, each with a shape from Sound 2. A sawtooth is the usual starting point because it has every harmonic for the filter to work on. A square or narrow pulse is hollower. Osc 2 detune sets the second oscillator a few cents off the first: the two drift in and out of phase and the sound becomes thick and moving. 5 to 15 cents is the classic “fat” sound; 0 is thin and still. Set Osc 2 octave to −1 for weight under a bass, or +1 for brightness. Noise adds breath, from Sound 3.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
2. Filter
The low-pass filter is where the character comes from. Cutoff sets how bright the note is, resonance adds the peak at the cutoff. The filter here is the steep 24 dB-per-octave kind.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
3. Envelopes: ADSR
An envelope is a shape that runs once each time you play a note. It has four stages:

Attack: how long it takes to rise from nothing to full when the key goes down.
Decay: how long it takes to fall from full to the sustain level.
Sustain: the level it holds while the key stays down (a level, not a time).
Release: how long it takes to fade to nothing after the key comes up.

The amp envelope shapes the loudness: a piano has fast attack, long decay, no sustain; an organ has instant attack, full sustain, instant release; a string pad has slow attack and slow release.
The filter envelope moves the cutoff, by up to Envelope amount octaves. This is the secret of most good synth sounds: real instruments are brightest at the start of a note. A fast filter attack and short decay give the “pew” of a synth bass; a slow attack gives a brass “swell”. The drawing under the controls shows both envelopes.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
4. LFO
The LFO (Sound 6) adds vibrato (→ Pitch) or a slow filter sweep (→ Cutoff).

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:
Recipes to try

Bass. Press Bass. Turn Envelope amount to 0: the note goes dull and loses its “pluck”. Put it back and change Decay in the filter envelope: short is a click, long is a wow.
From brass to strings. Press Brass, then raise the amp Attack to 0.3 s and set the filter Envelope amount to 0. The swell becomes a bowed string pad.
Pluck. Press Pluck and play fast. Everything happens in the filter envelope: sustain at 0, so every note closes down by itself.
No oscillator at all. Press Wind (noise): noise through a resonant band-pass, with the LFO moving the band. Play different keys: nothing changes, because noise has no pitch.

title: Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis
text:

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text: Good habits that make rehearsals start on time, keep the gear working, and keep your hearing for life.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Before you arrive

A stage plot: a simple drawing of where everyone stands, what they need (DI, mic, power, monitor).
An input list: channel 1 kick, 2 snare, … vocals. The sound person will love you.
Pack: instrument, cables, spares (Gear 2), tuner, capo or reeds or rosin, power supply, music, water, earplugs.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Setting up

Big things first: drums and amps in position, then keyboards and stands, then cables.
Power to each position; run cables along the edges, taped down across walkways.
Connect, then switch on in order: sources first, amps and speakers last (Gear 1).
Tune (the strobe tuner) before the sound check, then again before you start.
Sound check (Gear 3).
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Rehearsal etiquette

Don’t noodle while someone else is talking or sound checking.
Ask before touching someone else’s gear or settings.
Keep stage volume down; turn the amp toward yourself.
Mute or turn down before unplugging.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Packing down

Amps and speakers off first, then everything else.
Unplug by the plug; coil over-under, tie, put in the cable bag.
Instruments into cases first, so they don’t get knocked over.
Stands down, knobs tightened so parts don’t fall off.
A last walk round: adaptors, pedals, phone chargers and music left behind are the commonest losses.
Report anything broken. Tape “BAD” on it.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Lifting and carrying
Bend your knees, keep heavy things close to your body, ask for help with amps and cases over about 20 kg. Two people for a PA speaker on a stand.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears
text:
Protect your hearing
Hearing damage is permanent and painless, and it adds up. Tinnitus (ringing after a loud night) is a warning.

Safe-ish limits get short fast: about 85 dB for 8 hours, 94 dB for 1 hour, 100 dB for 15 minutes. A loud band rehearsal is often 100–110 dB.
Wear earplugs at rehearsals and gigs. Musician’s earplugs (flat response, about 15–25 dB) sound like the band, just quieter; foam plugs work but sound muffled.
Drummers and the players beside the drums need them most. Cymbals are very loud.
In-ears and headphones: keep the level as low as you can, take breaks.
Give your ears quiet time after loud exposure.
crumbs: Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text: A compressor turns loud sounds down. A gate does the opposite: it turns quiet sounds down, all the way to silence. Below its threshold it’s shut; when the sound gets loud enough, it opens. A transient shaper changes the start of each note without touching the rest. Both work on the shape in time of a sound, the envelope, after it has been recorded.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The noise gate



The source is drum hits with hiss and hum mixed in, like a noisy recording or a guitar amp buzzing between notes. The strip shows the level, the threshold (dashed) and where the gate is open (shaded).

Threshold: the gate opens when the level goes above it. Set it just above the noise and just below the quietest note you want to keep.
Attack: how fast it opens. Too slow and the start of each hit is cut off.
Hold: how long it stays open after the level falls, so it doesn’t flutter.
Release: how fast it closes. Too fast cuts off the tail of each note; too slow lets the noise back in.
Range: how far it closes. −80 dB is silence; −12 dB just tucks the noise down, which sounds more natural.

Try Clean up hiss, then raise the threshold too far and listen to the hits getting chopped.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The 80s gated snare
Choose 80s gated snare: there is now a big reverb before the gate, and the gate is keyed by the dry drums. Every hit gets a huge, explosive burst of reverb that stops dead a fraction of a second later instead of fading. Phil Collins’ “In the Air Tonight” made it famous in 1981 (the engineer Hugh Padgham found it by accident on a talkback mic), and it’s on half the pop records of the decade. Change Hold to change the length of the burst.

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
The transient shaper
The transient is the first few milliseconds of a sound: the stick hitting the drum, the pick on the string. The rest is the sustain (the drum ringing, the room).




Attack up: every hit gets punchier and closer. Down: softer and further away.
Sustain up: the ring and the room come forward. Down: the drums get tight and dry, as if the room were dead.

It does this with two envelope followers, one fast and one slow. Where the fast one is above the slow one, a hit is starting: that gets the attack amount. Where it’s below, the sound is ringing on: that gets the sustain amount. Unlike a compressor, it doesn’t care how loud the sound is, only whether it’s starting or fading. Try it on the Synth riff and on your microphone (clap).

title: Sound 15: Gates and Transients
text:
Next

Sound 16: Reverb

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
A pitched note has its energy at a few frequencies (the harmonics). Noise has its energy spread over all of them at once, with no pattern and no repeating shape. It’s the hiss of a cymbal, the breath in a flute, the “s” and “f” in speech, wind and rain. Synthesizers include a noise source for exactly these sounds.
How to use the page. Press ▶ to hear the colour you chose, or press one of the Made from noise buttons. Noise is loud for its size: start with the volume low.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
The colours of noise




White noise has equal energy at every frequency. Because each octave up holds twice as many frequencies as the one below, it sounds very bright: a hiss.
Pink noise has equal energy in every octave, so it falls away toward the highs. It sounds more even to the ear, like steady rain or a waterfall, and sound engineers use it to test speakers.
Brown noise (named after Brownian motion, not the colour) falls away faster still: a deep rumble, like surf heard from inside a house.

Watch the spectrum as you switch. White is flat, pink tilts down gently, brown tilts down steeply. The oscilloscope never settles into a shape, because noise never repeats.

title: Sound 3: Noise
text:
Sounds made from noise
Noise on its own is not very musical. Its use comes from shaping it: a filter picks out a band of frequencies, an envelope makes it short or long, and an LFO makes it move.







Button
Recipe




Wind
pink noise through a narrow band-pass filter whose centre drifts slowly


Surf
pink noise through a low-pass, both the volume and the brightness swelling every eight seconds


Hi-hat
white noise, only the highs, cut off within 50 ms (longer for the open hat)


Snare
a burst of noise for the wires with a short low tone for the drum head


Steam
white noise with the lows removed


Rain
soft pink noise for the background, plus thousands of tiny filtered clicks for drops



Every drum sound in the site’s backing band except the kick is made from noise in roughly this way.

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a guitarist who knows open chords and strumming but hasn’t played jazz. Its thirteen steps go in order of how simple the voicing is. First come more chord types in familiar shapes, then fewer strings, then fewer chord tones, then more colour. Guitar chord shapes by hand has the same chords in the order the hand finds them easy.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left and the nut at the top. Each dot shows its chord tone: R is the root, and 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on are counted up from it. The fret numbers under each diagram run from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Press ▶ to hear a shape. The staff writes the chords an octave above where they sound, which is how guitar music is written.
Each step has an ID, such as G-A3, that other lessons use to point back here.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A1 Open triads
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. A guitar has six strings, so some of those three tones are doubled: C x32010 is C–E–G–C–E, with the 3rd on two strings. The doubled tones and ringing open strings give the bright sound of folk and pop. The 3rd decides major or minor, and it is the only difference between E and Em.



Practice: loop C, Am, F, G (four-chord loops, loop 1) until the changes land in time with no gap. Play F as the small shape xx3211 until you reach the barre (G-A3).
Unlocks: the strummed styles of the Backing Track: Acoustic strum, Straight-eighth rock, Boom-chick.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A2 Fifths (power chords)
Root and 5th, sometimes with the octave on top. There is no 3rd, so the chord is neither major nor minor. Fifths stay clear under distortion, where the 3rds of two chords would clash, and they fit whatever 3rd the bass or the singer supplies. This is also the first time a chord leaves a tone out, which every later step does too. The shape is the same with the root on string 6 or on string 5, so one fingering moves anywhere.



Practice: play a 12-bar blues in fifths. Then rock between the 5th and the 6th on the middle string (E5 to E6 to E5), the classic rock-and-roll rhythm figure.
Unlocks: palm-muted eighth notes in rock and pop-punk.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
text:
G-A3 Barre chords: the E and A shapes
Any open shape can move up the neck if your index finger replaces the nut. The root is under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape and on string 5 for the A shape. Those two shapes give all twelve major and minor chords, and this is the point where the neck becomes a map rather than a list of chords. The physical side is in G-B8 and G-B9.



Practice: play one four-chord loop in three keys, naming each root as you land on it.
Unlocks: the same strums in every key; Motown / soul.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A4 Sus and add9
A sus chord replaces the 3rd with the 2nd (sus2) or the 4th (sus4). With no 3rd it is neither major nor minor, and it leans toward resolving: Dsus4 falls to D as G moves down to F♯. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up. It is sweet rather than tense. These are the colours of pop and 80s rock guitar, and the first chords in this sequence that go beyond a triad.



Practice: D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2, one bar each. Then alternate C and Cadd9.
Unlocks: sixteenth-note strums with hammer-ons, and fingerpicking (Travis pattern).
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A5 Dominant 7th
A dominant 7th is root, major 3rd, 5th and flat 7th. The 3rd and the ♭7 are a tritone apart, and a tritone wants to resolve. Going from G7 to C, the 3rd (B) rises a half step to C and the ♭7 (F) falls a half step to E. That pull is what makes a chord dominant, and it drives the blues and every jazz tune.



Practice: play G7 to C slowly and find the two notes that move by one fret. Then see blues for guitar.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle, and a 12-bar blues on I7, IV7 and V7.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A6 Minor 7th and major 7th
A minor 7th is a minor triad plus a ♭7. It sounds soft and open rather than dark. A major 7th is a major triad plus the 7th one fret below the root, and it sounds dreamy. Pop already uses both: Am7 and Cmaj7 turn up all over pop changes for guitar. In jazz these two types, together with the dominant 7th, make up most of the harmony.



Practice: Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7 (I–vi–ii–V) in open shapes. Then play it in F with barre shapes.
Unlocks: Bossa nova, and slow Charleston comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A7 Half-diminished and diminished 7th
Half-diminished (m7♭5) is a minor 7th with a flat 5th. It is chord vii in a major key (Bm7♭5 in C) and the ii chord in a minor key (see minor changes). A diminished 7th is a stack of minor 3rds, so the shape repeats every three frets with the same four notes. The F♯dim passing chord in pop changes is this chord.



Practice: slide a dim7 shape up three frets at a time. You’ll hear the same chord four times, with four different names.
Unlocks: the passing chords in turnarounds, and the minor-key ii–V–i.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A8 Shell voicings (root, 3rd, 7th)
The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones: they say what kind of chord it is. The 5th adds the least, because the bass and the key already imply it, so a shell leaves it out. Root, 3rd and 7th make a chord thin enough to sit under a singer or a solo, which is how a rhythm guitarist plays in a jazz band. Shells come with the root on string 6 (strings 6, 4 and 3) or on string 5 (strings 5, 4 and 2). The Chord Library calls these Shell (R-3-7).



Practice: play C7, F7 and G7 as shells and watch the 3rd and the 7th: each moves a fret or two when the chord changes.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, Reverse Charleston, and the Shell voicing in the Backing Track’s guitar menu.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
section: G-A9 Triads on the top strings
text:
G-A9 Triads on the top strings
Three strings and three notes, with nothing doubled. This is the cleanest chord on the guitar, and it sounds best in a band with a keyboard or a second guitar because it takes only a thin slice of the range. A triad has three positions, and each one moves the lowest note to the top. The shapes are small, so you can chain them with almost no movement. The Backing Track calls this Voice-led triads.



Practice: play C, F and G, choosing each time the shape nearest to the last.
Unlocks: funk sixteenths and reggae or ska off-beats on the top three strings.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A10 Drop 2 voicings
Start with a seventh chord in close position, its four tones packed inside an octave. Take the second note from the top and drop it an octave. The chord opens up enough to fit the fingers, and it still has all four tones. On strings 4, 3, 2 and 1, a ii–V–I in C moves every voice by a fret or two. That smooth movement between chords, the voice leading, is what jazz chord shapes are for.



Practice: play that ii–V–I, then move the same three shapes up five frets to F.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, with Bossa nova and Charleston comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A11 Drop 3 voicings
Drop the third voice from the top instead of the second, and the bass note moves down a string, leaving a string skipped in the middle. From the bottom up the tones are root, 7th, 3rd, 5th. Drop 3 sounds bigger than a shell and still has four notes. Guitarists use drop 3 when the chord needs a low root and weight, and drop 2 when it should sit higher and lighter.



Practice: play the ii–V–I in drop 3 (Dm7 x5x565, G7 3x343x, Cmaj7 x3x453), then in drop 2, and listen to how close the voice leading is.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing in the Backing Track, and slow ballad comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A12 Extensions: 9th and 13th
The 9th is the 2nd an octave up, the 11th is the 4th and the 13th is the 6th. An extension adds colour without changing what the chord does. C9 still pulls to F, only richer, and C13 is the dominant chord of a blues band’s horn section. Here’s a shortcut: an Em7 shape over a C bass note is Cmaj9, because E–G–B–D are the 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th of C.



Practice: swap each dominant 7th of a 12-bar blues for a 9th or a 13th.
Unlocks: funk, Boogaloo stabs, and the jazz blues.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
G-A13 Altered dominants
An altered dominant raises or lowers the 5th or the 9th to add tension just before the chord resolves. The ♭9 and ♯9 pull down toward the chord that follows, and the ♯5 pulls up toward its 3rd. Altered chords are short and high-energy, and they usually come at the end of a phrase. The 7♭9 shape, without its root, is a diminished 7th, which is why a dim7 shape can stand in for a 7♭9.



Practice: in a ii–V–I in C, play G7♯9 instead of G7 and listen to the tension release into Cmaj7.
Unlocks: endings, turnarounds and the last bar of a chorus in jazz comping.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz
text:
Where to go next

Guitar chord shapes by hand has the same chords in physical order, with what makes each one hard.
Piano chord voicings has the same ideas on the keyboard.
The Chord Library has every voicing of every chord: search drop2, shell, caged:E and so on.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
An equaliser (EQ) turns some frequencies up and others down. You met the parts on the filter page: high-pass, low-pass, shelves and bells. An EQ is several of them in a row, and it’s the most used tool in any recording studio. Every track in a mix gets some, to make room for the others.
How to use the page. The pink curve on the spectrum is the EQ: above the middle line is a boost, below is a cut. Use Bypass often. Your ears get used to a change within seconds, and only comparing tells you whether it’s better.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
The bands




High-pass (low cut): removes everything below a frequency. The most useful control on the desk: almost nothing except bass and kick needs anything below 80–100 Hz, and rumble there muddies everything.
Shelves lift or lower everything above (high shelf) or below (low shelf) a frequency, like the bass and treble knobs on a stereo.
Bells (peaking filters) boost or cut around one frequency. Q is how narrow: a high Q touches only a few notes’ worth of frequencies, a low Q a wide region.
Low-pass (high cut) removes the top: hiss, harshness, or everything at once for a muffled effect.

A rough map of what lives where:








Range
Called
Sounds like




20–60 Hz
sub
felt more than heard: kick drum thump, synth sub bass


60–250 Hz
bass
warmth and weight; too much is boomy


250–500 Hz
low mids
“mud” and “boxiness”: most mixes are cut a little here


500 Hz–2 kHz
mids
the body of most instruments; too much honks


2–5 kHz
upper mids
presence, the bite of a voice or guitar; too much is harsh


5–10 kHz
highs
clarity, the “s” sounds


10–20 kHz
air
sparkle and openness

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
Cut before you boost
Try Cut the mud and Presence on the chords and on your microphone. Engineers usually cut what’s wrong rather than boost what’s missing: a cut makes room, a boost makes everything louder and soon everything is fighting. Two sounds that both have a lot at 300 Hz will mask each other; cut one of them there, and both become clear.
Telephone keeps only 400 Hz to 3.2 kHz, the band a phone line carries. Scooped is the classic metal guitar curve: big lows and highs, a hole in the middle.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
Find the problem
Recordings often have one frequency that rings: a drum’s overtone, a boomy room, a harsh voice. The trick for finding it is boost and sweep:

Set Hidden problem to A ringing frequency. Something is now wrong with the sound.
Press Search (narrow boost): Bell 2 becomes a tall, narrow boost.
Sweep Bell 2 frequency slowly. At most places it just sounds odd; at the problem frequency the ring suddenly leaps out.
Now turn that boost into a cut (Bell 2 gain to about −12 dB) and listen: the ring is gone.
Press Reveal to see how close you were. Then try Boomy and Harsh.

title: Sound 11: The Equaliser
text:
Next

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text: When you map a recording in the Timestamp Notes, S stamps a section and gives it a label from a menu. This lesson covers what each label means, when to use letters instead of words, and how the page counts the choruses each player takes.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Two kinds of stamp

S marks a section: the place where a new part of the form starts. It gets a label from the menu, and the bar map, the chord grid, the phrases and Send on all use it.
C marks a note: anything else worth finding again (“drum fill”, “key change”, “wrong note at 1:12”). A note is just text, and it doesn’t split the song into sections.

Both kinds of stamp go in the same Timestamps list, in time order. Section stamps are tinted blue and have the menu.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
The words








Label
What it is
Where you hear it




Intro
Music before the first real section, often a vamp or the last bars of the tune
Pop, rock, jazz


Head
The tune itself, played straight through, before and after the solos
Jazz


Verse
Words that change each time over the same music
Songs


Pre-chorus
A short build that lifts the verse into the chorus
Pop


Chorus
The part that comes back with the same words: the hook
Songs


Bridge
Contrasting music, usually heard once or twice
Songs, jazz (the B of AABA)


Interlude
An instrumental passage between sung sections
Songs


Solo
One player improvising over the form. Choose the instrument (Sax solo, Piano solo…)
Jazz, rock

A written ensemble chorus, the whole band loud together, often after the solos
Big band, small group arrangements

Everywhere



The same word in pop and in jazz can mean different things. In a song a chorus is a section with the hook. In jazz a chorus is one time through the whole form: “he took three choruses” means the soloist went through the form three times.

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
The letters
Jazz standards and older songs are usually described by form letters: each new piece of music gets the next letter, and a piece that comes back gets its old letter.

AABA (32 bars, 8 each): I Got Rhythm, Satin Doll. The B is the bridge.
ABAC: All of Me. The second A returns, but the end goes somewhere new.
A A′: the A comes back with a different ending. A′ (“A prime”) means nearly A.

The menu starts by offering A. Once you’ve used A, it also offers A′ (A changed) and B (something new). Each letter you use adds the next one: B brings B′ and C, A′ brings A″. You never have to type a prime mark.
Letters aren’t numbered. An AABA tune should have three A’s, so they all stay “A”.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Numbering is automatic
Pick the same word twice and both are numbered: two Heads become Head 1 and Head 2 everywhere they appear (the bar map, the chord grid, the Notation page). Delete one and the other goes back to plain Head. Move a stamp earlier and the numbers follow time order, not the order you stamped them.
Need a label that isn’t on the menu? Choose Other… at the bottom and type it (“Vamp”, “Drum break”, “Trading 4s”). A typed label is kept exactly as you wrote it. The ▾ next to it takes you back to the menu.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Choruses: who soloed how long
Once the bars are tapped (B), the page measures each section and divides it by the length of one chorus:

One chorus is the length of the first Head stamp. If you stamped letters, it’s the A A B A (or whatever pattern repeats). If the guess is wrong, type the bar count into a chorus is __ bars.
Back-to-back stamps with the same label are one solo. It doesn’t matter whether you stamp the sax solo once or at the top of every chorus: three stamps of Sax solo, 32 bars each, make Sax 3 choruses.
Untapped bars are worked out from the tempo, so you can tap one chorus, stamp the rest with S and still get a count. The last section runs to the end of the recording.
A count of 1.5 means the solo stopped halfway through the form. That happens, but check that your stamp is in the right place.

In a song (no Head and no letters), sections can each be a different length, so a solo is counted in bars instead, along with the section it matches in length: “Guitar 8 bars (as long as the Verse)”. A last chorus tapped twice as long as the first plays its chords through twice rather than holding each one twice as long. If one section is a bar over a multiple of four and the next is a bar under (9 then 7), the Sections panel marks both with ⚠: one stamp is probably a bar off.
Fill from the tempo (in the Bar map panel) goes further: tap the head, stamp where each solo starts, and it puts in every bar after the taps. Between two stamps the bars are spread evenly, so a band that speeds up or slows down lands back on each stamp. A head or solo that comes out within about a tenth of a chorus of a whole number becomes that many choruses. The guessed bars are grey in the Bars table. Tap B on any downbeat where they drift: your tap is kept and the bars around it are worked out again. Clear guesses takes them all out.
Each count appears next to the solo’s first stamp, and the full list is under the Timestamps.
crumbs: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

title: Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song
text:
Exercise

Choose a jazz recording with a head and at least two solos.
Listen once and press S each time the form starts again. Choose Head, then the soloists.
Tap a chorus of bars (B).
Read the chorus counts. Do they match what you heard? If a count is a half, find the stamp that’s off.
Do it again with letters only (A, A, B, A…) and check that the chorus length comes out the same.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Watermelon Man is a 16-bar blues that a conga player can learn in an afternoon, once the tumbao is under the hands. If you have not played the tumbao yet, start with How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao. This page assumes the heel, toe, slap and open tones, and the part Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Congas alone to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and Leave out the congas to take over. Each step starts in its own style and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both. The sounds are General MIDI stand-ins, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones are approximations: listen to a real player for the sound.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The tune and its history
Herbie Hancock wrote Watermelon Man for his first album, Takin’ Off (Blue Note, 1962), with Freddie Hubbard, Dexter Gordon, Butch Warren and Billy Higgins on drums. No conga player is listed on that record. It is in F, in even eighths: Hancock said Higgins played “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. It goes at roughly 120 to 130 beats a minute.
Late in 1962 Hancock filled in on piano in the band of the conga player Mongo Santamaría for a weekend at a club in the Bronx, and Donald Byrd urged him to play the tune for Mongo. Mongo’s band recorded it on 17 December 1962 “in a cha-cha beat”, with Kako Baster on timbales, Victor Venegas on bass and Ray Lucas adding a backbeat on drums. The single came out on Battle in 1963 and reached the top ten or eleven of the Billboard Hot 100 (sources differ). It is slower than Hancock’s, and is often named as a starting point of boogaloo and Latin soul. A much later remake, on Head Hunters in 1973, has Bill Summers blowing into beer bottles after the Central African hindewhu.
What this lesson teaches, and what it does not. No published transcription of the conga part on Mongo’s record was found. What you learn here is the standard tumbao, the part a conga player plays in a cha-cha beat. Listen to the record and copy what you hear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Reading the part
Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space; a low drum, when there is one, sits on a lower space. A plain head is the open tone (or the bass tone), an ✕ is the slap, a triangle is heel or toe, and a diamond is the muted tone. Two lines of words sit under the notes: the stroke (H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muted, B bass) and the hand (L or R).

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
The form
It is a 16-bar blues: a 12-bar blues whose bars 9 and 10 (C7 and B♭7) are played three times. In F, with one chord to a bar:

Bars 1 to 4: F7, F7, F7, F7
Bars 5 to 8: B♭7, B♭7, F7, F7
Bars 9 to 12: C7, B♭7, C7, B♭7
Bars 13 to 16: C7, B♭7, F7, F7

The Backing Track has the same form as its “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset, with the band stopping on bar 14 (the break). The steps below use it.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
section: 1. The form, with the open tones only
text:
1. The form, with the open tones only
Start with the two open tones, on 4 and the and of 4, and nothing else. Count the sixteen bars out loud. Listen for the three C7 to B♭7 pairs in bars 9 to 14: that is the part of the form a 12-bar blues does not have.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
2. The right hand
Add the slap on 2. The right hand plays the slap, then the two open tones. The slap on 2 lands with the backbeat.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
3. The tumbao, slowly
Now the whole part: Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open, hands L L R L L L R R, one bar at a time, in a cha-cha beat at about 100 beats a minute. Do not speed up to catch the band; keep the left hand quiet and the slap and open tones clear.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
4. The break
On bar 14 the band stops. The congas play one open tone on beat 1 with the band, then nothing, and come back in on bar 15 with the band. Count the silent beats. The two bars shown large are bars 13 and 14.



The bar after the stop is the hard part: nothing in the band tells you the time but your own counting. Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud through bar 14.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
5. With the melody
The tune, written in F, above the chart. The band plays it on the piano with the congas. Tick Leave out the tune to hear the congas and the band alone. In this step the band plays straight through the break, so the melody is not cut off.



Read the melody as you play. The riff in bars 1 and 2 is the line everyone knows.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
6. Mongo’s way and Herbie’s way
The same part in two styles. The first plays the congas in the Cha-cha at a moderate tempo, as Mongo’s band recorded it, with the break on bar 14. The second is the Boogaloo at about 126, with straight eighths and the break, nearer Hancock’s own tempo. Change between them with the Feel menu at the bottom. The part is the same tumbao in both.
Mongo’s way: Cha-cha, a moderate tempo.



Herbie’s way: Boogaloo, about 126.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
7. Two drums
As an extension, the same form with two drums in the Son montuno: every second bar the right hand plays two open tones on the low drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel. Which bar of the pair takes the low drum depends on the clave, and this lesson does not say which way the clave runs on the record. A one-bar tumbao avoids the question: stay with step 6 until you can play it through without thinking.

title: Watermelon Man for Congas
text:
Where to go next

Play step 6 with the congas left out and the tumbao in your hands for ten choruses.
Learn the five strokes properly in How to Play Congas.
Blues for Drums has the same kind of steps for a drum kit.
Tools → Backing Track has the “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset and a Congas menu that works in any style.
Listen to Mongo Santamaría’s record and copy what you hear.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text: Chopping is cutting a sample into pieces so each can be played on its own. On an Akai MPC the pieces go onto the 16 pads; on a Roland SP-404 each pad holds a sample with its own start and end; in a DAW the pieces become slices of a clip or notes of a sampler.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
Three ways to cut

Equal slices: cut the loop into 16 equal parts. For a one-bar loop in 4/4 each slice is a sixteenth note; for two bars, an eighth. Quick, and it keeps the timing grid, but a slice can start just before or after a hit.
One a beat: cut at every beat (from the loop’s tempo). Good for chord samples, where each beat is a chord.
At the transients: cut where the sound suddenly gets louder (a transient: the attack of a drum or a plucked note). Each slice starts exactly on a hit, so it sounds clean; the slices are of different lengths.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
Try it




With 16 equal slices, play pads 1–16. Some slices start with a click or a bit of the hit before. Listen for it.
Switch to At the hits. Now pads start on kicks, snares and hats. Play pads 1–4: each is a clean one-shot.
Move a chop: drag one of the marker lines on the waveform left or right. The pad plays as you let go. Put a marker exactly at the start of a snare: the slice before it now ends cleanly too.
Load Old Soul Record (chords) from the menu and choose One a beat: each pad is now a chord. Play a new progression with them.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
text:
The art of the chop

Short chops (a single hit or a word) become an instrument: you play a new rhythm with them.
Long chops (a bar, a phrase) keep the feel of the original: you rearrange them like building blocks, as J Dilla and Pete Rock did with soul records.
Leave out the obvious bit. The famous hook of a record is the hardest to clear and the most recognised; a tiny chord stab from the middle of side B is yours to transform.
Fades: a slice that starts or ends in the middle of a sound clicks. This sampler fades each slice in and out over 1.5 ms; a DAW or MPC has fade or “attack/release” settings for the same reason.

title: Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing
section: The DJ’s version: loops and cue points
text:
The DJ’s version: loops and cue points
A DJ chops live. A cue point is a marked spot in a track to jump to; a loop repeats a stretch (a bar, four bars) until it is released. With hot cues on the four snare hits of a break, a DJ can “finger drum” a new pattern over the next record: a chop made in the moment. On the deck below, press CUE while stopped to set a cue point where you are, then ▶; press CUE while it plays and it jumps back and stops.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
A harmonic is the bell-like note you get when you touch a string lightly at the right spot instead of pressing it to the fret. The finger does not shorten the string: it stops the string from moving at that one point, so only the vibrations that already have a still point there can carry on. What is left is one of the string’s overtones, on its own. This lesson starts with the natural harmonics on open strings, explains where they are and what pitch each one gives, and then moves on to tapped, harp and pinch harmonics. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section.
How to use the page. Strings are numbered 1 (high E) to 6 (low E); tab has one line a string, high E on top. Start the volume low: the playable string in section 2 makes pure, ringing tones.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
1. What a harmonic is
A plucked string does not only swing as one long arc. At the same time it vibrates in 2 halves, in 3 thirds, in 4 quarters, and so on. Each of these patterns sounds a pitch: the whole string gives the note you hear (the fundamental), halves give twice its frequency, thirds three times, quarters four times. Together they are the harmonic series, and their mix is what makes a guitar sound like a guitar.
Each pattern has nodes, points that stay still, and between them antinodes, where the string swings most. Halves have a node in the middle. Thirds have nodes at one third and two thirds of the way along. When you touch the string lightly at one third of its length, every pattern that needs that point to move is choked off; the patterns that have a node there (thirds, sixths, ninths …) keep ringing. You hear the lowest of them: the 3rd harmonic.
Here is the series on the low E string (E2). Click a note to hear it; the numbers under the notes say how many parts the string is divided into, the numbers above how many cents each is from the nearest piano note.



The 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th harmonics are octaves and fifths of the open string, and nearly match the piano. The 5th harmonic is a major third, about 14 cents flat of the tempered G♯. That matters when you use harmonics to tune (section 8).
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
2. Where the natural harmonics are
The nut and the saddle are the string’s two ends, so the 12th fret, halfway, is the node for halves. Frets get closer together as they go up because each one shortens the string by the same ratio, so the other simple fractions land on or near particular frets:

A few things follow from the fractions:

One pitch, several places. Every node of a pattern gives the same note. The 7th and 19th frets give the same B; the 4th, 9th and 16th give the same G♯. The 7th fret harmonic and the 12th fret harmonic are not the same octave: thirds are higher than halves.
The higher the harmonic, the narrower the spot. The 12th is easy; the 5th-of-the-string spots near the 4th and 9th frets need you to be within a millimetre or two, a little toward the nut, and they ring quieter.
The spot is over the fret wire, not between frets where you would fret a note, because that is where the fractions land: at the 12th, 7th and 5th the node is right above the metal.

Click a node to hear the harmonic it leaves ringing; the line shows the pattern of the string for that harmonic, with its still points.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
3. Playing natural harmonics

Touch, don’t press. Lay the fleshy pad of a fretting finger on the string directly above the fret wire (12th to begin with). Just touching: the string should not reach the fret. Pressing is the most common reason a harmonic comes out as a dead thud.
Pick near the bridge. A firm pick stroke two or three fingers’ width from the saddle brings out the high patterns more than picking over the soundhole or neck pickup does.
Lift. Take the touching finger off the string straight after the pick stroke. The harmonic then rings on its own for as long as an open string would. Leave it on and the harmonic stays thin and dies.
Go in order. Get the 12th clean on all six strings, then the 7th, then the 5th, then the spots just behind the 4th and 9th, then just past the 3rd.

Several strings at once. Lay one finger flat across all six strings above the 12th fret and strum, then lift: a chord of harmonics, the open-string chord an octave up. The same across the 5th and 7th frets gives the bell chords in many intros.

On electric guitar, the bridge pickup and a little gain make harmonics jump out. On acoustic, pick harder than you think, near the bridge.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
4. Tapped and artificial harmonics
Natural harmonics only give the open strings’ overtones. To get harmonics of any note, fret the note, and the halfway point moves: it is now 12 frets above the fretted note. Fret the 3rd fret, and the node is over the 15th.

Tapped harmonic (T.H.): fret the note with the left hand, then strike the string sharply with a right-hand finger on the fret wire 12 frets higher and bounce straight off. The tap both starts the string and stops it at the node. Also works 5 and 7 frets above the fretted note (the 4th and 3rd harmonics), and over a whole chord shape: hold a chord at the 2nd fret, tap across the 14th.
Artificial harmonic (A.H.), picked: fret the note, touch the node (12 frets up) lightly with the right-hand index finger, and pluck the string with the thumb or a pick held between thumb and middle finger, behind the touching finger toward the bridge. Lift the index just after.
Harp harmonics: the same artificial harmonic, alternated with ordinary plucked notes from the ring finger, on neighbouring strings, so harmonics and normal notes overlap like a harp. Fret a chord, then: thumb plucks string 4 while the index touches 12 frets up, ring finger plucks string 3 normally, then the same on strings 3 and 2 … Go slowly; the hand shape takes weeks.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
5. Pinch harmonics
The squeal in rock and metal solos is a pinch harmonic (P.H., also “squealie”). It is an artificial harmonic made with the pick hand alone: the pick starts the string, and the edge of the thumb grazes it a split second later and stops it at a node.
The grip. Hold the pick so that only a little of the tip sticks out past the thumb, a couple of millimetres. Pick downward, and roll the thumb’s edge onto the string straight after the pick, as if the stroke ends with the thumb brushing it. Graze, don’t damp: touch and let go. Push the stroke through the string, like an ordinary downstroke, a little harder than usual.
Finding the spot. The harmonic only comes out where the thumb lands on a node, so slide the picking hand slowly from the neck pickup toward the bridge, picking all the way, and listen. You will hear different harmonics pop out in different places; the loud ones are usually between the pickups and just in front of the bridge pickup.
Why the spot moves. The node is a fraction of the length of the string that is vibrating, which runs from the fretted note to the saddle. Fret higher up and that length is shorter, so every node moves toward the bridge with it. On the 5th fret of the G string, the node one quarter of the way from the bridge is somewhere other than on the 12th fret. So for each note you play, the sweet spot is in a slightly different place: practise by playing one note and walking the hand, then a note five frets higher and finding the spot again.
Sound. Pinch harmonics are easiest with the bridge pickup and gain (overdrive or distortion), which bring up the quiet high overtone. On a clean amp or acoustic they still work, quietly. Add vibrato straight after the squeal, or pick the note and bend it up (see String Bends on Guitar): the harmonic bends with it, a whole step on the fretted note being a whole step on the harmonic.

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
7. Common faults and fixes







Fault
Fix




A dull thud, no ring
You are pressing. Touch so lightly the string could slide under the finger.


The normal note sounds, not the harmonic
You are between frets. Move the finger to sit right above the fret wire.


It rings for a moment, then dies
Lift the touching finger straight after picking.


The 4th/9th/3rd fret ones won’t come
They are narrow and just off the fret (see the table in section 2); creep the finger toward the nut a millimetre at a time, and pick nearer the bridge.


Neighbouring strings ring too
Mute them with the touching finger’s underside and the picking palm.


Pinch harmonics: just a normal note
Less pick showing; make the thumb actually touch the string; move the hand, the spot is small.


Pinch harmonics: a choked click
The thumb stays on the string. Graze and let go.


Pinch harmonics work on one note but not the next
The spot moved with the fretted note (section 5): walk the hand again.


Tapped harmonics buzz
Tap on the fret wire, not behind it, and bounce off at once.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
8. Harmonics for tuning
Because the 5th fret harmonic of one string and the 7th fret harmonic of the next one up are (on most string pairs) the same pitch, sounding them together lets you hear beats, a slow wah-wah, when they disagree, and tune until it stops. Two cautions: the 7th fret harmonic is a pure fifth, 2 cents wider than the tempered one, so tuning a whole guitar this way stacks small errors; and the G-to-B pair is a third and doesn’t work this way. Guitar tuning methods goes through this and other methods, and the Guitar tuning tool has a strobe to check each string.
crumbs: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

title: Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch
text:
9. Practice, step by step
Five to ten minutes a day, in this order. Move on when the step rings clean nine times in ten.

12th fret, each string. Touch, pick near the bridge, lift. Six strings, three times each.
12th, 7th, 5th on one string. Play them in turn and hear that the 7th is higher than the 12th and the 5th higher again. Check against section 2.
The narrow ones. Behind the 4th, behind the 9th, past the 3rd, on the low E. Compare the 4th and 9th: same note.
Chords of harmonics. One finger flat across the 12th, then the 7th, then the 5th, strum and lift. Then a little tune: 12th on strings 3, 2, 1, then 7th on strings 3, 2, 1, then 5th.
Tapped harmonics. Fret an E major shape at the open strings and tap the 12th fret wire across all strings; then a barre at the 3rd fret, tapping the 15th.
Artificial harmonics. One note at a time: fret, touch 12 frets up with the index, pluck with the thumb. Then a slow C major scale on one string this way.
Pinch harmonic hunt. Bridge pickup, some gain. Fret string 3 at the 7th fret; walk the pick hand from neck to bridge until it squeals. Then fret the 9th and find the new spot.
Pinch with vibrato and a bend. Squeal on string 3 fret 7, add vibrato; then squeal and bend a whole step to the pitch of fret 9.
In a phrase. Play a lick you know and end it on a pinch harmonic with vibrato.

Where to go next: String Bends on Guitar for the bends under a pinch harmonic, Tuning systems for why the 5th harmonic is flat of the piano, and Guitar tuning methods.

text:
