Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

Starting from the melody: hitting the change in bar 5, the blues and pentatonic scales, and a scale for each chord. Scales are shown as tablature, keyboard fingerings or a violin fingerboard, whichever you play.



Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

For any instrument that plays one note at a time. Roots, chord tones, guide-tone lines, a riff, and the melody of Blues in the Closet, written in your own key.



Lesson: Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues

What the chords of a blues are and how players vary them, from three chords to a jazz blues, with a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.



Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

Roots, then root and fifth, then the chord tones as a written line, then walking. Fretboard diagrams, bass-clef notation and the band's own bass line written out.



Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

Two- and three-note chords built from the 3rd and 7th, on strings 5 and 4 and on strings 4 and 3, with the same shapes a tritone higher. No barre chords.



Blues for Piano: From Roots to Rootless Voicings

Left-hand roots, guide tones in the right hand, three-note shells and rootless left-hand voicings, each on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.



Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

The two great left hands of early jazz piano, played on the band one at a time, side by side on a blues, and swapped: stride leaps between bass and chord, boogie-woogie walks in eighths.



Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

How to read a drum part, then the beat, the ride pattern, swing time, fills that mark the form, the shuffle, the slow 12/8 and straight eighths.



Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

Why swing eighths are written as plain eighths, how far the long-short can stretch with tempo and style, and the range of good readings, with Blues in the Closet swung and Watermelon Man straight for contrast. Every example plays, with a swing slider.



Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

For a drummer who can already play a basic beat. The three sounds of the hi-hat, then quarter notes, eighths, accents, off-beats, an open note, open off-beats, sixteenths with one hand and with two, the foot alone and the swing hi-hat.



How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao

The drums, how to sit, the five strokes (bass, open, muted, slap, heel-toe) and how they are written, then the tumbao built in six steps with the band: open tones, right hand, left hand, both hands, a cha-cha band and two drums.



Watermelon Man for Congas

The tumbao over a 16-bar blues: the form, the break on bar 14, the melody, and the same part in Mongo Santamaría's cha-cha and in a boogaloo.



Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

Matched grip (German, American, French) and traditional grip, fulcrum, rebound and the Moeller whip; then the other places kit players part ways: kit layout, left-handed and open-handed playing, throne height, pedal heel up or down, stick choice, and counting.



Playing Brushes

What brushes are, how to hold them, sweeps against taps, the circle and the half-moon patterns for ballads and swing, the ride on a brush, and when to use them.



How to Play Cajón

The Peruvian box drum: how to sit, the bass and slap tones, ghost notes, a basic rock and pop beat, a 6/8 feel, the Afro-Peruvian landó, and using brushes and extras.



First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

G, D, Em, C for a whole class at once. Drums, bass, guitar, keyboard and voice each have four levels, from a first day on the instrument to a rock beat, root eighths and a folk-rock strum. The band plays the level you pick.



Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

The four chords under most pop songs, made richer one move at a time: extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants and ii-V-Is. With a chorus you can build yourself and an ear test.



Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

The C, Am, F, G changes as fretboard diagrams: open shapes, extensions, passing chords and secondary dominants.



Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

The C, Am, F, G changes with a left-hand root and a right-hand chord, on a keyboard diagram and a grand staff.



Pop Changes for Bass: Roots and the Walking Line

The root of each chord, then the stepwise walking line through the passing chords, in bass clef and on a fretboard.



Guitar Chord Shapes: From Pop and Rock Toward Jazz

Thirteen steps from open triads and power chords through barre chords, 7ths, shells and top-string triads to drop 2, drop 3 and altered dominants, each with diagrams, a staff and sound.



Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

The same chords ordered by what the fretting hand finds hard, from one-finger shapes to barres, muted strings and stretches, with what goes wrong at each step.



Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar

From one finger on one string to trills, licks and the Sus embellishment on open D, A and C, each written in notation and tablature that plays.



Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

Why a beginner tunes by ear from day one: matching a reference pitch, hearing beats (the wobble two nearly-equal notes make), tuning up to the note, and tuning against a drone. Strengths and weaknesses of each.



Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves

Tuning the guitar to itself: the fifth-fret method, the harmonics method (and why its pure fourths are 2 cents off, and the G-to-B harmonic is 14 cents off), octave checks, and the final chord check. What each gets right and wrong.



Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits

Needle, clip-on and strobe tuners: how they hear a note, why the reading jumps at the attack, why a guitar in tune on a tuner can still sound out (intonation, finger pressure, old strings), and how to use a tuner without letting it replace your ear.



String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

Half-step, whole-step and 1½-step bends, curls, pre-bends, unison and double-stop bends, how they're written in tab, and the blue notes they reach in the A minor pentatonic box, with a drone to bend against.



Harmonics on Guitar: Natural, Tapped and Pinch

Natural harmonics at the 12th, 7th, 5th, 4th/9th and 3rd frets and why they are there, how to touch and lift, tapped and harp harmonics, pinch harmonics with gain, bends and vibrato, how harmonics are written, faults and fixes, and a practice plan.



Travis Picking on Guitar

The thumb alone, pinches, fingers between the thumb notes, then C, G, Am and D, chord changes, hammer-ons and pull-offs, and the band. Ends with a note on chicken pickin'.



Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

Thirteen steps from triads and inversions through slash chords, 7ths, guide tones and shells to rootless, drop 2, spread, quartal and upper-structure voicings.



Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

The same voicings ordered by what the hands find hard: span, black keys, two hands together, leaps, stretches and independence.



Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

Major and minor triads with the root, 3rd or 5th in the bass, their figured-bass names (<span class="fb one"><span>6</span></span> and <span class="fb"><span>6</span><span>4</span></span>) and slash-chord names (C/E, C/G), on piano and guitar.



Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

Breath, onsets, speech-level singing and the mix, words, safe belting, pentatonic runs, cry and flips, phrasing with a mic, and singing a third above. Exercises move into your range.



Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

Conversational tone, swing eighths and ghost notes, scat syllables, the blues scale, arpeggios and guide tones through a ii-V-I, back-phrasing a ballad, and trading fours.



Classical Singing: Breath, Pure Vowels and Legato

Appoggio breathing, onset and legato, the five Italian vowels, resonance, registers and the passaggio, the nine-note scale, messa di voce, vibrato, diction and solfège.



Lesson: Four-Chord Loops

The loops under a great many songs (I V vi IV, vi IV I V, the fifties loop, the turnaround, a borrowed chord, two minor loops) one at a time, each on a chart and a staff, with a loop builder and an ear test.



Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

Authentic, half, deceptive, plagal and backdoor endings, each as a four-bar phrase on a staff, with the argument for why the plagal "Amen" is not a cadence, a phrase builder and two ear tests.



Lesson: Write an Ending

The tune library's Unfinished Songs stop two bars short over V and I. Write the melody that ends them, in the Notation page, and hear it with the chords.



Lesson: Guide Tones

The 3rd and 7th of each chord written as a single line over four-chord loops, a two-five-one and the turnaround. The band plays the line.



Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

From natural-minor i, iv, v to the harmonic-minor V7, the Picardy third, a walking bass and the ii°-V-i, in A minor.



Lesson: Borrowed Chords

The minor iv, the ♭VII and the ♭VI borrowed into a major key, one at a time, with a chord-by-chord builder and an ear test.



Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes

I-vi-ii-V made richer: sevenths, a dominant on the vi, starting on the iii, tritone substitutions and the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.



Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody

One tune, Ode to Joy, with four sets of chords under it, played with the melody. Mix the settings two bars at a time.



Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

The four jobs in a rhythm section, built up one player at a time. Switch players in and out while the band plays and see each part written out.



Arranging 2: Bass and Drums

Why the bass follows the kick, how the groove sets the feel, walking in swing and the tumbao in Latin music.



Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards

Comping: strum patterns, voicing and register, the off-beat chop, jazz comping, and two chord players without a fight.



Arranging 4: The Organ

A playable tonewheel organ: pull the nine tonebars, switch the chorus, work the swell pedal and spin the Leslie, then hear it in the band.



Accompaniment Patterns

A lesson for every bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove and conga part the band plays, each built up from simpler ones, played on the band and written out.



Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

One melody as staff notation, jianpu, Hindustani and Carnatic sargam, a DAW piano roll and arrangement, a waveform and a spectrogram: what each shows, what it hides, and when to use it. With MYP and DP notes.



Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

Why a pure major third does not beat and the piano's does, the syntonic and Pythagorean commas, and what twelve equal steps cost. Hear both on sine waves, the drone and a chord keyboard, then meet meantone, well temperaments and tunings that are not twelve-note.



How a Strobe Tuner Works

The spinning disc and flashing lamp of the Strobotuner, why a pattern stands still (the wagon-wheel effect), one band for each partial, the multiply-and-average arithmetic of the software version, drift as beat rate and cents, stiff strings and weak fundamentals, and just against equal temperament. Watch it follow the page's own sound, no microphone.



Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

Why some partials are not whole-number multiples: string stiffness (with a calculator), old strings, mode locking, brass and clarinet, formants, marimba and xylophone bars, chimes, church bells, timpani and gamelan. What a player can change (levels, not pitch) and what only the maker can, with every instrument as a practice preset on the strobe tuner.



Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

The harmonics of a note written out over any root, with how far each is from the piano. Build square, triangle, sawtooth and pulse waves from sine waves.



Sound 2: Oscillators and Pulse-Width Modulation

The classic synth waves on an oscilloscope and spectrum, pulse width, and PWM.



Sound 3: Noise

White, pink and brown noise, and wind, surf, hi-hats, snares and rain made from it.



Sound 4: Filters

Low-pass, high-pass, resonance, band-pass, notch and EQ, on noise, music or your own voice.



Sound 5: Envelopes

Attack, decay, sustain and release: why a piano, an organ and a violin playing the same note sound different.



Sound 6: LFOs

Vibrato, tremolo, wah and auto-pan from one slow oscillator, and what happens when it speeds up.



Sound 7: Subtractive Synthesis

A two-oscillator synth with filter, envelopes and LFO, played from the keys or MIDI, with presets for bass, brass, pads and plucks.



Sound 8: FM Synthesis

Carrier, modulator, ratio and index: sidebands on the spectrum, and bells, electric piano and bass from two sine waves.



Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis

Morph through a table of wave shapes by hand or with an LFO.



Sound 10: Granular Synthesis

A sound cut into hundreds of grains: freeze it, stretch it without changing its pitch, or scatter it into a cloud. Record your own voice.



Sound 11: The Equaliser

High-pass, shelves and bells, what lives in each frequency range, cut before you boost, and finding a hidden ringing frequency by ear.



Sound 12: Distortion

Overdrive, distortion and fuzz told apart; soft clip, hard clip, tube-like, wavefolder and bit crusher, and the harmonics each one adds.



Sound 13: The Compressor

Threshold, ratio, knee, attack and release, with a live gain-reduction meter.



Sound 14: Sidechain

Music ducking under a kick drum, from invisible glue to EDM pumping, and radio-style ducking under a voice.



Sound 15: Gates and Transients

A noise gate, the 80s gated-reverb snare, and a transient shaper for punch or room.



Sound 16: Reverb

A convolution reverb with a room you build: decay, pre-delay, damping and early reflections; spring reverb, shimmer and freeze.



Sound 17: Delay

Slapback, tempo echoes, ping-pong, tape and dub feedback, and a glitch stutter that loops slices of the beat.



Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger

Moving short delays, the Doppler effect, and the comb filter.



Sound 19: Phaser

All-pass filters, phase and sweeping notches.



Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

Tremolo, auto-pan, and a spinning Leslie speaker with its horn and drum speeding up at different rates.



Sound 21: Pitch Effects

How a pitch shifter works, the octaver, a harmonizer that stays in key, and auto-tune from natural to robotic.



Sound 22: The Vocoder

Talk into the microphone and play chords: the voice shapes the synth band by band.



Sound 23: Stereo

Pan, the Haas effect and mid/side width on a vectorscope, and why you check a mix in mono.



Sound 24: The Signal Chain

The order of effects and why it matters, and gain staging: never clip a stage.



Sound 25: Chiptune

Four channels on a game console chip, and arpeggios so fast they turn into chords.



Recording 1: Gain Staging

Preamp gain, dBFS and headroom, pads and DI: record at −18 average, never in the red.



Recording 2: Microphones and Phantom Power

Dynamic, condenser and ribbon; +48 V and how not to pop it; polar patterns; which mic for what.



Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase

The inverse-square law, proximity effect, where to point it, keeping bleed out, the 3:1 rule and polarity.



Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones

When to use headphones and when speakers, closed vs open, latency and direct monitoring, the cue mix.



Recording 5: Mixing

Balance, pan, EQ, compression and space, in that order, with sends and automation.



Recording 6: Mastering

Tonal balance, glue, limiting to −1 dBTP, LUFS and streaming loudness, dither and delivery files.



Recording 7: Mono and Stereo

Stereo pairs, one earbud and summing to mono, live sound, speaker placement, laptops and two subwoofers.



DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

Bars, beats and the playhead; tempo, metronome and loop, and where they are in BandLab, Ableton and Logic.



DAW 2: Programming a Beat

The step sequencer: kick, snare and hi-hat on sixteen steps, accents and ghost notes.



DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

Notes as data: draw, move, velocity, transpose; record from the keyboard and quantize.



DAW 4: Arranging a Song

Clips on tracks; the band as session players; duplicate, split, drop parts out.



DAW 5: The Mixer

Faders in dB, pan, mute and solo, meters and clipping: fix a bad mix.



DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

Record from the microphone with speakers, then headphones, and measure the bleed; monitoring, feedback and latency.



DAW 7: Bounce, Export and Taking It Further

WAV and MIDI out, into BandLab, Ableton or Logic; what a full DAW adds.



DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

Step by step in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, linked to each manual: setup, import, record, automate, bounce.



Sampling 1: What a Sample Is

A piece of a recording used in a new one: one-shots, loops, breaks, and how producers and DJs each use them.



Sampling 2: Chopping and Slicing

Cut a loop into slices: equal slices, one a beat, or at the hits; move the chop points by hand.



Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch

Repitch (speed and pitch together, like a record) or time-stretch (apart); semitones, percentages, and the sound of each.



Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops

Play chops from pads, record a pattern over a click, quantize, overdub: the MPC and SP-404 way of making a beat.



Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample

Turn a sample into a new song: rearrange, re-pitch, reverse, filter, and the DJ's edits, mashups and live remixes.



Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

Two copyrights in every record, what clearing a sample means, the court cases, and where DJs stand.



DJ 1: The Gear

Turntables, CDJs, controllers and the mixer: what each part does, and the two decks and mixer you'll practise on.



DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear

Match the tempo with the pitch fader, line up the beats with nudges, and learn to hear which one is fast.



DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars

Dance music comes in 8-, 16- and 32-bar phrases; start the next track on a phrase so changes land together.



DJ 4: EQ Mixing and Transitions

Swap the basslines, filter in and out, the long blend and the quick cut: transitions on the mixer.



DJ 5: Scratching Basics

The baby scratch, forward, chirp and transformer: one hand on the record, one on the fader.



DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing

Mix tracks in compatible keys with the Camelot wheel, and why the pitch fader moves the key.



DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

Energy curves, sets that tell a story, preparing crates, and watching the dance floor to know what to play next.



Gear 1: Power and Safety

Amps last on, first off; sockets and extension leads; earth, hum and ground loops; adaptors.



Gear 2: Cables and Connectors

Jack, XLR, TRS and the rest; balanced and unbalanced; mic, instrument, line and speaker level; over-under.



Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

Instrument amps, powered and passive speakers, a mixer channel top to bottom, sound check and feedback.



Gear 4: Keyboards

Kinds of keyboard, outputs and the sustain pedal, Local Off and transpose, stand height and cleaning.



Gear 5: Setting Up, Packing Down and Your Ears

Stage plot, setup and pack-down order, rehearsal etiquette, lifting, and protecting your hearing.



Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care

Strings, tuning, climate, and when it needs a setup.



Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners

The bow and rosin, wiping down, fine tuners and pegs, the bridge, strings and humidity.



Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners

Assembling, reeds, swabbing after every practice, and signs of a leak.



Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

Fitting the kit to the player, tuning heads, cymbal felts and care.



Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

Stamp the sections, tap the bars, loop a verse: Timestamp Notes, and what to do when YouTube won't play.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
When a choir or a string section plays a note, no two players are exactly in tune or exactly in time. The tiny differences make the sound wide and shimmering instead of one thin line. A chorus effect fakes that with a single sound: it adds copies of the sound, each delayed by a few milliseconds, and an LFO keeps changing those delays.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. Use headphones if you can: the copies are spread left and right. The strip under the controls draws each copy’s delay time over the last four seconds.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text: The effect

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
section: Why a moving delay changes the pitch
text:
Why a moving delay changes the pitch
A delay on its own only makes a sound later. But when the delay is getting longer, the sound coming out is slowed down a little, so it’s a little flat. When the delay is getting shorter, the sound is sped up, so it’s a little sharp. It’s the Doppler effect of a passing siren. So an LFO on the delay time is a gentle vibrato on the copy. Mixed with the original, the slightly detuned copy beats against it, and that beating is the shimmer.
Press Vibrato: the mix is 100% wet, so you hear only the moving copy. Its pitch wobbles. Now press Chorus and the same wobble mixed with the dry sound becomes a shimmer.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The controls

Delay: the average delay. About 15 to 30 ms for chorus. Below 10 ms the copy no longer sounds like a separate player; above 35 ms it starts to sound like a slap-back echo (try Doubler: a single slowly moving copy at 35 ms sounds like the part was recorded twice).
Depth: how far the delay swings, and so how far the pitch wobbles.
Rate: how fast. Slow (0.3 to 1 Hz) is lush; fast is seasick.
Voices: more copies, each with its own swing, spread across the stereo field.
Feedback: feeds the delayed copy back into the delay.

title: Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger
text:
The flanger
Press Flanger. The delay is now very short (1 to 5 ms), and the feedback is high. At delays this short the copy doesn’t sound like a second player. Instead it cancels some frequencies and reinforces others in an evenly spaced pattern, a comb filter. As the delay changes, the teeth of the comb sweep up and down: the jet-plane “whoosh”. It was first done with two tape machines running together, an engineer pressing a thumb on the flange of one reel to slow it. Try it on the drum loop and on the noise source, where the moving comb is easiest to see on the spectrum.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text: Two beatmatched tracks in clashing keys sound sour in a long blend, especially with chords or vocals. Harmonic mixing chooses the next track by key, so blends sound like one piece of music.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
The Camelot wheel
The Camelot system (by Mark Davis; popularised by Mixed In Key) numbers the keys around a clock, 1 to 12, A for minor and B for major. It is the circle of fifths with easy names: one step round is a fifth up.

















1A A♭m
2A E♭m
3A B♭m
4A Fm
5A Cm
6A Gm
7A Dm
8A Am
9A Em
10A Bm
11A F♯m
12A C♯m




1B B
2B F♯
3B D♭
4B A♭
5B E♭
6B B♭
7B F
8B C
9B G
10B D
11B A
12B E



From a track in 8A (A minor), the safest moves are:

8A (the same key),
7A or 9A (one step: D minor or E minor, keys a fifth apart, sharing six of seven notes),
8B (the relative major, C major: the same notes).

Moving +2 (an “energy boost”, 8A → 10A) or across diagonally works sometimes, and is a choice, not a rule.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
section: The pitch fader moves the key
text:
The pitch fader moves the key
Without key lock, speeding a track up raises its key: about 6 % is one semitone. +3 % is a quarter-tone sharp, enough to clash with a track in the “same” key. The decks show it: the key readout adds the shift in semitones. Key lock (Master Tempo) keeps the key while the tempo changes, by time-stretching. Some DJs use the shift on purpose: a track pitched up 6 % moves one semitone, so 8A becomes 3A.

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
Practise



The loops are in different keys: Warehouse Am (8A), Neon Floor Em (9A), Late Bus Cm (5A), Concrete Fm (4A), Mirrorball G (9B).

A: Warehouse (8A). B: Neon Floor (9A), matched to 124. Blend with both full. One step on the wheel: it works.
Load Late Bus (5A) on B instead (match it to 124: +3.3 %). Three steps away: hear the chords rub.
Load Hey Now (acapella) (8A) on B over Warehouse (8A): same key. Then over Neon Floor on A (9A). Then over Mirrorball (9B, the relative major of 9A): which works best?
Watch the key readout as you push a pitch fader to +8 %: how far has the key moved?

title: DJ 6: Harmonic Mixing
text:
Notes

Software detects keys; it is right most of the time, not always. Trust your ears in the headphones.
Drum-only intros and outros have no key: mix in there and keys don’t matter.
The Camelot code is a nickname for the key: the Circle of Fifths tool shows the circle behind it.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
A vocoder makes an instrument talk. It takes two sounds: a modulator (usually a voice) and a carrier (usually a synth playing chords). It measures how loud each band of frequencies is in the voice, moment by moment, and sets the loudness of the same bands in the synth to match. The synth keeps its pitch and chords; the voice supplies the words. It’s the robot voice of Kraftwerk, Herbie Hancock, Daft Punk and Laurie Anderson. It was invented at Bell Labs in the 1930s to squeeze speech down telephone lines.
How to use the page. Put on headphones: the microphone hears the speakers otherwise. Choose Microphone as the modulator (or the built-in Robot voice if there’s no mic), press ▶, then talk or sing while you play chords on the computer keys, the on-screen keyboard or a MIDI keyboard. Until you play, a chord is held for you.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text: The vocoder

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
How it works
The vocoder is built from parts you have already met:

Split the voice into bands. A row of band-pass filters, each a different frequency from low to high, splits the voice into 16 or so bands.
Measure each band. An envelope follower on each band turns the wobbling band into a smooth level: how loud that band is right now. The bars under the controls show those levels.
Split the synth the same way. A second row of band-pass filters, at the same frequencies, splits the carrier.
Let the voice turn the synth up and down. Each band of the synth is turned up and down by the level of the matching band of the voice, and the bands are added back together.

A vowel is a pattern of loud bands (the formants, from the filter lesson), so the synth takes on the vowel. The pitch comes from the synth, which is why you can speak in a monotone and have it sing in chords.

title: Sound 22: The Vocoder
text:
Things to try

Bands. With 4 bands the words are barely understandable; with 16 they’re clear; with 32 it sounds almost like a voice through a synth-shaped filter. Old hardware vocoders had 8 to 20.
Band sharpness. Higher Q makes each band narrower: more ringing and more “robot”.
Envelope speed. Slow (5 Hz) blurs the words into a smooth pad; fast (60 Hz) keeps every consonant but gets gritty.
Let “s” sounds through. A synth has little energy in the very top, so “s”, “t” and “f” disappear. Real vocoders pass the voice’s top end straight through to keep the words clear.
Carrier. A sawtooth is best, because it has energy in every band for the voice to shape. A square works less well (it is missing every other harmonic). Noise as the carrier gives a whisper with no pitch at all.
Listen to the modulator or the carrier alone to hear what goes in.
Drum loop as the modulator makes the chord pulse in the rhythm of the drums, a trick used in dance music.

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords
text:
This lesson is for a pianist who can play triads. It puts the chords of the lesson on C, Am, F, G on the keyboard: a left-hand root and a close-position chord in the right hand. Each step has a keyboard diagram, the chart and a grand staff, and the band plays along.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Pop Changes for Piano: From Triads to Passing Chords

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text: Every piece of electric music gear starts at the wall socket. Most problems (hum, crackles, gear that won’t turn on, blown speakers) and the only really dangerous ones come from how it’s powered.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
section: The order: on last, off first
text:
The order: on last, off first
Speakers and amplifiers make a loud thump when anything before them is switched on or off, and big thumps damage speakers and ears.

Switching on: sources first (keyboards, pedals, mixer, computer, interface), amplifiers and powered speakers last, volume down.
Switching off: the reverse. Amps and speakers off first, then everything else.
Turn the volume down before plugging or unplugging any cable into a live amp.

Easy way to remember: amps are last on, first off.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
section: Sockets, power strips and extension leads
text:
Sockets, power strips and extension leads

One wall socket can supply a limited current. In India mains is 230 V, 50 Hz: the small 3-pin socket is 6 A (~1400 W) and the big one 16 A (in the US 15 A at 120 V; UK/EU 13–16 A at 230 V). Add up the watts printed on each piece of gear; a band’s backline plus a PA can get close.
Daisy-chaining power strips into power strips overloads the first one and its cable. One strip per socket.
Unroll extension reels fully: a coiled reel under load heats up and can melt.
Use strips with a surge protector for computers and digital gear; a cheap strip with no breaker is a fire risk.
Voltage swings, power cuts and the inverter/generator switching over send spikes. Where the supply is unsteady, run keyboards, mixers and computers through a stabiliser or UPS, and switch amps off (or down) before power returns after a cut. Many sockets in India have their own switch: turn it off before plugging in.
Plug adaptors (a 2-pin or UK plug in an Indian socket) often fit loosely and lose the earth: use a proper Indian-plug cable or a strip with an earth.
Keep drinks off amps and mixers, cables out of puddles, and water bottles on the floor, not on the keyboard.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Earth (ground) and hum
The third pin is the earth (ground). It’s there so that if something fails inside, the metal case can’t become live.

Never break, tape over or remove the earth pin, or use a “ground lift” plug on the power cable, to stop hum. That’s how musicians have been electrocuted.
Hum (a steady 50 or 60 Hz buzz and its harmonics) usually comes from a ground loop: two pieces of gear earthed at different sockets and also joined by an audio cable. Fixes, safest first:

Power everything that’s connected together from the same socket or strip.
Use balanced cables and DI boxes; press the DI’s ground lift switch (that lifts the audio shield, which is safe; the power earth stays connected).
Keep audio cables away from power cables, or cross them at right angles.
Laptops on chargers hum through their audio out: try running on battery.

Buzz that changes when you touch the strings on a guitar is shielding or grounding in the guitar or its cable, not the wall.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Power supplies

Wall warts (adaptors) must match the gear: voltage, polarity (centre positive or negative, shown by a little diagram), and at least the current (mA) it needs. Wrong voltage or polarity can kill a pedal or keyboard instantly. Label every adaptor with what it belongs to.
Pedalboards: an isolated-output power supply is quieter than a daisy-chain cable.
Travelling: 120 V gear (bought in the US) on India’s 230 V burns out unless it says “100–240 V”. Check the label before using a plug adaptor.
Batteries: take them out of pedals and wireless packs when stored; leaking batteries ruin the contacts. Unplug the input jack of a battery pedal to switch it off.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Phantom power and wireless

+48 V phantom power for condenser mics: switch it on with the channel muted and turn it off before unplugging (Recording 2).
Wireless mics and in-ears: fresh or fully charged batteries before every show, not “it still had a bar”.

title: Gear 1: Power and Safety
text:
Stay safe

A tingle from a microphone or guitar strings is a fault: stop, unplug, and tell someone in charge.
Outdoors, and in the monsoon, power must go through an RCD / RCCB / GFCI (a breaker that trips on a leak to earth).
Don’t open amps, especially valve (tube) amps: they hold lethal voltages after being unplugged.
Tape cables down or use cable ramps across walkways; trips are the most common injury at gigs.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
Shout at a cliff and your voice comes back a moment later: an echo. A delay effect records the sound and plays it back a set time later, mixed in with the original. Feed some of that copy back into the delay and it repeats again, and again, each time quieter. It’s the simplest effect there is, and the building block of chorus and flanger and of most of reverb.
How to use the page. The source starts as single hits, so each echo is easy to hear. The strip under the controls shows one hit and every echo that follows it, as tall as it is loud.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
The echo




Delay time: how long until the copy comes back. Under about 30 ms you don’t hear an echo at all, just a thicker sound (that’s where chorus and flanger live). From about 60 to 150 ms you hear a slapback. Longer, and you hear separate repeats.
Feedback: how much of each echo is sent round again. 0% is a single echo; 50% means each repeat is half as loud as the last. Push it past 100% and every repeat is louder: the echoes pile up into a roar (this delay squashes them so they can’t blow up; real tape echoes do the same).
Tone of the repeats: a low-pass inside the loop, so every trip round loses more top end. The echoes get darker as they fade, which is what tape and old analog delays did and why they sit so well behind the music.
Wow and flutter: tape never runs at quite a steady speed. A slow wobble (wow) and a fast one (flutter) bend the pitch of the repeats.
Ping-pong: two delays feeding each other, one on the left and one on the right, so the echoes bounce between your ears. Headphones on.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
The presets







Preset
Where you’ve heard it




Slapback
1950s rock ‘n’ roll: Elvis’s voice and Scotty Moore’s guitar at Sun Records, one quick echo from a second tape machine


Echo
a voice in a big space, a few repeats


Dotted eighth
the Edge (U2): the echo lands between the notes, so a plain run of eighth notes becomes a sixteenth-note pattern. Try it on the Synth riff


Ping-pong
a stereo bounce, timed to the beat


Tape echo
a Roland Space Echo or an Echoplex: dark, wobbly repeats


Dub
King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry: long, dark repeats that hang on after the band drops out


Runaway
feedback over 100%. While it plays, drag the Delay time: the repeats slide in pitch, the way a tape echo does when you turn its speed knob



Timing to the beat. At a tempo of B beats per minute, one beat lasts 60000 ÷ B milliseconds. The riff here is at 112 bpm, so a quarter note is 536 ms, an eighth note 268 ms, and a dotted eighth (three sixteenths) 402 ms. Most delays have a tap button or tempo sync to do this for you.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
Glitch: stutter and beat repeat
Electronic producers break the music on purpose. One of the commonest tricks is the stutter (or beat repeat): grab a tiny slice of the music and loop it, rat-a-tat-tat, for a beat or two.
It’s a delay used in a strange way. The delay time is set to the length of one slice. When a glitch fires, the input is cut and the feedback goes to exactly 100%, so the last slice goes round and round, never fading. When the glitch ends, the music comes back.




Slice: how long the looped bit is. Short slices (1/32, 1/64) loop so fast they buzz with a pitch of their own.
Chance: how likely a glitch is on each half beat. Press Glitch now to fire one yourself.
Pitch drift: the delay time shrinks (or grows) while the slice loops, so the repeats get faster and rise (a riser) or slow down and fall (a tape stop).
Crush the repeats and backwards slices add the other two classic glitch sounds: a bit crusher and a slice played in reverse.

Glitch effects are everywhere in electronic dance music, in Aphex Twin and Squarepusher, in trap hi-hat rolls, and in vocal chops in pop. Plug-ins like Ableton’s Beat Repeat and iZotope’s Stutter Edit are built on this idea. Used for a beat at the end of a phrase, it’s a fill; used everywhere, it’s annoying. Try your Microphone and say a sentence while it plays.

title: Sound 17: Delay
text:
Next

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text: A DAW (digital audio workstation) is a tape recorder, a mixing desk and a box of instruments in one program. BandLab, Ableton Live, Logic Pro, GarageBand, FL Studio, Reaper and Pro Tools all look different, but they are built from the same handful of parts. These lessons teach those parts on a DAW small enough to see all at once, played by the Backing Track band’s instruments. Each lesson ends with where the same thing is in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, so you can do it there next.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Time runs left to right
Every DAW draws the song as a timeline: time runs left to right, one row (a track) per instrument. The numbers along the top are the ruler, counted in bars. The red line is the playhead: where playback starts and where you are.
The counter by the buttons reads bar . beat . sixteenth: 3.2.1 is bar 3, beat 2, on the beat. This is how every DAW counts, and it’s why a DAW wants to know your tempo (BPM, beats a minute) before you start: bars only make sense at a tempo.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Try it

Press ▶ Play (or Space). Watch the playhead and the counter. Space again stops.
Click the ruler at bar 5: the playhead jumps there. Enter (or ⏮) goes back to the top.
Change the Tempo to 130 and play again. Everything is faster, nothing else changed: the notes are stored in bars and beats, not in seconds.
Switch on ♩ Click, the metronome: a high click on beat 1, a lower one on 2, 3 and 4.
Loop (also called cycle): the yellow bracket under the ruler. Drag along the ruler from bar 3 to bar 4. With ⟲ Loop on, playback goes round those two bars until you stop it. Practising one hard spot, or writing a part over a four-bar loop, is most of what people use a DAW for.
crumbs: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport

title: DAW 1: The Timeline and the Transport
text:
Why bars, not seconds
A DAW that knows the tempo can put a note on beat 3 rather than at 4.37 seconds. That is what lets you change the tempo later, line notes up to the grid, copy a bar and have it fit, and hear a click in time. Audio you record is stored in seconds but placed on the same bar grid. Set the tempo before you record, and record to the click, or the grid won’t line up with what you played.

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
This is the 12-bar blues for instruments that play one note at a time: violin, saxophones, and anything else with a single line. It starts with one note per chord and ends with a line that spells out a jazz blues. You need to be able to read notes in your instrument’s range. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom transposes the page. Violinists choose Violin, and the scale under Where the flat 7 comes from then also shows the finger for every note. Flutes stay on concert pitch. Alto and tenor players choose their saxophone, and every chart and line of notation is then written in their key, while the band plays in the concert key shown beside it. A B♭ tenor and an E♭ alto reading this page at the same time see different notes and sound the same ones.
How to use the page. Every step is a twelve-bar line. Under each note is the name of its place in the chord at that moment: R for the root, then 3, 5, ♭7. Press ▶ Play beside the notation to hear the line alone, or ▶ Play with the band to hear it over the rhythm section, where the piano plays it. Tick Leave out the melody to play it yourself. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation either way.
Sections 1 to 6 build the skills. Section 7 puts them to work on a tune, Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet. If you would rather start with the tune, go there first and come back.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after. A blues has three chords and three roots. Play each one as a long note and count the bars: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I.



A bass player would play these notes. Playing them yourself is the quickest way to hear where the form turns.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
2. Chord tones, and the 3rd and 7th
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord. Here are the four notes of each chord, played up from the root.



The 3rd and the 7th are the guide tones. They are the two notes that tell a listener which chord this is, and they are the notes a good melody leans on.

Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line. The explanation follows the key and instrument chosen in the strip at the bottom.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
3. Guide-tone lines
Play only a guide tone of each chord, and at each change move to the nearest guide tone of the new chord. The line barely moves: when I7 goes to IV7 the 3rd falls a half step and becomes the ♭7th of the new chord. One note per bar, and the whole harmony of the blues is in it.
Starting on the 3rd:



Starting on the 7th. Two players can take one line each.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
4. Guide tones in rhythm
The same notes become a background figure when they are given a rhythm. This one is the Charleston: a note on beat 1 and another on the “and” of 2. A horn section plays exactly this kind of thing behind a soloist.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
5. A riff
A riff is a short figure repeated through the form and adjusted to fit the chords. This one is the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 5th of the home chord. Over the IV chord only its first note changes: it drops a half step, which makes it the ♭7th of IV. Over the V chord the whole figure moves up to that chord.



Look at the names under the notes in bars 5 and 6. The fingers play almost the same thing, and every note has a new job.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
text:
6. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord, with a minor 3rd. Through ii7, V7 and I7 the guide-tone line steps down: the 7th of each chord falls to the 3rd of the next.



The chord tones of the same chorus:
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

title: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes
section: 7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford wrote this blues in the early 1950s. It is a riff blues: one two-bar idea, played three times over the twelve bars. Learn the first two bars and you know nearly all of it.




How it is built

Four notes. The whole melody uses the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. Look at the names under bars 1 and 2: R, 3, R, 4, 3, R.
Three lines. Bars 1 to 4, 5 to 8 and 9 to 12 are the same riff. Each ends on a long note, which is where the rhythm section answers.
Notes that arrive early. Several notes are tied across the barline. They are played an eighth note before the beat and held into the next bar. Clap the rhythm before you play it. These early notes are what make the riff swing.



The one note that changes
In bars 5 and 6 the riff’s second note is a half step lower than it was in bars 1 and 2. It is the only accidental in the tune. Over the home chord that note was the 3rd. The IV chord has that pitch a half step lower, as its ♭7th, so the melody moves with the chord. In bar 7 the home chord returns and so does the original note. This is the sound of a blues going to IV, and the melody tells you the chord has changed without any help from the band.
Hear that move by itself. This is the guide-tone line from section 3 on the tune’s changes. Play it, then play the tune again and listen for the same half step inside the riff.





The last line
Bars 9 and 10 are a two-five (ii7 then V7) instead of V then IV. The melody does not change at all, but look at the names under it: the same pitches are now the 9th and ♭7th of the ii chord. A riff this simple fits because every one of its notes belongs to the key.
The roots of the tune, to learn where the chords fall:





Practising it

Sing the riff with the band before you play it.
Play bars 1 and 2 alone until the tied notes sit right. Use ▶ Play beside the notation to check yourself.
Play the whole tune with Leave out the melody ticked.
Change the concert key. A riff you can play in three keys is a riff you know.

When the tune is secure, go on to the improvising lesson, which uses this melody as its starting point.
crumbs: Blues for Violin and Saxophone: Playing the Changes

text:
Where to go next

Change the concert key and play every step again. F, B♭, C and G are the keys a blues is most often called in.
Loop a chorus with the melody left out and make up your own line from the chord tones, landing on a guide tone at each change.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson and write its guide-tone line.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text: A loop is not a song. Arranging is laying parts out along the timeline so the song has sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro) and changes as it goes: instruments come in and drop out, the drums get busier for the chorus, everything stops for a beat. In a DAW you arrange by moving clips (Logic and BandLab call them regions) on the tracks.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Session players
Instead of writing every part, let the band write a start. Under the tracks, type chords (bars split by |), pick a Style and press Write the parts: the Backing Track band’s drummer, bassist and chord player each write their part into a clip at the playhead. Logic’s Drummer and Session Players, BandLab’s SongStarter and Ableton’s MIDI generators do the same job. The parts are now ordinary MIDI clips: open them in the editor and change any note.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Build a song

Press Write the parts with C | Am | F | G, Rock, 2 times. That’s 8 bars: call it the verse.
Move the playhead to bar 9 (click the ruler), type F | G | C | Am and write 2 times again: the chorus.
Select a clip and Duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D) to repeat a section. Set Song length longer first if you run out of room.
Drop a part out: delete the Chords clip in the first verse, or drag the drum clip later so the drums enter at bar 5. An arrangement is as much about who isn’t playing.
Split a clip at the playhead (put the playhead inside the clip, press Split) and delete the second half for a stop.
Drag a clip by its right edge to change its length; drag the clip to move it (hold Alt to move by beats, not bars), or onto another track.
Try a different Style for the chorus only: the band rewrites the clips under it, the verse stays.

title: DAW 4: Arranging a Song
text:
Common shapes

Build: start with one or two instruments, add one every 4 or 8 bars.
Contrast: verse sparse and low, chorus full and wide; a bridge in other chords.
Fewer is louder: dropping the drums for two bars makes their return hit harder.
Sections are usually 4, 8 or 16 bars. The DAW’s grid makes it easy to keep them that way.

Arranging for a band in more depth: Arranging 1: Who Plays What. Naming sections: Section labels.

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
This lesson is for a guitarist who knows the open chords. It puts the shapes of the lesson on C, Am, F, G on the neck. Each step has fretboard diagrams for its chords, the chart and the staff, and the band plays the chords on piano, guitar or organ (the Chords menu in the strip).
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
1. The basic chords
C, Am, F, G. The four chords as open shapes. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left and the nut is at the top. A dot labelled R is the root. In a key that has no open shape the diagram shows the barre shape instead.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
2. Extensions
Cadd9, Am7, Fadd9, Gsus2. Each of these is the basic shape with one finger moved or lifted. Check the diagrams for what changed: the new note carries a 9, 7 or 2.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
3. Passing chords
C, G/B | Am, C/G | F, F♯dim | G. The bass note moves by step. A slash chord such as G/B is the G chord with the note after the slash as its lowest note: the diagram shows the G shape, and you play B (string 5, second fret) beneath it.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords
text:
4. Secondary dominants
C, E7 | Am, C7 | F, D7 | G7. Four dominant sevenths. Each has one note from outside the key, and it is the one that leads into the next chord.
crumbs: Pop Changes for Guitar: From Open Chords to Passing Chords

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
The first lesson on this page’s loops stayed in major. Minor is different in one important way: the scale you play on is not the scale the chords come from. Natural minor has no leading tone, so the V chord is changed to get one. This lesson writes everything in A minor.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
1. The basic minor changes
Am, Dm, Em, Am: i, iv, v, i, all from the natural minor scale. The v chord, Em, is minor. It is pleasant and it is also weak: it has G, not G♯, so there is no leading tone to pull to A.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
2. The harmonic-minor V7
Am, Dm, E7, Am. One note changes, G to G♯, and the chord becomes the dominant. The G♯ is the leading tone and it rises to A. This is the chord that makes minor feel like a key and not a mode.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
3. The Picardy third
Am, Dm, E7, A. Finish on a major chord. The C of the A minor chord is raised to C♯. It is an old trick, for a hymn or a baroque piece: the music goes dark and the last chord turns the lights on.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
4. A walking bass
Am Am/G | Dm/F Dm | E7 | Am. The bass steps down A, G, F, then falls a third to D, and E7 and Am follow. The slash chord Am/G is an A minor chord over a G in the bass.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

title: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key
text:
5. ii° to V to i
Am, Dm, Bm7♭5 E7, Am. Put the half-diminished ii chord in front of the dominant. It is the minor version of the two-five: B, D, F, A, then E7. The bass falls a fifth from B to E, and again from E to A, the same circle-of-fifths motion as in the major two-five-one.
crumbs: Lesson: Changes in a Minor Key

text:

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text: This lesson explains how sampling law has worked, mainly in the United States, so you know which questions to ask. It is not legal advice: for a release that matters, ask a music lawyer or a sample-clearance service.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
Two copyrights in every recording
A commercial recording usually carries two separate copyrights:

The musical work (the composition: melody, harmony, words), owned by the songwriters and their publisher.
The sound recording (the “master”: that particular performance, captured), usually owned by the record label.

Sampling a recording uses both. Clearing a sample means getting permission (a licence) from the publisher and the master owner. If you replay (interpolate) the part yourself instead of sampling the record, you use only the composition, so you need only the publisher’s permission. That is why many producers re-record samples.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
What the courts have said

Grand Upright Music v. Warner Bros. Records (1991). Biz Markie’s “Alone Again” used a piece of Gilbert O’Sullivan’s “Alone Again (Naturally)” without permission. The judge found infringement and referred the case for criminal prosecution. After it, labels started clearing samples routinely.
Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music (1994). The US Supreme Court held that 2 Live Crew’s parody of “Oh, Pretty Woman” could be fair use: a new work that comments on the old one weighs strongly in its favour. Fair use is decided case by case; it is not a rule like “under two seconds is fine” (there is no such rule).
Newton v. Diamond (2004). The Beastie Boys licensed the recording of a flute passage from James Newton but not the composition. The court held the three-note composition use was too small to matter (de minimis).
Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (2005). A two-second guitar chord, pitched down and looped, from a Funkadelic recording. The Sixth Circuit court said that for sound recordings there is no “too small to matter”: “Get a license or do not sample.”
VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone (2016). A 0.23-second horn hit in Madonna’s “Vogue”. The Ninth Circuit disagreed with Bridgeport: a use too small for the public to recognise is de minimis. So US courts are split by region.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
How clearing works

Find out who owns the composition (the performing-rights databases, ASCAP / BMI / SOCAN / PRS, list publishers) and who owns the master (the label on the release, or its current owner).
Ask both, saying how much you used, how, and how the song will be released.
Expect an up-front fee, a share of the new song’s publishing, a royalty on sales, or a mix. A famous hook costs far more than an obscure bar, and an owner can simply say no.
Get it in writing before release. Clearing after a song is out is harder and dearer.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
The safe routes

Royalty-free sample packs and loops sold for production: read the licence (most allow use in your music, not resale of the samples).
Public domain: compositions whose copyright has expired. Note that a recording of an old composition can still be protected.
Creative Commons recordings, under the terms of their licence (CC BY: credit the creator).
Your own recordings: sample yourself, your band, the street. Every loop in these lessons was made on this site, so you may use them.
Replay the part (an interpolation) and clear only the composition.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law
text:
Where DJs stand

Playing records in public is a public performance of the songs. Venues (clubs, bars) normally hold blanket licences from the performing-rights organisations that cover the DJ playing commercially released music there.
Mixes posted online are copies and performances of every track in them. Streaming sites that host DJ mixes either hold licences for that (some have agreements with labels and rights organisations) or remove mixes when rights holders object.
Edits, bootlegs and mashups use others’ recordings in a new one: legally, they are unlicensed derivative works unless cleared. Many are played and tolerated in clubs; releasing or selling them is where the trouble starts.
crumbs: Sampling 6: Clearing Samples and the Law

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
Everything in the small DAW is in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, under other names and in other places. This lesson is a checklist for your first session in one of them, then a small project: bring in the song you made here, and add the things the small DAW can’t do.
Each step links to the page in that program’s own manual (BandLab Help Center, the Ableton Live 12 Reference Manual, the Logic Pro 12.3 User Guide). Menus move between versions: if a step doesn’t match what you see, the linked page is the one to trust.
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
Before you start

Headphones, wired. Bluetooth headphones add a delay you can hear: BandLab’s help puts wired at about 5–10 ms and Bluetooth anywhere from 34 to 300 ms (BandLab: what is latency?).
Your files from DAW 7: mini-daw.mid (the notes) and, if you like, mini-daw.wav (the mix, to compare with).
A name for the project, and a folder to keep it in.
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
The checklist

BandLabAbleton LiveLogic Pro


BandLab runs in the browser (and as a phone app). Projects are saved to your BandLab account, so there is no folder to choose. Keyboard shortcuts work only in the web Studio (shortcuts).

Open the Studio and start a new project (Getting started with the Studio).
Tempo and metronome. Open the arrow next to the metronome in the transport bar: tempo, click sound, click volume and a count-in for recording. M turns the click on and off (Using the metronome).
Bring in your MIDI file. The web Studio imports MIDI files as well as audio (WAV, MP3 and others) (supported formats). Then pick an instrument for each track; give the drum track a drum kit.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a MIDI region to edit its notes; select notes and quantize (right-click → Quantize, or Q) (Editing MIDI regions). Slice a region at the playhead with S, duplicate with Alt/Option-drag (Slicing and merging, Duplicating and extending).
Record audio. Add a Voice/Audio track, put your headphones on, and press R to record (R again stops). Hearing yourself (monitoring) is offered on Voice/Audio, Guitar and Bass tracks (Studio FAQ).
Fix the latency if your take lands late: BandLab has an automatic latency test; on iPhone and iPad it corrects itself (Fixing latency).
One effect, one automation move. Add an effect to the voice track (an EQ, a limiter), then switch on automation in the timeline and draw points so the voice comes up in the chorus (BandLab blog: the Mix Editor).
Download the mix. Project → Download → Mixdown As, then choose the format; single tracks can be downloaded as audio or MIDI (Downloading tracks, Exporting MIDI).



Live has two views: Arrangement (the timeline, as in these lessons) and Session (a grid of clips to launch). Tab switches. Work in Arrangement for this project. All shortcuts: Live keyboard shortcuts.

Set up audio. Live → Settings (Mac) or Options → Settings (Windows), Cmd/Ctrl+, → Audio: choose the driver and the input and output device (Audio settings; on Windows an ASIO driver is recommended; setting up an audio interface). The same page shows the buffer size and the overall latency.
Save the Set straight away (File → Save Live Set As). Live makes a Project folder for it; when you finish, File → Collect All and Save copies every sound the Set uses into that folder (saving Sets, collecting files).
Tempo and metronome: the tempo box and the metronome switch in the Control Bar (O); the count-in is in the menu next to the metronome (metronome settings, count-in).
Bring in your MIDI file: drag it from Live’s browser into the Arrangement, or Create → Import MIDI File (MIDI files). Each track arrives as a MIDI clip with no sound: drop an instrument on each, and a Drum Rack kit on the drum track.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Draw mode B; quantize Cmd/Ctrl+U; split Cmd/Ctrl+E; duplicate Cmd/Ctrl+D; loop the selection Cmd/Ctrl+L (splitting clips, the Arrangement loop).
Record audio. Insert an audio track (Create → Insert Audio Track), choose its input, arm it, and press the Arrangement Record button (F9) (choosing an input, arming tracks). An armed track is monitored by default (Auto); with speakers, set its monitor to Off (monitoring).
Fix the latency if your take lands late: Driver Error Compensation in Settings → Audio. It only applies to tracks with the monitor set to Off (Driver Error Compensation FAQ).
One effect, one automation move. Drag an audio effect onto the voice track. Press A to show automation, pick the track’s volume, and draw (or click) points so the voice comes up in the chorus (drawing and editing automation).
Export. File → Export Audio/Video (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R) for the mix; File → Export MIDI Clip for the notes of one clip (exporting audio, exporting MIDI).



Mac only. The user guide is for Logic Pro 12.3 (the version menu on each page goes back to older ones).

Set up audio. Logic Pro → Settings → Audio → Devices: the input and output device, and the I/O Buffer Size. Small for recording (less delay), large for mixing (more plug-ins); clicks and crackles mean it’s too small (Audio Devices settings, managing monitoring latency).
New project. File → New from Template (Cmd+N), New Project; open Details to set the tempo, key, time signature and the input and output device (Create projects). Every Cmd+S keeps a backup; File → Revert to goes back to one (alternatives and backups).
Metronome: K; count-in Shift+K; Control-click the metronome button to choose when it clicks (Use the metronome). Cycle: C (the cycle area).
Bring in your MIDI file: File → Import → MIDI File (it lands at the playhead), or drag it from the Finder into the Tracks area (Standard MIDI files). Choose a patch for each track.
Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a region for the Piano Roll; quantize with the Time Quantize menu and its Strength slider (it can always be undone) (quantize note timing). Edit → Split → Regions at Playhead (split regions), Edit → Repeat (repeat regions). Mixer: X. The band’s role is played by Session Players (Drummer, Bass Player, Keyboard Player) (Session Players); drum steps by the Step Sequencer (overview).
Record audio. Add Tracks (Option+Cmd+N) → Audio → Mic or Line, choose the Audio Input (Create tracks). Select the track, headphones on, R records, Space stops (record from a microphone). The guide itself says to use headphones when the metronome is on, so the click isn’t recorded.
Monitoring: the I button on the track header; it always adds some delay (input monitoring). Record → Low Latency Mode keeps it small (managing monitoring latency).
One effect, one automation move. Add a plug-in in an Audio FX slot (plug-ins). Press A to show automation, choose Volume, and click to add points (show automation, add points).
Bounce. File → Bounce → Project or Section; move the End a little past the last region so reverb tails aren’t cut off (bounce a project). Notes out: File → Export → Selection as MIDI File.
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
text:
The project
Rebuild your small-DAW song, then do three things it couldn’t:

Same song, new sounds. Import mini-daw.mid, choose instruments, match the tempo. Play both mixes: what changed?
Record one real part with a microphone, in headphones, to the click (DAW 6). Record it three times and keep the best. Real DAWs keep every pass (takes) and let you build one from the best bits (comping): Logic, Ableton.
Add one effect and one automation move. Reverb on the voice, the chorus louder than the verse.
Bounce it, listen on earbuds and on a phone speaker, and fix the loudest problem (Recording 5: Mixing).
crumbs: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

title: DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW
section: What you’ll meet that wasn’t here
text:
What you’ll meet that wasn’t here

A loop and sound library: BandLab’s Sounds, Live’s browser, Logic’s Apple Loops. Fast to start with; remember everyone else has them too.
Plug-ins: EQ, compressors, reverb, delay, amp models, synths. The sound-design lessons taught what they do; now it’s only finding them.
Automation: any knob can move by itself through the song.
Generated parts: Logic’s Session Players and BandLab’s SongStarter do what the band does in DAW 4.
Clip launching: Live’s Session View and Logic’s Live Loops, for trying ideas live before arranging them.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
A piano is slightly out of tune on purpose. Every chord on it, apart from the octave, is a little wrong, and the wrongness is spread so evenly that all twelve keys sound alike. The alternative is just intonation (JI), where intervals are tuned to the simple ratios that the harmonic series gives you, and they sound smooth and still. This lesson shows what each costs, with ears first and numbers second.
How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button. The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume (start low). The Drone button in the top navigation bar is the same drone as the one on this page. Click a heading to fold a section away, or use On this page on the right to jump (shift-click folds the others). The lesson on the harmonic series goes further into where the ratios come from.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: The harmonic series gives the ratios
text:
The harmonic series gives the ratios
A note on a real instrument is a stack of frequencies at whole-number multiples of the lowest, the fundamental: 1×, 2×, 3×, 4×, and so on. Those are the harmonics. Each interval between neighbouring harmonics is a simple ratio of whole numbers:



Between harmonics

Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 together are a major triad, 4:5:6. That is the reason a major chord sounds stable: it is already inside every note you hear. Below, the first sixteen harmonics are written out over any root, with how many cents each is from the nearest piano note. A cent is 1/100 of a piano half step, so an octave is 1200 cents. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen to the harmonics that are most out of tune with the piano (7, 11, 13 and 14).



Frequencies multiply, but we hear pitch by ratio: going up a fifth always multiplies the frequency by 3/2, whether you start on a low note or a high one. To compare ratios, take 1200 × log₂(ratio) to get cents. A pure fifth, 3:2, is 1200 × log₂(1.5) = 701.96 cents. A pure major third, 5:4, is 386.31 cents.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Why pure intervals do not beat
text:
Why pure intervals do not beat
When two notes are close in frequency, their waves line up and then fall out of step, over and over. The sound swells and fades at a rate equal to the difference in their frequencies. That is a beat: 440 Hz with 443 Hz beats three times a second.
Beating also happens between the harmonics of two different notes. In a pure major third (4:5), the 5th harmonic of the lower note and the 4th harmonic of the upper note are exactly the same frequency, so they simply reinforce each other. When the interval is slightly off, those two harmonics are a few hertz apart and beat. A pure fifth (2:3) has the same matching harmonics, the 3rd of the lower note and the 2nd of the upper.
The widget shows it. With Only the two harmonics that should match the sound is just two sine waves, and the picture is their sum: it swells and fades as they drift in and out of step. Switch the tuning between Just and Equal temperament and hear the beating start and stop. The wavy line is drawn slowed down; the real rate is in the text under the controls.



Now the same with all the harmonics of two notes, which is what a real chord does. Choose another interval with the Interval menu. Notice that the fifth beats slowly (it is only 2 cents off) and the thirds and sixths beat fast (14 to 16 cents off). That is why equal temperament is so much kinder to fifths than to thirds.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Two commas: why tuning cannot be perfect
text:
Two commas: why tuning cannot be perfect
Pure tuning runs into arithmetic. Two facts about ratios cannot both be true:

Stack twelve pure fifths (3:2) and you arrive at the note seven octaves up, almost. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² = 129.746; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is the Pythagorean comma, 531441:524288, or 23.46 cents, nearly a quarter of a half step.
Stack four pure fifths and reduce by two octaves and you get a major third, but a wide one: 81:64 (407.8 cents), compared with the pure 5:4 (386.3 cents). The difference, 81:80 or 21.51 cents, is the syntonic comma.

So the pure thirds of the harmonic series (5:4) and the pure fifths (3:2) are made of different building blocks, and they do not fit together. A tuning system is a decision about which of those to keep and which to spoil.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Just intonation, and why it cannot modulate
text:
Just intonation, and why it cannot modulate
In a just scale, every note is a whole-number ratio of the tonic (Do). The common major scale version is:



Do
Re
Mi

Do

The I, IV and V chords (Do–Mi–Sol, Fa–La–Do, Sol–Ti–Re) are pure 4:5:6 triads, and they sound beautifully still. The trouble starts with the other chords. The ii chord is Re–Fa–La: from Re (9/8) to La (5/3) the ratio is (5/3) ÷ (9/8) = 40/27, which is 680.4 cents. That is a fifth 21.5 cents flat, a syntonic comma off, and it sounds sour. To get a good ii chord you would need a different Re (10/9), but then the notes of V would be wrong. In the key of C, the note D has two jobs and a different pure frequency for each.
That is the main limit of just intonation on a fixed-pitch instrument (a keyboard, a fretted guitar, a marimba). Tune the keyboard for C major and the same keys give poor chords in D major or E♭ major. You would want more than 12 notes per octave, or a retune for each key. Voices, violins, trombones and other instruments that can adjust each note do this naturally: a choir singing Do–Mi–Sol will tune the triad pure, and a progression like C – Am – Dm – G – C will drift upward in pitch by a syntonic comma over each lap if every chord is tuned pure.
Here is the drone, held on Do with Mi and Sol above it (a major triad). Pure tunes Mi to 5/4 and Sol to 3/2 of Do; Equal uses the piano’s notes. Switch back and forth while it sounds. Listen for the third: in the pure setting the chord sits still, and in equal temperament it has a faint shimmer, the beating from the last section.



Try this: with the drone sounding, sing or play (on any instrument that can bend its pitch) the note Mi above the drone, first sliding toward the piano’s version, then toward the pure one. The pure one locks into the drone. It is the pitch that stops beating.

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Equal temperament: twelve equal steps
Equal temperament (12-TET) solves the key problem by making every half step the same size. An octave is a 2:1 ratio and has twelve steps, so each step multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12) = 1.059463. A semitone is exactly 100 cents, and every interval of the same size is the same in every key. Twelve fifths then come out to exactly seven octaves, and the Pythagorean comma is spread evenly: each fifth is narrowed by 23.46 ÷ 12 = 1.96 cents.
The price is that no interval except the octave is pure. The fifth is only 2 cents flat, which is close enough to ignore. But the thirds and sixths are 14 to 16 cents off, enough to hear:

In words: the tempered major third is about 14 cents sharp of the pure 5:4, the tempered fifth about 2 cents flat of 3:2, and the tempered minor third about 16 cents flat of 6:5. Thirds are the most exposed because the ear uses them to decide whether a chord is major or minor, and because the beating of two harmonics (the 5th and the 4th) falls in a region where the ear is most sensitive. The minor sixth and the major sixth are the thirds turned upside down, so they are wrong by the same amount.
Equal temperament is the standard for the piano, the guitar, MIDI and nearly every synthesizer. Its strength is that it lets you play in any key, modulate anywhere, and use chromatic and jazz harmony that no pure system supports. Many singers, string players and brass players move toward just intonation while they play, without thinking about it.
