title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Other systems, briefly
Equal temperament is one answer to the comma problem, and not the only one used.

Pythagorean tuning. All fifths are pure 3:2, and the thirds come out wide (81:64, 407.8 cents, 21.5 cents sharp of 5:4). It suits melody, with its sharp leading tones and bright, tense thirds, and it was the system of medieval Europe, whose music was built on fifths and fourths. One fifth, the wolf, is out by the Pythagorean comma (678.5 cents).
Quarter-comma meantone. Renaissance and early Baroque keyboards narrowed each fifth by a quarter of a syntonic comma (696.6 cents) so that the major thirds came out pure (386.3 cents). Chords in the home keys are lovely. The cost is an even worse wolf fifth (about 737.6 cents), and keys with many sharps or flats are unusable.
Well temperaments (Werckmeister, Vallotti, Kirnberger and others). Eighteenth-century tunings that spread the comma unevenly so that every key works but each has its own colour: keys near C have nearly pure thirds, and distant keys are tenser. In Werckmeister III four fifths (C–G, G–D, D–A, B–F♯) are narrowed by a quarter of the Pythagorean comma and the rest are pure. In Vallotti six fifths (F–C–G–D–A–E–B) are narrowed by a sixth of the comma and the rest are pure. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier (1722) has a prelude and fugue in all 24 keys, so it needs a tuning where every key is playable. Its exact temperament is still debated; “well tempered” did not mean equal. Many listeners find these keys have individual character, which equal temperament flattens.
Equal temperament gradually took over in the nineteenth century, as chromatic harmony and modulation made key colour impossible to keep.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Beyond twelve notes
Not all music divides the octave into twelve.

Arabic maqam. Many maqamat use the “neutral” second and third, about halfway between a minor and a major one (roughly 150 and 350 cents), notated with a half-flat sign. This is often described as quarter tones (24 notes to the octave), but the actual pitches vary by maqam, region and performer, and are set by ear.
Equal divisions other than 12. 19-TET has an almost pure minor third (315.8 cents against the 6:5 of 315.6) but a weak fifth (694.7). 31-TET has near-pure major thirds (387.1 cents) and a good fifth (696.8), and was proposed in the 16th century to improve on meantone. 53-TET has a fifth within 0.07 cent of 3:2 and a major third within 1.4 cents, which is why it is a favourite for theorists approximating just intonation. All need special keyboards or a computer.
Gamelan. Indonesian ensembles use two scales, five-note slendro (roughly equal steps of about 240 cents) and seven-note pelog (unequal steps, normally five of the seven in a piece). Every ensemble is tuned to itself, and no two are the same, so the instruments belong together. Paired instruments are often tuned slightly apart on purpose to give a shimmering beat, the ombak (“wave”), the same beating you heard above, used as a colour rather than avoided.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
section: Seeing it: a strobe tuner, pure intervals, and why pianos are stretched
text:
Seeing it: a strobe tuner, pure intervals, and why pianos are stretched
A needle tuner gives one number. A strobe tuner gives one row of moving stripes for every partial of the note you play. Row k listens at k times the pitch you are aiming at (the microphone signal is multiplied by a sine and cosine at that frequency and averaged; the phase of the result moves the stripes). If that partial is exactly where it should be, its stripes stand still. If it is sharp they drift to the right, and if flat to the left, at a speed equal to the error in Hz. Rows fade where the partial is weak, and the first tenth of a second of each note is ignored, because the attack is not a steady pitch.
Choose the target below: the equal-tempered note, a just interval over a tonic you pick, a step of 31-ET, or any number of cents above the note (350 is a neutral third). The conventional readout (nearest note and cents) is underneath. The microphone is asked for only when you press Start, and Stop lets it go. No microphone? The made-up string is a stack of oscillators you can detune.



Hear just intervals. With the tonic on A, the note E is aimed at 3:2 over A. Play (or sing) an E against an A drone (the Drone button in the top bar): when the beats stop, your E is the pure fifth, and every row stands still. It is about 2 cents wider than the piano’s E. Change the tonic to C: the target E is now the pure major third, 5:4, which is about 14 cents narrower than the piano’s. That is the number behind the beating in the widgets above, and the reason a choir with no keyboard drifts toward pure intervals.
Why a piano is stretched. The harmonic series of an ideal string is exactly 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. A real string has stiffness, so it resists bending near its ends, and the effect grows quickly with the partial number: partial k sounds at about k f √(1 + B k²), where B is the string’s inharmonicity (a mid-range piano string has B of the order of 0.0001 to 0.001, and the short thick bass strings and the shortest treble strings have more). Every upper partial is therefore sharp of the exact multiple. When two notes an octave apart are tuned, the beats a tuner listens to are between the upper note’s fundamental and the lower note’s second partial, which is already slightly sharp: so the upper note is tuned a little sharp of 2:1, and so on up the keyboard. The bass ends up flat and the treble sharp of the equal-tempered scale. This is called stretch tuning. Try it: set the source to the made-up string, press Start, and raise the stiffness. Row 1 stays still and the higher rows drift to the right, row 6 more than row 2. Notice that the readout above the bands, which reduces the whole sound to one pitch, is pulled sharp by the upper partials, while row 1 shows that the fundamental has not moved.
crumbs: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament

title: Tuning Systems: Just Intonation and Equal Temperament
text:
Things to try

In the major-third widget, set the lower note to 110 Hz, then 440 Hz. At which pitch is the tempered third’s beating faster? (The beat rate is in Hz, so it doubles per octave.)
In the second widget, step through the intervals in Equal temperament mode and rank them from most to least beating. The fifth and fourth should be at one end and the thirds and sixths at the other.
Start the drone on Do with Mi and Sol, set to Pure, and hum along. Switch to Equal and hum again. Can you feel your pitch pulled toward the pure Mi?
Play a D minor chord in the chord keyboard in just intonation and in equal temperament. Which sounds worse, and why? (The fifth D–A is 21.5 cents flat in the pure scale.)
In the stiff-string tuner, set the stiffness to 0 and then to 0.0020. At which row does the drift first pass 10 cents? (Row k is sharp by 600 × log₂(1 + B k²) cents, from the formula above.)
Calculate for yourself: the cents between two frequencies is 1200 × log₂(f₂ ÷ f₁). Check that A at 440 Hz and E at 660 Hz (a pure fifth) is 701.96 cents, and that the piano’s E is 659.26 Hz.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text: The bass and drums are the foundation. If they agree, a band can lose everyone else and still sound like a band. This page is about how they agree. How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
1. The bass follows the kick
The kick drum and the bass are both low and both short at the start of a note. When they land together they sound like one big instrument. When they land apart, the bottom of the band sounds busy and blurred.
Below, the drums play the same pop backbeat throughout. Try each bass line against it. Look at the bass staff and the kick drum (the lowest notes on the drum staff) and see where they line up.



The dotted line is the one the style was written with: the bass plays exactly where the kick plays. The others still work, but they make a different song: roots on every beat is plainer, eighths push harder, root and fifth sounds like country.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
2. The drums choose the feel
Now keep the bass line and change the groove. Each one divides the beat differently or puts the backbeat somewhere else.



Half-time moves the snare from 2 and 4 to 3 only: the chords go by just as fast but the song feels half as fast. Arrangers use it for a breakdown or a big final chorus. Four on the floor puts the kick on every beat, which is why the root-eighths bass now sounds like it’s doubling something.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
section: 3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
text:
3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time
In jazz the roles change. The ride cymbal carries the time, the kick drum mostly keeps out of the way, and the bass plays a note on every beat. That’s a walking line: the root on beat 1, other notes of the chord and scale in between, and a note on beat 4 that leads into the next chord.
Compare it with the lighter two-feel (half notes) that a band often plays on the melody before walking for the solos, and with plain chord tones.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
4. Latin: the bass anticipates
In son montuno and salsa, the bass plays the tumbao: it doesn’t land on beat 1 at all. The new chord’s root arrives early, on the and of 2 and on 4, and rings over the barline. The clave and congas mark the beat instead.



Switch the congas off, then the drums. With only the bass left, you can hear that it is always a beat ahead of the chord chart.

title: Arranging 2: Bass and Drums
text:
5. Try it

In section 1, play the Root eighths line, then switch the drums to Half-time in section 2. Which bass line would you choose for a half-time chorus?

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text: A drum kit that’s set up to fit the player is easier to play and easier on the body. Tuned and looked after, it sounds much better than an expensive kit that isn’t.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Setting up

Throne (stool) first: thighs level or sloping slightly down from the hips.
Snare between your knees, a few cm above them, flat or tilted slightly toward you.
Bass drum where your right foot (left, if left-footed) lands naturally on the pedal; spurs out so it doesn’t creep. A rug under the kit.
Hi-hat to the other side of the snare, its pedal where the other foot falls.
Toms close and angled toward you so the sticks hit the middle without reaching.
Cymbals: ride and crashes within reach, not so high you lift your shoulders.
Tighten every wing nut and memory lock. Felts and a plastic sleeve on every cymbal stand: metal touching the cymbal’s hole cracks it.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Tuning

Tighten the lugs in a star pattern, a quarter turn at a time, finger tight first, then with the key, so the head is even all round.
Tap 2–3 cm in from each lug: they should sound the same pitch.
The snare is tighter and higher; the snare wires under it are adjusted by the strainer knob until they respond crisply without choking the sound.
Toms get lower as they get bigger. Bass drum: a little above wrinkle-free, with a pillow or muffling inside if it booms too long.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Care

Heads wear: replace when dented, dead-sounding or won’t tune. Snare and batter heads go first.
Cymbals: hold by the edges, not the face. Clean (or not) with cymbal cleaner only; never polish a cymbal with household cleaner. Never fully tighten the stand’s wing nut on a cymbal: it needs to move, or it cracks.
Sticks: turn them as you play; replace splintered ones (splinters fly).
Hardware: a drop of oil on the pedals’ moving parts a few times a year; keep the springs adjusted equally.
Moving: cases or bags for every drum and a cymbal bag. Cymbals never in with the hardware.
Keep drums away from heaters and out of hot cars; the wood and the heads both suffer.
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Electronic kits

Same setup heights. Pad cables unplugged by the plug; don’t hit the rims of mesh pads hard without a rim zone.
Volume down before putting on headphones; drums are the most hearing-damaging instrument (Gear 5).
crumbs: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care

title: Gear 9: Drum Kit Setup and Care
text:
Hand drums
Hover any part of a drawing for its name.
Congas come in three sizes of the same barrel-shaped drum. Tuning bolts (lugs) pull the hoop down onto the head; tune with the drum standing, a quarter turn at a time round the drum, as on a kit.



Bongos are a joined pair played with the fingers, held between the knees or on a stand. They are tuned high and tight; loosen them after playing so the heads aren’t under tension all week.



Djembe is carved from one piece of wood with a goatskin head, tuned by its ropes. Tightening is a job for someone who has done it: a skin pulled too far splits.



Tabla is a pair from North India: the wooden dayan (right hand) is tuned to the key of the music by tapping the gatta and the rim with a small hammer; the metal bayan (left hand) gives the bass. The black syahi on each head is what makes them ring with a clear pitch. Keep them covered and never put them down on their heads.



Natural skins (all of these, often) go slack when it’s damp and tight when it’s dry: let a drum get used to the room before tuning, and keep them out of sun and away from heaters.

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
This lesson orders piano voicings by what the hands find hard, starting from a first lesson. Each step adds one task: more notes, a wider span, black keys, two hands at once, leaps, and finally hands that move independently. Each step says what makes the voicing easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Piano chord voicings has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, R for the root. The staff puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press Show finger numbers below to put the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. The span is the distance from a hand’s lowest note to its highest, counted in half steps: an octave is 12. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Finger numbers on piano and on guitar. The two instruments count differently. On piano the thumb is 1 and the fingers go 2, 3, 4 to the little finger, 5, in both hands. Because the hands are mirror images, the right hand plays a chord from the bottom 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1: the left hand’s little finger takes the lowest note. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1 and the little finger is 4 (the thumb, when it frets a bass note over the neck, is written T). So a “3” means the middle finger to a pianist and the ring finger to a guitarist. The fingerings here are the usual ones; a hand of a different size may choose another.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
Hand position
Set this up before the first chord, and check it when a voicing feels clumsy.

Sitting: sit on the front half of the stool, far enough from the keys that your forearms are level, or slope slightly down towards the keys, with your elbows a little in front of your body. A stool too low pushes the wrists up; too high pushes them down.
Fingers: curved, as if holding a ball. The knuckles are arched and the fingertip pad lands on the key. Fingers 2, 3 and 4 are about the same length when curved, so they land together.
Wrist: level with the back of the hand and the forearm, neither drooping below the keys nor lifted above them. The hand can float a little as it moves; it does not rest on the keys.
Thumb: it plays on its side, near the corner of the nail, not flat on its pad. Keep it relaxed and slightly curved, level with the other fingers.
Where on the key: play white keys near the front edge, where they go down most easily. Play a black key in the middle, not on its edge. When a chord mixes the two, the longer fingers (2, 3 and 4) usually take the black keys further back, while the thumb and little finger stay on the white keys at the front.
Easy because: a curved hand has every finger above its key, so the hand needs no tension to hold the position.
Hard because: the fingers tire when starting out, and it is tempting to flatten them to reach.
What goes wrong:

Flat fingers: the pad lies on the key, the hand has less strength, and the fingers play neighbouring keys too.
A dropped wrist, with the knuckles sinking below the hand.
The little finger collapses, and its first joint folds in.
The thumb plays flat on its pad and sticks out, and the hand twists.
Shoulders lifted, with the arms held up from the shoulder instead of hanging.


Practice: put the hand on C, E and G in 1-3-5 with the wrist level. Press each key, and check the wrist and finger tips between presses. Keep the fingers curved when the hand moves to the next chord.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B1 White-key triads, one hand



RH 1-3-5, and LH 5-3-1 an octave lower.

Easy because: each finger has a white key of its own: thumb, middle finger and little finger, with a key left out between each.
Hard because: the three notes have to sound together and evenly. The thumb is strongest, so the bottom note comes out loud and the top note thin.
What goes wrong:

The notes split instead of sounding as one chord.
The top note is lost.


Practice: play a chord, lift the hand, and put it back on the next chord without looking. Keep the wrist level.
Unlocks: P-A1.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands
text:
P-B2 Bass note plus triad: two hands




Easy because: the left hand plays one note, so it has one job.
Hard because: the two hands have to land together, and the right hand jumps a 4th or more between chords.
What goes wrong:

The stronger hand arrives first and the other drags.
One hand lifts early.
Watching one hand loses the other.


Practice: play C–Am–F–G in half notes, counting out loud. Close your eyes after one time through.
Unlocks: P-A1; Piano ballad with Long notes.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps
text:
P-B3 Inversions: small moves instead of jumps



RH 1-3-5 for root position and second inversion; 1-2-5 for first inversion.

Easy because: the hand moves by a step instead of a jump, and there are only two finger patterns.
Hard because: the span grows to 8 or 9 half steps. The open space in a 1-2-5 shape tempts fingers 3 and 4 to fill it.
What goes wrong:

Squeezing with finger 2, which makes the chord uneven.
Choosing the wrong finger for the new note.


Practice: play C in root position, first and second inversion, up the keyboard and back. Then do the same on F and G.
Unlocks: P-A2.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B4 Black keys in triads



All RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: in D, A and E the black key falls under finger 3, the longest finger, which reaches in easily.
Hard because: in B♭ and E♭ the thumb or finger 5 lands on a black key. Those fingers are short and prefer white keys, so the whole hand has to move further in toward the fallboard.
What goes wrong:

The thumb slips off the black key.
Finger 5 flattens.
Reading the key signature becomes a second task.


Practice: play D, A and E first, and B♭ and E♭ after them. Then do the same with the left hand.
Unlocks: every key in the Key menu of the lesson pages, and four-chord loops in all twelve keys.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B5 Two-note guide-tone shapes



RH 1-3 for the 4ths; 1-4 for the tritone.

Easy because: only two notes, so the hand is always relaxed. The span is 5 or 6.
Hard because: the interval changes from chord to chord (4th, tritone, 4th), so the fingers have to adjust each time.
What goes wrong:

Reaching with the arm instead of letting the fingers open.
Losing track of which note is the 3rd.


Practice: hold one pair, then change to the next while keeping the arm still.
Unlocks: P-A7; Charleston comping and blues guide tones. This step comes before four-note 7ths (P-B6) because two notes are easier on the hand. In the harmonic order it comes after them.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B6 Four-note 7ths in one hand



RH 1-2-3-5. The span is 10 or 11.

Easy because: the notes are a 3rd apart, so the fingers fall on every other key.
Hard because: the hand opens to a 7th, and finger 5 has to reach while fingers 2 and 3 stay curved.
What goes wrong:

The thumb lies flat.
Finger 5’s note is weak.
The chord comes out uneven.


Practice: play each chord, then its closest inversion (as in P-A6), and compare how the hand feels. If the hand aches, leave out the top note.
Unlocks: P-A5 and P-A6; the 7th chords in blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B7 Shells in the left hand
text:
P-B7 Shells in the left hand



LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3 (span 16), LH 5-1 and the right thumb on the top note.

Easy because: three notes in one hand, about the same span as P-B6.
Hard because: the left hand is usually the weaker one, and mistakes are easy to hear down low. The 1–7–3 order is a 10th wide, too wide for most hands to play alone.
What goes wrong:

The thumb hangs over the edge of the key.
The middle note doesn’t sound.


Practice: play the three shells slowly and listen for every note.
Unlocks: P-A8; solo piano.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand
text:
P-B8 Rootless voicings: four notes in the left hand



LH 5-3-2-1 throughout. The span is 9 to 11.

Easy because: the A and B forms alternate, so the hand moves by a step or less. The B forms are the narrowest.
Hard because: four fingers sound at once in the weaker hand, and you need the forms in every key. Black keys fall under different fingers in each key.
What goes wrong:

Forgetting which form comes next.
One note missing.


Practice: learn the chain in F first, which sits well under the left hand, and then the chain in C. Then add a bass line in the right hand.
Unlocks: P-A9; Jazz ballad, Bossa nova, Boogaloo.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord
text:
P-B9 Leaps: bass note, then chord



The left hand alone, as in stride or boom-chick: a low bass note, then a chord about an octave and a half higher.

Easy because: the shapes are triads you already know.
Hard because: the hand jumps 1½ octaves on the beat. The eyes want to follow the hand, and the rhythm slips.
What goes wrong:

The chord is late or too loud because the hand crashes onto it.
Looking down and losing the place.


Practice: left hand only, bass–chord–bass–chord, with a metronome at 60. Move in an arc and shape the chord in the air before it lands. Close your eyes once the landing is reliable.
Unlocks: stride and boom-chick left hands; country and folk comping.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves
text:
P-B10 Stacked 4ths: one shape that moves



RH 1-3-5, span 10. For the So What chord, LH 5-2-1 and RH 1-3.

Easy because: every interval is the same, so there is one hand shape.
Hard because: each stack of 4ths lands on a different mix of black and white keys, so the same shape feels different in each place.
What goes wrong:

The hand follows the key colours and loses the shape.


Practice: slide the stack of 4ths up the white keys from D to D, one hand at a time, noticing which positions feel best.
Unlocks: P-A12; modal jazz.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
text:
P-B11 Wide spans: octaves, 9ths and 10ths



LH 5-1 for the octave, the 9th and the 10th. LH 5-2-1, rolled, for C–G–E.

Easy because: most adult hands can play an octave, and a 9th is possible with a firm wrist.
Hard because: a 10th is beyond most hands played as one chord.
What goes wrong:

Forcing the stretch. Roll the chord from the bottom instead, and never play through pain.


Practice: roll C–G–E slowly and listen for the three notes blending into one sound. Then play it with the pedal.
Unlocks: P-A11; Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Piano ballad.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard
section: P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand
text:
P-B12 Independence: a held shell, a moving right hand



LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.

Easy because: the left hand holds still, and the right hand plays a plain triad.
Hard because: the hands play different rhythms, three notes each, and each hand plays a different chord.
What goes wrong:

Both hands playing on the same beat.
The black keys in the right-hand triad (C♯, F♯) being missed.


Practice: hold the shell on beat 1 and play the right-hand triad on the “and” of 2. Then on the “and” of 4. Tap your foot on the beat.
Unlocks: P-A13; Charleston, Reverse Charleston, Boogaloo stabs and Son montuno.
crumbs: Piano Voicings by Hand: From Easy to Hard

title: Conga part: Tumbao
text:
This is a lesson on one conga part the Backing Track band plays: Tumbao. It is built up from 3 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read the band’s last four bars on the staff underneath. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.
All the accompaniment patterns · Conga parts

title: Conga part: Tumbao
text:
The pattern
The basic conga part, on one drum with the hands alternating: left-hand heel on 1, left-hand toe on the and of 1, a right-hand slap on 2, left toe on the and of 2, left heel on 3, left toe on the and of 3, then two right-hand open tones on 4 and the and of 4. Heel and toe are quiet; slap and open tones carry.
It belongs in Son montuno, Cha-cha and Boogaloo. Here it is in the cha-cha style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
section: Step 1: Open tones only (learning the tumbao, 1)
text:
Step 1: Open tones only (learning the tumbao, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the two right-hand open tones of the tumbao, on 4 and the and of 4. The first thing to play.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
section: Step 2: Right hand alone (learning the tumbao, 2)
text:
Step 2: Right hand alone (learning the tumbao, 2)
The right hand of the tumbao by itself: a slap on 2, then open tones on 4 and the and of 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
section: Step 3: Left hand alone (learning the tumbao, 3)
text:
Step 3: Left hand alone (learning the tumbao, 3)
The left hand of the tumbao by itself: heel on 1, toe on the and of 1, toe on the and of 2, heel on 3, toe on the and of 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The bass plays with you; switch the drums and chords on when it is steady.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
text:
Step 4: Tumbao, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Both hands: heel, toe, slap, toe, heel, toe, open, open. Heel and toe quiet; slap and open tones carry.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
section: Step 5: Up to tempo, with the band
text:
Step 5: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s congas off and take the part yourself.

title: Conga part: Tumbao
text:
In other styles
The same conga part in other styles it fits. The other players change; yours does not. Notice how the same part sounds different in a different band.
Son montuno



Boogaloo

section: How it relates to the other patterns
text:

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
text:
This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat. It is built up from a simpler pattern, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.
All the accompaniment patterns · Comping rhythms

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
text:
The pattern
The chords play the 3-2 son clave over two bars. First bar (shown): 1, the and of 2, 4. Second bar: 2 and 3. Faith, Desire, I Want Candy.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
text:
Step 1: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
Start with something simpler. Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
section: Step 2: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat, slowly
text:
Step 2: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Two bars: the tresillo (1, the and of 2, 4) in the first, then 2 and 3 in the second. That is the 3-2 son clave. Clap it before you play it.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
section: Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
text:
Step 3: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 112 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
text:
Step 4: On the guitar
The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
section: Step 5: Two chords in a bar
text:
Step 5: Two chords in a bar
Harder: now some bars have two chords, two beats each. The pattern keeps its rhythm and changes chord where the bar does: watch the staff for the hit that lands on beat 3.

title: Comping rhythm: 3-2 clave / Bo Diddley beat
section: How it relates to the other patterns
text:
How it relates to the other patterns

Leads to: The Barbara Ann rhythm, Groups: 3+3+3+3+2+2: the patterns that use this one as a step.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
text:
The pattern
Chords on the and of 1 and the and of 3, never on a downbeat.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
text:
Step 1: Charleston
Start with something simpler. A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
text:
Step 2: Reverse Charleston
The Charleston displaced: a short chord on the and of 1 and a held one on beat 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
text:
Step 3: Off-beats, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Chords on the and of 1 and the and of 3, never on a downbeat. Keep them short and light; they float on top of the walking bass.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
section: Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band

Step 4: Up to tempo, with the band
The whole band, at 120 beats a minute. Play along, then switch the band’s chord player off and take the part yourself.

title: Comping rhythm: Off-beats
text:
Step 5: On the guitar

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: one open note
text:
The pattern
Eighth notes on the closed hi-hat, with the and of 4 left open. The foot and the stick close it again on beat 1 of the next bar. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock, Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Dance pop and Boogaloo. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: one open note
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Maiden Voyage
text:
This is a lesson on one comping rhythm the Backing Track band plays: Maiden Voyage. It is built up from 2 simpler patterns, one step at a time, and every step is played by the band and written out as it plays. How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read the band’s last four bars on the staff underneath. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.
All the accompaniment patterns · Comping rhythms

title: Comping rhythm: Maiden Voyage
text:
The pattern
A two-bar pattern of held chords: 1, the and of 2 and 4 (held over the barline), then the and of 2 and 4.
It belongs in Boogaloo and Bossa nova. Here it is in the bossa nova style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Maiden Voyage
text:

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:
The pattern
Chords on the and of 2 and the and of 4. The second one anticipates the next bar’s chord and is held across the barline.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:

Start with something simpler. A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:
Step 2: Off-beats
Chords on the and of 1 and the and of 3, never on a downbeat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Red Garland
text:
Step 3: Red Garland, slowly

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Bass line: Footprints: waltz ostinato
text:
The pattern
A two-bar figure in 3/4 (one bar of 6/4): root, fifth, octave in quarter notes, then the third above that octave held for two beats and the fifth to lead back.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Footprints: waltz ostinato
text:
Step 1: Root and fifth
Start with something simpler. The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Footprints: waltz ostinato
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. A two-bar figure in 3/4: root, fifth, octave in the first bar, then the third above the octave held for two beats and the fifth leading back down. Feel it as one long bar of six.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
The pattern
Follows the Feel menu. Swing: the ride pattern, hi-hat foot on 2 and 4, a feathered kick and a little snare. Straight eighths: eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, cross-stick on 2 and 4.
It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad, Boogaloo and Stride piano. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Jazz time
text:
Step 2: Ride pattern (learning swing, 2)
The swing ride pattern and nothing else: the cymbal on every beat with a skip note before 3 and before 1 (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a), and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Jump blues
text:
The pattern
The blues shuffle pushed harder: swung eighths on the cymbal, the kick feathered on all four beats, and a loud backbeat on the snare on 2 and 4. In 3/4 the snare on 2 and 3.
It belongs in Jump blues and Boogie-woogie. Here it is in the jump blues style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Jump blues
text:
Step 1: Blues shuffle
Start with something simpler. Swung eighths all the way through on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. The Chicago blues beat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The blues shuffle, harder: swung eighths on the cymbal, the snare hit hard on 2 and 4, and the kick played softly on all four beats (feathered: felt more than heard). Get the shuffle steady, then add the kick on 2 and 4 under the snare, quietly.

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
The pattern
Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.
It belongs in Dance pop, Straight-eighth rock and Reggaeton. Here it is in the dance pop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
Step 2: Ballad: syncopated
Three held sounds a bar: the chord on beat 1, its top two notes on the and of 2 and on beat 4 (3+3+2).
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
Step 3: 3+3+2 (tresillo), slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Three held chords grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Count eight eighths and play on 1, 4 and 7. Hold each chord until the next.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)

title: Comping rhythm: 3+3+2 (tresillo)
text:
Step 5: On the guitar
The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

title: Drum groove: Funk
text:
The pattern
Snare on 2 and 4 with a syncopated kick: beat 1, the and of 2 and the and of 3. Eighths on the cymbal.
It belongs in Boogaloo and Straight-eighth rock. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Funk
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Funk
text:
Step 2: Rock backbeat
Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Snare on 2 and 4, eighths on the cymbal, and a syncopated kick: 1, the and of 2, the and of 3. Practise the kick against the hat alone first.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:
The pattern
Quarter notes: the chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4, over held left-hand octaves on the root. On the piano with the Standard voicing the chord is a triad in first inversion.
It belongs in Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Folk carol, Hymn (four parts) and 12/8 doo-wop. Here it is in the piano ballad style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:

Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: rocking
text:
Step 2: Hymn: four parts
Every chord played once and held until the next one. On the piano or organ it is four parts: the root in the left hand and three voices above it that move as little as possible from chord to chord. It follows the chart’s chords, so a carol written with a chord on every beat sounds like the hymnal.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Left hand: an octave on the root, held. Right hand in quarter notes: the whole chord on 1, the thumb on 2, the top two notes on 3, the thumb on 4. The right hand rocks between the thumb and the top.

title: Drum groove: 12/8
text:
The pattern
Three eighths to every beat on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, backbeat on 2 and 4. In 4/4 the eighths are triplets.
It belongs in 12/8 doo-wop. Here it is in the 12/8 doo-wop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

text:

Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The first rock beat. In 3/4: hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: 12/8
text:
Step 2: Blues shuffle
Swung eighths all the way through on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. The Chicago blues beat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

The strum most songbooks start with: down on 1, down-up on 2, then up, down-up through 3 and 4 (the hand misses the strings on beat 3).

title: Bass line: Bossa nova
text:
The pattern
Root on 1 and fifth on 3, each one set up by an eighth note just before it: the fifth on the and of 2, the next chord’s root on the and of 4.
It belongs in Bossa nova. Here it is in the bossa nova style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Bossa nova
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Bossa nova
text:
Step 2: Root and fifth
The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

How to play it. Root on 1, fifth on 3, and each one set up by an eighth note just before it: the fifth on the and of 2, and on the and of 4 the root of the next bar’s chord. The low notes sound like a heartbeat: long, short-long, short.

The pattern

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie octaves
text:
The pattern
Rolling octaves: the root and the root an octave higher in swung eighths, low on every beat and high on every and, the same every bar. A chord that arrives on beat 3 starts again from its low root.
It belongs in Boogie-woogie and Jump blues. Here it is in the boogie-woogie style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie octaves
text:
Step 1: Roots on every beat
Start with something simpler. The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie octaves
text:
Step 2: Octaves (disco)
The root on every beat and the root an octave up on every off-beat.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie octaves
text:
Step 3: Boogie-woogie octaves, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Root low, octave high, in swung eighths: the low note on the beat, the high one on the and. Keep the hand loose and let it roll rather than hit. Each new chord starts on its low root.

text:
The pattern
The Charleston displaced: a short chord on the and of 1 and a held one on beat 3.
It belongs in Swing. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Reverse Charleston
text:

title: Comping rhythm: Reverse Charleston
text:

A held chord on beat 1 and a short one on the and of 2. The first comping rhythm most players learn.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
The pattern
Four on the floor: kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4, a closed hi-hat on each beat and an open one on every off-beat (the stick closing it each time). The Four on the floor groove without the clap.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock, Piano ballad, Acoustic strum, Dance pop and Boogaloo. Here it is in the dance pop style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: open off-beats
text:
Step 2: Hi-hat: off-beats only
The closed hi-hat plays only the ands, 1-and 2-and 3-and 4-and. Kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4. In 3/4: kick on 1 and 2, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Four on the floor: kick every beat, snare on 2 and 4, a closed hat on each beat and an open one on every and. The foot opens and closes in eighths.

title: Conga part: Tumbao, two drums
text:
The pattern
The tumbao in the first bar. In the second, the right hand plays two open tones on the lower drum, on the and of 2 and on 3, in place of the toe and the heel; then the left-hand toe and the two open tones of beat 4 on the higher drum. The low drum belongs to the bar with three clave notes, which is the second bar of the 2-3 clave.
It belongs in Son montuno, Cha-cha and Boogaloo. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Conga part: Tumbao, two drums
text:

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
The pattern
The Cuban bass line that never plays beat 1: the fifth on the and of 2, then on beat 4 the root of the NEXT bar’s chord, held over the barline.
It belongs in Son montuno and Cha-cha. Here it is in the son montuno style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
Step 1: Root and fifth
Start with something simpler. The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
Step 2: Bossa nova
Root on 1 and fifth on 3, each one set up by an eighth note just before it: the fifth on the and of 2, the next chord’s root on the and of 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Tumbao
text:
Step 3: Tumbao, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Do not play on beat 1. The fifth lands on the and of 2; on beat 4 you play the root of the next bar’s chord early and hold it across the barline. Count aloud and clap beat 1 while you play, so you feel where the chord changes even though you are ahead of it.

text:
Step 1: Root and fifth
Start with something simpler. The boom of boom-chick: the root on beat 1 and the fifth on beat 3, short, the same every bar. In 3/4 it is one note a bar, root one bar and fifth the next.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Motown: root, fifth, octave
text:
Step 2: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3)
The root on beat 1, again on the and of 2 and on beat 3, the same rhythm as the kick drum. Every second bar ends with an eighth note that leads into the next chord.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Motown: root, fifth, octave
section: Step 3: Motown: root, fifth, octave, slowly
text:
Step 3: Motown: root, fifth, octave, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. A two-bar line. The first bar is the dotted rhythm with the fifth on beat 3, then octave and fifth in eighths. The second bar leads by step into the next chord. Play it lightly and short; a Motown bass part bounces.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
The pattern
Eight swung eighth notes a bar walking up the chord and back down: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd, the same every bar. It is the boogie-woogie pianist’s left hand, played on the bass. A chord that arrives on beat 3 starts the walk again from its root.
It belongs in Boogie-woogie and Jump blues. Here it is in the boogie-woogie style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 1: Roots on every beat
Start with something simpler. The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogie-woogie
text:
Step 3: Boogie-woogie, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Eight swung eighths a bar, up the chord and back down: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd. Learn the shape on one chord until the hand knows it, then move it up a fourth for the IV chord and a fifth for the V. The shape stays the same; only the root changes. Lean on beats 1 and 3.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
The pattern
One note on every beat (four quarter notes in 4/4, three in 3/4, dotted quarters in 12/8): the root on beat 1 when the chord changes, chord tones and scale steps in between, and an approach note on beat 4 that leads into the next bar.
It belongs in Swing and Jazz ballad. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:
Step 2: Two-feel
Half notes on beats 1 and 3, root then fifth, with an occasional pickup into the next bar. The lighter feel a band often plays on the head before the bass starts to walk.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Walking
text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Beat 1: the root. Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones or scale steps. Beat 4: a note one fret above or below the next bar’s root. Start from the chord tones of the step before and change only beat 4, then free up beats 2 and 3.

title: Interactive Tools
text: Each tool below is used in the lessons listed under it. The foot of every lesson also lists the other lessons sharing its tools. Written by node scripts/tool-catalog.cjs.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text: A DJ plays recorded music for people, one track flowing into the next. The job needs two (or more) sources you can start, stop and speed up independently, and a mixer to blend them, with headphones to hear the next track before anyone else does.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
The decks

Turntables. The Technics SL-1200 (1972 onwards) became the club standard: a direct-drive motor that gets to speed in under a second, a heavy platter, and a pitch fader (±8 %, later ±16 % on some models). A slipmat lets the record slip over the spinning platter, so you can hold the record still while the platter turns, then let go on the beat.
CDJs (Pioneer’s name, now used for all such players) play files from USB sticks. A jog wheel stands in for the record: touch the top to scratch, turn the side to nudge. Tempo range, cue and loop buttons, key lock (Master Tempo) and a waveform display.
DVS (digital vinyl systems): turntables playing records of a timecode signal that software reads, so a laptop file follows the record’s speed and direction. Serato, rekordbox and Traktor all offer it with supported audio interfaces.
Controllers: two jog wheels, a mixer and pads in one box, for DJ software on a laptop. Cheaper and lighter; the same skills.

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
The mixer
Each channel has, top to bottom: gain (trim the input so loud and quiet tracks match), EQ (usually three bands: high, mid, low, cutting well below the boost, so a band can be nearly “killed”), often a filter, a cue button (send this channel to the headphones), and the channel fader. Then the crossfader blends the two sides, and the master sets the output level.

Headphones: the cue mix (or “cue/master”) knob blends what you’ve cued with the master. Some DJs use split cue: cue in one ear, master in the other.
Crossfader curve: smooth (both sides at full in the middle, for long blends) or sharp (a cut, for scratching: the sound comes in within a millimetre of the edge).

title: DJ 1: The Gear
text:
Your decks
The widget below is the practice rig for these lessons: two decks and a two-channel mixer. Everything here works with a mouse or a finger.




Press ▶ on deck A. Notice the platter turning, the waveform scrolling past the red line (now), and the time readout.
Stop and start it again: the “motor” takes a moment to reach speed and to stop, as a real turntable does.
Pull the Lo knob on channel A all the way down: the kick and bass vanish. Bring it back.
Move the crossfader from A to B, with deck B playing. Then press CUE on channel B, and click Listen: speakers to switch to what the headphones would hear. A browser has one output, so this is how you hear the cue here; with Split cue ticked and headphones on, cue is in the left ear and the master in the right.
Drag the label of a playing record: you are holding it. Move it back and forth. Then drag the rim (the outer ring) while it plays: the side of the platter, to speed it up or slow it down a touch (a nudge).

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
A needle tuner gives you one number. A strobe tuner gives you a picture that stands still when the note is in tune, and drifts one way if you are sharp and the other way if you are flat. It is the most precise tuner there is, and the way it works is a lovely piece of physics that you can play with. This lesson builds one from the spinning disc of the 1930s to the few lines of arithmetic in the tuner on this site, with a widget at every step. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. The pictures with a Pause button move on their own; the sliders change what they show. The sound widgets have a ▶ button, and the bar at the foot of the window sets the volume (start low). Nothing here needs a microphone: the last two widgets listen to the page’s own sound. The Strobe tuner button in the top bar is the same tuner on every page of the site, and works with the microphone, with the page’s sound, with a video on the page, or with another browser tab. For where the numbers 3:2 and 5:4 come from see the harmonic series; for what the tuner is used to compare, see tuning systems.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
1. The mechanical strobe tuner
The first strobe tuners (the Conn Strobotuner, 1936, is the famous one) had no electronics to speak of. A small motor spun a disc at a fixed, very steady speed. Printed on the disc were rings of black and white segments, a different number in each ring, one ring for each note (or octave of a note) to be tuned. A microphone and an amplifier fed the note you were playing to a neon lamp behind the disc, and the lamp flashed once for every cycle of the note’s sound. You looked at the disc through the flashes.
Take a simple disc with rings of 8, 16, 24 and 32 segment pairs, turning 13.75 times a second (825 rpm). The 8-pair ring sweeps 8 × 13.75 = 110 pairs past any fixed spot every second, the 16-pair ring 220, and so on. So ring 1 is a ruler for 110 Hz (the A two octaves below the A at 440), ring 2 for 220 Hz, ring 3 for 330 and ring 4 for 440. Set the lamp to flash at 110 times a second and look at ring 1: each flash lights the disc at the moment it has turned exactly 8 pairs further round, which looks exactly like the last picture. The ring appears to stand still.
Now play 112 Hz, a little sharp. The flashes come slightly faster than the ring’s pairs pass, so each flash catches the ring a little further round than the last, and it creeps round at 2 pairs a second, the difference between the note and the ring’s frequency. Flat, and it creeps the other way. That is the whole idea: the speed of the creep is the number of hertz you are away, and its direction is sharp or flat. The disc really turns 825 rpm; the lamp’s light is what makes the difference visible.



Try this. Set the lamp to Steady and the disc is a grey blur: without the flashes there is nothing to see, since the disc turns too fast to follow. Switch to Flashing and slide the note: ring 1 stops at 110 Hz, ring 2 at 220 Hz, and so on. Between those, every ring crawls or blurs. Press Match the nearest ring to see the one that stops.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 2. Why a pattern stands still: aliasing
text:
2. Why a pattern stands still: aliasing
The trick of “looking at something in flashes” has a name, stroboscopic aliasing, and you have seen it in films, where a car’s wheels appear to stand still or turn backwards. A film camera takes (say) 24 pictures a second. If a spoked wheel turns a little less than one spoke-gap between pictures, the spokes look as if they have moved forward a little. If it turns a little more, they look as if they have moved back. And if it moves exactly one spoke-gap each picture, the wheel stands still although it is turning fast.
What you see is the difference between the wheel’s rate (spokes passing a point per second) and the flash rate, wrapped round so it is never more than half a flash away from zero:

apparent rate = (spokes × turns per second) − (flashes per second) × (the whole number that makes this as small as it can be)

The widget below has a wheel with eight identical spokes on the left (the truth, drawn continuously) and the same wheel as the strobe light shows it on the right. Give the wheel a speed, give the strobe a rate, and watch.



Things to find: the wheel at 2 turns a second has 16 spokes passing a point each second; at 16 flashes a second it stands still. Raise the flash rate to 20 and the spokes appear to go backwards. Drop it to 8 flashes a second and it stands still again: the wheel moves two spoke-gaps between flashes, and the spokes all look the same. Tick Mark one spoke and both stillnesses go, because the marked spoke is now different from the others: only 2 flashes a second (one whole turn between flashes) stands still.
In the disc tuner the wheel was the disc ring and the flash rate the note. A tuner lights up with a pattern that stands still only when the note is an exact multiple of the ring’s rate. That is the mechanical strobe tuner, and the rest of the lesson is the same idea done with arithmetic.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
3. One band, one partial
A real note is not one frequency. A guitar string vibrates in halves, thirds, and so on all at once, so the sound has a stack of partials at (nearly) 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. See the harmonic series for why. A lamp that flashes with the wave flashes at the fundamental but also with the partials, so on a disc tuner the rings for 1×, 2×, 3× each get their own pattern, and they all stand still together when the string is in tune. That is a mixed blessing: you can read several rings at once, and each ring is a different ruler.
The tuner on this site makes that explicit. It has one band (a row of stripes) for each partial. Band k is a ruler tuned to k times the reference pitch. The sound has a partial at k times the string’s own fundamental. If the string is exactly at the reference, partial k matches band k and the stripes stand still. If the string is c cents sharp, partial k is at k × f × 2^(c/1200), so band k drifts at

drift (Hz) = k × fref × (2^(c/1200) − 1)

which is k times faster for the kth band. The upper bands are k times more sensitive: a small error shows on band 6 six times sooner than on band 1.
Here are the bands with no microphone: a computed string, so you can see what a tuner should show for a given error. The small picture above shows the string’s partials (bars) against the bands’ rulers (the vertical lines).



Set the String is off by slider to +8 cents: all six bands drift to the right, band 6 six times faster than band 1. Now add stiffness. A real string is a little stiff, like a thin rod, and a stiff string’s partials are pushed up: partial k is at k f √(1 + B k²), so the high partials are sharp even when the fundamental is on the note. You will see the lower bands stand still and the higher ones drift right: the string is in tune where it matters, and the strobe shows exactly how much its upper partials are stretched.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 4. The software version: multiply and average
text:
4. The software version: multiply and average
A computer cannot spin a disc, but it can do what the disc and the lamp do together, with two multiplications. This is called demodulation, and radios do it too. For band k, keep two reference waves going, a cosine and a sine at k × fref. Multiply the incoming sound, sample by sample, by each of them, then average (a low-pass filter) the results.
Why it works: multiplying two sine waves gives two new ones, at the difference and at the sum of their frequencies. The sum is fast and the average wipes it out. The difference is slow: it is zero if the sound is exactly at the reference, and then the average is a steady number; if the sound is 0.5 Hz sharp, the average is a number that swings slowly at 0.5 Hz. The cosine’s average and the sine’s average are two numbers I and Q, and together they are the corner of a right-angled triangle, a point on a circle. The angle of that point is the phase: where the stripes are. If the note is in tune, the point stays put; otherwise it goes round the circle once for every Hz of difference, counter-clockwise if sharp and clockwise if flat. The stripes you see are drawn at that angle.
The widget runs the arithmetic on a slowed-down signal, so you can watch each step. The reference is 4 Hz (instead of 110 Hz or more) and the “note” is a slider. Step through it.



Check that the averaged traces (step 4) are a cosine and a sine of the difference frequency: at a note 4.5 Hz against the 4 Hz reference they swing at 0.5 Hz, and the dot on the circle goes round once in two seconds. At exactly 4.0 Hz nothing moves. The sum frequency, 8.5 Hz, which you see in the products at step 3, is gone from step 4. (The first second or so is the average filling up, and the tuner ignores it. The real tuner also ignores the first 100 ms of every note, the pluck, since the attack is a noisy burst.)
The bank of bands in apps/shared/pitch-detect.js does exactly this, at the sound card’s sample rate, for each of up to ten bands at once. It reads the angle every 128 samples and works out the drift in hertz from how fast the angle turns; the cents are then 1200 × log₂((kf + drift) / kf).

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 5. Drift is the beat rate; hertz to cents
text:
5. Drift is the beat rate; hertz to cents
The drift in hertz is exactly the beat rate you would hear if you played the reference and your note together. A note 3 Hz sharp of the reference beats 3 times a second against it, and the stripes go round 3 times a second. That is how a piano tuner sets a string by ear against a fork, and the strobe is the same measurement made visible and made at every partial.
To turn hertz into cents, remember that a cent is a ratio, not a number of hertz. One cent is a factor of 2^(1/1200), about 1.000578. So the same pitch error is a small drift at a low note and a bigger one at a high note:









Reference
1 cent is
10 cents is
One stripe passes every, at 1 cent




A2, 110 Hz
0.064 Hz
0.64 Hz

A3, 220 Hz
0.127 Hz
1.27 Hz

A4, 440 Hz
0.254 Hz

It also explains why strobe tuners are so exact for low notes. To see 1 cent on the open low E string of a guitar (82 Hz), band 1 needs 20 seconds to cross one stripe; band 6, being tuned to 494 Hz, crosses six times quicker. Using the higher bands is how you resolve small errors on a low string quickly. The calculator below does the sum.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
6. Why several bands help
If the fundamental were always the loudest partial, one band would do. Two things make that untrue for a guitar.
A weak fundamental. On the low strings of a guitar and on a bass, the speaker or pickup and the string itself give a fundamental that is often weaker than the second or third partial. A tuner that listens for the lowest frequency, or that computes one pitch from the whole waveform, can then jump to the octave above or flicker between two answers. A strobe tuner has no such trouble: the rows are independent, and the bands that have a strong partial are bright and the others fade. In the tuner below, turn the fundamental down to 5% and the first row fades while the others stay bright; the readout above the bands (which is a single pitch worked out by a different method) may get unsettled, and the rows are still telling the truth.
Stiff strings. Real strings are stiff, so the upper partials are pushed sharp by k f (√(1 + B k²) − 1) as in section 3. A piano’s bass strings and a guitar’s thickest strings are the stretched ones. Tuning by the fundamental (row 1) leaves the upper partials a few cents sharp, which is why a piano tuner stretches the octaves: they tune the octave so that the partials beat as little as possible, not the fundamentals. Look at the rows with the stiffness at 0.0008 and decide which row you would trust.



Press Start (nothing here opens the microphone: the source is the made-up string), then drag Fundamental’s strength up and down, and String is off by to a few cents. Row 1 is the one a single-pitch tuner would trust. Notice that when you detune the string every row moves together, row k by k times as much.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 7. Just and equal temperament, on the bands
text:
7. Just and equal temperament, on the bands
Tuning systems shows that the pure major third, 5:4 (386.3 cents), is 13.7 cents narrower than the piano’s 400. A strobe tuner makes this visible, because it needs a target: it can be set to 12-tone equal temperament or to a just interval over a tonic, and then it shows how far the note you are playing is from that.
The widget gives the tuner a target (the note and its tuning system) and tunes a computed string to either system. When both agree, every band stands still. When the string is just and the target equal (or the other way round), the whole stack drifts, and the higher bands drift faster.



Pick Major third with the target 12-ET and the string Just over C: the string (327.0 Hz) is 13.7 cents flat of the piano’s E (329.6 Hz), so band 1 drifts left at about 2.6 Hz, and band 6 six times faster, which is a blur on the screen (as the fast wheel was in section 2) but is still read in cents in the number beside the band. Set the target to Just over C and the string stands still. For the fifth the difference is only 2 cents, a slow creep of 0.4 Hz. That is the size of the compromise a piano makes in every chord.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
section: 8. Watch it follow this page’s own sound
text:
8. Watch it follow this page’s own sound
The tuner does not need a microphone to listen. Each sound the site makes (the lesson widgets, the drone and metronome in the top bar, the chord keyboard, the Backing Track) hands its output to a small registry, AudioTap, and the tuner can listen to that instead: choose This page’s sound. It works with headphones on, there is nothing to pick up from a room, and it hears nothing but the page.
Below, the oscillator plays a sine wave at 221 Hz. The tuner’s target is A3 = 220 Hz, which is 7.8 cents flat of it. Press ▶ on the oscillator, then Start on the tuner (the source is already This page’s sound) and watch the bands drift to the right. Slide the oscillator’s frequency down through 220 Hz and the stripes slow down, stop, and reverse. The sine has only one partial, so only row 1 is bright.






Switch the oscillator’s wave to sawtooth or square and the other rows light up: those waves are sums of partials at whole-number multiples (see the harmonic series), so they stand still on the bands together.
The same choice is in the Strobe tuner in the top bar, which also has two sources that never touch the microphone: a video or audio file on the page (the Timestamp Notes player, say), and another browser tab (a YouTube video, in Chrome: it asks which tab to share, and you must tick “Share tab audio”). Try the top-bar tuner while the drone is playing: it listens to the drone through exactly the same tap.

title: How a Strobe Tuner Works
text:
Things to try

In the wheel, set 3 turns a second. At what flash rate does the eight-spoke wheel stand still? (24, since 24 spokes pass a point each second.) Which lower rates do it too, without a marked spoke? (12, 8, 6 and so on: 24 divided by a whole number.) With a marked spoke? (3, or 1.5, 1: only a whole number of turns between flashes.)
In the disc, play 165 Hz. Does any ring stop? (No: it is halfway between ring 1 at 110 and ring 2 at 220, so both are 55 pairs a second out and blur.) Then play 220, and then 224, and find which way the ring creeps.
In the bands widget, find the stiffness at which band 6 is 10 cents sharp with the string in tune. (600 × log₂(1 + B × 36) = 10 gives B of about 0.00032.)
In the demodulation widget, set the note to 3.5 Hz, then 4.5 Hz. The dot goes round in opposite directions. Which direction means sharp?
At 220 Hz, how many cents is a drift of 0.5 Hz on band 1? On band 3? (Convert with 1200 × log₂(1 + drift / (k f)): 3.9 cents and 1.3 cents.)
In the last widget, tune the oscillator to 220 Hz, then play a sawtooth. Which rows light up, and do they all stand still?
