title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text: Guitars and basses (acoustic and electric) need little care, but they do need some: clean strings, a stable climate, and a check of the setup now and then.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Every time you play

Wash your hands first. Sweat and oil kill strings and grime the fingerboard.
Wipe the strings, underneath too, and the back of the neck, with a dry cloth when you finish.
Put it in its case or gig bag or on a stand. Never leaning on an amp or a wall; that’s how necks break.
Use a strap lock or check the strap ends; dropped guitars crack at the headstock.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Tuning

Tune up to the note (if it’s sharp, go below and come back up), so the string holds.
Standard tuning E A D G B E (bass E A D G); tune often with a tuner.
If it won’t stay in tune: new strings still stretching, worn strings, temperature change, or the string slipping at the tuner.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Strings

Change them when they sound dull, won’t stay in tune, feel rough, or are discoloured. Every month or two for regular players; basses less often.
Steel strings on acoustics and electrics; nylon strings only on classical guitars. Never put steel strings on a classical guitar: the tension can pull the bridge off.
Change one or a few at a time on guitars with a floating tremolo, so the bridge stays put.
Stretch new strings: pull each gently up from the fingerboard and retune, a few times.
Cut the ends; they’re sharp. Wear eye protection the first time you cut strings.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Climate

Wood moves with humidity: in dry air (winter heating) the frets can stick out at the edges and acoustic tops can crack; in damp air the action rises.
Keep it at room temperature; never in a hot car. Let it warm up in its case after coming in from the cold.
An acoustic in a dry winter: a soundhole or case humidifier. In the monsoon or a humid city: silica gel or a two-way humidity pack in the case, and wipe strings after playing, since they rust fast in damp air.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
The setup
The setup is how the guitar is adjusted: neck relief (the truss rod), string height (action), intonation, and the nut. A good setup makes a cheap guitar easy to play. Signs you need one:

Strings are high and hard to press down, or buzz against the frets.
Notes up the neck are out of tune even when the open string is in tune (intonation).
After changing to a different string gauge, or with the seasons.

The truss rod adjustment should be done by a teacher or tech the first few times: a little goes a long way, and forcing it can break it.

title: Gear 6: Guitar and Bass Care
text:
Electrics

Crackling when you turn a knob: dust in the pot; a squirt of contact cleaner (by a tech) or work the knob.
Crackle when you move the cable: the jack socket or the cable (Gear 2).
Unplug the cable from active basses and acoustic pickups when not playing; it switches the battery off.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text: Saxophones are tough metal tubes, but their pads, springs and keys are delicate, and they get wet every time you play. Clean and dry it after every practice and it will stay airtight, which is what makes it play easily.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Assembling

Reed in your mouth first to wet it while you set up (or soak it a minute in water).
Neck strap on, hooked to the ring on the sax’s back.
Remove the end plug. Fit the neck: hold it by its socket, twist gently, and tighten the screw. Don’t grab the octave key on the neck; it bends.
Mouthpiece on the neck cork, about halfway (it sets the tuning: further on = sharper). Grease the cork if it’s stiff.
Reed flat against the table of the mouthpiece, its tip lined up with the tip of the mouthpiece, a hair’s width of black showing. Ligature over it, screws snug, not crushing.
Always lift the sax by the body and bell, never by the keys or rods.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Reeds

Reeds come in strengths (1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 …). Most beginners start at 2 or 2.5.
Rotate three or four, numbered, so none wears out too fast. Keep them in a ventilated reed case, flat.
Break in new reeds: play each only a few minutes a day for the first few days.
After playing, rinse the reed in clean water, wipe it from heel to tip, and let it dry before closing the case.
Don’t share reeds, and don’t chew or bite them.
Mould on a reed (black, green or fuzzy spots) means throw it away. In humid weather, store reeds with a humidity pack rather than shut in a damp box, and swap reeds every few weeks even if they still play.
A chipped, cracked or warped reed squeaks and buzzes: throw it away.
Never leave the reed on the mouthpiece in the case; it warps.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
After every practice

Take off the reed, wipe it, put it in its case.
Take off the mouthpiece; run water through it (cool, not hot) or swab it, and dry.
Swab the body: drop the weighted end of the pull-through into the bell, turn the sax so it falls out of the top, pull it through gently. Two or three times.
Swab the neck with a neck swab.
Wipe the pads that stick (often the G♯ and octave pads) with pad paper if they’re tacky.
Wipe fingerprints off with a soft cloth.
Put the end plug in and everything in its place in the case, latches closed.

Don’t leave a swab inside the sax: it holds the moisture against the pads.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Mould
A wet sax shut in its case grows mould: in the mouthpiece, the neck, the swab, the case lining, and on the pads. It smells musty, can make you ill, and rots pads. It’s worst in humid weather (the monsoon, coastal cities).

Swab and dry after every practice; let the swab dry outside the case, and wash it every week or two.
Wash the mouthpiece weekly in lukewarm water with a little mild soap and a mouthpiece brush; rinse and dry. (Not hot water: it can discolour or warp hard rubber.)
Leave the case open for a while after practice in a dry room, so it airs out; keep silica gel in the case.
If the case smells musty or you see spots: clean the mouthpiece and neck, air and sun the empty case, and have the pads checked. Throw away any mouldy reeds.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
What not to do

No polish on lacquer; no metal polish. Just a soft cloth.
Don’t eat sweets or drink sugary drinks before playing: sugar sticks the pads. Rinse your mouth first.
Don’t stand it on its bell, or lay it on a chair. A sax stand or the case.
Don’t oil or adjust the keys and screws yourself.
Don’t put music or a lyre in the case where it presses on the keys.

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Signs it needs a repair

Notes that won’t sound, low notes that gurgle, or it got hard to play: a leak (a pad not sealing). Often after a knock.
A key that sticks, sits crooked, or is slow to return: a bent rod or a loose spring.
A buzz or rattle from the body. Missing felts or corks.
Take it to a repair technician every year or so for a check (a “play condition” service).

title: Gear 8: Saxophone Care for Beginners
text:
Next

Gear 9: Drum Care

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text: Tremolo is the volume going up and down, over and over. It’s one of the oldest effects: guitar amps had it built in from the 1950s, long before pedals. An LFO does the work. Move the position instead of the volume and it’s auto-pan. Spin a real speaker and you get both at once, plus a pitch wobble: the rotary speaker.
crumbs: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text:
Tremolo and auto-pan




Rate: how many times a second. Slow is a throb; fast is a shimmer.
Depth: how far the volume falls. At 100% it goes all the way to silence.
Shape: a sine wave swells smoothly; a square chops the sound on and off (Chopper).

Try Surf tremolo on the Synth riff, then switch to Auto-pan with headphones on: the chords float from ear to ear. Push the rate up past about 15 Hz on the LFO page and tremolo stops sounding like a wobble and starts sounding like a new tone: that’s amplitude modulation, a cousin of FM.
Guitarists say “tremolo” for two different things, confusingly: the tremolo arm on a Stratocaster actually bends the pitch (that’s vibrato), while a tremolo effect changes the volume. Fender named them backwards in the 1950s and the names stuck.
crumbs: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker

title: Sound 20: Tremolo and the Rotary Speaker
text:
The rotary speaker
Don Leslie built a speaker cabinet for the Hammond organ in the 1940s with two spinning parts: a horn for the high frequencies and a drum for the low ones. As each turns toward you it gets louder, higher in pitch (the Doppler effect, as when a siren passes) and moves across the stereo field.




Slow (chorale) and Fast (tremolo): the two speeds. Organists switch between them in the middle of a song. Press Slow ⇄ Fast while it plays and listen to the change: the light horn gets up to speed in about a second, while the heavy drum takes several. That lurch, the two parts going at different speeds for a moment, is the sound people love.
Crossover: where the highs (horn) and lows (drum) are split.
Amp drive: the Leslie’s own valve amp, pushed until it growls.

Try it on the Synth riff and your Microphone as well. The Beatles put voices and guitars through a Leslie (“Tomorrow Never Knows”), and Stevie Ray Vaughan’s “Cold Shot” guitar is one.

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
This lesson is for a drummer who can already play a basic beat: the bass drum on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4, and something steady on top. It is about the “something on top”, and about everything the hi-hat can do besides keeping time. You need a hi-hat with a pedal, a snare and a bass drum. Each step is a little harder than the one before; stay on a step until you can play it through the whole chorus without watching your hands.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the groove written large and the whole chorus on a drum staff. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the note that is sounding lights up in the notation. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. The straight steps are played over four bars of F7 by the Straight-eighth rock or Acoustic strum band, and the swing steps over the 12-bar blues by the Swing band. Each step starts at its own tempo; the strip at the bottom changes the tempo, and the Feel menu changes the band. If you cannot yet play a step at its tempo, slow it down until you can.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
text:
0. The three sounds of the hi-hat
The hi-hat is two cymbals on a stand, one above the other, with a pedal that opens and closes them. That gives it three sounds you will use all through this lesson.

Closed, with the stick. The pedal is down, the cymbals are together, and you hit the top one. A short, tight “tick”. This is the hi-hat sound you hear in most rock.
Open, with the stick. You let the pedal up a little, so the cymbals are apart, and hit. The sound rings and hisses until something stops it.
Closed, with the foot. You press the pedal and the cymbals come together on their own, with no stick. A soft “chick”.

Click a button to hear each one, and the last button to hear an open note being closed.


Closed, stick


Open, stick


Closed, foot


Open, then the foot


Here is how each is written. All three are an ✕, because they are cymbals. A closed note sits above the staff. An open note is the same ✕ with a small circle over it. A note played with the foot is an ✕ below the staff, and its stem points down like the bass drum’s. Click a head to hear it.



The foot closes the cymbals, and that stops an open note. When the cymbals come together, whatever was ringing ends. So an open hi-hat rings until the next closed note or the next foot note cuts it off, whichever comes first. On this page the band’s drummer does the same: press “Open, then the foot” and listen to the open note stop dead. Hearing where an open note ends is as important as hearing where it starts.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
text:
1. Quarter notes on the closed hi-hat
The plainest rock beat. The closed hi-hat plays all four beats, the bass drum plays on 1 and 3, and the snare plays on 2 and 4. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud and make the hi-hat as even as the clock.



Two things at once, then three. Start with the hi-hat and the snare alone; add the bass drum when the hands are steady. The hi-hat does not slow down when the snare lands.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
text:
2. Eighth notes: the basic rock beat
Now the hi-hat plays twice as often, eight notes to the bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The notes on the numbers fall with the bass drum and the snare; the notes on the “ands” fall in between. The bass drum is still on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4.



Keep the right hand moving in one smooth, even stroke, down on the beat and down on the “and”, and let the snare and the bass drum fit themselves around it.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
3. Accents
The same eighth notes, but now they are not all the same. Lean on the notes that fall on the beats and play the “ands” lightly. The usual way to get this is to hit the beats with the shoulder of the stick, on the edge of the hi-hat, and the “ands” with the tip, on top of it; the beats come out louder and brighter, the “ands” softer. The groove starts to breathe.
In the notation, an accent mark (>) is written over each note that is meant to be louder than its neighbours. Look for the mark over the beats in the staff below; the “ands” have none.



Listen with Drums alone. Then play it on a practice pad and try making the difference between the two kinds of note smaller and larger.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
4. The off-beats alone
Take the hi-hat off the beats and play it only on the “ands”: and of 1, and of 2, and of 3, and of 4. The bass drum plays on every beat, and the snare is still on 2 and 4. The beats are now played by the feet and the left hand, and the right hand plays in the gaps.



Say “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” out loud, and tap your foot on the numbers. The hi-hat sits on the words you say between the taps.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
5. Opening the hi-hat
Go back to the eighth notes of step 2, and open the hi-hat once: on the and of 4, the last note of the bar. Open it as you hit, let it ring through the end of the bar, and close it on the 1 of the next bar, with the stick and the foot together. Because the cymbals come together, the open note stops right where beat 1 starts.



The open note is written with the small circle. The foot note under the staff, on beat 1 of each bar, is the pedal closing the cymbals. Play it once with the stick alone and once with the foot as well, and listen for the difference.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
section: 6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
text:
6. Open on every off-beat: four on the floor
The groove of a dance floor. The bass drum plays on every beat, the snare on 2 and 4, and the hi-hat plays closed on the beats and open on every “and”. Each closed note on the next beat shuts the open one before it, so you hear a “tss-tick, tss-tick” pattern. Your foot has to lift the pedal for each “and” and press it down again for each beat.



This is the same groove as “Four on the floor” in the Drums menu of the Backing Track, with the clap taken off so that you can hear the hi-hat by itself.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
7. Sixteenth notes with one hand
At a slow tempo the hi-hat can play four notes to every beat: sixteenths. Count “1 e and a 2 e and a 3 e and a 4 e and a”. One hand plays them all, sixteen to the bar. Play the beats a little stronger than the rest. The bass drum is on 1 and 3, the snare on 2 and 4.



Start very slowly. A slow tempo is the whole point of this step: you are learning to keep sixteen even notes going while the other hand and both feet do something else. Speed up by a few beats a minute at a time.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
8. Sixteenth notes with two hands
Now use both hands on the hi-hat, right, left, right, left on the four notes of a beat. Both hands play on the hi-hat. On beats 2 and 4 the right hand has a different job: it comes off the hi-hat to play the snare. So the hi-hat is silent on those two notes, and you play fourteen hi-hat notes to the bar instead of sixteen.



The gap in the hi-hat on 2 and 4 is where the snare sits. Listen for it: the left hand keeps the sixteenths going without a break, and the snare lands in the space the right hand leaves.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
9. The foot alone
Now the hi-hat’s foot, which keeps time in a different way. First the jazz setting: time is played on the ride cymbal, and the hi-hat foot closes the cymbals on 2 and 4. The foot is the “chick” that goes with the ride pattern.



Next, a rock beat played on the ride cymbal, with eighth notes on the ride, the bass drum on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4, and the foot closing the hi-hat on all four beats. The right hand is on the ride cymbal, so the hi-hat is played by the foot alone. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” with your foot first, then add the rest.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
10. The swing hi-hat
The ride pattern of swing time, played on the hi-hat itself. The pattern is the same as on the ride: a note on each beat, with a skip note after beats 2 and 4. The cymbals are open on 1 and 3, so they ring, and closed on 2 and 4, where the foot closes them with the stick. The skip notes after 2 and 4 are closed. The eighths are swung: the first is long and the second short.



The foot notes on 2 and 4 under the staff are what stop the open notes, and so make the “tss-chick” of swing time. Listen with Drums alone, and notice where the open notes end.
crumbs: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths

title: Hi-Hat Grooves: From Quarter Notes to Sixteenths
text:
Where to go next

Play step 2 or 3 with the drums left out and keep the form of the vamp for ten choruses.
For the beat that goes with the 12-bar blues, the ride pattern and the shuffle, go to Blues for Drums.
Tools → Backing Track has every groove on this page in its Drums menu, under the names that start “Hi-hat”. The Cymbal menu has “Closed hi-hat”, which puts the hi-hat in place of the ride in the other grooves.

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
An arrangement is a set of decisions about who plays what, where, and when they keep quiet. This series takes the site’s backing band apart one player at a time. Each example below is the band itself: press ▶ Play, then use the buttons under Who plays to switch players in and out while it runs. Under the buttons, the last four bars the band played are written out, one staff per player, so you can see what you are hearing.
The four lessons:
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
1. Four jobs
A rhythm section shares out four jobs:

Time. The drums say where the beat is and how it is divided: straight or swung, busy or calm. Everyone else leans on them.
The bottom. The bass says which chord this is by playing its root, mostly on the strong beats, and it ties the harmony to the drums’ rhythm.
The harmony and the inner rhythm. Guitar and keyboards fill the middle: the rest of the chord, played in a pattern that sits between the drums’ hits.
The melody. A singer or soloist. The rhythm section’s job is to leave room for it.

A band sounds good when those jobs don’t step on each other. Most of arranging is deciding who doesn’t play.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 2. Build it up one player at a time
text:
2. Build it up one player at a time
Start with only the drums, then add the bass, then the guitar. Listen for what each player adds. The drums alone have rhythm but no key. The bass adds the chord changes. The guitar adds the colour of each chord (major or minor) and fills the gaps in the rhythm.



Now take one away at a time. Without the bass, the band suddenly sounds thin and high. Without the drums, the guitar and bass have to keep time themselves and they sound loose. Without the guitar, the bass and drums still hold the song up: that’s why they are called the foundation.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
section: 3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
text:
3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house
Look at the written parts while the band plays. The bass sits low, under the bass clef. The guitar sits in the middle. The drums aren’t pitched, but the kick is low, the snare is in the middle and the cymbals are high.
When two players share a register they blur together. The easiest fix is to move one of them. Here the piano comps in a ballad, then plays the same notes an octave higher, then an octave lower. Hear how the low one gets in the way of the bass and muddies the chords, and how the high one leaves the middle empty for a singer.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
4. Same chords, three bands
A style is a set of these decisions made together. These three play the same four chords. Switch players off in each to hear how the jobs are shared out differently.
Rock: bass on every eighth note, guitar strumming eighths, a backbeat on 2 and 4. Everyone plays the same grid, so it drives.



Reggae: the guitar plays only on the off-beats and the drums leave beat 1 empty. The bass carries the downbeat by itself. Take the bass out and the beat is gone.



Swing: the bass walks a note on every beat, the ride cymbal plays the swung pattern, and the piano plays short chords now and then, mostly off the beat. The piano part changes every time round: in jazz the comping is a conversation, not a fixed pattern.
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band
text:
5. Try it

In each example, find the one player you could lose with the least damage. That player is the first to drop out when a singer comes in.
Turn on only bass and drums in the reggae example, then only guitar and drums. Which pair still sounds like reggae?
Next: Bass and drums.



  Tempo 
  ■ Stop
crumbs: Arranging 1: Who Plays What in a Band

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
A bend pushes or pulls a fretted string sideways across the fret so that its pitch rises smoothly, with no second pick stroke. It is the guitar’s version of a singer sliding up to a note, and it is the main way a guitarist reaches the notes between the piano’s keys. This lesson builds the technique first, then the habit of bending to a target pitch, then the variants, and then where bends go in a blues in A. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Strings are numbered 1 (high E) to 6 (low E). Tablature has one line a string, the high E on top, and a number for the fret. The Drone button in the top bar is the same drone as the one in section 2: keep it sounding on A while you practise, because a bend is only right or wrong against something that stays still. Start the volume low.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
1. The mechanics
Support fingers. One finger alone cannot move a string a whole step. Bend with the ring finger (3) and put the middle (2) and, if you can, the index (1) on the same string, one fret behind it, so that three fingers push together. The fingers behind are not decoration: they share the load and keep the string from sliding off the fret. For a small bend (a half step) with the middle finger, the index finger backs it. When the bend is on the note you are fretting with the little finger, the ring finger backs it.
Push or pull? The string goes across the neck, so it has to go one way or the other.

On the thin strings (1 to 3, the high E, B and G) the usual way is to push the string up toward the ceiling, away from the palm.
On the thick strings (4 to 6) the usual way is to pull it down toward the floor, so that the string does not run off the edge of the fretboard and the pull is not blocked by the neighbouring string. Many players use this for the G string too, and a few bend the B string down. Either direction gives the same note: use whichever your hand finds steadier.

It is the wrist. The bend comes from rotating the forearm and wrist, as if turning a doorknob, and not from squeezing the fingers sideways. The fingers keep their shape and the hand turns about the line of the forearm. Beginners squeeze and the bend stalls at a half step, and the hand tires.
Thumb. Two usual ways, and both are right:

Thumb over the top of the neck, anchored on the low E string. The thumb damps that string and gives the hand a pivot to turn about. This suits push bends.
Thumb behind the neck, as in classical position. It gives more leverage for a pull bend.

Mute the other strings. A bend gets sloppy from strings that were not meant to ring. The fingertip that frets the bend mutes the string below it, the underside of the same finger mutes the one above, and the picking hand’s palm rests lightly at the bridge. The strings you do not bend ring only if you let them.
String gauge and place on the neck. Lighter strings (for example a set of .009 to .042) bend more easily than heavier ones (.011 and up), and are easier on beginners’ fingertips. Heavier strings give a fatter sound and more tension to play against. A longer scale length makes strings tighter, and so does a lower tuning, so a given set bends differently on different guitars. Within one guitar: the frets near the 5th to 12th are friendliest for most players. Near the nut a bend stretches more string and takes more push, and above the 12th the string is short and stiff, so the same push moves it less and the last bit of the bend is hard to hold. Thick strings take the most effort. This is why a first bend is usually on the G or B string at the 7th or 8th fret.
Practice: no pitch goals yet. Fret the G string at the 7th fret (D) with the ring finger, and put the middle and index fingers on frets 6 and 5 of the same string. Rotate the wrist slowly until the pitch has gone up as far as it will, then let it down slowly. Do ten. The bent note should be clean, with no buzzing from the string touching the next fret or ringing neighbours.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
2. Bending in tune
A bend is a slide with no frets in it, so nothing tells you when you have arrived. The fix is to hear the target first. Before you bend, fret the target note (the note a half step, whole step or more above where you start), play it, then go back, play the lower note and bend until it matches. After a few days your ear carries the target and you can skip the check.

The bendboard below shows a bend three ways at once, and lets you try it. On the left is the neck as you see it in tab (the high E on top, the frets running to the right), with box 1 in grey. The filled dot is your finger and the string curves away from it toward the next string by as much as you bend. The dashed dot is the fret that sounds the target pitch, and the arrow between them carries the tab mark: ¼, ½, full, 1½, PB (pre-bend) or R (release). The gauge beside it counts the bend in cents, with ticks at 100, 200 and 300 and the blue-note zones shaded (around 316 to 350 cents above the root for the blue third, and around 583 for the blue fifth). The trace underneath is the pitch against time, with the target shape in dark grey.

Drag the dot toward the next string (or use the Bend slider, or the arrow keys on the dot): a tone glides with it, and the readout says how many cents you are off the target.
Start and Target play the two notes, and Play the shape bends the note for you along the dark line (pick bend, bend and release, pre-bend and release, or vibrato on a bend).
Listen and compare opens the microphone (only when you press it) and draws the pitch of your own guitar over the target: play the first note when the line begins. It needs the guitar in standard tuning and one note at a time.
MIDI wheel lets the pitch wheel or the mod wheel of a MIDI keyboard do the bending.

Choose a bend from box 1 (each one is a note from section 5, with its string and fret). Target, then bend is the practice routine in sound. A bend that is a few cents off beats against the target and against the drone.

The drone, tuned to A and with the E above it:



On the gauge and the trace, a bend that lands inside a blue zone is the blue note: it is neither the piano’s minor third nor its major third. Compare the solid orange line (you) with the dark line (the target): where they drift apart, the sound beats against the target.
Check against something that does not move. The drone is one. Another is the same note on another string: to bend the G string’s 7th fret (D) up a whole step to E, fret the E on the B string (5th fret), pick it, then bend and compare. Hearing two strings settle into one pitch is the most reliable test you have.
Hold the bend with a strobe. A bend that is nearly right looks right on a needle. A strobe shows each partial of the string, and a bend you hold still at the target makes its stripes stand still. Set it to the target note (here E, the pitch of the 9th fret on the G string), press Start, bend, and hold: stripes drifting right mean you are sharp, left flat, and the speed is how far. Use it for long held bends and for the end of a bend with vibrato. Wait a moment after the pick strikes: the attack is ignored.

Tune the guitar first. A bend can’t be in tune with a guitar that isn’t.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
3. Variants
All of these start with the same push. What changes is when the bend happens.

Bend and release. Pick the lower note, bend up to the target, then let the string back down to the start while the note is still sounding. Written 7b9r7.
Pre-bend, and pre-bend and release. Bend the string silently, before the pick strikes it, to the target pitch. Strike it, and then (if it is a pre-bend and release) let it back down. The ear never hears the lower note first. Written PB and PB R. This is harder than it sounds because there is no sliding to correct with: the bend is right or wrong before you hear it. Check against the target note as in section 2.
Unison bend. Two strings play the same pitch: fret the lower string (for example the G string at the 7th fret, D) and, on the next string up, the note a whole step higher (the B string at the 5th fret, E), pick both, and bend the lower one up to meet the one that stays still. You hear one note thicken, then split and merge. A slightly out-of-tune unison beats, which is the sound of a bend that is not quite there.
Double-stop bend. Two strings sound at once, and one or both are bent. With a double stop on strings 2 and 3, bend them together a whole step, or bend one and keep the other still. Listen for it in rock-and-roll and blues lead playing.
Oblique bend. One string is held still (often an open string, or a high fretted note) while another is bent against it. The distance between the two changes while one note does not.
Vibrato on a bend. Reach the target, then wobble the pitch a little below and up to it (and not above it) with small quick rotations of the wrist. A bend with vibrato is how most guitarists end a held note. Keep the target as the top of the wobble.
Quarter-tone bends, the “curl”. A tiny bend, about half a fret. It is not meant to arrive anywhere on the piano. See section 5.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
4. How bends are written
In tablature a bend is a curved arrow from the fret number up to a bracket or the target number, with a word or number over the tip saying how far:

7b9 (text tab)

(9)
the pitch the bend is aimed at, as a fret number in brackets



The staff may also show the target note as a grace note, or a slur with “bend” over it. In plain text tab, the bend and release shown in the picture are written like this, on the B string:
e|----------------------------|
B|--8b10----8b10r8------------|
G|----------------------------|

and a pre-bend and release (fret 8, bent silently to the pitch of fret 10, picked, then let down):

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
5. Bends in the blues
The minor pentatonic scale on the 5th fret (“box 1”) in A is the first place most guitarists use bends. The scale below is written on a staff in A (with the notes’ names); press ▶ Play to hear it, and use the table beneath for the strings and frets.



Box 1 in A, with the string and fret where each note is (string 1 is the high E). Every string has two notes in the box, at the 5th fret and at the 7th or 8th:








Degree

1 (root)

Bends that blues players reach for early (strings and frets as in the table; the target of each bend is a pitch you can also fret one or two frets up):

4 to 5, a whole step. D to E. On string 3 (G), fret 7 (D), bend to E (the pitch of fret 9). This is a favourite because the 5 is the strongest note against the I chord, and the 4 is the weakest, so the bend is a movement from tension to rest. In tab: G|--7b9--.
♭7 to root, a whole step. G to A. On string 2 (B), fret 8 (G), bend a whole step to A (the pitch of fret 10). The ♭7 pulls towards the root the way it does in the dominant chord. In tab: B|--8b10--.
♭3 up toward the major 3. C toward C♯. On string 1 (high E), fret 8 (or string 3, fret 5), bend a little, about a quarter-tone. The note is not C and not C♯. This is the blue third, between the minor third of the scale and the major third of the A7 chord sounding under it. In tab: a 1/4 over the arrow, not a number of frets.
5 up a step and a half. E up to G, the ♭7. On string 2 (B), fret 5, bend three frets’ worth, to the pitch of fret 8. This is the 1½-step bend of section 2, and takes all three fingers. In tab: B|--5b8--.
♭5 bends. The blues scale adds ♭5 (E♭ in A). On string 3, fret 8 (E♭), bend a half step to E, from the ♭5 to the 5. In tab: G|--8b9--. Likewise a half-step bend from 4 (D, fret 7) to ♭5 (E♭, fret 8): G|--7b8--.

Practise each of them against the A drone from section 2: the whole-step bends of D and G should land on notes (E and A) that are in the drone, so that you hear them lock.

Between the piano’s notes
A piano or a fretted guitar plays the third as either the minor third (300 cents above the root) or the major third (400). The blues third is neither. It sits in the middle, near 350 cents, which is the region of a neutral third. Measurements of recorded blues singing and playing show this. Cutting (2019, Empirical Musicology Review) found clusters of blue-note pitches near 319, 583 and 1038 cents above the tonic, in between the equal-tempered notes at 300 and 400, 500 and 600, and 1000 and 1100. A guitar with frets can’t play those notes on a fretted string. A bend can. This is why the bends in the box are not “mistakes to be corrected”: they are the way the guitar reaches notes the frets leave out.
Hear it in the tool below, with the A drone sounding if you like. Each button plays A (220 Hz) with a second note above it: the minor third, a note 319 cents up (the first of Cutting’s clusters), the neutral third at 350, and the major third. The last button slides from the minor third to the major third; listen for where it stops sounding like either. None of the notes between the minor and major third has a fret.

  Minor third, neutral third, major third
  
    Minor third, 300 cents (C)
    Blue third, 319 cents
    Neutral third, 350 cents
    Major third, 400 cents (C♯)
    Slide from 300 to 400
  
  A220 plus the interval above it, on a sine tone.

Listen to. Pick one phrase from each of these players’ recordings and try to copy its bend.

B.B. King, “The Thrill Is Gone” (1969): the vibrato that ends his phrases, and bends that sing like a voice.
Albert King, “Born Under a Bad Sign” (1967): long, wide bends on the high strings.
Freddie King, “Hide Away” (instrumental, early 1960s): bends inside a driving shuffle.
Stevie Ray Vaughan, “Pride and Joy” and “Texas Flood” (both from the early 1980s): big bends and a heavy touch.

These are pointers for your ears. Check the recordings before repeating any detail about them.
crumbs: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune

title: String Bends on Guitar: Bending in Tune
text:
6. Practice, step by step
Spend a few minutes on each step, slowly. Do not move on until the previous step is clean three times in a row. Keep the A drone going.

No pitch. Section 1’s practice: ten slow bends with three fingers, then ten releases.
Half step. Fret the target (G string fret 8, E♭), then the start (fret 7, D). Bend until they match. Repeat 10 times; switch to the B string, fret 8 to 9.
Whole step. String 3 fret 7 to the pitch of fret 9. Fret fret 9 first, play it, play fret 7, bend. Aim for the drone’s E.
Whole step, no check. Hear the target in your head, bend, then check with the fretted note afterwards.
Whole step with release. Bend, hold for four slow beats, release to the start without letting the note go sharp or flat on the way down.
Pre-bend and release. Bend silently, pick, release. Check the pitch of the pre-bend against the fretted target before you pick.
Step and a half. String 2: fret 5 to the pitch of fret 8. Use all three fingers.
Vibrato on the bend. Bend to the target, hold it, and add a small wobble that does not drop below the start.
The curl. On string 1 fret 8, bend a little, to between C and C♯, listening for the point where it sounds neither minor nor major. Compare with the neutral third button.
In a phrase. Play four bars over a 12-bar blues in A (the band in Blues for Guitar can play the chords in A) using only the bends 4 to 5 and ♭7 to the root, resting between them.

Where to go next: Hammer-ons and pull-offs for the other ways of changing pitch without picking, Blues for Guitar for the chords under the solo, and Tuning systems for why a pure interval and a piano’s interval are not the same.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text: A dot adds half the value of the note again. A dotted half note (normally two beats) becomes three beats. A dotted quarter becomes one-and-a-half.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
The dotted-quarter-plus-eighth figure
The classic figure is a dotted quarter followed by an eighth — the “long- short” pattern you hear at the start of countless tunes. It’s tricky because the eighth note lands on the and of beat two, not on a beat.

title: Lesson: Dotted Rhythms
text:
Practice steps

Chant a steady “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”.
Hold the dotted quarter across “1 & 2”, then say the eighth on “&”.
Try it slowly, then bring it up to tempo.

Then go to Practice → Tunes and find a tune that uses this figure. Play it a few times and listen for the long-short.






Tip



Notice this lesson tracks separately from the quarter-note lesson — the report will show your time on each page, not just “lessons” as a lump.

title: Motown / soul
text: Open the Motown / soul style in the Backing Track

title: Motown / soul
text:
What it is
The 1960s Detroit sound of Motown Records: a snare (often with a tambourine) hitting every beat, a busy electric bass, guitars chopping chords, and a song built for radio and dancing.

title: Motown / soul
text:
A little history
Berry Gordy started Motown in Detroit in 1959. Its records were cut by a house band later known as the Funk Brothers: drummer Benny Benjamin, bassist James Jamerson, pianist Earl Van Dyke, and others, playing in Studio A (“the Snakepit”). The songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland wrote the mid-’60s run of hits for the Supremes and the Four Tops, many on a stomping four-beat snare. Jamerson’s bass lines, played with one finger on a Fender Precision, moved far more than any pattern can show. The band played uncredited until the film Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002).

title: Motown / soul
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Motown: root, fifth, octave, a stand-in for Jamerson’s lines.
Comping: the two-bar rhythm of You Can’t Hurry Love. Drums: snare on every beat.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text: Open the Boogie-woogie style in the Backing Track

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
What it is
Blues piano with a left hand that never stops: eight notes to the bar, swung, repeating one figure up and down the chord while the right hand plays riffs, tremolos and blue notes against it. It is almost always a 12-bar blues.
Boogie-woogie and stride are close relations: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a band into the left hand, and the same pianists often played both. Stride’s left hand leaps between bass and chord on the beats; boogie-woogie’s walks along the bass in eighth notes. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
A little history
The style began in the lumber, turpentine and railroad camps of Texas and Louisiana in the first years of the 1900s, played on “barrelhouse” pianos in the camps’ bars, and travelled north with the migration. In Chicago in the 1920s it was the music of rent parties, as stride was in Harlem. Pinetop Smith’s Pine Top’s Boogie Woogie (1928) gave the style its name; Jimmy Yancey, Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons played it in Chicago.
In December 1938 the producer John Hammond put Ammons, Lewis and Pete Johnson on stage at Carnegie Hall in the From Spirituals to Swing concert, and boogie-woogie became a national craze. Big bands arranged it (Count Basie’s Boogie Woogie, Tommy Dorsey’s version of Pinetop’s piece), and the Andrews Sisters sang it. Its eight-to-the-bar bass went into jump blues, rhythm and blues and early rock and roll: Chuck Berry’s guitar plays a boogie left hand.

title: Boogie-Woogie
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths walking up the chord and back down, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd, every bar. The pianist’s left hand, on the bass.
Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords against the bass.
Drums: Blues shuffle: swung eighths on the cymbal, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Boogie-woogie pianists have dozens of left-hand patterns (rolling octaves, the Yancey bass, broken sixths) and their right hands play the lead. The band’s bassist has one pattern and its pianist one riff, so a melody or a solo on top is your part.

title: Tango
text: Open the Tango style in the Backing Track

title: Tango
text:
What it is
The dance music of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in 2/4 or 4/4, played here on its oldest rhythm: the habanera (dotted eighth, sixteenth, two eighths), which also underlies the 3+3+2 of a lot of later pop.

title: Tango
text:
A little history
The habanera was a Cuban song and dance of the mid-1800s that spread through Spain, Mexico and the Río de la Plata ports (Bizet borrowed one for Carmen, 1875). In the poor neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires in the 1880s and ’90s it mixed with the milonga, Spanish and Italian song, and African Argentine candombe into the tango. Early groups were flute, violin and guitar; the bandoneón (a German button accordion) arrived around 1900 and became the tango’s voice. Carlos Gardel’s Mi noche triste (1917) began the sung tango. The 1940s orquestas típicas (Juan D’Arienzo, Aníbal Troilo, Osvaldo Pugliese) moved to a driving marcato in four; from the 1950s Astor Piazzolla’s nuevo tango added jazz and classical counterpoint.
The band plays the habanera rhythm, the older and more widely useful of tango’s rhythms; the four-beat marcato of the dance orchestras is not modelled.

title: Waltz (in one)
text: Open the Waltz (in one) style in the Backing Track

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
What it is
A fast 3/4 in which the listener feels one beat a bar, not three: the bass on 1, light chords on 2 and 3, brushes, bars grouped in fours.

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
A little history
The waltz rose from Austrian and South German country dances in the late 1700s and took over the ballrooms of Vienna in the early 1800s with Joseph Lanner and the Strauss family (Johann Strauss II’s The Blue Danube, 1867). Played fast, the pulse is one per bar, and phrases come in fours and eights. The waltz then spread everywhere: music-hall and parlour songs, country waltzes (Tennessee Waltz), jazz waltzes, and many carols and folk songs that are sung in a quick 3/4.

title: Waltz (in one)
text:
The band’s version

Bass: root on 1 (root one bar, fifth the next). Comping: waltz. Drums: brushed waltz.

title: Jazz ballad
text: Open the Jazz ballad style in the Backing Track

title: Jazz ballad
text:
What it is
A slow standard played by a jazz rhythm section: the bass on beats 1 and 3 (a two-feel), held chords on the piano, and brushes stirring the snare or a soft ride. The band leaves room for the melody.

title: Jazz ballad
text:
A little history
The two-feel is older than walking bass. New Orleans and 1920s dance bands put the tuba or string bass on 1 and 3, and when the bass began walking in the 1930s (see Swing), the two-feel stayed on as the lighter gear: bands play the head of a tune in two and start walking for the solos. On ballads it never has to leave. Brushes, used on drums since the 1920s, became the ballad sound through drummers such as Jo Jones and later Philly Joe Jones and Ed Thigpen. Pianists filled the long chords with the rich voicings that came from Ellington, Billy Strayhorn and later Bill Evans.

title: Jazz ballad
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Two-feel: root on 1, fifth on 3, now and then a pickup into the next bar.
Comping: long held chords (pad).
Drums: quiet time. Voicings: rootless, with unmarked extensions.

title: Ska / reggae
text: Open the Ska / reggae style in the Backing Track

title: Ska / reggae
text:
What it is
Jamaican popular music since about 1960: guitar and keyboard chords on the off-beats (the skank), a bass that carries the melody of the groove, and, in reggae, a one-drop drum beat with nothing on beat 1 and the kick and snare (or rim) together on beat 3.

title: Ska / reggae
text:
A little history
Ska (c. 1960-66) came from Jamaican musicians playing American R&B for sound systems and stressing the off-beat; studio bands such as the Skatalites played it fast with horns. Around 1966 the tempo slowed into rocksteady, with the bass more prominent (Alton Ellis, the Paragons). By 1968 the beat had changed again into reggae: Toots and the Maytals’ Do the Reggay (1968) is one of the first records to use the word. Drummer Carlton Barrett of Bob Marley’s Wailers made the one-drop the standard reggae beat, and Island Records’ Catch a Fire (1973) took the Wailers worldwide. Later strands include dub, roots, lovers rock, dancehall (see Reggaeton) and Britain’s 2 Tone ska revival (c. 1979).

title: Ska / reggae
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Roots on every beat, plainer than a real reggae bass line, which moves and leaves gaps.
Comping: off-beat chords. Drums: one-drop.

title: Son montuno
text: Open the Son montuno style in the Backing Track

title: Son montuno
text:
What it is
The groove of Cuban son and of salsa: a two-bar repeating piano figure (the montuno or guajeo), a bass that plays ahead of the beat (the tumbao), and a clave pattern every part is fitted to.

title: Son montuno
text:
A little history
Son grew up in eastern Cuba and reached Havana around 1910-20, played by small groups on tres (a guitar with three doubled strings), guitar, bongó, maracas, claves and a marímbula or bass. The second half of a son, the montuno, is a vamp where a lead singer improvises against a chorus. In the late 1930s and 1940s Arsenio Rodríguez enlarged the group into the conjunto: piano, trumpets, and a conga. He is credited with the anticipated bass: the bass skips beat 1 and lands on the and of 2 and on 4, so that each chord is heard a little before the bar it belongs to. Mambo bands (Pérez Prado, Machito) and the New York salsa of the 1960s and ’70s (Eddie Palmieri, Fania Records) built on the same parts.
Clave is the two-bar rhythm (3-2: three hits then two; or 2-3) that the parts are written around. The band plays 2-3.

title: Son montuno
text:
The band’s version

Bass: tumbao, anticipating each bar. Comping: the two-bar montuno.
Drums: clave. Congas: a tumbao moving to the second drum every other bar.

title: Bossa nova
text: Open the Bossa nova style in the Backing Track

title: Bossa nova
text:
What it is
Brazilian song style from Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s: samba slowed and quietened for a voice and a nylon-string guitar. The guitarist’s thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 (in 2/4 counting, the two beats of the bar) while the fingers play syncopated chords that repeat over two bars.

title: Bossa nova
text:
A little history
Samba’s percussion section (the surdo bass drum, tamborim, agogô) was too loud for the small apartments and clubs of Copacabana. João Gilberto moved the parts onto the guitar: the thumb took the surdo, the fingers took the tamborim’s syncopations. His single Chega de Saudade (1958, song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes) is usually called the first bossa nova record. Jobim’s harmony (major sevenths, ninths, chromatic inner lines) came from jazz and from Debussy and Ravel.
American jazz musicians took it up after Charlie Byrd and Stan Getz’s Jazz Samba (1962). Getz/Gilberto (recorded 1963, released 1964), with Astrud Gilberto singing The Girl from Ipanema, made it a world style. Jazz drummers turned the guitar’s rhythm into the brush or cross-stick pattern the band plays: a two-bar figure close to the son clave, over a steady bass drum on 1 and 3.

title: Bossa nova
text:
The band’s version

Bass: root and fifth with pickups. Comping: the two-bar pattern.
Drums: bossa clave on the cross-stick. Voicings: jazz voicings with added 9ths.
Feel: straight eighths. Bossa never swings.

title: Cha-cha

title: Cha-cha
text:
What it is
A medium-tempo Cuban dance rhythm, steadier and simpler than mambo, with a cowbell on every beat and the three quick steps (cha-cha-chá) on beat 3, the and of 3, and beat 4.

title: Cha-cha
text:
A little history
Violinist Enrique Jorrín, of the charanga orchestra Orquesta América, wrote La engañadora (1951, recorded 1953). The orchestra’s dancers found its rhythm easier than the danzón-mambo, and the steps’ scuffing sound named the dance. Charangas played it on flute, violins, piano, bass, timbales, güiro and conga; Orquesta Aragón made it famous across Latin America. By the late 1950s it was a ballroom dance in the US and Europe, and American pop recorded “cha-cha” versions of everything.

title: Cha-cha
text:
The band’s version

Bass: the cha-cha bass line. Comping: chords on the cha-cha figure.
Drums: a bell on the beats. Congas: a tumbao. Voicings: plain triads and sevenths.

title: Dance pop
text: Open the Dance pop style in the Backing Track

title: Dance pop
text:
What it is
The disco beat and its descendants: a kick drum on every beat (four on the floor), the open hi-hat on every off-beat, a bass jumping between the root and its octave, and chords on a 3+3+2.

title: Dance pop
text:
A little history
Disco grew out of New York and Philadelphia clubs in the early 1970s. Earl Young, the drummer of Philadelphia International’s house band MFSB, is often credited with the steady kick and open hi-hat (The Love I Lost, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, 1973). The octave bass became disco’s other mark (Chic’s Bernard Edwards). Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (1977) put the beat on synthesizers and pointed toward house and techno (Chicago and Detroit, mid-1980s). Since then the four-on-the-floor beat has stayed at the centre of dance pop: Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Daft Punk, Dua Lipa.

title: Dance pop
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Octaves. Comping: a 3+3+2, on the electric piano. Drums: four on the floor.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text: Open the Hymn (four parts) style in the Backing Track

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
What it is
Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
A little history
Martin Luther’s chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach’s four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s wrote the texts; the collection Hymns Ancient and Modern (1861) and The English Hymnal (1906, music edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

title: Hymn (four parts)
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Held roots. Comping: hymn: three voices over the root. Drums: none.
Choose Church organ as the instrument for the other obvious sound.

title: Swing
text: Open the Swing style in the Backing Track

title: Swing
text:
What it is
The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a) with the hi-hat closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that “comps” (accompanies, complements): short chords placed off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

title: Swing
text:
A little history
In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1 and 3 (the two-beat feel; see Jazz ballad). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s, bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That “All-American Rhythm Section” is where the modern swing feel comes from.
In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the snare and bass drum for accents (“dropping bombs”). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans, Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band’s piano uses here.

title: Swing
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Walking: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
Comping: syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
Drums: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
Voicings: rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band’s bassist is a beginner’s model.

title: Jump Blues
text: Open the Jump blues style in the Backing Track

title: Jump Blues
text:
What it is
Up-tempo blues for dancing, played by small bands of the 1940s: a rhythm section, two or three horns riffing together, and a singer. The bass plays the boogie-woogie left hand, the drums play a shuffle with a hard backbeat on 2 and 4, and the horns and piano play short riffs. It is the bridge from swing and boogie-woogie to rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

title: Jump Blues
text:
A little history
When the big bands became too costly during the Second World War, many of their players formed small groups that kept the swing bands’ riffs and the boogie-woogie bass but played them louder, on the backbeat, for dancers and jukeboxes. Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five were the most popular: Caldonia (1945) and Choo Choo Ch’Boogie (1946) topped the race-record charts, which Billboard renamed rhythm and blues in 1949. Big Joe Turner, Wynonie Harris, Roy Brown and Amos Milburn sang it; Lionel Hampton’s Flying Home gave it a honking tenor sax. By the early 1950s the same music, with an electric guitar in front, was being called rock and roll.

title: Jump Blues
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogie-woogie: swung eighths, root 3rd 5th 6th flat-7th 6th 5th 3rd.
Comping: Boogie-woogie right hand: a two-bar riff of short swung chords.
Drums: Jump blues: the shuffle on the cymbal, the kick feathered on every beat, a loud snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

The horns are what most people remember of a jump band, and the band has none. Play the riffs yourself, or sing.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text: Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
What it is
The basic rock band: drums with a snare backbeat on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
A little history
Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early ’50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s, records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then punk’s down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre of the style.

title: Straight-eighth rock
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: down-up eighths on the guitar. Drums: a backbeat whose kick varies from bar to bar. Chords are pushed (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives one symbol to each sound, so a singer can read the same sounds in any language. Click a symbol for a description and reference words in English (General American and RP), Hindi, Marathi, German, French, Korean and Japanese. A language is left blank where it does not have the sound.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Find and filter



Tick languages to dim every symbol that none of them uses, and to list only those languages in the detail panel. Search matches symbols, descriptive names, words, romanisations and glosses.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Vowels
Tongue height runs down the page (close to open) and tongue position across it (front, central, back). Drag anywhere on the chart, away from the symbols, to hear a synthesised vowel glide through the space: up and down moves the first formant, across moves the second. Rounding, voice and pitch sit below the chart; Hold keeps the sound going so you can click symbols to glide between them. The chart also takes arrow keys and Space. What the synthesiser is doing, and what F1 and F2 mean: Formants: what makes a vowel.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Consonants
The main chart of consonants made with air from the lungs: place of articulation across, manner down.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Affricates and other consonants
Sounds that do not fit the main chart’s grid: affricates (a stop released into a fricative), glides and a few more.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Modified sounds
Aspirated, breathy-voiced and tense stops, and nasal vowels.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Stop series by language
The same stops are organised differently in each language. Click a symbol.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Diacritics and marks
Small marks that change a symbol, and the marks that show length, stress and linking.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Notes for singers


How classical diction uses IPA
A transcription records sounds, not spelling. Coaches and diction books write a song’s text in IPA so everyone sings the same vowels and consonants, then add stress, linking and the places where a sung line differs from speech. Learn the sounds once and you can read the transcription for any language you meet.


Pure vowels
Most sung languages here are built on steady vowels (Italian, German, French, Japanese, Hindi, Marathi, Korean). In English, [eɪ], [oʊ] and [aɪ] are diphthongs: sing the first element for nearly the whole note and add the second at the very end. Italianate five-vowel thinking ([a e i o u], with open and closed e and o) is a good basis for all of them.


English
General American and RP differ most in r (after vowels), in the vowels of bath, lot and thought, and in the flap [ɾ] of water. Unstressed syllables have schwa in speech, but singers often give them a clearer vowel on long notes. Aspiration of initial p, t, k is a strong cue for audibility.


German
Final voiced stops are voiceless (Tag [taːk]). Two ch sounds: [ç] after front vowels and l, n, r; [x] after a, o, u, au. Vowel length is meaningful, and the stage r is the tongue-tip trill [r] while everyday speech uses [ʁ]. Vowel-initial stressed syllables begin with a light glottal onset [ʔ].


French
No diphthongs and no aspiration. Four nasal vowels, front rounded vowels [y ø œ], and the mute e, which is pronounced when sung. Liaison and enchaînement link words, and French syllables are even in stress.


Hindi and Marathi
Keep dental (त द) and retroflex (ट ड) apart, and learn the four-way contrast (p, pʰ, b, bʱ). Hindi drops the inherent a at the end of words, and sometimes inside them; sung text may restore it. Marathi has the extra affricates [t͡s d͡z] and the retroflex lateral [ɭ].


Korean
Three kinds of stop: lax, tense and aspirated. Lax stops are voiced between vowels. Tense and aspirated stops raise the pitch of the following vowel in speech. Final stops are unreleased.


Japanese
Five vowels, with [ɯ̟ᵝ] spread-lip rather than rounded. Long vowels, double consonants and moraic ん count as extra time. Vowels i and u are often devoiced between voiceless consonants in speech. Japanese [ɾ] is a single tap.

title: IPA Chart for Singers
text:
Language notes


About the examples
Examples use broad transcription of standard forms: General American and RP, Standard Hindi, Standard Marathi, Standard German, Metropolitan French, Seoul Korean and Tokyo Japanese. Individual speakers, regions and poetic or sung styles differ. For Devanagari, Hangul and kana the highlighted piece is the written syllable containing the sound (Devanagari and Hangul write a syllable as a unit); romanisation is a transliteration, not IPA. Check anything you will perform with a native speaker or diction coach.


Hindi and Marathi
Both use the Devanagari script. Hindi has the Persian-Arabic sounds [f z x ɣ q] in loanwords, shown with a dot (nuqta) under the letter; many speakers replace them with native sounds. Marathi usually does not write the nuqta; its loan sounds are often assimilated. Marathi च and ज are [t͡s d͡z] before a, ā, u, o, and [t͡ʃ d͡ʒ] before i, e.


Korean
Hangul writes sounds in syllable blocks. The Korean vowel ㅡ is [ɯ], and ㅓ [ʌ]. Final consonants are pronounced differently from initial ones.


Japanese
Written in kana and kanji; the examples give kana. The し and ち sounds are alveolo-palatal ([ɕ], [t͡ɕ]) and ふ is [ɸɯ̟ᵝ].


Symbols without examples
Some symbols (for example ɨ, ʉ, ɘ, ɵ, ɤ, ɞ, ɶ) are on the chart but are not separate sounds in any of the seven languages here. They are shown dashed and have no reference words.
