title: Accompaniment Styles
text:
These patterns are built into the accompaniment engine and can be selected on any tune page.
    Each style adapts automatically to the tune's meter and chord chart.
    Styles marked any meter work in 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, and 6/8; fixed-meter styles
    fall back to block chords when the meter doesn't match. Examples shown in C major at 110 bpm.
  

  
    By genre
    By instrument
    Backing Track band
  

  
  

  
  

    
      Jazz
      

        
          
            Jazz Charleston
            charleston
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Chord on beat 1 and the and-of-2, leaving beats 3 and 4 open. Named for the 1920s dance; the defining syncopation of early jazz and Swing Era big-band writing.
          
            Jazz
            Swing
            Piano
            Full band
          
        

        
          
            Jazz waltz
            jazzwaltz
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          Swung bass on beat 1, ride-cymbal implied chord on beat 3. The feel of bebop and post-bop piano trios — Evans, Peterson, Monk in 3/4.
          
            Jazz
            Bebop
            Piano trio
          
        

        
          
            Walking bass
            walk
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass moves in step-wise quarter notes through chord tones and approach notes; right-hand comping on beats 2 and 4 (Charleston rhythm). The defining texture of jazz trio and big-band rhythm-section playing from bebop onward.
          
            Jazz
            Bebop
            Piano
            Bass
          
        

      
    

    
      Latin
      

        
          
            Bossa nova
            bossa
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Tresillo-derived bass pattern with chords on the off-beats; ride cymbal and side-stick percussion. Rooted in the guitar style of João Gilberto and the samba-jazz fusion of late-1950s Rio.
          
            Latin
            Jazz
            Brazilian
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Tango
            tango
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Habanera rhythmic cell in the bass (long–short–short–long) with syncopated chords. Descended from Cuban contradanza via the Argentine arrabal — the tresillo pattern that underlies both the habanera and early tango.
          
            Latin
            Argentine
            Cuban
            Bandoneón
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Son montuno
            montuno
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Cuban piano tumbao: bass-chord-chord repeating against the clave. The foundational piano pattern of son cubano and salsa; the rhythmic motor behind virtually all Afro-Cuban popular music.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Salsa
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Cha-cha
            chacha
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beat 1, chord on 2, then three quick chords on "3–and–4" — the "1·2·cha-cha-chá" count. Evolved from the mambo in 1950s Cuba; named for the shuffling footwork of dancers.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Piano
            Full band
          
        

        
          
            Calypso / mento
            calypso
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, light chords on every upbeat — the Trinidadian and Jamaican "afterbeat." Mento is the Jamaican root form; calypso developed in Trinidad. Both patterns flowed into ska and reggae.
          
            Latin
            Caribbean
            Roots
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Samba
            samba
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Surdo-style kick on beats 2 and 4 (absent on beat 1), snare on beat 3, hi-hat fills every eighth. The rhythmic foundation of Brazilian carnival parade music; transferred to the drum kit from the samba bateria.
          
            Latin
            Brazilian
            Drum set
            Bateria
          
        

        
          
            Mambo
            mambo
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation), snare on beat 3, hi-hats throughout. Developed in 1940s Havana by Dámaso Pérez Prado; bridged Cuban son and American big-band.
          
            Latin
            Cuban
            Drum set
            Full band
          
        

      
    

    
      Funk & R&B
      

        
          
            Funk
            funk
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat anchors the eighth-note pulse. James Brown's drummers — Clyde Stubblefield and John "Jabo" Starks — defined this feel.
          
            Funk
            R&B
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            Half-time feel
            halftime
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Snare moves to beat 3 (rather than 2 and 4), making 2 bars feel like 1. Common in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges where the tempo needs to feel broader without actually slowing down.
          
            Pop
            Hip-hop
            Rock
            Drum set
          
        

        
          
            New Orleans second line
            secondline
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Kick on every beat; snare on the "and-of-1" and "and-of-3." The marching parade groove of New Orleans brass bands; adopted by jazz funk, R&B, and rock drummers (the Meters, Allen Toussaint, Dr. John).
          
            Funk
            New Orleans
            Jazz
            Drum set
            Marching
          
        

      
    

    
      Waltz & Dance
      

        
          
            Waltz
            waltz
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beat 1, chord on beats 2 and 3. The universal dance-band formula for 3/4 time. The slight delay before the chord creates the characteristic lilt that distinguishes waltz from a march.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Piano
            Orchestra
          
        

        
          
            Viennese waltz
            viennese
            3/4
            ▶
          
          
          A short downbeat chord followed by slightly-early beats 2 and 3 (the "anticipated" Viennese lilt). The elastic timing distinguishes the Strauss concert hall waltz from the plainer ballroom waltz.
          
            Dance
            Classical
            Romantic
            Orchestra
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Boom-chick
            oompah
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root on the downbeat, chord on every other beat. The engine of polka, march, and German dance-band styles; derived from tuba–horn interplay in brass ensembles.
          
            Folk
            Polka
            March
            Brass
            Accordion
          
        

      
    

    
      Folk & Country
      

        
          
            Folk — alternating bass
            folk
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Alternating root–fifth bass note with a chord on the off-beat. The defining guitar and banjo accompaniment pattern in American folk, bluegrass, and country; also called the "Carter scratch."
          
            Folk
            Country
            Bluegrass
            Guitar
            Banjo
          
        

      
    

    
      Pop & Rock
      

        
          
            Pop / ballad
            pop
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Bass on beats 1 and 3, steady quarter-note chords on all beats. The most common piano and keyboard pattern in popular music since the 1950s.
          
            Pop
            Rock
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Driving 8ths
            driving8
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Steady eighth-note chords with no gaps. Propulsive and energetic; fills every subdivision. Found across rock, country, and pop guitar — sometimes called a "strum pattern."
          
            Rock
            Country
            Pop
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Offbeat chords
            offbeat
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Chord only on the off-beats, silence on the downbeats. The defining rhythmic gesture of ska and reggae; known as the "skank" or "chop." In reggae, the kick lands on beat 3 (the "one-drop").
          
            Ska
            Reggae
            Guitar
            Keyboard
          
        

      
    

    
      Classical & Piano
      

        
          
            Block chords
            block
            any
            ▶
          
          
          All voices together on every beat, sustained until the next chord. The simplest possible accompaniment; used for chorale writing, teaching chord shapes, and very slow tempos.
          
            Classical
            Chorale
            Piano
            Keyboard
          
        

        
          
            Piano arpeggio ↑
            arpflow
            4/4
            ▶
          
          
          Rising arpeggios through the full bar (root–third–fifth–octave). Characteristic of Romantic-era piano writing and nocturne accompaniment; adds forward motion when chord changes are sparse.
          
            Classical
            Romantic
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Arpeggio (root–5th)
            arpcell
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root and fifth as individual tones in a repeating per-beat cell. Creates a light, open texture that suggests harmonic motion without dense block chords; useful for harp or guitar figuration.
          
            Classical
            Pop
            Harp
            Guitar
            Piano
          
        

        
          
            Bass line (roots)
            bassroot
            any
            ▶
          
          
          Root note only in the bass, no chord voices above. Use as a harmonic foundation when the melody instrument carries the full harmonic content, or when learning to hear bass motion in isolation.
          
            Teaching
            Minimal
            Bass
          
        

      
    

  

  
  

    
      Piano & Keyboard
      
        
          Block chordsblockany
          Sustained block voicing on every beat. The starting point for learning chord shapes and for chorale-style writing.
          ClassicalChorale
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Left-hand bass on 1, right-hand chord on 2–3. The standard piano waltz texture from Chopin through the ballroom repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Pop / balladpopany
          Bass on 1 and 3, chords on every beat. Ubiquitous in pop piano; easy to adapt to either hands-together or stride-style playing.
          PopRock
        
        
          Piano arpeggio ↑arpflow4/4
          Rising broken chord through the full bar. Nocturne and ballad texture; standard left-hand figure in Romantic piano writing.
          ClassicalRomantic
        
        
          Viennese waltzviennese3/4
          Elastic 3/4 with the characteristic early-beat anticipation. Strauss orchestra and salon piano repertoire.
          DanceClassical
        
        
          Jazz Charlestoncharleston4/4
          Syncopated 4/4 comping with a chord on beat 1 and the and-of-2. Common in Stride, Swing, and mainstream jazz piano.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Jazz waltzjazzwaltz3/4
          Swung bass on 1, light chord on 3. The texture of jazz piano trios playing in 3 — Evans, Peterson, Monk.
          JazzBebop
        
      
    

    
      Guitar & Plucked Strings
      
        
          Folk — alternating bassfolkany
          Thumb alternates root–fifth in the bass; fingers strum the chord on the off-beat. The foundational fingerpicking and flatpicking pattern in folk, bluegrass, and country guitar.
          FolkCountryBluegrass
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving8any
          Steady downstroke eighth notes, no rests. The strum pattern behind countless rock, country, and pop songs.
          RockCountryPop
        
        
          Offbeat chordsoffbeatany
          The ska/reggae "skank": chord only between the beats. In reggae the downstroke is muted, leaving only the upstroke chop.
          SkaReggae
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Tresillo bass with off-beat chords. João Gilberto's original bossa guitar part is the blueprint; the pattern is also widely adapted to keyboard.
          LatinBrazilianJazz
        
        
          Arpeggio (root–5th)arpcellany
          Open-voiced ascending tones per beat. Evokes harp, classical guitar, and lute figuration; widely used in Renaissance and Baroque lute tablature.
          ClassicalPop
        
      
    

    
      Brass & Ensemble
      
        
          Boom-chickoompahany
          Tuba carries the root on 1; horns answer with the chord on 2 (and 4). The pattern maps directly to the brass section interplay in polka bands, march bands, and German Blasmusik.
          PolkaMarchFolk
        
        
          Tangotango4/4
          Habanera cell in the bass with syncopated upper chords. In Argentine tango this interplay moves between bandoneón and piano; in orchestral tango (Piazzolla) it drives the entire ensemble.
          LatinArgentine
        
      
    

    
      Bass & Foundation
      
        
          Bass line (roots)bassrootany
          Root note only, no chords. Use this when practicing bass lines in isolation, or when the melody is dense enough to imply the harmony on its own.
          TeachingMinimal
        
      
    

    
      Drum Set
      
        
          Backbeatbackbeat4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The universal pop and rock groove; the first drum pattern most students encounter.
          PopRock
        
        
          Driving 8thsdriving84/4
          Continuous eighth notes on the hi-hat with backbeat snare. Energetic pop and rock feel; common in anthemic and uptempo styles.
          PopRock
        
        
          Ska / reggae (one-drop)ska4/4
          Kick displaced to beat 3; snare and hi-hat emphasise the off-beats. The rhythmic foundation of ska, rocksteady, and roots reggae.
          ReggaeSka
        
        
          Swing — ride cymbalswing_ride4/4
          Swung ride pattern with kick and snare on beats 2 and 4. The standard jazz ride pattern from Swing through bebop.
          JazzSwing
        
        
          Swing — hi-hatswing_hats4/4
          Swung quarter-note hi-hat pulse; lighter texture than ride-cymbal swing. Used in small-group jazz and ballad settings.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Swing — open hi-hatswing_hats_open4/4
          Swung hi-hat opening on beats 2 and 4; airy, washy texture. Common in contemporary jazz and fusion where the drummer wants more cymbal wash than the closed-hat version.
          JazzFusion
        
        
          Swing — brushesswing_brushes4/4
          Wire-brush swirl with soft backbeat. Quiet jazz trio and intimate club setting; the standard brush technique for standards and ballads.
          JazzBallad
        
        
          Jazz waltz — ridejazzwaltz_ride3/4
          Swung ride in 3; kick on beat 1, light snare elsewhere. The jazz-waltz drum feel behind Bill Evans, Miles Davis, and the post-bop trio repertoire.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Jazz waltz — hi-hatjazzwaltz_hats3/4
          Closed hi-hat pulse in 3 with a light swing feel; more understated than the ride-cymbal version. Used in intimate trio settings where the drummer wants less projection.
          JazzWaltz
        
        
          Bossa novabossa4/4
          Ride cymbal tresillo with side-stick; the drum kit adaptation of Brazilian percussion. Foundational in bossa nova and samba-jazz.
          LatinBossa
        
        
          Tango (habanera)tango4/4
          Habanera kick cell with closed hi-hat. The rhythmic engine of Argentine tango and early-20th-century Latin dance music.
          LatinTango
        
        
          Son montuno (clave)montuno4/4
          Cuban clave rhythm on the kick; snare and hi-hat fill the groove. The drum kit version of the son montuno pattern.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Waltzwaltz3/4
          Kick on beat 1, hi-hat on 2 and 3. Straightforward triple-meter groove for waltzes, country, and folksong accompaniment.
          DanceFolk
        
        
          Compound (6/8)compound66/8
          Kick on the two main beats, hi-hat subdivisions filling the compound pulse. Used in jigs, compound-feel pop, and gospel 6/8.
          FolkGospel
        
        
          Half-time feelhalftime4/4
          Snare on beat 3 only; kick and hi-hat fill the rest. Makes the bar feel twice as wide without changing tempo. Widely used in hip-hop, stadium rock, and ballad bridges.
          PopHip-hopRock
        
        
          Funkfunk4/4
          Kick on beats 1 and 3; syncopated snare on the "and-of-2" and "and-of-4"; hi-hat on all eighths. The foundational James Brown / Clyde Stubblefield groove.
          FunkR&B
        
        
          New Orleans second linesecondline4/4
          Kick on every beat, snare on the upbeats of 1 and 3. The marching street-parade groove; adopted by the Meters, Dr. John, and rock drummers worldwide.
          FunkNew Orleans
        
        
          Sambasamba4/4
          Surdo kick on beats 2 and 4; snare on beat 3; hi-hat throughout. The drum kit adaptation of the samba bateria; common in Brazilian jazz and fusion.
          LatinBrazilian
        
        
          Mambomambo4/4
          Kick on beat 1 and the "and-of-3" (a clave-derived anticipation); snare on beat 3. The driving groove of 1940s Havana; ancestor of modern salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Calypso / mentocalypso4/4
          Floating kick (no downbeat on 1); side-stick on beat 3; hi-hat emphasises the upbeats. The Trinidadian and Jamaican afterbeat; ancestral to ska and reggae.
          CaribbeanReggae
        
      
    

    
      Hand Percussion
      
        
          Bongo — martillobongo_martillo4/4
          Steady eighth-note alternation between hi and lo bongo; the "hammer" pattern. The default timekeeping groove in Cuban son and salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Bongo — quarterbongo_slow4/4
          Quarter-note hi/lo alternation; a relaxed, open texture. Works well as a simplified bongo part for classroom or beginner settings.
          LatinTeaching
        
        
          Conga — tumbaoconga_tumbao4/4
          Open tone on the and-of-4, muted tones elsewhere. The foundational Cuban conga pattern; ubiquitous in salsa and son.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — tumbao (dense)conga_tumbao_dense4/4
          Eight-note tumbao with slap and open tone variations; a fuller, more active feel than the standard four-note version.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — sonconga_son4/4
          Alternating lo-conga open tones across the bar; simpler and more open than the tumbao. Common in son cubano and early salsa.
          LatinCuban
        
        
          Conga — waltzconga_waltz3/4
          Conga tones on the three main beats in 3/4; pairs with Latin waltz and compound-feel songs.
          LatinWaltz
        
        
          Conga — 6/8conga_6_86/8
          Open and muted conga tones across the compound-triple pulse. Works with 6/8 Afro-Cuban styles and compound jigs.
          LatinAfro-Cuban

The routine

title: Vocal Warm-up
text:
How it works

Body first, then breath, then voice. Stretches loosen the neck, shoulders, jaw and ribs, which all pull on the larynx. Breathing steps wake up the low, wide breath. The singing starts on hums and lip trills (semi-occluded sounds that are easy on the folds) and only then opens onto vowels, wider leaps and the top of the range.
The piano plays the starting chord, then the pattern with you, then moves up a half step. It climbs from the low middle of your voice to a comfortable top (not your highest note) and comes back down. Set Range if it sits too high or low.
The band plays two short grooves: one to sing a scale over as the key climbs, and a slow one to hum over as a cool-down.
Gentle routines stay lower, shorter and softer; Performing soon adds agility and a wider top, and ends ready rather than cooled down.







Warning



Stop if anything hurts, tickles or feels tight. Warm-ups should feel easy: if a note strains, let the pattern go by and come back on the way down. Sip water between steps.

title: How published sources classify Herbie Hancock’s “Watermelon Man” with respect to the blues
text:
Note on method: quotes below come from WebFetch page summaries (a small model extracting text), so treat wording as near-exact but not guaranteed verbatim. No print source (Gioia, Real Book, Sher, Aebersold, Grove, Penguin, Pond, Gluck) could be read directly.




No lead-sheet or book source could be verified. Every web database/education page that states a form calls it a 16-bar blues (or “altered”/“extended” blues). Gioia’s entry (p. 446) exists but its wording was not obtained.




Standard Repertoire (standardrepertoire.com) lists length “16 bars” and subtitles it “Altered blues recorded by Herbie as a hard bop song, and later in a fusion style”; it lists style as “Swing” (an oddity). — Standard Repertoire
AllSolos lists form as “Blues - 16 bars”, “built on an extended blues structure”, “bluesy, danceable riff”. — AllSolos
Learn Jazz Standards: “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove, originally a latin-rock style, and later funk.” — learnjazzstandards.com
Ted Gioia, The Jazz Standards (Oxford, 2012): a Google Books catalog page indicates the Watermelon Man entry is on p. 446 (per search-tool summary). Entry text NOT obtained. — Google Books
Swiss-jazz.ch lead sheet PDF (Flavio Goulart de Andrade, 2007) exists; its search snippet shows changes F7 / B-flat 7 / C7 pattern, but the PDF is image-only and could not be read or verified. — PDF





Amateur/educational databases converge on “16-bar blues” with qualifiers “altered” or “extended”; none say “not a blues”.





Real Book (Hal Leonard), New Real Book (Sher), iReal Pro, jazzstandards.com (search returned no page), Aebersold volumes, Hal Leonard Play-Along: no labels found/verifiable.
Gioia’s exact wording unavailable.







Education sites teach it as a 16-bar blues: bars 1-8 like a normal blues, bars 9-16 an extended/varied ending. Wikipedia’s “Sixteen-bar blues” cites it only uncited.




Jazzfuel (Nick Lea): “essentially a sixteen-bar blues”; “the first 8 bars mimic a classic blues exactly”; “the following 8 are an elongated variation of the regular final section”; “a healthy dose of the blues with a bit of gospel thrown in”; also “‘straight-eighths’ latin-rock style groove” and “an early example of what would become known as Latin boogaloo”. — Jazzfuel
FretDojo: “it’s a 16 bar blues, rather than a 12 bar blues” (extra changes from bar 8 to 12); piano riff “combines elements of bebop, jazz and R&B – with a pop twist to boot.” — FretDojo
Wikipedia “Sixteen-bar blues”: “This can be heard, for example, in ‘Watermelon Man’ by Herbie Hancock.” No inline citation; the preceding variation sentence is tagged [citation needed]; none of the three listed references (Horn 1994 review; Hal Leonard “The Blues” 1995 pp. 112-113) mention the tune. Trace ends there: unsourced. — Wikipedia
Old Wikipedia mirror (2006 snapshot): 16-bar form “is considered an elongated 12 bar blues” (via search summary; I did not open the page). — mirror
Harmonica forum post (via search summary, unopened): first eight bars match a 12-bar blues; the second eight alternate IV and V three times. — forum
Jazzguitar.be lesson/forum exist but returned 403/blog not read directly. — jazzguitar.be





The “elongated 12-bar blues” framing (bars 1-8 blues-like) is the common teaching line; it is a form claim, not a genre claim.





Mark Levine, Berklee, Open Music Theory, musictheory.net, StudyBass, school band arrangements: nothing found.







Critics use genre labels (hard bop, soul jazz, funk, jazz-funk, boogaloo) and “bluesy”; none found calls it a 12/16-bar “blues” formally, and none found denies it. No dissent located.




Wikipedia (composition): “‘Watermelon Man’ is written in a sixteen-bar blues form.” (uncited); infobox genres “Hard bop”, “soul jazz” (uncited); “The tune drew on elements of R&B, soul jazz, and bebop” (Creswell, 1001 Songs, 2006, p. 333); first version “recorded in a hard bop style” (Brackett, New Rolling Stone Album Guide, 2004, p. 361); Head Hunters “funk version” (Brackett); Santamaria cha-cha (Gerard 2001); boogaloo origin (Flores 2000, p. 93); “over two hundred” recordings (Santoro 2004 p. 86). — Wikipedia
Wikipedia (Takin’ Off): “The bluesy track ‘Watermelon Man’…” cited to Martin & Waters 2005, p. 311; album genres soul jazz, hard bop; AllMusic Steve Huey (2011) 4.5 stars; Penguin Guide (Cook & Morton, 9th ed. 2008, p. 640) 3.5 stars; review texts not shown. — Wikipedia
Search summary of Huey’s AllMusic review (reprint, not read directly): hard bop with “funky piano riffing”; Huey calls “Empty Pockets” bluesy rather than Watermelon Man. Unverified. — Takin’ Off summary
uDiscover (Charles Waring): Hancock quoted calling it “funky”; 1973 version “a radical jazz-funk makeover”. — uDiscover
Superbrass (search snippet): “based on a 16 bar blues riff” drawing on R&B, soul, jazz, bebop, gospel. — Superbrass





Dominant critical frame: soul-jazz/hard bop/funk with a blues-derived form; “bluesy” is common, “a blues” is mostly in education/form descriptions.





Grove, Gioia History of Jazz, Gluck, Pond (Head Hunters), actual AllMusic and Penguin text: not accessed. No source arguing “not a blues” found (absence after limited search).







Only the Grammy Hall of Fame fact (Santamaria’s version, inducted 1998) turned up; no official description of its form.




Santamaria’s version inducted into Grammy Hall of Fame 1998, #10 Hot 100 April 1963 — Wikipedia





Library of Congress (National Recording Registry) and Blue Note descriptions: not found.






Support: nearly all form descriptions say 16-bar blues; sole concern is that it is an extended/altered one (bars 9-16 vary the 12-bar ending) and genre labels are soul jazz/funk/boogaloo.
Weakest link: Wikipedia sixteen-bar page unsourced; print authorities unverified.

title: Definitions of “a blues”: form, harmony, melody, genre; status of 8-/16-bar and blues-derived tunes
text:
Research limits: paywalled/print sources (Grove, Levine, Coker, Aebersold, Kubik, Evans, Oliver, Titon, Schuller, Murray, Baraka) were NOT directly accessible; claims about them are only as reported by the secondary/open sources cited. Items from memory only are listed under Gaps as leads, not findings.




Reference/pedagogical works treat the 12-bar, I-IV-V, dominant-7th, AAB, blue-note package as the prototype. Scholars note it is a standardization (commercial recording era) and not a universal criterion; early blues had no single structure.




Blues is described as both a genre and a form; defining elements listed as call-and-response, blues scale, specific chord progressions, blue notes (flattened 3rd/5th/7th); “few characteristics common to all blues”. — Wikipedia, Blues (secondary/popular)
12-bar form: three closely related chords (I, IV, V) in fixed order, commonly dominant 7ths, often ending in a turnaround; became increasingly common in the 1920s-30s with recorded singers. — Wikipedia, Blues
Early blues lacked a standard structure: Howard W. Odum documented secular songs c.1908-10 with freely repeated/extended verses; David Evans notes standardization came through commercial recording; pre-1920 field recordings (Lead Belly, Henry Thomas) show many structures other than 8/12/16 bars; Walter Vinson’s “Sitting on Top of the World” is 9 bars. — Wikipedia, Blues (relaying Evans/Odum; check originals)
Lyric AAB: single line repeated four times in early verses; AAB became most common in first decades of 20th c.; W.C. Handy said AAB avoided the “monotony of lines repeated three times”; early published examples “Dallas Blues” (Wand, 1912), “St. Louis Blues” (Handy, 1914). — Wikipedia, Blues
Scholarly baseline in MTO: blues “usually associated with strophic form”, “a series of verses, with a 12-bar blues progression underlying an aab melodic and lyrical structure”, citing Titon (1977, 142), Taft (1983, xiii), von Appen & Frei-Hauenschild (2015, 48-49); de Clercq (2012, 124) calls the 12-bar aab the “classic” approach, dominant 1925-1966 in Carter’s corpus. — Carter, “Beyond Strophic: Prolonged Refrains, Choruses, and Bridges in the Blues, 1923-1966,” Music Theory Online 25.3 (2025)
Newman White (1929, 207): “the stanza, and not the song, is the only true unit” (blues stanza as unit of analysis). — Carter, MTO (same link)
Open Music Theory (Hughes/Lavengood, Gotham et al.): dominant 7th is the defining feature of blues harmony; all chords in standard 12-bar are dominant 7ths; blues emphasises plagal over authentic cadence. — search summary of Open Music Theory “Blues Harmony” (page itself returned 403; summary only)
Titon: “downhome blues scale” derived from 1926-30 recordings, spans a tenth rather than an octave (Titon 1977, 155, as reported). Titon’s study rests on 47 transcriptions (44 downhome + 3 vaudeville), mostly first stanza only. — Hein, “Blues tonality”; review/search result on Titon
Van der Merwe (1992, 119, 123): most altered degrees are 3rd, 7th, 5th, 6th; thirds in performance are mostly neutral rather than major/minor; blue notes have “melodic dissonance”. — Hein, “Blues tonality” (secondary report of Origins of the Popular Style)
Everett (2004, 17): blues melodies decorate major-mode harmony; blues tritones/half steps “intrinsically dissonant”. — Hein, “Blues tonality” (secondary)





A rigorous “is it a blues” test must separate prototype (12-bar AAB I-IV-V7) from criteria actually necessary; scholars (Evans via Wikipedia, Odum) show the prototype is historically a later standardization.





Could not access Grove “Blues” (Evans/Oliver), New Grove Dictionary of Jazz (Kernfeld), Schuller, Baraka, Murray’s text itself, or Evans’s Big Road Blues; no direct quotation obtained.







Reference and instructional sources uniformly treat 8-bar and 16-bar forms as blues forms (variants of the 12-bar, or of the 8-bar), and list “Watermelon Man” as a 16-bar blues. But these sources are mostly popular/pedagogical and tertiary; the one peer-reviewed treatment found (Carter, MTO 2025) frames 16-bar as a verse-chorus (8+8) hybrid and argues the blues is “inherently hybrid”, so non-12-bar forms remain blues.




8-bar blues: “second most common blues form” (Riker, Complete Blues Guitar Method, 1994, p. 91); IV typically at bar 3 not 5; I-V in bar 2 a characteristic (Riker); “common to folk, rock, and jazz forms” (Barrett 2000, p. 8). Examples: “Trouble in Mind” (Hill, 1926), “How Long Blues” (Carr, 1928), “Nobody Knows You When You’re Down and Out” (B. Smith, 1929), “Key to the Highway” (Broonzy, 1941), “Worried Life Blues” (Big Maceo, 1941; “probably the most common eight-bar progression”). — Wikipedia, Eight-bar blues
16-bar blues: “a variation on the standard twelve-bar blues, or less commonly on the eight-bar blues”; most versions lengthen one section or repeat a middle section/transition; also common in ragtime (Horn 1994, Popular Music 13/3, 366-369, review). Examples: “Hoochie Coochie Man” (extends opening tonic section), “Going Down the Road Feeling Bad” (repeats middle section), “Watermelon Man” (repeats the transition between chord 9 [V] and 10 [IV] twice – claim flagged “citation needed”). — Wikipedia, Sixteen-bar blues
Wikipedia “Blues” lists “Watermelon Man” and “Sweet 16 Bars” (Ray Charles) with 8/16-bar progressions. — Wikipedia, Blues
“Varying the section lengths can produce eight-bar or sixteen-bar blues” (unsourced). — Wikipedia, Twelve-bar blues
Music-theory-for-dummies style sources also list 24- and 32-bar blues. — Dummies, popular genres and forms (search snippet only)
Scholarly classification of 16 bars: de Clercq (2012, 142) calls an 8+8 form “hybrid 16-bar blues”; Carter reads it as verse (8) + chorus (8), clearer verse-chorus form; also 4+8 “prolonged refrain” (Titon 1977a, 326 n.46, “quatrain-refrain”), a “chorusification” of the 12-bar scheme. — Carter, MTO 2025
Carter’s inclusion criterion is genre-based: songs “typically categorized as a ‘blues’ song”; core claim: “Blues that connected with the popular mainstream formally and otherwise did not cease to be blues”; “the blues is an inherently hybrid genre at its heart” (citing Wald 2004, xiii-xiv, 232; Floyd 1995, 78); critiques Middleton (1972, 52-53) as “enforcing a notion of blues purity”. — Carter, MTO 2025
Von Appen & Frei-Hauenschild (2015, 22-23) define a harmonic “scheme” (slow harmonic rhythm, conventional pattern) – a way to treat blues as a scheme rather than a fixed bar count. — Carter, MTO 2025





Two classification logics: (a) “variant” (extension of 12-bar by lengthening/repeating a section) – puts Watermelon Man inside blues; (b) “hybrid/verse-chorus” – depends on whether sections are derived from blues phrase structure. Watermelon Man’s 8+8 vs 12+4 reading matters (see section 5).
Support for 8-/16-bar status is mostly pedagogical/encyclopedic; a report should flag that evidence quality.





No Grove/Evans/Oliver/Titon statement on 8- or 16-bar forms found. No peer-reviewed source naming Watermelon Man found. “Trouble in Mind” 1926 recording attribution disagrees across sources (Bertha “Chippie” Hill vs Bertha Hill) – unresolved.







Little reliable material was accessible. Jazz-theory texts accessible via secondary sources treat “blues” as a named chord-change form with jazz variants (bebop blues, minor blues); I found no source defining “blues-based” vs “a blues.”




“Blues changes” = twelve-bar progression; jazz variant “bebop blues” resembles Parker’s “Now’s the Time,” “Billie’s Bounce,” Rollins’s “Tenor Madness” (Spitzer 2001, Jazz Theory Handbook, p. 62); minor 12-bar blues examples: Coltrane’s “Equinox,” “Mr. P.C.” (Spitzer 2001, p. 63); V chord may be V7 or v7. — Wikipedia, Twelve-bar blues
Quick-change (“quick to four”) variant, IV in bar 2 (McCumber 2006, p. 25); V-IV-I-I in third line considered standard in shuffle blues (Gerow & Tanner 1984, p. 37). — same
Albert Murray separates “blues” as mood from “blues music” (essentially dance music): “The blues as such are synonymous with low spirits. Blues music is not.”; blues idiom = stylized music of creative artists. — Washington Examiner; Pistelli on The Hero and the Blues (secondary)
Wikipedia: “blues” as a distinct genre arose with the 1920s recording industry and Great Migration, as a marketing term; musicians often called themselves “songsters”. — Wikipedia, Blues





“Blues” can denote (1) form/changes, (2) idiom (Murray), (3) marketing genre – these yield different answers for Watermelon Man.





No access to Levine, Coker, Aebersold, Berklee, Kernfeld, Real Book genre labels. Web search for Levine returned only spam PDF sites (discarded). “Blues-based/bluesy” distinctions: nothing found.







Scholars generally treat blues tonality as a scale/pitch-set phenomenon (blue notes, neutral intervals) layered over, or in tension with, major-mode I-IV-V harmony; several argue for a distinct system. No consensus; dominant-7th tonic as a stable tonic is widely noted.




Kubik: blues tonality grounded in lower/middle overtones of scales degrees 1 and 4 (Kubik 2008, 176-177); blue notes “in tune” relative to original pitch set; V7 “frequently absent, especially in rural blues” (Kubik 2005, 207). — Hein, “Blues tonality” (secondary relay; verify against Kubik, Africa and the Blues 1999 / 2005-2008 works)
Fahey (on Charley Patton): two “blues modes” – Dorian+Mixolydian union, and Mixolydian alone. — Hein
Tagg: blues scale as extension of minor pentatonic; blues tonality substitutes a major triad for the tonic of diatonic minor/Dorian; loop grooves create “places to be” rather than large-scale tonal scheme. — Hein (2009; no page)
Weisethaunet (2001, 101): blue notes as expressive pitch play inseparable from rhythm and timbre. Tallmadge (1984, 155): pitches as “mobile, unstable units”. Cutting (2018): vocal-pitch analysis, three blue-note clusters (neutral third, between 4 and #4, around b7); possible derivation from just 5:6:7:9. Jaffe (2011, 35-37) defends “major blues scale” and bVI7. Tymoczko (2011, 374) reads blues as deliberate harmonic clash (disputed by Hein). — Hein
Dominant-7th chords in blues “default sound rather than a force pulling toward resolution” (interpretive). — Beatkitchen (low-grade, popular)





The “dominant-seventh tonic is stable” idea and the Tagg/Fahey modal accounts mean I7-IV7-V7 harmony can itself signal blues tonality independent of bar count.





Not obtained: Gauldin, Doll Hearing Harmony, Moore, Everett primary texts; Van der Merwe and Kubik primary pages (reported only via Hein, a blog).








“essentially a sixteen-bar blues: the first 8 bars mimic a classic blues exactly, whilst the following 8 are an elongated variation of the regular final section”; in F, straight-eighths groove; “a healthy dose of the blues with a bit of gospel”. — JazzFuel, Watermelon Man (popular)
Chart (F): F7 x4 | Bb7 x2, F7 x2 | C7 Bb7 C7 Bb7 | C7 Bb7 F7 x2 (i.e. I7 4 bars, IV7 2, I7 2, then V7/IV7 alternation 4, then V7 IV7 I7 I7). — saxstation (teaching site; one source; verify against the published lead sheet)
Wikipedia lists it under 16-bar blues (repeat of the V-IV transition), flagged “citation needed”. — Wikipedia, Sixteen-bar blues





On the saxstation chart, bars 1-8 are I-I-I-I-IV-IV-I-I (a blues first 8 with the 12-bar’s bars 1-8 in standard order), bars 9-16 are V-IV-V-IV-V-IV-I-I = the 12-bar’s V-IV-I-I tail with the V-IV doubled. So it is read as 12-bar + repeated V-IV (a “variant” account) – but a 4/4/8 or 8/8 (verse/refrain) view is also possible; sources disagree with each other on which framing.
Under criteria from sections 1-4: dominant-7th I-IV-V ✔; extended 12-bar phrase logic ✔; AAB lyric N/A (instrumental; melody is riff-based – not checked); blue-note melody not verified here.





No tune’s melody/scale analysis found; no peer-reviewed source on Watermelon Man; no confirmation of Hancock’s own genre description.

title: Definitions of “a blues”: form, harmony, melody, genre; status of 8-/16-bar and blues-derived tunes
text:
Reference/pedagogical works treat the 12-bar, I-IV-V, dominant-7th, AAB, blue-note package as the prototype. Scholars note it is a standardization (commercial recording era) and not a universal criterion; early blues had no single structure.




Blues is described as both a genre and a form; defining elements listed as call-and-response, blues scale, specific chord progressions, blue notes (flattened 3rd/5th/7th); “few characteristics common to all blues”. — Wikipedia, Blues (secondary/popular)
12-bar form: three closely related chords (I, IV, V) in fixed order, commonly dominant 7ths, often ending in a turnaround; became increasingly common in the 1920s-30s with recorded singers. — Wikipedia, Blues
Early blues lacked a standard structure: Howard W. Odum documented secular songs c.1908-10 with freely repeated/extended verses; David Evans notes standardization came through commercial recording; pre-1920 field recordings (Lead Belly, Henry Thomas) show many structures other than 8/12/16 bars; Walter Vinson’s “Sitting on Top of the World” is 9 bars. — Wikipedia, Blues (relaying Evans/Odum; check originals)
Lyric AAB: single line repeated four times in early verses; AAB became most common in first decades of 20th c.; W.C. Handy said AAB avoided the “monotony of lines repeated three times”; early published examples “Dallas Blues” (Wand, 1912), “St. Louis Blues” (Handy, 1914). — Wikipedia, Blues
Scholarly baseline in MTO: blues “usually associated with strophic form”, “a series of verses, with a 12-bar blues progression underlying an aab melodic and lyrical structure”, citing Titon (1977, 142), Taft (1983, xiii), von Appen & Frei-Hauenschild (2015, 48-49); de Clercq (2012, 124) calls the 12-bar aab the “classic” approach, dominant 1925-1966 in Carter’s corpus. — Carter, “Beyond Strophic: Prolonged Refrains, Choruses, and Bridges in the Blues, 1923-1966,” Music Theory Online 25.3 (2025)
Newman White (1929, 207): “the stanza, and not the song, is the only true unit” (blues stanza as unit of analysis). — Carter, MTO (same link)
Open Music Theory (Hughes/Lavengood, Gotham et al.): dominant 7th is the defining feature of blues harmony; all chords in standard 12-bar are dominant 7ths; blues emphasises plagal over authentic cadence. — search summary of Open Music Theory “Blues Harmony” (page itself returned 403; summary only)
Titon: “downhome blues scale” derived from 1926-30 recordings, spans a tenth rather than an octave (Titon 1977, 155, as reported). Titon’s study rests on 47 transcriptions (44 downhome + 3 vaudeville), mostly first stanza only. — Hein, “Blues tonality”; review/search result on Titon

title: Watermelon Man (Hancock, 1962): form, harmony, origins, later versions
text:
Method note: about 15 web calls. I did not reach a Real Book / Hal Leonard chart, jazzstandards.com, iReal Pro, the Hancock memoir text, Pond’s book, or the NPR transcript (the NPR fetch timed out twice; jazzguitar.be returned 403). Hancock quotes below are taken from secondary pages that quote him, not from the primary text. I could not check them against the memoir.




The head is 16 bars in F. It is a 12-bar-blues skeleton with the last four-plus bars reworked: bars 1-8 are a standard blues opening, and the bar 9-10 pair (C7 / Bb7) is stated three times before a 2-bar return to F7. Every source with chords uses dominant sevenths on F, Bb and C only; none shows an Eb7 or other bVII chord in the 1962 head.




Bar-by-bar chart (one community forum post, not an authoritative lead sheet): bars 1-4 F7; 5-6 Bb7; 7-8 F7; 9 C7; 10 Bb7; 11 C7; 12 Bb7; 13 C7; 14 Bb7; 15-16 F7. The key is not stated on the page. The page itself calls the form “a blues modified a little bit”. — saxstation.com
Ethan Hein’s analysis agrees with that chart: “It’s essentially a twelve-bar blues in F, but with bars nine and ten repeated three times.” He adds that the last two bars are harmonically identical to the first four, so chorus boundaries are hard to hear, and Hancock exploits this on the 1973 recording. (Counting: 8 + 3x2 + 2 = 16.) — Ethan Hein
Key of F: “It is most commonly played in the key of F”; “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove, originally a latin-rock style, and later funk.” — learnjazzstandards.com. Hooktheory also lists F major (128 BPM, 4/4) with I7, IV7 and V7 chords, though the page’s chord-string notation is unclear. — Hooktheory
JazzFuel says: 16-bar blues, “first 8 bars follow a classic blues pattern, and the last 8 are an extended variation of the final section”; written in F; no chord changes given. It points to a Hancock-chaired Jazz Day score (jazzday.com, “WATERMELON-MAN-s2-Full-Score.pdf”) that I did not retrieve. — JazzFuel
Wikipedia: “sixteen-bar blues form”, drawing on R&B, soul jazz and bebop; Hancock’s chordal work draws on gospel. — Wikipedia
The Herbie Hancock official site’s Takin’ Off page quotes the liner notes as “a strongly gospel-infused 16-bar theme”. It says the opening piano vamp is a gospel-style figure (quarter rest, two eighths, an eighth and a dotted quarter), the horns state the theme mainly in unison, solos run Hubbard, Gordon, Hancock, and the master runs 7:09. It says Lion immediately heard the potential in the “modified blues”. — herbiehancock.com
A UVM blog says dominant sevenths on “the four chords of the original” (contrast Cantaloupe Island’s minor sevenths) and a 16-bar form with a similar bassline and piano figure to Cantaloupe Island. I count three chords in the saxstation chart, so “four” disagrees with that chart. — UVM blog
Personnel: Hancock, Dexter Gordon, Freddie Hubbard, Butch Warren, Billy Higgins. Recorded May 1962 (uDiscover). — Wikipedia; uDiscover
Billy Higgins’ feel, per Hancock (via uDiscover, quoting Possibilities): “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz” and a “great funky-jazz flavor”. — uDiscover





The C7 (V) to Bb7 (IV) alternation in bars 9-14 is a V-IV oscillation, which is a normal blues turnaround element, not a bVII-IV cadence. The suggested Eb7 does not appear in any source I found for the 1962 head; the only flat-side chords found are in the 1973 version (section 3).
This is a 12-bar blues with bars 9-12 (V IV V IV) stretched by one extra V-IV pair and a 2-bar tonic tag, which matches “sixteen-bar blues” usage.





No published lead sheet checked (Real Book, Hancock songbook, iReal, jazzstandards.com). Whether published charts differ from the record (e.g. substituted chords, 9ths, or a different key) is unverified.
No source I found describes the melody note by note (blue notes, minor pentatonic, blues scale). Only the general descriptions above exist. The melody having blue thirds or a minor pentatonic basis is unverified here; an ABC transcription from the Jazz Day score would settle it.
No source describes the bass line in detail beyond “similar bassline and piano accompaniment figure” to Cantaloupe Island, and the gospel-style piano vamp rhythm above. Whether the vamp is in F with b7 chord tones is not stated.
No source found for whether F is the written key in the Real Book.







Hancock ties the tune to the cry and horse-drawn wagon of a Chicago watermelon seller, says it took about 15 minutes to write, and says he wanted something real rather than a purely commercial tune. In the sources I reached he does not call it “a blues” or “bluesy”; that word comes from secondary writers.




1962 Takin’ Off liner notes (Hancock): “In reflecting on my childhood I recalled the cry of the watermelon man making his rounds through the back streets and alleys” (truncated in the source). Leonard Feather’s notes mention the 1938 Ellington record of the same title: “No connection.” — herbiehancock.com. Another page gives the same line with “Chicago’s South Side” wording, which is a secondary quotation. — Wikipedia, citing Santoro 2004 p. 86
Possibilities (2014), as quoted by uDiscover: “I grew up hearing the clackety-clack, clackety-clack of his horse-drawn wagon.” / “I’d heard the rhythmic clacking so many times, it was easy to turn it into a song patter.” / “I wrote out a funky arrangement, with the melody lilting over a rhythmic pattern”. Also “The only moment I remember worrying about was just before we played ‘Watermelon Man.’” — uDiscover. Not verified against the book.
MOJO interview: “the thing that kept hitting me was the watermelon man”; the vendor went “through the cobblestone alleys of Chicago with a horse-drawn carriage on wagonwheels, not tyres”; “It took 15 minutes to write.”; “I don’t wanna write a, quote, commercial tune just for the heck of it. I want it to be real.”; Donald Byrd’s advice: “half the record is for yourself, and half the record is for the company.” On the blues generally: “I’m from Chicago so I heard the real blues” and “I heard the real blues, Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf and a bunch of others.” — MOJO
Wikipedia states Hancock wrote the tune to help sell his debut and it was the first piece he composed with a commercial goal; he did not regard it as a sellout and called it one of his strongest pieces structurally (Lyons, 1989). That is Wikipedia’s paraphrase, not an exact Hancock quote. — Wikipedia
Ethan Hein says Hancock got the idea by transcribing street calls from women in his neighbourhood, citing context from a 1985 Steven Feld interview (a different quote from that interview about Ba-Benzele: “I could do it but I know that it’s OK ’cause its just a brothers kind of thing.”). — Ethan Hein
Liner notes via the official site: Hancock played the tune for Alfred Lion at his Blue Note audition and Lion asked for more originals. Donald Byrd urged him to play it for Mongo and to form Hancock Music publishing. — herbiehancock.com





The only “bluesy/soul-jazz” characterisation I found comes from reviewers and the label-site notes (“modified blues”, “gospel-infused”). Hancock’s own words in the reached sources stress street-vendor calls, Chicago, gospel/R&B listening and a commercial but “real” intent. The report should not attribute “blues” to Hancock.





Did not read the NPR 2014 transcript (https://www.npr.org/transcripts/354871509 surfaced in search but the fetch timed out), JazzTimes, DownBeat, Guardian, or the memoir text. The Lyons 1989 and Santoro 2004 citations are only second-hand through Wikipedia. Exact memoir wording about the “women calling out” or any “bluesy” intention is not located. One search summary said the mother was involved; no source confirmed this.







Mongo’s hit keeps the same 16-bar form and F7/Bb7/C7 harmony, slower, with a Latin (guajira-based) groove and congas, and one analyst hears two extra groove bars on the second head. It reached No. 10 on the Hot 100 (some sources say 11).




Hancock briefly subbed for Chick Corea in Mongo’s band; Donald Byrd urged him to play the tune; Mongo recorded a three-minute radio version on 17 Dec 1962, re-recorded for Battle; released early 1963 (infobox Feb 1963); No. 10 Hot 100 in April 1963; Grammy Hall of Fame 1998; sometimes called the start of boogaloo. — Wikipedia. JazzTimes also says No. 10. — JazzTimes obituary. Conflict: uDiscover says “No. 11”. — uDiscover
Form per Ethan Hein: the same as Hancock’s except that “on the second pass through the head Mongo adds two bars of groove”; slower, guajira-based Latin groove, melody dragged behind the beat. — Ethan Hein
Hancock (1998 notes, via official site): Mongo said “Keep playing!” and described it as “a tune the Cubans sang up in the mountains, a folk tune.” — herbiehancock.com





No chord chart for Mongo’s version; the claim that harmony is unchanged rests on Hein’s “form matches” statement only. Published sources on the Battle record’s tempo, key and arrangement credits were not reached.







The 1973 track is a re-arrangement in funk: about 75 BPM, no solos, an added chord and a new section modulating up a minor third replace the final bars. Sources agree on the Hindewhu intro; the details of the added chords vary.




Reworked by Hancock and Harvey Mason; only Head Hunters track not written for the album; 6:29. Personnel: Hancock (Rhodes, clavinet, synths), Maupin (soprano), Summers (percussion, beer bottle), Mason, Paul Jackson. — Wikipedia: Head Hunters; Wikipedia
Wikipedia: Hancock “added an eight-bar section”; Summers blows into bottles for the intro and outro imitating hindewhu; inspiration was the 1966 recording by Simha Arom and Geneviève Taurelle (the Ba-Benzele Pygmies). Wikipedia’s Head Hunters article marks the beer-bottle credit “[citation needed]”. — Wikipedia
Hein’s section map: about 75 BPM; no solos; “The last two bars of the form are replaced by a new section whose key jumps up a minor third”; sections labelled A (first half of 1962 head), B (bars 9-12 of the 1962 version) and C (new). Sequence: 15-bar hindewhu intro, bass enters (4), drums enter (4), clavinet (8), B (6), C (9), A (7, first Eb held over from the final Gb7 of C), B (6), C (3), A (7), B (6), C (9), outro groove (7), hindewhu fade. — Ethan Hein
UVM blog: the 1973 version kept “its progression (expanded to include one more chord, Ab7) and a vestige of its melody” and added a new groove and electric instruments. — UVM blog
Hein notes Madonna’s “Sanctuary” sample is a Mixolydian groove clashing with a natural-minor melody on top. — Ethan Hein





Hein’s “Gb7” and UVM’s “Ab7” are two different flat-side chords (a minor third above F7 would put chords in Ab). They may both be real (both are bVII-side/bIII-side colour); I cannot reconcile them without a transcription. Both are the only place any flat-side chord appears, and they belong to the 1973 version only.
The 1973 head is a re-built form that is no longer a plain 16-bar blues; the groove (Mixolydian vamp) is still blues-derived.





Pond’s 2005 book, the Head Hunters liner notes, and a Hancock 1979 Down Beat quote (“the attention is on the rhythmic interplay…”, via Wikipedia) were not read. No reliable chart of the 1973 harmony found. Bar counts in Hein’s map do not obviously sum to a single-form repeat; treat as one listener’s analysis.








Baba Brooks, “Watermelon Man Ska” (1963); the Manish Boys played it live 1964 (no recording); Manfred Mann EP “The One in the Middle” (1965); Big Mama Thornton at Newport Folk Festival (1969); David Benoit (2003). — Wikipedia
Wikipedia says the tune has been recorded over two hundred times. — same source.





Jon Hendricks lyrics and Manfred Mann’s form were not found. No form data on any of these covers.

title: Watermelon Man (Hancock, 1962): form, harmony, origins, later versions
text:
The head is 16 bars in F. It is a 12-bar-blues skeleton with the last four-plus bars reworked: bars 1-8 are a standard blues opening, and the bar 9-10 pair (C7 / Bb7) is stated three times before a 2-bar return to F7. Every source with chords uses dominant sevenths on F, Bb and C only; none shows an Eb7 or other bVII chord in the 1962 head.




Bar-by-bar chart (one community forum post, not an authoritative lead sheet): bars 1-4 F7; 5-6 Bb7; 7-8 F7; 9 C7; 10 Bb7; 11 C7; 12 Bb7; 13 C7; 14 Bb7; 15-16 F7. The key is not stated on the page. The page itself calls the form “a blues modified a little bit”. — saxstation.com
Ethan Hein’s analysis agrees with that chart: “It’s essentially a twelve-bar blues in F, but with bars nine and ten repeated three times.” He adds that the last two bars are harmonically identical to the first four, so chorus boundaries are hard to hear, and Hancock exploits this on the 1973 recording. (Counting: 8 + 3x2 + 2 = 16.) — Ethan Hein
Key of F: “It is most commonly played in the key of F”; “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove, originally a latin-rock style, and later funk.” — learnjazzstandards.com. Hooktheory also lists F major (128 BPM, 4/4) with I7, IV7 and V7 chords, though the page’s chord-string notation is unclear. — Hooktheory
JazzFuel says: 16-bar blues, “first 8 bars follow a classic blues pattern, and the last 8 are an extended variation of the final section”; written in F; no chord changes given. It points to a Hancock-chaired Jazz Day score (jazzday.com, “WATERMELON-MAN-s2-Full-Score.pdf”) that I did not retrieve. — JazzFuel
Wikipedia: “sixteen-bar blues form”, drawing on R&B, soul jazz and bebop; Hancock’s chordal work draws on gospel. — Wikipedia
The Herbie Hancock official site’s Takin’ Off page quotes the liner notes as “a strongly gospel-infused 16-bar theme”. It says the opening piano vamp is a gospel-style figure (quarter rest, two eighths, an eighth and a dotted quarter), the horns state the theme mainly in unison, solos run Hubbard, Gordon, Hancock, and the master runs 7:09. It says Lion immediately heard the potential in the “modified blues”. — herbiehancock.com
A UVM blog says dominant sevenths on “the four chords of the original” (contrast Cantaloupe Island’s minor sevenths) and a 16-bar form with a similar bassline and piano figure to Cantaloupe Island. I count three chords in the saxstation chart, so “four” disagrees with that chart. — UVM blog
Personnel: Hancock, Dexter Gordon, Freddie Hubbard, Butch Warren, Billy Higgins. Recorded May 1962 (uDiscover). — Wikipedia; uDiscover
Billy Higgins’ feel, per Hancock (via uDiscover, quoting Possibilities): “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz” and a “great funky-jazz flavor”. — uDiscover





The C7 (V) to Bb7 (IV) alternation in bars 9-14 is a V-IV oscillation, which is a normal blues turnaround element, not a bVII-IV cadence. The suggested Eb7 does not appear in any source I found for the 1962 head; the only flat-side chords found are in the 1973 version (section 3).
This is a 12-bar blues with bars 9-12 (V IV V IV) stretched by one extra V-IV pair and a 2-bar tonic tag, which matches “sixteen-bar blues” usage.





No published lead sheet checked (Real Book, Hancock songbook, iReal, jazzstandards.com). Whether published charts differ from the record (e.g. substituted chords, 9ths, or a different key) is unverified.
No source I found describes the melody note by note (blue notes, minor pentatonic, blues scale). Only the general descriptions above exist. The melody having blue thirds or a minor pentatonic basis is unverified here; an ABC transcription from the Jazz Day score would settle it.
No source describes the bass line in detail beyond “similar bassline and piano accompaniment figure” to Cantaloupe Island, and the gospel-style piano vamp rhythm above. Whether the vamp is in F with b7 chord tones is not stated.
No source found for whether F is the written key in the Real Book.

title: Watermelon Man (Hancock, 1962): form, harmony, origins, later versions
text:
Hancock ties the tune to the cry and horse-drawn wagon of a Chicago watermelon seller, says it took about 15 minutes to write, and says he wanted something real rather than a purely commercial tune. In the sources I reached he does not call it “a blues” or “bluesy”; that word comes from secondary writers.




1962 Takin’ Off liner notes (Hancock): “In reflecting on my childhood I recalled the cry of the watermelon man making his rounds through the back streets and alleys” (truncated in the source). Leonard Feather’s notes mention the 1938 Ellington record of the same title: “No connection.” — herbiehancock.com. Another page gives the same line with “Chicago’s South Side” wording, which is a secondary quotation. — Wikipedia, citing Santoro 2004 p. 86
Possibilities (2014), as quoted by uDiscover: “I grew up hearing the clackety-clack, clackety-clack of his horse-drawn wagon.” / “I’d heard the rhythmic clacking so many times, it was easy to turn it into a song patter.” / “I wrote out a funky arrangement, with the melody lilting over a rhythmic pattern”. Also “The only moment I remember worrying about was just before we played ‘Watermelon Man.’” — uDiscover. Not verified against the book.
MOJO interview: “the thing that kept hitting me was the watermelon man”; the vendor went “through the cobblestone alleys of Chicago with a horse-drawn carriage on wagonwheels, not tyres”; “It took 15 minutes to write.”; “I don’t wanna write a, quote, commercial tune just for the heck of it. I want it to be real.”; Donald Byrd’s advice: “half the record is for yourself, and half the record is for the company.” On the blues generally: “I’m from Chicago so I heard the real blues” and “I heard the real blues, Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf and a bunch of others.” — MOJO

That is Wikipedia’s paraphrase, not an exact Hancock quote. — Wikipedia

title: Guitar and Bass Setup Check
text:
A guitar that's hard to play, buzzes, or won't play in tune up the neck usually needs an adjustment, not a new guitar. Work through the
checks below with the instrument in tune (tune it here) and in your playing position. Each answer
goes into the list at the bottom: what's wrong, what to change, and who should change it: you, your teacher, or a repair tech.
Answers are kept in this browser.

Before anyone turns anything: the truss rod is a steel rod inside the neck. A quarter turn at a time, never forced,
and wait for the neck to settle before judging. Bridge screws are safe to turn and easy to undo; nut slots and acoustic saddles are not
(material taken off doesn't come back). When in doubt, it's a tech's job: a setup costs about as much as a few sets of strings.


  The instrument
  What is it? 
  Clear answers
  



  1. Neck relief: is the neck bowed?
  A neck should bow very slightly forward under string tension, so the vibrating string clears the frets. Put a capo at the 1st fret.
  With your right hand (or arm), press the lowest string down at the fret where the neck meets the body (around fret 14–17). The string is now a
  straight edge. Look at the gap between the string and the top of the 7th or 8th fret, and tap the string there: a tiny click means a small gap.
  The gap
  
    not checked
    none: the string touches, no click
    barely: a faint click
    a sheet of paper's thickness, a clear click
    a business card fits
    more than a business card
  
  or feeler gauge, mm 
  



  2. Where does it buzz?
  Play every string at every fret in each zone, at the strength you normally play (not harder: everything buzzes if you dig in). Listen
  acoustically, not through an amp: tick each place where a note buzzes or dies early. This is your ear's job, and the most telling test on the page.
  
  Only at one fret, on several strings?
  



  3. String height (action)
  Measure from the top of the 12th fret to the bottom of the string, with a steel ruler that reads half millimetres (no capo, nothing pressed).
  Lowest string, mm 
  Highest string, mm 
  



  4. The nut
  Press a string at the 3rd fret, and look at (and tap) the string over the 1st fret. Then play an open chord, then the same notes fretted near
  the nut: if the fretted ones sound sharp to your ear, the nut is likely high.
  Gap at the 1st fret
  not checkednone: string touches the 1st fret
  tiny: you can just see it, a clickclearly visible, and first-fret notes sound sharp



  5. Intonation: does it play in tune up the neck?
  On each string, play the harmonic at the 12th fret (touch lightly right over the fret wire, pick, lift), then press the 12th
  fret and pick. They are the same note when the string length is right. Listen first: is the fretted note the same, higher, or lower? Then let the
  microphone measure it (🎤 buttons; let each note ring for two seconds). Retune the open string before each one.
  
  With old strings this test lies: they play sharp up the neck however the saddles are set. Fit new strings first if they're
  more than a few months old.



  6. Anything else?
  
     It won't stay in tune
     Fret ends feel sharp at the edge of the neck
     Dents worn into the frets under the strings
     The bridge is lifting at the back (acoustic)
     A crack anywhere
     The truss rod won't turn, or is already very tight
     Crackles or cuts out (electric)
  



  What to do

title: Notation Rules
text:
What the entry pages do with the keys you play: which notes are chords and which melody, where each one lands on the bars, how long it is written, how it is spelled. Part 1 runs the engine on a take (a preset, or the log the Chord Entry page keeps) and shows what every rule decided; change a setting and see what it would have written. Part 2 is the rules themselves, with the numbers the engine really uses.

  
    1. Try it
    
      Start from
      Load the last take from Chord Entry
    
    A take log is what the Chord Entry page copies with Copy the take log: every key and pedal event with its time, and the settings. Paste one here and Load it. The settings below then work on the same playing, so you can see what a different rule setting would have written.
    
    Load this logDownload the log
    

    
      EntryChordsMelodyChords and melody (split)
      Key
      Meter4/43/46/812/82/45/4
      Bars
      Tempo
      SwingSwung (by the tempo)StraightAs in the log
      Shortest noteEighthSixteenth
    
    
       Notes struck together are written as a chord
      Together within (ms)
      A chord closes after (ms)
      Snap chords toBarHalf barBeatEighth note
      Melody from
       Slash chords
    
    
      BeamsWithin a beatWithin half a barNone
      SyncopationAs playedTied across the middle of the barTied across every beat
      Short detached notesNote and restStaccato note
      Long notes before a restThe simplest nearby lengthAs released
      TripletsNeverWhere the playing fits
      Notes before bar 1Leave them outWrite them (a pickup bar)
      Grace notes within (ms)
    

    What did I mean?
    
    What was written
    
    
    The take against the bars
    
    a chord's notes as playeda melody note as playedthe melody as writtena chord as placedthe pedal held

    Bars
    Melody notes, one by one
    Chords, one by one
    Pedal
    Copy a report of this run
    The report holds the log, the settings as set here, what was written and every table above. It is everything needed to run the same take again, so it is the thing to send when a take comes out wrong.
  

  
    2. The rules
    In the order the engine applies them. Each rule says what it does, the number it uses (the numbers are read from the engine, not typed here) and where to see it in the tables above. Chords and melody are the same take: the keys you play are sorted into one or the other first (rule 1), and then each follows its own rules.

    Time
    T1The clock: beats from the first downbeat
      Every key and pedal event carries a time in milliseconds from the first downbeat after the count-in (negative in the count-in). A beat is 60 / tempo seconds; in 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 a beat is a dotted quarter, as the band counts it. On a click the page subtracts the sound card's output latency, and the Timing offset or Nudge field moves everything by the milliseconds you give it (a positive number is earlier).
      Seen in: the log's events, and the played column of the note and chord tables.
    T2The bars, and how the pedal changes them
      The take starts with the meter chosen and that many bars. The beat never moves; only where bars begin does. Hold the pedal (MIDI controller ) across two downbeats and the bars from the first of them on are as long as the gap between them, in whole beats. Notes within  beats count as one strike (a chord is one downbeat); only the first and last strike while the pedal is down are used. The gap and the first downbeat are rounded to whole beats.
      A change that falls inside a bar cuts that bar short (a 2/4 bar in a 4/4 tune). A change less than one beat after a bar line moves back to the bar line. In compound meters the new length is counted in dotted quarters, so three beats make 9/8. A second change must come after the first. Over chords already entered the bars are fixed and the pedal is ignored.
      Seen in: the Bars table and the Pedal table (its strikes are the beats it used).
    T3Swing: a swung off-beat is put back on the even grid
      When the playing is read as swung, the second eighth of each beat is taken to sit late: at a fraction s of the beat (0.5 would be straight). s comes from the tempo: 0.68 − 0.08 × clamp((bpm − 100)/120) − 0.05 × clamp((bpm − 220)/80), so it is about 0.68 at a ballad tempo and 0.60 near 220. A time that far into the beat is moved back to the half beat (unswing) before it is rounded to the grid. This is why swung eighths come out as plain eighth notes, and the band swings them again when it plays them. Bars in compound meters are always read straight. Chords are unswung the same way before they snap to the grid.
      Seen in: unswung in the note table (units from the first bar, before rounding) and the Swing setting above.
    T5Pickups: notes before the first bar
      A note (or chord) struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is taken as on it. Struck earlier than that, in the count-in, it is dropped, unless Notes before bar 1: Write them is on: then the earliest such note sets the length of a short bar in front of bar 1, rounded up to whole beats (never longer than the count-in), and everything is written in it, with no meter mark. The chart then reads it as a pickup (anacrusis). A chart that already has a pickup bar uses its length.
      On the Backing Track page, when the take starts at a later bar (a section, or "Start at bar"), the count-in is the bar before the one recorded from, so notes played in it are written at the end of that bar: a pickup into a verse goes at the end of the interlude before it. Only at the very start of the tune does a pickup get a short bar of its own.
      Seen in: the Bars table (a short first bar), the note table (bar 1 is the pickup) and the roll (the count-in is to the left of the first line).
    T4The grid: rounded to the nearest eighth or sixteenth
      A melody note's start is rounded to the nearest eighth note (or sixteenth, if chosen); the unit is an eighth, so a beat is 2 units in x/4 and 3 in compound meters. A note struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat is moved onto it; one struck earlier than that is dropped. A note that rounds to the same spot as the next one is dropped and the later one stays. A note after the last bar is dropped. Chords snap by the Snap setting instead (a bar, half bar, beat or eighth).
      Seen in: on grid and result in the note table.

    Notes
    N1Which keys are chords and which are melody
      In a chords take every key goes to the chord reader; in a melody take every key goes to the melody line. In a split take the keys below the split key are chords and the split key and those above it are melody. The pedal strikes count notes from either side.
      Seen in: the Entry and Melody-from settings; the roll shows chord notes in orange and melody notes in teal.
    N2Notes struck together
      Melody notes struck within  ms of the first of them are one strike. By default only the highest is written and the others are left out; with Notes struck together are written as a chord all of them are written as an ABC chord, [CEG], with one length. A note struck later than that window is a new note.
      Seen in: left out in the note table, and the notes column (several pitches are one strike).
    N3One note at a time
      The line is one voice: a new note ends the one before it, even if you are still holding it.
    N4How long a note is written
      A note lasts until the next note starts (it is written legato), unless the gap between its release and the next start is  of an eighth or more: then it is written as released (rounded to the grid) and a rest follows. The last note is written to its release. A note is never shorter than one grid step. A note cannot run past the next note or the last bar line.
      So a line played short and detached, as swing is, is written with full note values and no rests unless a gap is clear.
      Where a rest does follow a note longer than an eighth (the end of a phrase), the moment you let go is not much of a guide: with Long notes before a rest: The simplest nearby length (the default) the note ends wherever, near the release, the note and the rest after it are simplest to write. The end may move up to  of the note's length (at least one grid step, at most a beat). The candidates are scored by the written symbols of the note and the rest (a dotted one counts one and a half), an end that is off the beat, and the distance moved; holding the note right on to the next one, losing a rest that was played, costs  more. So a quarter let go a sixteenth early is a quarter, not a dotted eighth and a sixteenth rest, while a dotted quarter and a clear eighth rest stay as played. As released writes the release rounded to the grid.
      Seen in: length in the note table says which case applied and the gap it measured.
    N5Bar lines, chord changes and ties
      A note that runs over a bar line is split and tied. A note that runs over a chord change is split at the change and tied, so each chord symbol sits above the note under it. Only lengths that are written as one note are used:  grid steps (a dotted note is 3 or 6); any other length is split into those and tied.
    N6Spelling: which letter and which accidental
      Notes of the key are spelled as the key spells them. A note outside the key takes whichever of its sharp and flat spellings is nearer the middle of the key on the line of fifths (centre + ); when they are equally near, the flat. So in C: E♭, A♭, B♭, F♯ and D♭; in F: G♭ (not F♯) and A♭.
      An accidental is written only where it differs from the key signature or from what the same letter in the same octave had earlier in that bar. Octaves: middle C is C, the C above it c, then c'; below, C,.

    N7Detached notes: staccato
      By default a short note followed by a rest is written as the note and the rest (an eighth and an eighth rest). With Short detached notes: Staccato note, a note followed by a rest exactly as long as itself, where the two together make a length that can be written, is written as one staccato note of both: eighths with eighth rests become staccato quarters. A staccato note is played by the band at half its length. (Triplet notes are not changed.)
      Seen in: length in the note table ("a note and an equal rest are written as a staccato note of both").
    N8Triplets
      Off by default. When on, each beat of a simple meter whose beat is two units (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, …; not 6/8 and the like, where the beat is already three) is read as three even parts if its notes fit thirds of the beat better than the eighth-note grid by more than  of a beat (summed over the beat's onsets). The check is made on the raw time (a swung off-beat is compared after the swing is taken out, so a swung pair is not mistaken for a triplet; the same pair read as straight is). A beat read as triplets is written under a bracket: three notes (3CDE, or a quarter and an eighth (3:2:2C2D. Only whole beats are triplets (no quarter-note triplets over two beats, no sixteenth sextuplets yet).
      Seen in: triplet in the note table gives the two numbers compared.
    N9Grace notes
      Off by default. When on, a note whose next note starts within the chosen milliseconds (never more than  of a beat, a thirty-second note) is not a note of its own but a slashed grace note of the next one: {/D}E. A run of such notes is all grace notes of the first note after them. This is for the quick note into a blue note; it is why a note that was struck first but let go before the next began is not folded into a chord (rule N2 only joins notes that are still held together). The band does not play grace notes back.
      Seen in: graces in the note table.
    N10Parallel thirds and other double stops
      Above the split key (or in a melody take) two notes struck together are one melody note. With Notes struck together are written as a chord on, both are written in one bracket ([CE], [DF], …) with one length, tied as a pair; with it off only the top one is written. They never reach the chord reader, so they are not named as a chord. Notes of the pair that are struck slightly apart still count as together if they are inside the Together-within window and the first is still held when the second arrives.

    Chords
    C1When a chord is finished
      A chord is closed  ms after its first note. Keys still held from the chord before count as part of the next one, unless three or more new keys arrived. It is timed at its first note.
      Seen in: the Chords table, notes played.
    C2Naming a chord
      Every note played must be accounted for by the chord (the Director page, by contrast, accepts extra notes). Every pitch class played is tried as the root against the table below. A reading in which every note is a chord tone wins; a perfect fifth may be left out of any chord of four or more notes. If two readings fit equally (C6 and Am7), the lowest note played decides; then the reading whose root is nearer the key; then the order in the table. If nothing fits exactly, the closest match is written and the chord is marked as a guess. Two or more different notes are needed. Inversions are written as plain chords unless Slash chords is on (C with E at the bottom is then C/E).
      Seen in: candidates in the Chords table: the five best readings, best first.
      
    C3Where a chord goes
      A chord is timed at its first note. Its position in the bar is unswung (T3), then moved to the nearest point of the Snap setting. A chord struck up to  of a beat before the first downbeat goes on it. The chord sits there until the next one.

    Writing it down
    W2Beams
      In ABC a space between notes breaks a beam, so the notation joins eighth notes (and shorter) by writing them without a space: within a beat by default, or within half a bar (four eighths in 4/4; three in 6/8 and the other compound meters are a beat already) with Beams: Within half a bar, or not at all. A rest, a note longer than an eighth, a chord change that starts a new group, or a triplet bracket ends a beam; a triplet is beamed under its own bracket.
    W3Syncopation: ties across the beat
      Jazz writes a quarter note on the “and” of 2 as one quarter. Classical notation writes it as two tied eighths. Syncopation: Tied across the middle of the bar splits a note that starts after the first beat and runs over the middle of the bar (beat 3 in 4/4; a half note on beat 2 too). Tied across every beat also splits a note that starts off the beat and runs over any beat. A note that starts on a beat, or on the bar's first beat, keeps its length. Only the written ABC changes (the band hears the same notes).
    W1The ABC
      Bars of four to a line (the melody bars are written with the beams and ties above); M: is the opening meter and a bar of another meter gets [M:n/d] in front of it. The unit is a quarter note when nothing in an x/4 take sits between the beats, else an eighth, else a sixteenth when sixteenths were used. Chord symbols are quoted above the note or rest at their position. Rests fill what is left.

title: Tune Your Guitar by Ear
text:
Pick a way to tune, then follow the steps one string at a time. The fretboard shows where to put your fingers; click any
spot on it to hear that note. No guitar knowledge needed: strings are numbered 6 (the thickest, nearest your chin) to 1 (the thinnest),
and frets are counted from the end where the tuning pegs are.

Your ear is the tuner. Every method here asks you to listen: to two notes agreeing, to a wobble slowing
down, to a chord sounding sweet. The microphone reading is there to check your ear, not to replace it. With Ear first ticked it stays
blurred until you've said what you hear. Start that habit today: musicians who only tune by looking at a screen can't hear when they've drifted
out of tune halfway through a song.


  1. Your guitar and how you'll tune it
  
    Tuning
