  With speakers, the page's own reference and drone reach the microphone too: stop them, or use headphones, when you check.
  Keys: Space reference, ← → strings, d drone, m microphone.



  Tips that apply to every method
  
    Tune up to the note. If a string is sharp, go below the note and come back up. The string then holds its pitch better.
    Turn while the string rings. Small turns. You hear the change happen.
    Hum or sing the note. If you can sing the reference and then sing the string, your ear is doing the work.
    Finish with a chord. Every method ends at your ear: strum something and adjust any string that sounds sour.
    New strings stretch and go flat for a day or two. Tune, play, tune again.
  
  Why there are several methods, and what each gets wrong: Tuning 1: your ear and beats,
  Tuning 2: fifth-fret, harmonics, octaves,
  Tuning 3: tuners and their limits. Something always out however you tune?
  The Setup Check finds out whether the guitar needs an adjustment.

title: Tap Latency
text:
How late each of Tap Along's buttons lands behind the beat you hear. Use the
  phone and the headphones or speaker you'll mark songs with (Bluetooth adds a lot), turn the ringer on (on an iPhone the silent switch
  mutes this page), and press Start. After four clicks to count you in, tap button 1 on the next twelve clicks, then
  button 2, then button 3, the way you'd tap along to a song. Listen to the clicks rather than watching the screen.

  
    Tempo 80100120
    Start
  
  
  
  
  The lag is the median of the last ten taps (the first two settle in); the spread shows how steady they were.
  Most people tap a little ahead of a metronome, so a small or negative lag is normal. With Sync, Tap Along takes off
  what the buttons have in common anyway. What matters most is the difference between buttons.

A slash sets the lowest note, so C/E is C in first inversion and plain C starts in root position. While this box has anything in it, the diagrams above the cards come from here instead of the chord list.
      
    
    
      Piano: Right hand
      Piano: Left hand
      Piano: Two hands
    
    Voice leading auto-picks each chord's voicing to minimize motion from the previous chord; on fretted instruments that means the smallest move for the fretting hand. Fretboard: one finger per fret from the lowest fretted note; a barre is finger 1. Piano two-hand: left hand in red, right in gray; a root-position or drop voicing puts the bass note in the left hand and the rest in the right, a rootless or inverted four-note chord is split two and two. The voice-led triad and two-note styles always do this on one string set: pick a different shape under any chord and the chords after it follow. title: Emo / pop-punk
text: Open the Emo / pop-punk style in the Backing Track

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
What it is
Guitar-band rock at punk tempos with melodic, often confessional singing: a distorted guitar chugging palm-muted power chords in the verse, ringing open in the chorus, over root eighths and a rock beat, with half-time choruses and breakdowns.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
A little history
Emo (“emotional hardcore”) began in Washington, D.C., in 1985 with Rites of Spring and Embrace, who took hardcore punk’s speed into more personal songs. The 1990s brought a quieter, intricate “Midwest emo” (Cap’n Jazz, American Football). Pop-punk runs from the Buzzcocks and the Ramones to Green Day’s Dookie (1994), which sold millions, then Blink-182. Around 2000-2007 the two merged into a mainstream sound: Jimmy Eat World, My Chemical Romance, Fall Out Boy, Paramore. It came back in the 2020s, from Olivia Rodrigo to a revival of the bands themselves.

title: Emo / pop-punk
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root eighths. Comping: palm-muted chugging in verses, open strumming in Chorus bars.
Drums: rock backbeat; mark bars Half-time for a half-time chorus or breakdown.

title: Boogaloo
text: Open the Boogaloo style in the Backing Track

title: Boogaloo
text:
What it is
A jazz band playing straight (not swung) eighth notes over a repeated bass figure, with piano or organ chords locked to the riff and a backbeat on the drums. It sits between hard bop, R&B and Latin music.

title: Boogaloo
text:
A little history
The word covers two related things from the mid-1960s. Latin boogaloo was a New York dance music that mixed Cuban son and mambo with R&B; Joe Cuba’s Bang! Bang! (1966) and Pete Rodríguez’s I Like It Like That (1967) were hits. In jazz, soul jazz players on labels like Blue Note took up the same straight eighths. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (1962) and Lee Morgan’s The Sidewinder (recorded 1963) came first, and Lou Donaldson’s Alligator Bogaloo (1967) put the name on the jazz version. Drummers such as Idris Muhammad and Bernard Purdie played a backbeat with busy sixteenth-note hi-hats; the tunes were often blues forms over one riff. Mongo Santamaría’s cover of Watermelon Man (1963) carried the Latin side, with congas, back into the charts, which is why the band adds a conga tumbao.

title: Boogaloo
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Boogaloo riff: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, fifth and flat seventh on 4.
Comping: stabs on the same rhythm as the riff.
Drums: straight-eighth backbeat. Congas: a tumbao.
Voicings: rootless jazz voicings.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text: Open the Freylekhs / polka style in the Backing Track

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
What it is
The fast 2/4 of Eastern European dance music: the bass on every beat, alternating root and fifth, and the full chord on every off-beat (oom-pa oom-pa). A freylekhs (“joyful”) is the most common klezmer dance tune; the polka is its Central European cousin.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
A little history
The polka started in Bohemia in the 1830s and was danced across Europe and America within a decade. Its bands (brass, then accordion) gave it the bass-and-off-beat accompaniment. Klezmer is the instrumental music of Ashkenazi Jewish weddings in Eastern Europe. Immigrant clarinettists Naftule Brandwein and Dave Tarras recorded it in New York in the 1920s, with bands that played the same driving off-beats on piano, brass and drums. It faded after the war and came back in the 1970s revival (the Klezmorim, Andy Statman, Kapelye, later the Klezmatics). Songs like Hava Nagila and Hanukkah songs are still played this way.

title: Freylekhs / polka
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth on every beat, with a run up into the next bar now and then.
Comping: chords on the off-beats. In half-time bars the piano switches to ballad patterns.

title: Country train beat
text: Open the Country train beat style in the Backing Track

title: Country train beat
text:
What it is
The country rhythm that sounds like a steam train: a snare (often with brushes) on every eighth note, accented on 2 and 4, a bass on root and fifth, and a boom-chicka guitar.

title: Country train beat
text:
A little history
The sound is most associated with Johnny Cash’s Tennessee Two at Sun Records in Memphis: Luther Perkins’ muted boom-chicka electric guitar and Marshall Grant’s slapped bass on Folsom Prison Blues (1955) and I Walk the Line (1956). Drummer W. S. Holland joined in 1960 and the train beat became a drum pattern. Train songs had been part of country and blues since the 1920s (Jimmie Rodgers), and the beat has stayed in rockabilly, bluegrass-flavoured country and country rock.

title: Country train beat
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: a boom-chicka strum. Drums: train beat.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text: Open the 12/8 doo-wop style in the Backing Track

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
What it is
The slow 1950s ballad: piano chords repeated in triplets, three to every beat, over a slow backbeat, usually on the I-vi-IV-V chords, behind a lead singer and vocal group.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
A little history
Doo-wop came from African American vocal groups on street corners in New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Chicago in the late 1940s and ’50s, following the Ink Spots and the Mills Brothers. The backing singers sang nonsense syllables (doo-wop, sh-boom) in place of instruments. On record, small bands added a pianist hammering triplets, an idea from New Orleans rhythm and blues (Fats Domino) and the slow blues. The same 12/8 feel carries soul ballads into the 1960s, from Etta James’s At Last onward.

title: 12/8 doo-wop
text:
The band’s version

Bass: 12/8 ballad. Comping: triplets. Drums: slow 12/8 backbeat.
On a 4/4 chart the band plays the triplets over each beat.

title: Ragtime
text: Open the Ragtime style in the Backing Track

title: Ragtime
text:
What it is
Composed piano music from about 1895 to 1920, built like a march: several 16-bar strains, a left hand that plays a bass note on the beat and a chord off it, and a right hand whose melody is syncopated (“ragged”) against that steady left hand. Its eighth notes are straight, not swung.
Ragtime is where stride came from: the stride left hand is the ragtime left hand, played faster and swung, with songs and the blues in place of written rags. The lesson Two Left Hands plays the two one after the other.

title: Ragtime
text:
A little history
Ragtime grew among Black pianists in the saloons and dance halls of the Mississippi valley in the 1890s, and became the first African American music to sell across the country, mostly as sheet music for parlour pianos. Scott Joplin’s Maple Leaf Rag (1899), published in Sedalia, Missouri, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Joplin, James Scott and Joseph Lamb wrote the “classic rags”; Tin Pan Alley turned out ragtime songs by the thousand. Bands played rags too, and ragtime fed straight into early jazz in New Orleans and into Harlem stride.
It was largely forgotten until the 1970s, when Joshua Rifkin’s recordings of Joplin and the film The Sting (1973), with Marvin Hamlisch’s arrangement of The Entertainer, brought it back.

title: Ragtime
text:
The band’s version

Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 and the chord on 2 and 4, in straight time.
Bass: Root and fifth on 1 and 3, like the tuba in a march band.
Drums: Boom-chick: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

A rag is written down, and its right-hand melody is the point. The band plays only the left hand’s pattern; the ragged melody is yours.

What it is
Traditional carols played by a folk-rock band: a strummed steel-string guitar, upright bass on 1 and 3, light brushes. Between the four-part hymn and acoustic strum.

title: Folk carol
text:
A little history
Many English carols are older than the hymns sung beside them: dance songs and wassails collected by Cecil Sharp and Ralph Vaughan Williams in the early 1900s and published in The Oxford Book of Carols (1928). The British folk revival of the 1960s and the folk-rock bands that followed (Steeleye Span, Fairport Convention) played them with guitars, fiddles and drums, and many carol albums since have done the same.

title: Calypso
text:
What it is
The topical song of Trinidad: a singer (the calypsonian) with a witty, often political lyric over a bouncing 2/4, with a strummed guitar or cuatro, a bass on root and fifth, and chords on the off-beats.

title: Calypso
text:
A little history
Calypso (earlier kaiso) grew out of the songs of Trinidad’s Carnival in the 1800s: the chantwell leading call-and-response songs in French Creole, stick-fighting songs, and the music of the Spanish Venezuelan string bands. By the 1910s-20s it was sung in English and recorded in New York. Calypso tents competed each Carnival season, and singers took grand names: Atilla the Hun, Roaring Lion, Lord Invader, Lord Kitchener, the Mighty Sparrow. Lord Invader’s Rum and Coca-Cola (sung at the 1943 Carnival) became an American hit for the Andrews Sisters in 1945, and Invader later won a lawsuit over its royalties; and Harry Belafonte’s album Calypso (1956) was the first LP to sell a million copies. Jamaica’s mento is a cousin, and in the 1970s Lord Shorty mixed calypso with Indian rhythms into soca, now Carnival’s main music.

title: Calypso
text:
The band’s version

Bass: Root and fifth. Comping: chords on every off-beat. Drums: a calypso beat.

title: Stride Piano
text: Open the Stride piano style in the Backing Track

title: Stride Piano
text:
What it is
Solo piano music from Harlem in the late 1910s to the 1930s. The left hand does the work of a whole rhythm section: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4, the hand leaping (“striding”) between them on every beat. The right hand plays the melody, decorated, over it.
Stride and boogie-woogie grew up side by side: both are piano music for dancing at parties, both put a whole band into the left hand, and both feed into swing. They differ in what the left hand does. The lesson Two Left Hands plays them side by side.

title: Stride Piano
text:
A little history
Stride comes out of ragtime. A Scott Joplin rag already has the oom-pah left hand, written as a march. In New York around the First World War, pianists such as James P. Johnson, Luckey Roberts and Willie “The Lion” Smith played it faster and swung it, took it from rags to popular songs and the blues, and added runs, tenths and cross-rhythms. They played at rent parties, where tenants paid the rent by charging for food, drink and music, and in cutting contests against each other. Johnson’s Carolina Shout was the test piece: Duke Ellington learned it from a piano roll, slowed down.
Johnson’s pupil Fats Waller made stride popular on records and radio, from 1934 with a small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm: bass, drums and guitar playing in two under the piano’s left hand. That is the sound this style copies. Art Tatum took stride to its technical limit; Count Basie began as a stride pianist and pared it down to almost nothing; Thelonious Monk kept stride passages in his playing all his life.
Johnson also wrote Charleston (1923). Its rhythm, a long note on 1 and a short one on the and of 2, is the Charleston comping figure jazz pianists still use.

title: Stride Piano
text:
The band’s version

Comping: Stride: on the piano, a low bass note on 1 and 3 (the root as an octave where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
Bass: Two-feel: half notes on 1 and 3, with the piano’s left hand.
Drums: Jazz time, lightly.
Voicings: plain triads and seventh chords, all their notes.

Real stride left hands reach for tenths, walk them up and down between chords, and break the pattern for a run; the right hand carries the tune. The band’s pianist keeps the pattern and plays no melody. That is your part.

title: Boom-chick
text: Open the Boom-chick style in the Backing Track

title: Boom-chick
text:
What it is
The oldest accompaniment in popular music: a bass note on the strong beats and a chord on the weak ones. In 2/4 or 4/4 it is boom-chick; in 3/4 it is oom-pah-pah.

title: Boom-chick
text:
A little history
Brass bands and dance orchestras of the 1800s split the beat between the tuba (or bass) and the horns or second violins: marches, polkas and waltzes all run on it, and so does the stride and ragtime piano left hand (bass note, chord, bass note, chord). Guitarists in American old-time and country music used the same idea, a thumbed bass on the beat and a strum after it: Maybelle Carter’s guitar with the Carter Family from 1927, and later the folk revival. Sing-along songs from campfire to music hall still use it.

title: Boom-chick
text:

title: Acoustic strum
text: Open the Acoustic strum style in the Backing Track

title: Acoustic strum
text:
What it is
The singer-songwriter’s band: a steel-string acoustic guitar strumming a syncopated pattern (down, down-up, up-down-up), a bass and kick together on 1, the and of 2, and 3, and a light backbeat.

title: Acoustic strum
text:
A little history
The steel-string guitar became a popular accompanying instrument through country and blues players in the 1920s-30s and the folk revival of the 1950s-60s (Woody Guthrie, then Bob Dylan, Joan Baez). From the late 1960s singer-songwriters (James Taylor, Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens) put a band around the strummed guitar. The 1990s Britpop and “unplugged” years (Oasis’s Wonderwall) and the 2000s-2010s folk-pop of Jason Mraz, Mumford & Sons and Ed Sheeran kept it among the most common sounds in pop.

title: Acoustic strum
text:

title: Piano ballad

title: Piano ballad
text:
What it is
The slow pop or rock song led from the piano: octaves in the left hand, the chord broken or rocked in the right (often in first inversion, so the top moves smoothly), and a band that comes in half-time, with the backbeat on beat 3.

title: Piano ballad
text:
A little history
The piano was the home instrument of popular song long before rock: Tin Pan Alley sold sheet music for it. In the 1970s singer-songwriters at the piano (Carole King’s Tapestry, 1971; Elton John; Billy Joel) made the piano ballad a staple of rock. The 1980s power ballad put it under big drums, and from the 2000s Coldplay, Alicia Keys and Adele (Someone Like You, 2011, over nothing but broken piano chords) kept it at the top of the charts.

title: Piano ballad
text:
The band’s version

Comping: three right-hand patterns (rocking, half-broken, syncopated) in four-bar spans.
Bass and drums: half time; a quiet kick and a cross-stick on 3. The hi-hat sits low.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text: Open the John Prine Fingerpicking style in the Backing Track

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
What it is
A steel-string guitar played with the thumb and fingers at once: the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat while the fingers pluck the chord on the off-beats or pinch with the thumb. No drums, an upright bass doubling the thumb.

title: John Prine Fingerpicking
text:
A little history
Alternating-thumb picking runs back to Black guitarists in the South of the 1920s: Mississippi John Hurt recorded for OKeh in 1928, and Elizabeth Cotten played Freight Train left-handed. In Kentucky, Arnold Shultz, Ike Everly and Mose Rager handed it to Merle Travis, after whom “Travis picking” is named, and Chet Atkins spread it through country guitar. The 1960s folk revival brought it to singer-songwriters. John Prine (1946-2020), the Chicago postman whose first album (John Prine, 1971) contains Paradise, Hello in There and Angel from Montgomery, played a plain thumb-and-fingers style under plain-spoken songs.

text:

Comping: the prine and travis patterns. Bass: root and fifth with the thumb. Drums: none.

title: Reggaeton
text: Open the Reggaeton style in the Backing Track

title: Reggaeton
text:
What it is
Spanish-language dance music from Puerto Rico and Panama, built on the dembow: the kick on every beat, and the snare on the last sixteenth of beat 1 and the and of 2 (and again in beats 3 and 4), a 3+3+2 in sixteenths over each half bar, under long synth chords and a rapped or sung vocal.

title: Reggaeton
text:
A little history
The rhythm is named after Shabba Ranks’ Jamaican dancehall record Dem Bow (1990), whose riddim (the backing track, by Steely & Clevie, built on their Poco Man Jam) was copied everywhere. In Panama, artists such as El General sang Spanish lyrics over dancehall riddims (reggae en español). In Puerto Rico in the 1990s DJ Playero and others made underground mixtapes on the same beats; the name reggaeton took hold around the turn of the century. Daddy Yankee’s Gasolina (2004) was the international breakthrough, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s Despacito (2017) one of the most-streamed songs ever, and Bad Bunny the genre’s biggest star of the 2020s.

title: Reggaeton
text:

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text: Tonal patterns are short groups of pitches we learn by ear first, with solfège, before we ever name a key signature. The foundation is the major tonic and dominant.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Stepwise motion
The most basic tonal pattern is stepwise: Do – Re – Mi – Fa – Sol and back down. Sing it on a neutral syllable first, then with solfège, then connect it to what you see on the staff.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Tonic and dominant

Tonic (Do – Mi – Sol): the “home” chord, restful.
Dominant (Sol – Ti – Re): the “tension” chord that wants to resolve home.

Hearing the difference between these two is the single most important tonal skill in beginning band.

title: Lesson: Do, Re, Mi (Tonal Patterns)
text:
Practice steps

Sing Do, then find Sol.
Sing the tonic arpeggio, then the dominant.
Go to Practice → Tonal Patterns and play major stepwise patterns, singing along with solfège.

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Pop singing sounds like talking on pitch. The words come first, the tone stays close to your speaking voice, and the style lives in small things: how a note starts, a little cry or breath, a run at the end of a line. This lesson builds those things one at a time, from breathing to riffs and harmony.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. The exercises are written for a middle voice. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower, as usual. Exercises marked Step up climb a half step each time you press it, the way a warm-up works through the range. Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Breath and posture
Stand as if you were about to talk to a friend across the room: feet under the hips, knees soft, head level, shoulders loose. Breathe in low and quietly, so the belly and lower ribs widen and the shoulders don’t rise. Then let the air out slowly and steadily, without squeezing.
Exercise: hiss out on “sss” for a count of 8, then 12, then 16, keeping the sound even. Then do the same on a hum.
The aim isn’t a huge breath. It’s a steady one you don’t have to fight.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Starting the note: the onset
A note can start three ways:

Breathy: air first, then sound, as in a sigh, “hhhey”.
Hard: a little click of the vocal folds first, as in “uh-oh!”.
Balanced: air and sound together.

Pop uses all three for effect, but a balanced onset is home base. Sing the five notes below on “mum”, starting each note gently with the M.



Now sing the first note three times, once with each onset: “hhhum”, “’um” and “um”. Hear the difference, then go back to the balanced one.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Speech level and the mix
Your speaking voice and your high, light voice (head voice) join somewhere around the middle of your range. Pop singers keep the sound speech-like through that join. That blend is the mix. The safest way to find it is with exercises that keep the throat easy: lip trills (a horse’s “brrr”) and a bratty “nay”.
Sing this on a lip trill first, then on “nay” (bright and a bit nasal, like a teasing kid). Let the sound stay small at the top. Don’t shout up there.



As you step up, the top note will want to “flip” into a lighter sound. Let it flip at first. Over weeks, the “nay” helps the flip smooth out into a mix.

If your jaw juts or your neck tightens at the top, go back down two steps and make the sound smaller. Pop high notes come from a lighter, more speech-like voice, not from more push.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Vowels and words
Sing the words the way you’d say them: “love” is “luv”, not an operatic “lahv”. Two habits help.

Sing on the vowel and get to the consonant late. In “night”, hold “ah” and save the “-eet” ending for the very end of the note.
Narrow the vowel a little on high notes. “Ah” leans toward “uh”, and “ee” toward “ih”. The word still reads, and the throat stays easier.

Sing this line on “I can’t stop thinking ’bout you”, holding the vowels and putting the consonants late.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Belt, carefully
Belting is the strong, speech-like sound of pop and musical theatre on high notes, like a call across a playground: “Hey!”. Done well it is bright and forward, not shouted. Keep it short at first, and keep it well inside your comfort zone.




Belt for a few minutes at a time, not a whole session. If you feel any squeeze in your throat, go back to “nay” (the previous section). A teacher in person is the best guide for belting.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Riffs and runs
A run is a quick string of notes on one syllable, usually at the end of a phrase. Most pop runs come from the pentatonic scale. Learn each run slowly, on “ah”, until every note is clean. Then speed it up.
This run starts on A minor pentatonic: A, C, D, E, G.



And a common descending one from C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A.



Practice: sing each run at half speed with a metronome, then at full speed. A clean slow run is worth more than a fast blur.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Style: cry, breath and flips
These colours are what make a singer sound like pop:

Cry: a slight whimper or sob in the tone, like the edge of tears. It lightens the sound and helps it climb.
Breathy tone: let a little air into the start of a quiet phrase for intimacy. Don’t use it all the time, or the voice tires.
Flip (a yodel break): let the voice jump into a lighter sound for a moment on the way up, as in many folk and R&B lines.
Fry: the creaky sound at the bottom of the voice, used to start a phrase. Keep it light and brief.

Sing the line below twice: plainly, then adding a flip on the high note and a little breath at the start.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Phrasing and the mic

Sit a little behind the beat. Pop singers often land a word just after the beat, like a relaxed conversation. Try a line both ways with the Backing Track playing.
Shape each phrase. Most lines rise toward an important word and fall away after it.
Use the mic. Sing close (a finger or two away) for quiet, intimate lines. Pull back a few inches for loud notes, so they don’t blast. Point the mic at your mouth, not your chin.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Harmony: singing a third above
Backing vocals often sing a third above the melody: two scale steps higher, moving in parallel with it. Sing the melody below, then sing the harmony line written above it.



Practice: play it and sing the melody (the lower line), then the harmony. Then sing the harmony while the recording plays the melody.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic
text:
Where to go next

Jazz singing: swing, scat and singing the changes.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Four-chord loops: sing melodies and harmonies over the loops of most pop songs.
crumbs: Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic

title: DAW 7: Bounce, Export and Taking It Further
section: What this small DAW leaves out
text:
What this small DAW leaves out
Real DAWs do much more. In the order you’ll want them:

Audio editing: many takes of one part and the best bits of each (comping), fades, time-stretching (Recording 1: Gain Staging, Recording 2: Microphones).
Effects / plug-ins on each track: EQ, compression, reverb, delay (Sound 11: The Equaliser onwards).
Sends and buses: one reverb shared by many tracks (Recording 5: Mixing).
Automation: a fader or knob that moves by itself as the song plays.
Meter and tempo changes, takes and comping, time-stretching audio, software synths (the sound-design lessons).

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
The music of 1980s home computers and game consoles wasn’t recorded. A small sound chip played it live, note by note, as the game ran. The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES, 1983 in Japan as the Famicom) had two pulse waves, one triangle wave and one noise channel, plus a channel for short, low-quality samples that most games barely used. The Game Boy had nearly the same four: two pulses, a small wave channel of your own design, and noise. The Commodore 64’s SID chip had three voices.
Each channel could play one note at a time. That’s four notes in all, and one of them is noise, so it can’t hold a pitch. Composers such as Koji Kondo (Super Mario Bros., 1985), Hirokazu Tanaka, Tim Follin, and on the Commodore 64 Rob Hubbard and Martin Galway still wrote full arrangements: melody, harmony, bass and drums. The music people now call chiptune grew out of the tricks they used to do it.
How to use the page. Press ▶ to hear a four-bar tune written for the four channels. The buttons mute and unmute each channel. Hold two or three keys (computer keys, the keyboard below, or MIDI) and the chord channel arpeggiates your chord in place of the song’s. Start with the volume low.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Four channels



Every channel has a job, and the jobs follow from what each channel can do:








Channel
What it can do
What composers gave it




Pulse 1
a pulse wave at 12.5%, 25% or 50% width, 16 volume levels
the melody


Pulse 2
the same
harmony, a counter-melody, or an echo of the melody


Triangle
a triangle wave, an octave lower than the pulses, no volume control: on or off
the bass


Noise
noise, high or low, 16 volume levels
the drums



The pulse width is the instrument choice. 50% is the hollow square wave (odd harmonics only; Sound 2). 25% is fuller and more nasal, and 12.5% is thin and buzzy. Try both pulse widths while the tune plays. Composers often changed the width partway through a note to give it more movement.
Because the triangle has no volume control, chip bass lines never fade. A note sounds at full level until it’s cut off, so bass lines are written as bouncing octaves or with short gaps to make the rhythm. Drums are short bursts of noise: a low, quick one for the kick, a brighter one for the snare, a tiny high one for the hi-hat (built the same way as in Sound 3). Mute the other three channels to hear how little each drum is.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Rows and frames
The music was played by a small program that ran once every screen refresh: 60 times a second on American and Japanese machines (50 in Europe). Each run is a frame. Nothing in the music could happen between frames, so every note change, volume step and vibrato wobble fell on a 1/60-second grid.
Composers wrote in trackers: a spreadsheet of notes, one column per channel, read from top to bottom. Each line is a row, and the “speed” is how many frames a row lasts. Six frames a row, with four rows to a beat, gives 150 beats per minute. Tempo only comes in steps: move Frames per row and the tempo jumps between fixed values. Some composers alternated two speeds from row to row to get a tempo in between.
The program also made the expressive details by hand. The melody’s volume steps down frame by frame after each attack (you can see the steps in the oscilloscope), and after a long note has sounded for a while its pitch starts to wobble. That’s vibrato, written in software. Turn it off to hear how flat the long notes sound without it.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Chords from one channel
With one channel for the melody, one for the bass and one for drums, only one channel is left for harmony. One channel can play one note. A chord needs at least three.
The answer was the arpeggio: play the chord’s notes one after another, so fast that the ear can’t hear them as separate notes. Played every frame or every other frame, that’s 30 to 60 notes a second. Below about 50 ms per note, the ear stops following a tune and hears a texture instead: a buzzing, shimmering chord. It’s the most recognisable chiptune sound.
Compare the three settings of Chords on pulse 2:

Arpeggio (one channel): what the composers actually did.
Root only: what you’d get from that channel without the trick. The harmony is gone, and the F and C bars sound like they’re missing something.
Real chord (three channels): what the chip couldn’t do. It’s smoother, but now three channels are busy with one chord and there’s nothing left for the tune or drums.

Then go back to Arpeggio and slow it down with Frames per arpeggio note. At 12 or 15 frames a note you hear a tune of single notes going up and down. Speed it back up and somewhere around 4 to 6 frames the separate notes merge into a chord. The pattern matters less at full speed: Up, Up and down and Up, then the octave all sound like the same chord, each with a slightly different buzz.
In trackers this became a one-line effect: 047 on a note means “add 4 and then 7 semitones above it, each for one frame, over and over”: a major chord on one channel. 037 is minor.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Write your own: a tracker
This is the same tune in a tracker, laid out the way chip composers wrote it. Each column is a channel, each line is a row, and time runs down the page. The shaded lines are beats, and the darker ones start a bar. Press ▶ and edit while it plays: a change is heard the next time that row comes round.



What to type in a cell:








Column
Type
Example




Pulse 1, Triangle
a note: letter, - or #, octave
A-4, C#5


Pulse 2
a note, then an arpeggio effect 0xy
A-4 037 (minor), C-5 047 (major)


Noise
K kick, S snare, H hi-hat
S


any
--- stops the note; an empty cell lets it ring on




In the effect 0xy, x and y are how many semitones above the note to add. They’re written in hexadecimal, so C means 12, an octave. 037 is a minor triad, 047 a major one, 038 a minor triad in first inversion (the C chord in bar 3), 05C a fourth plus an octave, and 07C the open fifth heard in a lot of game music. Arrow keys and Enter move around the grid. Click a cell and play a note on MIDI or the on-screen keyboard to write that note in (Pulse 2 keeps its effect). Frames per arpeggio note starts at 1 here, which is how trackers play 0xy.
Some things to try:

Change the chords: make bar 2 F-4 037 (F minor) and hear the whole tune go darker.
Give the triangle a walking bass line, a note every beat, instead of octaves.
Write a drum fill in the last bar: an S on every row.
Speed up to 3 frames per row and write a run of sixteenths that no one could play.

Your grid is kept in this browser. Example tune brings back the original, and Clear empties everything.

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Music no one can play
Write that arpeggio out as sheet music and it isn’t playable. At 150 bpm, a new note every two frames is 12 notes per beat: steady 48th-note triplets. A note every frame is 24 to a beat. The fastest human trills and tremolos reach roughly 15 to 20 notes a second, and only on two notes, not a chord broken note by note. A pianist playing a chip tune “as written” would need to play the melody plus a chord broken into 30 notes a second in the other hand, perfectly even, for the whole song.
Composers knew no one would ever play it. The parts were written for a machine, so the usual limits of hands, breath and bows didn’t apply. Some of them made a style of that:

Rob Hubbard (Monty on the Run, 1985) and Martin Galway on the Commodore 64 wrote long, fast arpeggio passages and pitch slides that are part of the melody, not hidden behind it.
Tim Follin’s NES music (Silver Surfer, 1990) has arpeggios, echoes and runs at speeds that sound like a much bigger chip.
Fast single-note runs, octave leaps every frame, and drum fills on the noise channel quicker than any drummer are common.

Other tricks came from the same limits:

Echo: pulse 2 plays the melody a few rows late and quieter, to sound like a delay (Sound 17) the chip didn’t have.
Channel stealing: a sound effect (a jump, a coin) takes over a pulse channel for a moment, and that part of the music drops out. Composers planned the music so that it still made sense with a part missing.
Pitch sweeps: a note sliding down fast is a laser, or, on the triangle, a kick drum with more punch than noise alone gives.
Shared drums: a quick noise hit and a triangle blip together, so a snare has a pitched body (Sound 3 builds a snare the same way).

title: Sound 25: Chiptune
text:
Chiptune today
Many musicians still write for these chips, on the original machines or in trackers such as FamiTracker and LSDj (which runs on a Game Boy). They follow the old limits on purpose: four channels, frame timing, arpeggiated chords. A lot of the sound is the struggle with the limits. Pop and electronic producers also use pulse waves and fast arpeggios, without the limits, when they want that sound.

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
There is no single right way to write music down. A notation is a tool. Each one shows some things clearly and leaves others out, and each belongs to a tradition whose players read it fluently. This lesson writes one melody six ways so you can compare them side by side, then says when to reach for each.
The melody is the opening of Mò Lì Huā (茉莉花, Jasmine Flower), a Chinese folk song known across the world. It uses only five notes (a pentatonic scale), which also exists in Indian music: Hindustani musicians call that scale rāg Bhūpālī and Carnatic musicians rāga Mōhanam. So it can be written naturally in every system on this page.
▶ Hear the melody

Every example below is this same phrase.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
section: The six notations at a glance
text:
The six notations at a glance









Notation
Shows well
Leaves out or blurs
Typical home




Staff (Western) notation
exact pitch and rhythm, harmony, several parts at once
tuning between the 12 notes, ornaments of other traditions, timbre
Western classical, jazz, film, band, most published music


Jianpu (numbered notation)
scale degrees, rhythm, lyrics; quick to write and to transpose
harmony and multiple parts are clumsy
Chinese folk, pop and instrumental music; also Indonesia, Japan


Sargam (Hindustani and Carnatic)
scale degrees in a rāga, rhythm against the tāla cycle
the ornaments (gamaka, mīnd) that matter most; it’s a memory aid, not a full score
Indian classical teaching and composition


DAW screenshot (piano roll, arrangement)
exact timing, velocity, structure, layers, effects and automation
key, harmony and musical meaning; it is a picture of data, not something to read
electronic, pop production, any music made in a computer


Waveform
loudness over time, where sounds start, silence, clipping
pitch, harmony, almost everything else
editing audio, checking timing and dynamics


Spectrogram
which frequencies sound when: timbre, harmonics, vibrato
it’s hard to read notes, rhythm or harmony from it, especially with several instruments
acoustics, voice, sound design, analysis of non-pitched music
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Staff notation



Five lines, notes placed on lines and spaces for pitch, note shapes for length. Its strengths: exact pitch (every one of the 12 notes in every octave), exact rhythm, and many parts at once lined up vertically, so harmony and counterpoint can be seen. That’s why orchestral, choral and band music, and almost all analysis of Western harmony, uses it.
Its weaknesses: it assumes the 12 equal notes of a piano, so pitches between them (blue notes, Arabic maqām, Indian shruti, the slides of Chinese erhu playing) need extra signs or prose. It also needs training to read quickly.
Use it when: writing for Western instruments or ensembles; analysing harmony, voice leading or form in Western music; when exact rhythm and pitch must be communicated to a reader who will play it.






MYP and DP notes: staff notation






MYP: you don’t have to use staff notation in MYP Music, but when you analyse Western music, short notated examples (a motif, a chord progression) are the clearest evidence. Label what you’re showing: circle the motif and name it, write the chord symbols above. In your process journal, a scan of a hand-written sketch is fine.
DP: when you discuss a Western work in the Exploring music in context portfolio or an analysis, quote short, annotated excerpts with bar numbers instead of long unmarked pages, and say where they come from. For your own compositions, staff notation is expected where the music is written for performers to read; use notation software and check that what is written matches what you intend to be played.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Jianpu (numbered notation)



Jianpu (简谱, “simplified notation”) numbers the notes of the scale: 1 to 7 are do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. The key is given at the start (1 = F means do is F). A dot above a number puts it an octave up, a dot below an octave down. A plain number lasts one beat; each line under a number halves it; a dash after it adds a beat. Bar lines are as in staff notation.
It was spread in China in the early 20th century from a French numbered system, and is still how most Chinese musicians write and read folk songs, pop songs and parts for traditional instruments like the erhu, pipa and dizi. Because it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches, the same page can be played in any key just by changing “1 =”.
Use it when: writing or studying Chinese music, or when the players read jianpu; writing a single melody with lyrics quickly; teaching melodies by scale degree (it pairs naturally with tonal solfège).






MYP and DP notes: jianpu






MYP: if you investigate a Chinese musical tradition (Criterion A, Investigating), showing the music in jianpu, with a short key that explains the dots, lines and dashes, demonstrates that you understand how the tradition itself writes music. Put staff notation next to it if your reader won’t know jianpu.
DP: in the portfolio or an analysis, quoting music from a Chinese tradition in its own notation is a sign of working in context. Provide a legend the first time, and if you compare it with a Western piece, a parallel staff version helps the examiner follow. Don’t just transcribe it into staff notation and leave the original out.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Sargam: Hindustani and Carnatic notation
Indian classical music names the notes of the scale Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni (sargam), shortened to their first letters. Sa is the home note, chosen by the singer; like jianpu, it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches. The two classical traditions write it a little differently.

Hindustani (North Indian): Bhatkhande notation



Developed by Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande in the early 20th century. Each box is one mātrā (beat). Notes sharing a beat are joined by a curve beneath. A dot above a note is the upper octave (Ṡ), a dot below is the lower. A dash holds the previous note (some books use the Devanagari sign ऽ instead). Underneath, the tāla (the rhythmic cycle) is marked: X is sam, the first and strongest beat, and 0 is khālī, the “empty” beat. This melody fits exactly one cycle of the eight-beat Keherwā tāla. A flat (komal) note is shown by a line under it, and the raised Ma (tīvra) by a line above.


Carnatic (South Indian): swara notation



Carnatic notation writes the swaras in lower-case letters (s r g m p d n), with dots for octaves, a comma to extend a note by one time unit and a semicolon for two. The tāla is marked with bar lines at the end of each section: one line after the laghu (four beats here) and after each drutam (two beats), and a double line at the end of the cycle. Eight beats is Ādi tāla, the most common Carnatic tāla, so this melody fills exactly one cycle of it too.


What sargam leaves out
The most important part of a rāga is how notes are approached: slides (mīnd), oscillations (gamaka), which notes are lingered on. The written swaras give the skeleton only, and students learn the rest by ear from a teacher. Many pieces are never written at all. So sargam notation is a reliable memory aid and teaching tool, not a complete score.
Use it when: studying, teaching or composing in an Indian tradition; showing the shape of a rāga; showing how a melody sits against a tāla cycle.






MYP and DP notes: sargam






MYP: in an investigation of Indian music, use the tradition’s own terms (rāga, tāla, sam, khālī, swara) and its notation for short examples. Explain in your own words what the notation cannot show, such as gamaka, and support it with a timestamped recording (“listen at 1:42 for the slide from Ga to Re”).
DP: for the portfolio or an analysis of Indian music, sargam with a legend, plus precise timestamps in a named recording, is stronger evidence than a staff transcription alone. Staff notation can’t show the shruti and gamaka you’d be discussing. If you do transcribe to staff for comparison, say what it loses. Name the tradition (Hindustani or Carnatic), and the rāga and tāla.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
DAW screenshots






A digital audio workstation (DAW) shows music the way the computer stores it. The piano roll (top) is a grid: time runs left to right, pitch bottom to top, each bar is a note, and its shade is how hard it is played (velocity). The arrangement view (bottom) shows every track as a lane of blocks (regions or clips), with lines for automation: a volume fade, a filter opening.
What it’s good at: exact timing and velocity, how a track is layered and structured, which sounds, effects and automation were used. For electronic music, hip hop and most pop production, this is the score: the music was never written any other way.
What it’s bad at: it doesn’t tell the reader the key, the chords or the beat they should feel. It’s a picture to be explained, not something a performer can read. A wall of tiny clips means nothing without labels.
Use it when: the music was made in a DAW; showing production decisions (layers, effects, automation, edits); showing a process (before and after).






MYP and DP notes: DAW screenshots






MYP: screenshots are excellent process-journal evidence for Criterion B (Developing) and C (Creating): show a “before” and “after” with a sentence on why you changed it. Crop to what matters, zoom so it’s readable, and add arrows and labels. A full-screen screenshot of the whole project with no annotation shows very little.
DP: in the Experimenting with music report and in production-based Presenting music or HL project work, annotated DAW screenshots are often the most appropriate evidence for music created in a DAW. Annotate them: name the track, the plug-in and the setting, and say what musical effect it had. Pair a screenshot with a timestamp in the audio (“the filter opens at 0:48”). For anything that will be performed by players, include a readable score or lead sheet as well.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Waveforms



A waveform draws the sound itself: how far the speaker cone moves, over time. Zoomed out (top), it shows loudness over time: where notes start, how they fade, where the silences are, and whether the recording is clipping (flat-topped at the edges). Zoomed right in (bottom), you can see individual cycles of the wave (see Sound 1).
That’s about all it shows. You cannot read the pitches, the harmony or the instruments from it.
Use it when: showing where an edit, an entry or a hit happens; comparing the dynamics of two performances or two masters; showing that a recording is too quiet or distorted.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Spectrograms



A spectrogram shows time left to right, frequency bottom to top, and loudness as brightness. Each note appears as a stack of lines (its harmonics), so it shows timbre, vibrato and which frequencies are present when. Here you can see the melody’s notes, each with its harmonics above, and the slight vibrato on the long notes.
With one clean instrument, it can be surprisingly readable. With a full band it becomes a dense cloud from which notes, chords and rhythm are very hard to pick out. Specialists use it for voice (formants), acoustics, birdsong, and for music where pitch isn’t the point: electronic textures, noise music, extended techniques.
Use it when: your point is about timbre, a sound’s frequency content, vibrato or a texture with no clear notes, and only with labels that point at what to look at.






MYP and DP notes: waveforms and spectrograms






MYP and DP alike: use them only when they show the point you’re making (dynamics, timing, timbre), and say what to look at. A waveform or spectrogram dropped in as decoration isn’t evidence of anything, and it won’t stand in for notation. One cropped, labelled image with a timestamp beats a full-track screenshot.
DP: in an analysis of electronic or non-notated music, a spectrogram with a labelled feature (“the sweep from 200 Hz to 5 kHz is the filter opening”) can support a point about timbre or production that no score could show. Keep it as support for your writing, not a substitute.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

title: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation
text:
Choosing: a short checklist

Whose music is it? Use the notation the tradition itself uses (staff for a Bach chorale, jianpu for a Chinese folk song, sargam for a bandish, a DAW view for a track made in Ableton), and add a translation only if your reader needs it.
What’s the point you’re making? Harmony → staff. Scale degrees and melody → jianpu or sargam. Production → DAW. Dynamics or timing of a recording → waveform. Timbre → spectrogram.
Who has to read it? A performer needs something playable. An examiner needs something labelled.
What does it leave out? Say so, and fill the gap with a recording and a timestamp.
Crop, label, cite. Short excerpts, bar numbers or timestamps, the source of every example.







MYP and DP notes: presenting evidence in general






Legends. The first time you use any notation your reader might not know (jianpu, sargam, a graphic score), give a two-line key.
Accuracy. Wrong notes or rhythms in a notated example undermine the point it makes. Check every example against the recording.
Citations. Every quoted score, recording and screenshot of someone else’s work needs a source.
Recordings and timestamps. For music that isn’t primarily written down, the recording is the primary source, and a timestamp is your “bar number”.
Your own work. In both programmes, evidence of process (sketches, screenshots of versions, short recordings of tries) counts. Date it and say what changed.
crumbs: Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

The Notation page has a lot on it. These steps show it to you a part at a time: you only see a part once a step needs it, and each step asks you to write something specific before the next one opens. Your work is checked as you go.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text: With no reference at all, you can still tune the guitar to itself: get one string right (or just leave it where it is), and tune the others from it. The pitch may not match a piano, but the guitar will agree with itself, which matters more when you play alone. Each method compares two notes that should be the same, so you listen for the beating of Tuning 1 to stop. Every method is in the tuning tool, drawn on a fretboard.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
1. The fifth-fret method
Press string 6 at the 5th fret: that’s A, the note of open string 5. Tune string 5 to it. Then string 5 fret 5 gives string 4, and string 4 fret 5 gives string 3. String 3 (G) to string 2 (B) is a smaller gap: use the 4th fret. Then string 2 fret 5 gives string 1. (On a bass, the 5th fret every time.)







Strengths
Weaknesses




Needs nothing; easy to remember
Errors add up: a 3-cent mistake on each step leaves string 1 up to 15 cents off string 6


Gives equal temperament, the tuning the frets are made for
A fretted note is only as good as the guitar’s intonation and your finger: press hard and it goes sharp


Teaches where the notes are on the neck
The first note dies away while you tune the second

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
2. The harmonics method
Touch a string lightly over the 5th fret wire (don’t press), pick and lift: a bell-like harmonic, two octaves above the open string. The harmonic over the 7th fret of the next string is the same note, and harmonics ring for a long time, so you can play both and tune while they beat. (How to play harmonics: Guitar harmonics.)
The catch: harmonics are notes from the harmonic series, which is pure, while frets are equal-tempered. The 5th-fret harmonic is the string’s 4th harmonic, the 7th-fret one its 3rd, so matching them makes the two strings a pure fourth (ratio 4:3, 498 cents) instead of the frets’ 500 cents: 2 cents narrow. Hear the difference:



Tune strings 6 → 5 → 4 → 3 that way and string 3 ends about 6 cents flat of where the frets want it. Two cents on one string is nothing; six starts to show in chords.
The G-to-B trap. An old instruction says: harmonic at the 4th fret of string 3 against open string 2. The 4th-fret harmonic is the string’s 5th harmonic, a pure major third, which is 14 cents flatter than the frets’ major third. Tuned that way, the B string is 14 cents flat: clearly sour in a G or E chord. Use instead the 7th-fret harmonic of string 6 (a B) against open string 2, and the 5th-fret harmonic of string 6 (an E) against open string 1: unisons, off by only 2 cents and 0. The tuning tool does this.







Strengths
Weaknesses




Harmonics ring on while you turn the peg: both hands free
Pure intervals: 2 cents a step, adding up


No fretting, so finger pressure and fret errors don’t enter
Wrong pairs (the G–B 4th-fret one) are badly out


Clear beats, easy to hear
Hard to play harmonics on day one; weak on some guitars

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
3. Octaves and unisons
Some shapes give the octave of an open string: string 4 fret 2 is the E an octave above string 6. String 3 fret 2 is the A above string 5, string 2 fret 3 the D above string 4, string 1 fret 3 the G above string 3. Strings 6 and 1 are two octaves apart. An octave in tune sounds like one fat note; out of tune it shimmers. Octaves don’t add up errors the way a chain does: each one compares against a string further away, so they catch the drift of the other two methods.

title: Tuning 2: Fifth-Fret, Harmonics and Octaves
text:
4. The last check: a chord
Every method ends at your ear. Strum chords that use all six strings (E, A minor, G, C, D) and listen. If one sounds sour, play its strings two at a time to find the culprit. A small adjustment that makes the chords you play sound right is the right adjustment, even if the tuner disagrees by a cent or two. (Guitarists sometimes shade the B string a little flat for this reason.)



Method
Accuracy
Best for




Reference by ear
~10–20 cents note-by-note, much better with beats
Matching a band, any tuning


Drone
very fine
Practice; training the ear


Fifth-fret
adds up, 5–15 cents worst
No device at all


Harmonics
2 cents a step, ~6 worst; 14 with the wrong pair
Fast, hands free


Octaves
fine, doesn’t add up
Checking the others


Tuner
~1 cent, if used well
Stage, loud rooms: see Tuning 3

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text: Each track ends in a channel strip in the mixer: a fader for its level, a pan control for where it sits left to right, mute and solo, and a meter. All the strips add up in the master strip, which is what you hear and what is saved when you bounce. The mixer is the same in every DAW; only the colours change.

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text:
The controls

Fader, in decibels (dB). 0 dB leaves the track as it is; −6 dB is about half its voltage, and to the ear a little under half as loud takes about −10 dB. Faders move in dB because the ear hears in ratios.
Pan: C is the middle, L100 / R100 hard left / right. Kick, snare, bass and the lead stay in the middle; spread the rest.
Mute (M) silences a track; Solo (S) silences every other track. Solo is for finding a problem; judge balance with everything playing.
Meter: how loud the track is, with a white peak mark. Green is fine, yellow is getting loud, red is close to 0 dBFS, the most a digital file can hold. Past it the waveform is cut off: clipping, a harsh crackle. The CLIP light stays lit once it happens (click it to reset).

title: DAW 5: The Mixer
text:
Fix a bad mix
This mix is wrong on purpose: the keys and guitar are too loud, the bass is nearly gone, the drums are buried, and everything is in the middle.

Play it. Is the master’s CLIP light coming on? Pull the Master down until it stops, then leave it there.
Start with the drums and bass: bring them up until the groove is solid.
Bring the keys and guitar down until they sit around the groove, not on top of it. Turning things down is most of mixing.
Pan the guitar to L40 and the keys to R40. Listen to how they stop fighting.
Solo the bass to hear what it’s doing, then un-solo. Mute the guitar: is the song better without it?
Double-click any fader or pan to put it back to 0 / centre.




The rest of mixing (EQ, compression, reverb on sends, references) is in Recording 5: Mixing; level and headroom before the mix in Recording 1: Gain Staging.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text: A triad has three notes: the root, the 3rd and the 5th. You can stack them in any order. The note you put lowest decides which inversion you are playing. The chord keeps its name, because the three notes are the same. Only the arrangement changes, and with it the sound and the way the hand moves. This lesson covers major and minor triads: how to build the three positions, what they are called, and how to write them. Press ▶ to hear a shape.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
section: Root position, first inversion, second inversion
text:
Root position, first inversion, second inversion
In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is lowest. In second inversion the 5th is lowest. To invert a chord, take the lowest note and move it to the top, an octave higher. Do it once for first inversion and twice for second inversion. Do it a third time and you are back in root position, an octave up.
Finger numbers. Press Show finger numbers to see the fingering in the dots instead of the chord tones. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, in both hands, so the right hand plays a root-position triad 1-3-5 and the left hand 5-3-1. On guitar the index finger is 1 and the little finger 4. Notice that on piano the inversions change the fingering (first inversion in the right hand is 1-2-5), because the wide gap moves.






Look at the dots. In the first chord the root is on the bottom. In the second the 3rd is on the bottom and the root has moved to the top. In the third the 5th is on the bottom. The same three letters, C, E and G, are in all of them.
Telling them apart on the page. Look at the lowest note and ask what it is for the chord. If it is the root, the chord is in root position. A 3rd means first inversion, and a 5th means second inversion. The way the notes sit also gives a clue. In root position the notes are stacked in 3rds (C to E to G). In first inversion the top two notes are a 4th apart (G to C). In second inversion the bottom two notes are a 4th apart (G to C).
Practice: play C in root position, then first inversion, then second inversion, then root position an octave higher. Say the name of the lowest note each time. Repeat on F and G.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Minor triads
Minor triads invert in the same way. The only difference is that the 3rd is a half step lower.



The intervals inside the chord are the thing that changes. A major triad is a major 3rd with a minor 3rd on top; a minor triad is the reverse. So root-position Am (A C E) has a minor 3rd (A to C) and then a major 3rd (C to E). First inversion (C E A) has a major 3rd and then a 4th. Second inversion (E A C) has a 4th and then a minor 3rd. Whatever the quality, a 4th sits at the top of first inversion and at the bottom of second inversion, and that 4th is how you spot an inversion by eye.
Practice: play Am in the three positions, then C and Am one after the other in first inversion. Notice that the two chords share two notes, and only one finger moves.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: figured bass
Classical musicians have a shorthand for the inversions that goes back to the 1600s. It is called figured bass, and it labels the chord by the intervals above the lowest note. You will still see it in theory books and in Roman-numeral analysis.










Position

The 6 stands for the interval of a 6th above the bass note. In first inversion of C, the bass is E and the other notes are G (a 3rd up) and C (a 6th up). In second inversion, the bass is G, with C above it (a 4th up) and E (a 6th up). The figure for first inversion is simply 6, because the 3rd is understood and left unwritten. The second inversion needs both numbers, 64.
With Roman numerals the figures go beside the numeral: I is a tonic triad in root position, I6 is in first inversion, and I64 is in second inversion. In C major, I6 is C/E and I64 is C/G.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Names: slash chords
Pop, rock and jazz players use a simpler system. They write the chord, a slash, and then the bass note. C/E means a C chord with E in the bass: first inversion. C/G means a C chord with G in the bass: second inversion. A plain C means the root is in the bass, although the player decides which notes go above.

Say it as “C over E”. The note after the slash is always the bass. A slash chord can also have a bass note that isn’t in the chord at all, such as C/D. That is not an inversion, and we leave it for another lesson. Chart writers use the slash form because it tells the bassist what to play, and the chord symbol alone does not.

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Inversions on the guitar
On the guitar an inversion is a different set of strings and frets, and the shape moves anywhere on the neck if it has no open string. These are on strings 3, 2 and 1. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Compare the F shapes with the C shapes on the piano above.






The numbers under each diagram are the frets from the low E string to the high E string, and x is a string you don’t play. Move any of these along the neck and the root moves with it. The F shapes become G shapes two frets higher. More about moveable shapes is in Guitar chord shapes by hand.
Practice: play the three F shapes in order, then slide each up two frets and name the new chord.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion
text:
Why use them: voice leading
Without inversions, every chord change makes the hand jump. With them you can choose the position of each chord so that the notes move as little as possible, and some notes stay where they are. This is voice leading. It makes a progression sound smooth and connected, and it is much easier on the hand. For example, going from C to Am to F, the top note C stays put in all three chords, as the root, the 3rd and the 5th, while the other notes move a step at most. That example is worked out in piano chord voicings, and Piano voicings by hand shows how it feels under the fingers.
Practice: play C, then F in second inversion (F/C), then C again. The C stays where it is, and the other two notes each move a step. Then play C, F in root position, C and feel how much farther the hand travels.
crumbs: Inversions: Root Position, First and Second Inversion

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
A hammer-on and a pull-off make a second note without a second pick stroke. The fretting hand does the work. This lesson builds both from one finger on one string up to licks, scale runs and chord embellishments. Each step says what makes it easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong, then gives something to practice. The same technique is the left-hand half of Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs.
How to read the examples. Each exercise is written on a staff and in tablature. Tablature has one line a string, the high E on top, and a number for the fret. A slur between two notes is a hammer-on (the second note is higher, marked H) or a pull-off (the second note is lower, marked P), and both notes lie on one string. The staff is written an octave above where a guitar sounds, as guitarists read it. Press ▶ to hear it. The player picks every note, so on the recording the hammer-ons and pull-offs are separate soft attacks. Listen for the pitches and the rhythm and make the legato yourself. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger).

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
1. One finger on one string
Pick the open G string once. Then bring finger 2 down on the 2nd fret from above, quickly, with the tip, just behind the fret wire. The string rings the higher note with no pick. That is a hammer-on.




Easy because: one finger, one string and one pick stroke.
Hard because: the finger has to land hard enough to sound a note with nothing but its own speed. A soft landing gives a faint or no note.
What goes wrong:

The finger lands flat or too far back from the fret, and the note is dull or buzzes.
The hand lifts the finger a long way before it falls. A short, quick drop is enough, and it keeps the hand relaxed.
The other fingers fly up in sympathy. Let them hang near the strings.


Practice: ten hammer-ons in a row, each one picked once, with a rest between. Listen for the hammered note being as loud as the picked one. That takes some weeks to get.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 2. From an open string: each finger
text:
2. From an open string: each finger
An open string is the easiest start, because no finger is holding the lower note. On the high E string, hammer each finger in turn: finger 1 at fret 1, finger 2 at fret 2, finger 3 at fret 3, finger 4 at fret 4.




Easy because: the open string is a fixed, ringing starting point.
Hard because: fingers 3 and 4 are weaker than 1 and 2, and they land softly at first.
What goes wrong: the weak fingers give the faintest notes. A finger landing next to the fret rather than behind it, a thumb riding over the neck, and the wrist drooping all make it worse.

Practice: the same drill on every string. Spend most of the time on fingers 3 and 4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
3. Fretted to fretted
Now the lower note is fretted too. Press finger 1 down on the 2nd fret of the A string and pick. Finger 1 stays down while finger 2 hammers onto fret 3. When the higher finger lands it shortens the string, and the higher note sounds. Then try fret 4 with finger 3, then move up one fret and do it again.




Easy because: you already know both halves. The picked note is a plain fretted note, and the hammer is the move from section 2.
Hard because: two fingers have to be placed at once, one to keep the lower note ringing and one to hammer.
What goes wrong: the lower finger relaxes when the upper one lands and the first note dies. The hammer lands on a different string from the one picked. The hammered note is quieter than the picked one.

Practice: hold finger 1 down and hammer with finger 2, then 3, then 4, up and down the neck on one string.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
4. Pull-offs
A pull-off is the mirror image. Put two fingers down on the same string, the upper one at the higher fret and the lower one at the lower fret. Pick, then pull the upper finger off, and as it leaves, pull it a little sideways, toward the floor, so that it plucks the string. The lower finger or the open string rings.



Then with the lower note fretted:




Easy because: a pull-off is a hammer-on backwards. Section 3’s two-finger shape is the same.
Hard because: the lower finger must already be in place before the pull. A pull-off that only lifts the finger sounds weak. It has to flick.
What goes wrong:

The upper finger lifts straight up and the lower note is barely heard.
The finger drags across the next string and mutes it or sounds it.
The lower finger is not down yet when the upper one leaves.


Practice: put both fingers down, pick, and pull off. Play the picked note and the pulled note at an even loudness. Do the open-string version on every string, then the fretted one.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
5. Trills and hammer-pull loops
Put the two together. Pick once, hammer on, pull off, hammer on, and keep going, and the picked note turns into a trill. This is how guitarists get a long, fluttering note out of one pick stroke, and it is a fine test of both techniques at once.



Make it faster by halving the note values. Then end with a picked note, so the trill has a landing.




Easy because: nothing new: a hammer-on, a pull-off and a repeat.
Hard because: the notes have to stay even and loud while the hand tires.
What goes wrong: the notes fade away as the hand tires. The rhythm rushes. The lower finger gets pushed off when the upper finger hammers.

Practice: one measure at a slow tempo, with a metronome, and then speed up 4 beats a minute at a time. Stop when the notes begin to fade. Try it with fingers 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 and 3-4.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
text:
6. In licks and scale runs
A lick is a short phrase. Written below are three, all in the key of A minor, in the first of the pentatonic positions, with the index finger on the 5th fret. Each slur is on one string. The first goes up with hammer-ons and the second comes down with pull-offs:



The third is in the open position and mixes both. The hammer-on from the open D string, and the pull-off back to the open G string, are the sound of a lot of blues and country playing:




Easy because: a pentatonic run is only two notes a string, and each pair is a hammer-on or a pull-off you know.
Hard because: the picks and the slurs alternate, and the hand has to change strings after each pair.
What goes wrong: the picked note at the start of each pair is rushed, and then the slurred notes sound like they are in a hurry. Playing it fast without the pick on the first note of each pair is the quickest way to lose the beat.

Practice: play the first two bars with a metronome at 70, and say the rhythm out loud, “one-and two-and”. When the slurred notes are as loud as the picked ones, speed up.

title: Hammer-ons and Pull-offs on Guitar
section: 7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
text:
7. Inside chord shapes: the Sus embellishment
Hammer-ons and pull-offs also decorate a chord. The best known is the Sus embellishment: strum an open chord, then hammer one finger onto a note next to a chord tone, so that the chord briefly becomes a sus chord, and pull it off to come home again. Jimi Hendrix used the idea all through Little Wing and Castles Made of Sand, and rock, folk and country guitarists use it all the time. On D, A and C the moving finger is the little finger or the ring finger on the top strings, and the rest of the chord stays put.
D. Strum D. The finger on the high E string (fret 2) stays down. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the same string: the 3rd of the chord (F♯) becomes the 4th (G), and D becomes Dsus4. Pull off to come back.






A. Strum A. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of the B string, over the finger that holds fret 2: A becomes Asus4.






C. Strum C. The high E string is open. Hammer the little finger onto fret 3 of that string, then pull off. The top note moves from E to G and back.







Easy because: the chord is already under your hand. Only one finger moves, and only one fret.
Hard because: the hammering finger is the little finger, and it has to land without touching the next string or lifting a finger that is holding the chord.
What goes wrong:

The chord gets thinner because a finger of the shape lifted when the pinky came down.
The pinky lands on the pad instead of the tip, and mutes the string next to it.
It is played so fast and so loud that it stops sounding like a chord with a flourish.


Practice: strum the chord once, then hammer and pull off with a steady pulse, one decoration to a chord. Play along with the band: the chart is D, A, C, D, one bar each. Do the embellishment on each chord in time.



Unlocks: Travis picking with hammer-ons and pull-offs; the open-chord decorations of pop changes for guitar; guitar chord shapes by hand.
