title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
This lesson is for a pianist who plays pop and rock chords and hasn’t yet met jazz voicings. Its thirteen steps each change one thing from the step before: how many notes, which chord tones, or where they sit. Piano voicings by hand has the same chords in the order the hands find them easy.
How to read the diagrams. Each keyboard shows one voicing. The dots carry the chord tones, counted up from the root: R, 3, 5, ♭7, 9 and so on. The root is a filled square. The staff underneath puts the right hand on the treble clef and the left hand on the bass clef. Press ▶ to hear a voicing.
Fingers are numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger), listed from the lowest note up. Middle C is C4.
Each step has an ID, such as P-A3, that other lessons use to point back here. The chords stay the same throughout: C, Am, F and G for pop, and Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 for the ii–V–I. That way a step here can be played with the same notes as its partner in the physical order.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
text:
P-A1 Root-position triads over a bass root
A triad is root, 3rd and 5th. The 3rd decides major or minor, and the 5th gives weight. The left hand names the chord with its root, and the right hand fills it in. This is the sound of most pop piano, and every later step rearranges these notes or adds to them.



Fingering: LH 5 on the root. RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play the four chords on a steady beat. Notice that the right hand jumps every time. The next step gets rid of the jumps.
Unlocks: Piano ballad with Long notes or Quarter-note chords.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
text:
P-A2 Inversions and smooth voice leading
Inverting a triad moves its lowest note to the top, so the hand can stay in one place. Here the note C stays put through the first three chords: it is the root of C, the 3rd of Am and the 5th of F. The other notes move by a step at most. This is voice leading: each note travels as little as it can, and the chords sound connected. The bass root still names the chord.



Fingering: RH root position 1-3-5, first inversion (3rd at the bottom) 1-2-5, second inversion (5th at the bottom) 1-3-5.
Practice: loop the four chords with your eyes closed after the first time round. The hand moves no more than a finger’s width. Then play the loop in F and in G.
Unlocks: Ballad: rocking, Ballad: half-broken, Arpeggio up and down.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A3 Sus and add9
Sus2 and sus4 replace the 3rd with the 2nd or the 4th. The chord is then neither major nor minor, and it wants to settle. Add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 9th, the 2nd an octave up, for the shimmering open sound of pop ballads. Put the 9th above the 3rd, not right next to the root, or it rubs.



Fingering: sus2 1-2-5; sus4 1-4-5; Cadd9 (3–5–9) 1-2-5.
Practice: play Gsus4 and then G. One finger moves, as C falls to B. Then go from C to Cadd9.
Unlocks: Piano ballad, Arpeggio low and high; the Cadd9 bars of pop changes for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
text:
P-A4 Slash chords: a moving bass under still triads
The two hands now do separate jobs. The left hand walks the bass line C, B, A, G, F, F♯, G, and the right hand holds triads that barely move. A triad over a bass note other than its root makes a new chord with a new name. F over G, the last chord here, is the first jazz-flavoured sound in the sequence: G with ♭7, 9 and 11. P-A13 comes back to the idea.



Practice: play only the bass line, then only the right hand, then both together, slowly. Keep the right hand soft and let the bass line sing.
Unlocks: the passing chords in pop changes; Motown / soul.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
text:
P-A5 Seventh chords in close position
A seventh chord stacks one more 3rd on the triad, and the kind of 7th sets the colour. A major 7th (B in Cmaj7) is bright and floating. A ♭7 (B♭ in C7) is bluesy and restless. In a minor chord the ♭7 is soft. A dominant 7th has a tritone between its 3rd and its 7th (B and F in G7), which wants to resolve.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5.
Practice: play C, Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7, changing one finger at a time, and put each colour into words.
Unlocks: Medium swing with Quarter-note chords; the 7th chords in blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A6 Inverted 7ths: the ii–V–I
Choose each inversion so that the hand barely moves. From Dm7 to G7, F and D stay, A falls to G and C falls to B. From G7 to Cmaj7, F falls to E, D falls to C, and G and B stay. Each time, the 7th of one chord falls a step to the 3rd of the next: C to B, then F to E. That falling 7th is the engine of jazz harmony.



Fingering: RH 1-2-3-5 for each.
Practice: loop the three chords in time and sing the top line, D–D–C. Then move to F (Gm7, C7, Fmaj7) and B♭.
Unlocks: Medium swing, Charleston, and ii–V–I turnarounds.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A7 Guide tones: 3rd and 7th
The 3rd and the 7th are the only tones that tell major from minor and dominant from major 7th, so two notes can stand for the whole chord. The root belongs to the bass, and the 5th adds little. Follow the lines: C falls to B while F holds, then F falls to E while B holds. Guide tones goes further.



Fingering: RH 1-3 for a 4th; 1-4 for the tritone.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in guide tones, then sing each line. Add a top note of your own, any chord tone.
Unlocks: Charleston and Reverse Charleston without clutter; blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A8 Shells: 1–3–7 and 1–7–3
A shell is root, 3rd and 7th in the left hand alone, which leaves the right hand free for a melody. In 1–3–7 order the shape spans a 7th and sits comfortably under one hand. In 1–7–3 order the 3rd is on top, a 10th above the root. That sounds more open, and it is the classic jazz left hand, but most hands need the right thumb to take the 3rd. The root is in the shell because, with no bass player, someone has to play it.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1 for 1–3–7. For 1–7–3, LH 5-1 on root and 7th, and RH 1 on the 3rd.
Practice: play the ii–V–I in the left hand only, then add a melody in the right. Alternate 1–3–7 and 1–7–3 (Dm7 1–3–7, G7 1–7–3, Cmaj7 1–3–7) so the hand hardly moves.
Unlocks: solo piano and comping without a bass; blues for piano.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
text:
P-A9 Rootless voicings, A and B
With a bass player covering the root, the left hand plays the 3rd, the 7th and two colour tones: the 9th, plus the 13th on a dominant. Form A has the 3rd at the bottom and form B has the 7th at the bottom. Alternate them and each chord is only a step from the last. This has been the left-hand sound of jazz piano since the 1950s, and the site’s jazz styles use it. The Chord Library calls these Rootless A/B.



Fingering: LH 5-3-2-1 for A forms; 5-3-2-1 or 5-4-2-1 for B forms.
Practice: play the first chain (A–B–A) on a metronome, with the bass line D, G, C in the right hand. Then learn the chain that starts on B.
Unlocks: Jazz ballad, Medium swing with Charleston, Bossa nova, and Boogaloo.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A10 Drop 2
Take a four-note chord in close position and drop its second-highest note an octave. Dm7 in close position is D–F–A–C. The second note from the top is A, which drops to A3. The chord now spreads over an octave and a half, with the root back in the middle, and it sounds fuller and more orchestral. Put a melody note on top of a close chord, drop the second voice, and you have harmonised the melody.



Fingering: LH 2-1, RH 1-4 or 1-5.
Practice: take the first phrase of a melody you know. Play each melody note as the top of a close chord, then drop the second voice. Drop 3, where the third voice from the top drops, is the same idea one voice lower.
Unlocks: block-chord melody (George Shearing, Bill Evans), and Long notes under a singer.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
section: P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
text:
P-A11 Spread voicings: low 5th, upper triad
An open 5th low in the left hand is the cleanest bass a piano has, because it stays out of the muddy middle register. Above it, the right hand plays a triad built from the 3rd, 7th and 9th. For Cmaj9 that is E–B–D, a little like an Em triad over C, which is why a rich chord can feel simple to play. The site has no voicing style for spread voicings yet.



Fingering: LH 5-1, RH 1-3-5 (or 1-4-5 where the lower gap is wide).
Practice: hold the low 5th with the pedal, then place the right hand above it. Learn the low 5th as one shape.
Unlocks: Arpeggio low and high, Ballad: syncopated, Jazz ballad, and gospel and singer-songwriter ballads.
crumbs: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A12 Quartal voicings
Stacking 4ths leaves no 3rd in the chord, so it is neither major nor minor. It sounds open, modern and modal. The best-known example is the “So What” voicing from Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue (1959): three 4ths and a major 3rd on top. Every interval in a stack of 4ths is the same, so the shape can slide up and down and keep its sound. The site has no quartal voicing style yet.



Fingering: LH 5-2-1 with RH 1-3 for the So What chord; RH 1-3-5 for a three-note stack.
Practice: play the So What chord, then the same shape a half step higher, and back. Then slide a three-note stack up the white keys from D.
Unlocks: modal jazz and Bossa nova.

title: Piano Chord Voicings: From Pop Triads Toward Jazz
text:
P-A13 Upper-structure triads
The left hand plays a shell that fixes the chord’s name and type. The right hand plays a plain major triad built from the extensions above it. D major over a C shell gives Cmaj7 with a 9th, a ♯11 and a 13th. A major over a G7 shell is the same colour on a dominant. This is P-A4’s idea again: a triad over a different bass note. The site has no voicing style for upper structures yet.



Fingering: LH 5-3-1, RH 1-3-5.
Practice: play G7 as a shell, then place the A triad on top. Then try the D♭ triad and hear how strongly it pulls to C.
Unlocks: ballad endings, tags and turnarounds; reharmonising.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
The pattern
Stride with a wider left hand: on beat 1 a tenth (the root with the chord’s 3rd an octave above it, together); on beat 3 the fifth, or, when the chord is about to change, a tenth walking to a step from the next root. Chords in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. A tenth that would crowd the chords is played as its low note alone. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 1: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Start with something simpler. Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 2: Stride
The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride in tenths
text:
Step 3: Stride in tenths, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The stride left hand, stretched: on beat 1 the root with the 3rd an octave above it, both at once (roll them if your hand will not reach). On beat 3 the fifth, or, before a chord change, a tenth a step away from the next root, so the bass walks into it. Learn the leaps first with single notes, then add the top of each tenth.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern
text:
The pattern
The same thumb on every beat: root, inner string, alternate bass, inner string. The fingers pinch with it on beat 1, then play between the thumb’s notes: the and of 2, the and of 3, the and of 4.
It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: Travis pattern
text:
Step 1: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
Start with something simpler. Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
The pattern
The backbeat at half speed: kick on 1 and the and of 2, one snare on beat 3.
It belongs in Piano ballad, Straight-eighth rock and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
Step 1: Hi-hat: eighth notes
Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every eighth note, all of one weight, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The basic rock beat. In 3/4: six eighths, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Half-time
text:
Step 2: Rock backbeat
Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

How to play it. The backbeat at half speed: kick on 1 and the and of 2, a single snare on beat 3. The chords go as fast, the song feels slower.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride
text:
The pattern
The stride pianist’s left hand: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 (the root in octaves where a chord starts, its fifth on beat 3) and the chord in the middle of the keyboard on beats 2 and 4. In 3/4 the bass on 1 and the chord on 2 and 3. On the guitar it is plain boom-chick.
It belongs in Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the stride piano style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride
text:
Step 1: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
Start with something simpler. Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Stride
text:
Step 2: Stride, slowly
Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. The left hand alone first: a low octave on the root on beat 1, a chord about two octaves higher on beat 2, the fifth down low on beat 3, the chord again on 4. Look at where the hand lands, not where it has been: the leap down is the hard one. Keep the bass notes short and the chords lighter. When it is steady, let the band’s bass and drums join.

The pattern
After Jimmy Yancey’s slow-blues left hand: root on 1, fifth on the and of 1, root on the and of 2, fifth on 3, root on 4. A lilting, habanera-like figure for a slow blues. A chord that arrives on beat 3 starts on its root.

text:

title: Bass line: Yancey figure
text:
Step 2: Tango (habanera)
The habanera rhythm: root held for a beat and a half, the fifth on the and of 2, then the root an octave up on 3 and the fifth on 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:
The pattern
The ride pattern played on the hi-hat itself: open on 1 and 3, closed on 2 and 4 with the skip note after them, the foot closing the cymbals on 2 and 4. Swung. Nothing else.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:

Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Drum groove: Hi-hat: swing time
text:
Step 2: Ride pattern (learning swing, 2)
The swing ride pattern and nothing else: the cymbal on every beat with a skip note before 3 and before 1 (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a), and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Ballad: syncopated

Three held chords in a bar of eight eighth notes, grouped 3+3+2: beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4. Clocks, Shape of You, Eye of the Tiger.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

text:
The pattern

title: Bass line: Octaves (disco)
text:
Step 1: Roots on every beat
Start with something simpler. The root of the chord on every beat and nothing else. The plainest line there is, under driving eighths or a strummed song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Octaves (disco)
text:
Step 2: Root eighths
The root on every eighth note, the beats a little louder: the rock bass line under With or Without You and a thousand others.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
The pattern
The boogaloo riff, but about half the four-bar phrases end with a bar of walking quarter notes that leads into the next phrase, and now and then two bars.
It belongs in Boogaloo. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 1: Boogaloo riff
Start with something simpler. A repeated straight-eighths figure: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, then a fifth and flat seventh on beat 4 leading back to the root. The kind of line under Watermelon Man. In 6/8 and 12/8 it becomes a shuffle: each beat played long-short, climbing root, 3rd, 5th, 6th.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 2: Chord tones (learning to walk)
The chord spelled out, one note on every beat: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, the same in every bar. When a bar has two chords, each gets its root and one more note. A step between playing roots and walking.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff, walking at times
text:
Step 3: Walking
One note on every beat (four quarter notes in 4/4, three in 3/4, dotted quarters in 12/8): the root on beat 1 when the chord changes, chord tones and scale steps in between, and an approach note on beat 4 that leads into the next bar.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

How to play it. Riff most of the time; at the end of some four-bar phrases, walk one bar of quarter notes into the next phrase. The skill is the switch: feel where the phrase ends and land on the next root exactly on 1.

text:

It belongs in Swing, Jazz ballad and Stride piano. Here it is in the swing style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Drum groove: Ride pattern (learning swing, 2)
text:
Step 1: Quarter notes (learning swing, 1)
Start with something simpler. Only the beat: the cymbal on 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. No kick, no snare, no fills. The first thing to play on a blues.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
text:
The pattern
Short chords on the beats the bass leaves free: 2 and 4 in 4/4, 2 and 3 in a waltz. Goes with the Root and fifth bass line.
It belongs in Boom-chick, Country train beat, Motown / soul, Folk carol, Stride piano and Ragtime. Here it is in the boom-chick style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
text:
Step 1: Quarter-note chords
Start with something simpler. The chord on every beat, held. On the piano the left hand adds the root underneath as each chord arrives: Let It Be, Imagine, Someone Like You.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah
text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. Short chords on 2 and 4 where the bass leaves room (on 2 and 3 in a waltz). On piano: left hand plays the bass on 1 and 3, right hand the chord on 2 and 4. On guitar: pick the bass note, then strum the chord.
The band plays it on piano here; the step after next has it on guitar.

The same rhythm on the guitar. On guitar each chord is a strum or a pluck of a chord shape; a short chord is choked by easing the fretting hand off the strings.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:
The pattern
A repeated straight-eighths figure: root on 1, root pushed on the and of 2, then a fifth and flat seventh on beat 4 leading back to the root. The kind of line under Watermelon Man. In 6/8 and 12/8 it becomes a shuffle: each beat played long-short, climbing root, 3rd, 5th, 6th.
It belongs in Boogaloo. Here it is in the boogaloo style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:
Step 1: Roots on 1 and 3
Start with something simpler. The root on beats 1 and 3, held; one note a bar in 3/4. A chord that changes in between gets its root when it arrives.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:
Step 2: Dotted (1, and of 2, 3)
The root on beat 1, again on the and of 2 and on beat 3, the same rhythm as the kick drum. Every second bar ends with an eighth note that leads into the next chord.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Bass line: Boogaloo riff
text:

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.
How to play it. A straight-eighths riff: root on 1, root again on the and of 2, then fifth and flat seventh on beat 4 climbing back to the root. The push on the and of 2 is the same one as the dotted line; the ending is new. Play every bar the same.

The pattern
Eighths on the cymbal and a full snare on 2 and 4. The kick changes over four bars: 1, 3 and the and of 3; then 1, the and of 2 and 3; the last bar adds a pickup on the and of 4. Sixteenth-note fills.
It belongs in Straight-eighth rock and Emo / pop-punk. Here it is in the straight-eighth rock style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

text:

Start with something simpler. Closed hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The first rock beat. In 3/4: hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1, snare on 3.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums play alone first; switch the bass and chords on when it is steady.

This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

Step 2: Roots on every beat

Step 3: Chord tones (learning to walk), slowly

How to play it. Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, one to a beat, the same shape every bar. On a minor seventh chord the 3rd is three frets above the root; on a dominant or major chord, four. Say the chord tones as you play them.

text:

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
text:
The pattern
Thumb and fingers, after John Prine. The thumb plays every beat on the low strings: the root, an inner string, the alternate bass, the inner string again. The fingers pinch a treble string with the thumb on 2 and 4 and add the string below it on the and after. In 3/4 the pinches are on 2 and 3.
It belongs in John Prine Fingerpicking, Boom-chick, Acoustic strum, Folk carol and Country train beat. Here it is in the john prine fingerpicking style with the whole band. Switch the other players off to hear it alone.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and
section: Step 1: Strum: downstrokes on the beat
text:
Step 1: Strum: downstrokes on the beat
Start with something simpler. One ringing downstroke on every beat. The first strum to learn, and the usual one for a slow song.
This is a pattern of its own: the lesson on it takes it further. Here it is only a step on the way, slowly. The drums keep time with you; switch the others on when it is steady.

title: Comping rhythm: Fingerpicking: thumb, pinch-and

Step 2: Boom-chick / oom-pah-pah

Now the pattern itself. Compare it with the step before: press each button while the band plays and watch what changes on the staff.

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
Stride and boogie-woogie are the two great left hands of early jazz piano. Both are solo piano music for dancing, both swing, and both make the pianist’s left hand do the work of a bass player and a rhythm guitarist at once. They do it in opposite ways: stride leaps, boogie-woogie walks. This page plays them on the band one at a time, then side by side, then swaps their parts.
How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read the band’s last four bars on the staff underneath. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down. For the history of each, see the Style Notes on Stride piano and Boogie-woogie.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
1. Where they meet

Rent parties. In the 1920s, tenants in Harlem and on Chicago’s South Side paid the rent by throwing a party with food, drink and a pianist. Harlem’s pianists played stride; Chicago’s played boogie-woogie. One piano had to be the whole band.
The left hand keeps time. In both, the left hand never stops and never changes its pattern much. The right hand is free to play the tune, riffs and runs on top.
Swing eighths. Both are swung: the eighth notes go long-short.
The same players. Count Basie began as a stride pianist taught by Fats Waller, and his band recorded Boogie Woogie in 1936. Fats Waller played boogie-woogie too, and the boogie-woogie pianists knew stride.
Where they went. Stride turned into swing piano (Teddy Wilson, Art Tatum, Basie); boogie-woogie into jump blues and rock and roll.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
2. Stride: bass, chord, bass, chord
The stride left hand plays a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. Here the band’s pianist plays only that left hand. Compare it with plain boom-chick, where the bass note is left to the bass player.



What to look for. On the staff the left hand jumps about two octaves on every beat. Stride pianists practise the jump with their eyes on the landing note: the low one. Start with the root on 1 and 3, then play the fifth on 3. Full lesson: Stride.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
3. Boogie-woogie: eight to the bar
The boogie-woogie left hand walks up the chord and back down in swung eighth notes: root, 3rd, 5th, 6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd. The band gives it to the bass player. Compare it with the simpler lines it is built from.



What to look for. The shape is the same on every chord; only the root moves. On the piano the hand stays in one position, fingers 5 1 on the root and 6th. Full lesson: Boogie-woogie.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
section: 4. Side by side on a blues
text:
4. Side by side on a blues
The same 12-bar blues in C, once in each style, with the whole band. Listen to the bottom of the band: stride bounces between low and middle on the beats; boogie-woogie rolls along underneath in eighths.
Stride



Boogie-woogie



The charts differ too. A stride player on a blues borrows the songs’ turnarounds (A7, D7, G7 leading home); a boogie-woogie player keeps to three chords, because the left hand is the interest.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
5. Swap the parts
Both styles’ parts can be played in the other’s band. Below is the boogie-woogie band; swap its bass and piano for stride’s and back. The drums keep the shuffle.



The last one is busy: two left hands at once, one leaping, one walking. Real players choose one.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
section: 6. Before and after: ragtime and jump blues
text:
6. Before and after: ragtime and jump blues
Stride came from ragtime: the same left hand in straight eighths, under a written, syncopated melody. Boogie-woogie went into jump blues: the same bass in a small band, with a hard backbeat on the drums. Switch between each pair and listen for what changes and what stays.






See the Style Notes on Ragtime and Jump blues.
crumbs: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie

title: Two Left Hands: Stride and Boogie-Woogie
text:
7. Try it

Pianists: switch the band’s piano off in section 2 and play the stride left hand yourself, slowly. Then switch the bass off in section 3 and play the boogie line with your left hand.
Bass players: the boogie-woogie line is a classic bass part in its own right. Play it on a 12-bar blues in section 4.
Listen to Fats Waller’s Handful of Keys and Albert Ammons’s Boogie Woogie Stomp back to back.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text: The chord instruments fill the middle of the band. They play the notes the bass leaves out, in a rhythm that fits between the drums’ hits. This is called comping (short for accompanying). How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
1. The rhythm is the part
A guitar part is mostly a rhythm. The chords here never change, only the strumming pattern. Each one gives the same song a different energy.



Under a singer, long chords and fingerpicking leave the most room. Down-up eighths fill everything and suit a loud chorus. Many arrangements go from sparse in the verse to full in the chorus with the same chords.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
2. Voicing: which notes, how high
The same chord can be played with all six strings ringing (an open chord) or as three notes higher up the neck (a triad). Open chords fill the whole range from low to high. A small triad stays out of the bass’s way and out of the singer’s.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
3. Off the beat: the chop
In reggae and ska the guitar plays only on the off-beats: short and choked. Motown guitarists did something similar on 2 and 4, doubling the snare. A chord instrument that plays very little can still be the part everyone remembers.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
4. Jazz comping: piano and guitar
In jazz, the piano doesn’t play a pattern. It plays short chords, mostly off the beat, and answers the soloist. It also leaves out the root (the bass has it) and plays rootless voicings: the 3rd, 7th and colour notes.



A swing-era guitarist (Freddie Green in the Count Basie band) did the opposite: a short three-note chord on every beat, felt more than heard. Here are the two together. That’s what the next section is about.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
5. Two chord players at once
Two chord instruments that both play busy patterns in the same register fight. The fix is to give them different jobs: one plays the rhythm, the other holds long chords, or one plays low and the other high. The band does this by itself when a second chord player is added: switch each one off in turn.
Swing: piano comps, the guitar plays four to the bar.



Rock: the guitar strums, an organ holds long chords behind it. This is the classic “pad” organ of 60s and 70s rock and soul.



The organ is its own world. The next lesson takes it apart.

title: Arranging 3: Guitar and Keyboards
text:
6. Try it

In section 2, pick Open chords and turn the bass off. Then pick Triads. Which one needs the bass more?
In section 5, switch off the drums and bass and listen to only the two chord players. Can you hear which one keeps the rhythm and which one holds the harmony?



  Tempo 
  ■ Stop

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text: Digital pianos, stage pianos, synths and MIDI controllers look alike and are set up alike. Here’s what the connections do, and how to look after them.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Kinds of keyboard

Digital piano: weighted keys, built-in speakers, mostly piano sounds. Good for practice.
Stage piano / workstation: weighted or semi-weighted keys, many sounds, no speakers (needs an amp or PA).
Synthesizer: sound design controls (filter, envelopes; the Sound lessons), usually light synth-action keys.
MIDI controller: no sounds of its own. It sends MIDI to a computer or another instrument.
Arranger keyboard: auto-accompaniment styles and built-in speakers.

Key count: 88 is a full piano; 61 and 76 are common on stage; 25–49 for controllers.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Connections

Outputs: usually L/Mono and R (1/4”). Mono gig? Use only L/Mono; the keyboard then sums both sides. Stereo: both, into two channels panned left and right, or a stereo DI.
Headphones: often mutes the speakers. Turn the volume down before putting them on.
Sustain pedal: plug it in before switching on; many keyboards read the pedal’s polarity at power-up, and if it was plugged in later the sustain works backwards (on when lifted). Fix: switch off, plug in, switch on with the foot off. Or use the polarity switch on the pedal.
Expression pedal: volume or other control, a separate TRS jack.
MIDI: USB to a computer (the site’s Notation page can take a MIDI keyboard in Chrome), or 5-pin MIDI Out → In to another instrument.
Power: many keyboards use a specific adaptor: wrong voltage or polarity can kill them (Gear 1).

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Settings worth knowing

Local Off: the keys stop playing the keyboard’s own sounds and only send MIDI. Use it when the computer plays the sound back, or you’ll hear two of everything.
Transpose: shifts all keys. Easy to leave on by accident: if you sound in the wrong key, check it first.
Split / Layer: two sounds on two halves, or two at once.
Touch / velocity curve: lighter or heavier response.
Volume slider: keep it fairly high (around ¾) and do the balance on the mixer, for less noise.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:
Setup and care

Stand: an X stand at a height where your forearms are level with the keys (elbows slightly above). Tighten every knob; check it doesn’t wobble.
Dust cover when not in use; no drinks on top.
Cleaning: unplugged, a soft cloth very slightly damp with water (a drop of mild soap). Never spray onto the keys. Liquid between keys breaks contacts.
Moving: a padded bag or case, keys facing your body. Don’t stand it on its end without a case.
Cold: a keyboard brought in from a cold car should warm up before switching on, so condensation doesn’t form.
Sticking or dead key: note which one and report it; don’t prise keys up.

title: Gear 4: Keyboards
text:

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
This is how a guitarist plays chords in a band on a 12-bar blues without a single barre chord: two or three well-chosen notes, moved by a fret at a time. You need to know how to fret a note and how the strings are numbered (6 is the low E, 1 is the high E). For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear it. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its guitarist plays exactly the notes in the diagrams, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the guitar to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. Find the key note on string 6. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on string 5. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on string 5. Three chords, three notes, and the hand stays where it is.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.



Play one long note per bar with the band and count the form: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Knowing where the roots are is what lets you find every chord shape that follows.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
2. What the 3rd and 7th do
A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the root, the 3rd, the 5th and the 7th. They do different jobs.

The root names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
The 5th adds weight and not much else.
The 3rd says whether the chord is major or minor.
The 7th says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a dominant seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord’s character. They are called the guide tones. Play only those two notes and a listener still hears the chord, especially with a bass player underneath. The diagrams show all four notes of each chord, with the guide tones filled in. Click a chord name to hear the four notes climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



From the root: the 3rd is one string up and one fret back, the 5th is one string up and two frets on, and the ♭7th is two strings up at the same fret as the root.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
3. Guide tones on strings 5 and 4
Now play just the 3rd and 7th, as a two-note chord on strings 5 and 4. Look at the Superimposed view to see what makes this worth learning: the three chords are the same two-finger shape, one fret apart. From the I chord, move both fingers down one fret for IV and up one fret for V.
That works because the 3rd of one chord is a half step from the 7th of the next. Going from I7 to IV7, the 3rd drops a fret and becomes the ♭7th, and the ♭7th drops a fret and becomes the 3rd. Switch the labels to chord tones and watch the two notes swap names.
Up a tritone. The 3rd and ♭7th of a dominant chord are six frets’ worth of pitch apart, an interval called a tritone, and a tritone turned upside down is still a tritone. So the same two-finger shape six frets higher gives the same two notes of the same chord, with the 3rd and ♭7th changing places. Press Up a tritone to move all three chords there. That gives every chord two homes on each pair of strings. In keys where the lower home would run off the end of the neck (F and G♭ here), the diagrams start in the upper one, so the three shapes always stay one fret apart.



The hollow dot is the root. Where one is shown it is in reach on string 6 and you can add it; where none is shown, leave it to the bass player.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
text:
4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root
The same pairs one string set higher sit under roots on both low strings, so every chord can have its root added. These three-note chords are shell voicings: root, 3rd and 7th with the 5th left out. A chord with its root on string 6 has the 7th on string 4 and the 3rd on string 3. A chord with its root on string 5 has the 3rd on string 4 and the 7th on string 3. Mute string 5 with the side of your finger when the root is on string 6.
First the two notes alone:



Then with the root. This is the rhythm guitar sound of the swing era. Up a tritone here moves each chord to its other shell: the root changes string and the 3rd and 7th change places above it.



The band’s guitarist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that rhythm, then try four even strokes to the bar (set the feel and tempo to taste).
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord: its 3rd is one fret lower than a dominant chord’s. In a shell with the root on string 6, that puts the 7th and the minor 3rd at the same fret, under one finger.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Press Superimposed to see how little the hand moves through ii7, V7 and I7.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here it is with the shells from step 4 underneath.



Comp under the tune with a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3, and leave the riff room. Then look at the guide tones alone. The riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a fret to become the ♭7th of IV, which is exactly what your guide-tone shape does at the same moment.
crumbs: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords

title: Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place. Start with F, B♭, A and C.
Loop a chorus with the guitar left out and comp for yourself.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and find the guide tones of each new chord from its root.
The Chord Sheet tool (Tools menu) draws these and fuller voicings for any chords you type in, one at a time or superimposed.

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
You can buy a tuner for the price of a sandwich, so why learn to tune by ear? Because playing in tune is something you hear, not something you see. A string drifts during a song, a singer goes a little flat, the band’s keyboard is tuned slightly high: a screen can’t fix any of that for you, and your ear can. Tuning is the best ear training a guitarist gets, and you do it every time you pick the guitar up. This lesson and the next two compare the ways of tuning, and what each is good and bad at. Practise them in the tuning tool.
Words. Strings are numbered 6 (thickest) to 1 (thinnest). Flat means too low, sharp too high. A cent is a hundredth of a half step (one fret): most people can’t hear 5 cents on one note alone, but they can hear it easily as beating between two notes.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
1. Matching a reference
The simplest method: something plays the right note (a piano, a tuning fork, an app, the tuning tool’s Play reference), and you make the string match.

Listen to the reference. Hum it.
Pick the open string. Is it higher or lower than what you hummed? Say it out loud.
Turn the peg while the string rings, a little at a time.








Strengths
Weaknesses




Needs nothing but a reference; works in any tuning
A note heard one after another is hard to judge closer than about 10–20 cents


Trains the most important skill: is it higher or lower?
Low strings are harder to hear than high ones


Works with any reference, including a bandmate’s note
You need a reference that is itself in tune
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
section: 2. Beats: the wobble you tune by
text:
2. Beats: the wobble you tune by
Play two notes that are nearly the same and you hear a slow wah-wah-wah. That’s beating: the two waves slide in and out of step. The beat rate is the difference between the two frequencies: notes at 110 and 111 Hz beat once a second, 110 and 113 three times. So the beats tell you how far off you are, and they slow down as you get closer. In tune, they stop. This is far more precise than comparing notes one after another, and it’s what every method in these lessons relies on.
Hear it: the widget below plays two notes. Pick P8 (an octave) or P5, and switch between just (whole-number ratios, no beating) and equal (the guitar’s frets, a slow beat).



Tune up to the note. If you’re sharp, go below and come back up. The gear in the tuning peg then holds against the string’s pull, and the string stays put.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
3. Tuning to a drone
A drone is a note that keeps sounding. Tune a string against it and you hear the beating the whole time, so you can turn the peg and listen at once. The drone on this site (the Drone button in the top bar, or the one below) holds a note and its fifth; the tuning tool puts one on each string’s note.






Strengths
Weaknesses




The ear hears beats continuously: very precise
A drone on E and B tunes those strings best; the others want their own drone note


Trains hearing in tune against something, the way you play with a band
A pure fifth in the drone isn’t quite the guitar’s fifth (2 cents): see Tuning 2


No microphone, works in a noisy room with headphones
Needs a device



Listening and not listening. Practise both: tune to the drone, then turn the drone off and play a chord. Does it still sound right? Then turn it back on and check. The tool’s Listening switch does the same with the microphone: tune with it off, and only then turn it on to see how close your ear got.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner
text:
4. A practice plan

Every day, tune by ear first, then check with the microphone in the tool, with Ear first ticked: guess flat, in tune or sharp before the reading shows. Watch your score improve.
Detune one string on purpose (a quarter turn) and find it by strumming a chord.
Sing each open string’s note before you play it.

Next: Tuning 2: fifth-fret, harmonics and octaves.
crumbs: Tuning 1: Your Ear Is the Tuner

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
A clip on an instrument track holds MIDI notes, not sound. Each note is only: which key, when, how long, and how hard (velocity). The instrument turns them into sound when you play. So you can change any note, the tempo, or the instrument afterwards, and nothing is lost. That is the big difference from audio, a recording of sound, which you can cut and move but not re-voice note by note.
The piano roll shows the notes: pitch up the side (a piano keyboard on its edge), time across, each note a bar whose length is its length.
crumbs: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
Writing notes
The Keys track below has the four chords of a C Am F G loop as whole notes, and an empty Bass clip is waiting.

Click the clip on the Keys track. Its notes show in the piano roll. Click a key on the left to hear it.
Draw: click an empty spot to write a note one grid step long. Drag the note up or down to change its pitch, drag its right end to make it longer.
Velocity: the bars under the notes. Drag them down for softer notes. Shift+click several notes to select them, then use the Velocity slider.
Transpose: select notes (or none, for all) and press +12 / −12 for an octave, +1 / −1 for a semitone.
Select the Bass clip and write a bass line: one note a bar, the chord’s root (C, A, F, G), then try root on 1 and 3.
crumbs: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

title: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI
text:
Recording and quantizing
Clicking notes in is precise but slow. Most people record from a keyboard and then fix the timing.

Select a track (click its name). Press ● Rec (or R): one bar of clicks to count you in, then it records. Play with the computer keyboard (A W S E D F T G Y H U J K: the white and black keys from C; Z / X octave down / up) or a MIDI keyboard plugged in (Chrome or Edge). Space stops; the take becomes a new clip.
Your notes will be a little early or late: that’s human. Quantize (Q) moves them onto the grid. Set Grid to the smallest note you played first.
Quantize 50% moves them only half way: tighter, still human. Producers often quantize less than fully for this reason.
Undo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z) whenever an edit goes wrong. Every DAW keeps a long undo history: use it freely.

Quantizing to the wrong grid is the commonest beginner mistake: triplets forced onto a 1/16 grid, or a swung part straightened. Listen after you quantize.
crumbs: DAW 3: The Piano Roll and MIDI

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
This lesson orders chord shapes by what the fretting hand finds hard, starting from a first lesson on guitar. Each step adds one physical demand: more fingers, a stretch, a barre, a muted string, a shift along the neck. Each step says what makes the shape easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Guitar chord shapes has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.
How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left. Each dot shows its chord tone, R for the root. The numbers under each diagram are the frets from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Press ▶ to hear a shape.
Finger numbers and barres. The button below puts the finger numbers in the dots instead of the chord tones, on every diagram on the page. Where one finger lies across several strings, a shaded bar joins those dots. The bar is drawn only where a barre is new: the small barre in G-B6, the first full barres in G-B8 and G-B9, and the barre with a silent string in G-B13. Tick the box to draw it on every diagram.
Finger numbers on guitar and on piano. The two instruments count differently. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1, then middle 2, ring 3 and little finger 4, and a thumb fretting a bass note over the top of the neck is written T. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, and the left hand is numbered the same way as the right, so its little finger plays the lowest note. A “3” is the ring finger to a guitarist and the middle finger to a pianist. Picking-hand fingers on guitar have letters of their own (p, i, m, a), so they are never mixed up with these.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Hand position
Good position is what makes every shape below easier, so set it up before the first chord and check it again whenever a shape feels hard.

Thumb: behind the neck, roughly opposite finger 2, with the pad (not the flat of the thumb) on the wood. It is a rest to push against, not a clamp. Squeezing harder does not make the note clearer.
Fingertips: arch each finger so that the tip comes down on the string from above, just behind the fret wire (the side towards the tuning pegs). Close to the fret needs the least pressure and buzzes least. The middle of the gap between frets needs more pressure and still buzzes.
Fingers: curved, with the knuckle joints bent. A curved finger lets the strings next to it ring.
Wrist and elbow: the wrist stays fairly straight, not bent sharply down or back, and the elbow hangs relaxed instead of pinned to the ribs or lifted. The palm stays a little away from the neck, so there is a gap you could slide a finger through.
Guitar angle: sit with the guitar body against your right thigh and the neck pointing slightly upward. Looking down at the fretboard should not need you to twist your wrist.
Easy because: with the thumb behind the neck, the fingers fall on the frets and need very little effort.
Hard because: it is not how the hand sits when it rests, so for the first weeks it takes thought.
What goes wrong:

The thumb climbs over the top of the neck. That makes the fingers flat, and they mute the strings next to them. (An occasional thumb over the top for a bass note is fine: that is the T in the diagrams.)
Flat fingers: the pad lies on the string and touches its neighbour.
The tip sits in the middle of the fret space, or on the fret wire, and the note buzzes or dies.
The wrist collapses and the palm presses on the neck, which is tiring and slows changes.
Long nails stop the fingertip landing; trim the fretting hand’s nails short.


Practice: place the fingers of a chord one at a time, checking each tip. Pick the strings one by one. If a string buzzes, move that fingertip closer to the fret before pressing harder.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B1 One or two fingers



Em7 takes finger 2. Em uses 2 and 3, and E5 does too, with the higher strings left silent. E7 uses fingers 2 and 1, and Am7 uses 2 and 1.

Easy because: one or two fingers, no stretch, and everything is within two frets.
Hard because: each finger has to press firmly enough to make a clean note, and the strum has to land on the right strings.
What goes wrong:

Fingertips hurt for the first week or two.
A string buzzes when the finger sits back from the fret instead of just behind it.
A fingertip leans on the next string and mutes it.


Practice: hold Em and pick one string at a time, so you can hear that each one rings. Five minutes a day builds calluses.
Unlocks: two-chord strums; G-A1 and G-A2.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B2 Three fingers, close together



Am and E are the same shape, moved over one string; both are fingered 2-3-1. A is 1-2-3, or a small index-finger barre across three strings. D is 1-3-2, with finger 1 on string 3, finger 3 on string 2 and finger 2 on string 1. Dm is the same three fingers in a different order, 2-3-1. D7 is 2-1-3: it is D with the middle finger moved to the other side, so the three fingers sit close together as in D.

Easy because: the fingers stay together and no finger reaches across another.
Hard because: three fingers have to land at once, and in A they crowd into one fret.
What goes wrong:

In D and D7, finger 3 touches the high E string and mutes it.
In A, the fingers collide.
Changing between E and A is slow.


Practice: move from Am to E. Fingers 2 and 3 move across one string together, and finger 1 stays on its fret, moving from string 2 to string 3. Go as slowly as you need to keep the shape.
Unlocks: four-chord loops that use only these chords; Boom-chick.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B3 Reaching: C and G



C is fingered 3-2-1, from string 5 up to string 2. Cadd9 adds finger 4 on string 2 in place of finger 1. G is 2-1-3, or 3-2-4 with finger 4 on both of the top two strings.

Easy because: everything is within the first three frets.
Hard because: in C the fingers spread diagonally over three frets and three strings. In G the fingers are far apart across the neck, and the strings between them have to ring open.
What goes wrong:

In C, finger 1 leans on the high E string.
The thumb rides high over the neck, which shortens the reach. Keep it low, behind the neck.


A note on the B string in G. In G the B string rings open, and it sits right beside the finger on the high E string. That finger, finger 3 or 4, can lean back and touch the B string, and then the string goes dull or silent. The chord is still G, because the B on string 5 still sounds, but it is thinner and the strum sounds uneven. To avoid it, press with the tip and keep the knuckle arched. Damping the B string can also be a choice: let the finger on string 1 lie lightly against it, and the chord loses one of its two B’s and sounds more open. The X in the second diagram marks the B string damped.



Practice: form C, lift all three fingers together, and put them down again without looking. Repeat ten times.
Unlocks: C, Am, F, G, and the pop changes of G-A1 and G-A4.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B4 Four fingers: open 7ths



C7 is C with finger 4 added on string 3. B7 uses all four fingers in a cluster: 2-1-3-4. Fmaj7 is a small shape on the top four strings.

Easy because: each shape is a small change from one you already know.
Hard because: four fingers are down at once, including the weak little finger, and B7 is a cramped cluster.
What goes wrong:

The little finger lands on the pad instead of the tip and mutes the next string.
The change from C to C7 is slow because finger 4 starts far away.


Practice: hold C and tap finger 4 on and off string 3, fret 3 (C to C7 and back), without lifting the other fingers.
Unlocks: Blues shuffle and the open-position 12-bar blues; G-A5.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B5 Reach: a wide stretch



The reach of a hand is how far apart the fingers can press at once. G7 is G with the little finger’s note moved down: finger 3 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1. The fingers sit on the two outer strings and on opposite sides of the neck, so the hand opens as wide as it does in any open chord. Compare it with G above it.

Easy because: only three fingers, and the strings between them ring open.
Hard because: the hand has to open across all six strings and three frets at the same time. Small hands feel it most.
What goes wrong:

The thumb creeps up over the neck, which shortens the reach and makes it worse.
Finger 1 reaches the high E string at an angle and touches the string next to it.
The wrist bends sharply to make up the distance. Keep it fairly straight, with the elbow close to the body.


Practice: form G, then change to G7 by lifting finger 3 and putting down finger 1, with fingers 2 and 3 staying where they are. Do not hurry. If the stretch hurts, stop and rest, and do a little each day. The span grows with patience.
Unlocks: the G7 in blues and country changes; G-A5.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B6 Two strings under one finger
text:
G-B6 Two strings under one finger



In Dm7, finger 1 lies flat across strings 2 and 1 at the first fret. In F, fingers 3 and 2 go down beside that small barre.

Easy because: the barre covers only two strings.
Hard because: for the first time, one finger presses two strings, and it has to lie flat rather than on its tip.
What goes wrong:

String 2 is dull because it falls in the crease of the finger. Roll the finger slightly onto its outer edge.
The thumb creeps around the front of the neck.


Practice: put finger 1 alone across strings 2 and 1 and pick each string, until both ring. Then add the other fingers.
Unlocks: the F chord in the pop changes.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B7 Top-string triads



Moveable shapes. A chord shape can slide up and down the neck as long as it has no open string. An open string stays at the same pitch when the hand moves, so the shape would change. If every note is fretted, the whole shape moves together, and the chord’s name changes with the root. Of the shapes above, C xxx010 and Am xxx210 use open strings and stay where they are. C xxx553, C xxx988 and F xxx565 are fully fretted, so they move. The same is true of the barre chords in G-B8 and G-B9.
Three positions of the same triad. A triad has three notes, and any of them can be the lowest. On strings 3, 2 and 1 these are the moveable shapes. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Find the root and you know the chord.






In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is the lowest, and in second inversion the 5th is. The inversions lesson explains the names and how to write them, and pianists can see the same idea in piano inversions. The next step is voice leading: when you change chords, choose the inversion that is nearest, so each note moves a fret or two, or stays put. That is how a few small shapes on the top strings can follow a whole progression, and it is where this lesson leads.

Easy because: only three notes, and at most three fingers.
Hard because: strings 6, 5 and 4 must stay silent. Either pick only the top three strings, or let your fretting fingers rest lightly against the low strings to damp them. Higher up the neck the frets get closer together.
What goes wrong:

The open low strings ring.
The pick catches string 4.
The chord sounds thin. It is meant to: it is one part in a band.


Practice: play the three C shapes in a loop, picking the strings one at a time and then together.
Unlocks: funk and reggae chops; G-A9.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B8 Full barre, E shape



Finger 1 lies across all six strings, and the other fingers make the E shape in front of it: the open E chord, fingered 2-3-4 instead of 1-2-3, moved up so that the barre does the nut’s job. The root is on string 6, under the barre. Here the barre is at fret 5, which makes these A, Am, A7 and Am7.
Start at fret 5, not at F. The usual first barre chord is F, at fret 1, and it is the hardest place to learn it. Near the nut the strings sit highest above the frets and are under the most tension there, so the barre has to press hardest, and the frets are widest, so the hand has to stretch furthest. Around fret 5, closer to the bridge, the strings give more easily and the frets are closer together. Get the shape ringing there, then move it down a fret at a time (A♭, G, G♭) until you reach F. G-B10 does that move on purpose.

Easy because: the shape on top of the barre is E, which you already know.
Hard because: one finger presses six strings, which takes strength, and the hand tires quickly.
What goes wrong:

Strings buzz. Put the barre right behind the fret, and roll the finger so that its firmer outer edge, not the soft pad, meets the strings.
String 2 or 3 falls in a crease of the finger.
The elbow sticks out.

Fm and Fm7 are a little easier, since they need fewer fingers on top of the barre.

Practice: play the barre alone at fret 5, no other fingers, until all six strings ring. Hold for 10 seconds and rest for 20. Or put a capo at fret 5 and play E shapes above it, then do the capo’s job with your finger. When fret 5 is easy, do the same at fret 3, then fret 1.
Unlocks: every major and minor chord; G-A3.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B9 Barre, A shape
The A shape: the open A chord with a barre behind it on string 5, the root under the barre. String 6 is not played. At fret 5 these are D, Dm, Dm7, D7 and Dmaj7; the same shapes at fret 1 are B♭, B♭m and the rest, where the stretch and the pressure are greater for the same reasons as F.




Easy because: the barre covers five strings, not six.
Hard because: three fingers squeeze into one fret space on adjacent strings. Many players flatten finger 3 across strings 4, 3 and 2 instead, which takes practice of its own.
What goes wrong:

When finger 3 lies flat, it mutes string 1.
Finger 1 bends at the knuckle and lets string 1 go dead.


Practice: play Dm at fret 5 with the barre and finger 3 only, then add fingers 4 and 2. Then move it down to Cm (fret 3) and Bm (fret 2).
Unlocks: barre chords anywhere on the neck.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck
text:
G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck



The first three are the E shape (root on string 6) at frets 5, 3 and 1: A, G and F. The last three are the A shape (root on string 5) at frets 5, 3 and 2: Dm, Cm and Bm. They are written in that order, from fret 5 down, so that the move takes you from the easy end of the neck toward the hard one. Name the chord by the note under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape, on string 5 for the A shape.

Easy because: the shape doesn’t change, only the fret.
Hard because: you have to find the new fret without looking, and release just enough pressure to slide without the strings squeaking, all without dropping the beat.
What goes wrong:

A gap between chords.
Landing a fret off.
A scrape on the slide. Ease off the pressure, but don’t lift the fingers.


Practice: slide A down to G and back on a steady beat, then G down to F, using the fret markers at 3, 5, 7 and 9 as landmarks.
Unlocks: I–IV–V and the 12-bar blues in barre chords, in any key.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B11 Barre 7ths: finger independence



A7 and Am7 are the E shape at fret 5 with a finger taken away, so the barre itself plays the 7th on string 4; F7 is the same at fret 1. D7, Dmaj7 and Cmaj7 are the A shape, with the root on string 5. Learn them at fret 5 first, as in G-B8.

Easy because: A7 and Am7 are barres you already know, with a finger taken away.
Hard because: the little finger now has to press at the far end of a barre. Cmaj7 x35453 needs fingers 2, 3 and 4 spread across strings 4, 3 and 2.
What goes wrong:

The little finger collapses and mutes a neighbouring string.
It hasn’t the strength yet.


Practice: hold a barre and tap finger 4 on one string, fret by fret.
Unlocks: Bossa nova in barre positions; G-A6.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
G-B12 Skipped strings: shells



In the shapes with the root on string 6, the underside of finger 1 (on the root) also touches string 5 to mute it. In the shapes with the root on string 5, the finger on the root leans against string 4.

Easy because: three notes, three fingers, and the shapes move anywhere.
Hard because: the skipped string must not sound. It is muted by a finger resting on it without pressing, and the strings above the shape are muted too.
What goes wrong:

The skipped string rings, because the muting finger isn’t touching it.
Playing too hard, which brings the muted strings back.


Practice: strum all six strings with the shape held. Only three notes should come out.
Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, and blues for guitar; G-A8.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3
text:
G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3




Easy because: the shapes are a barre plus at most two notes, and Cm7 is a barre alone.
Hard because: you need barre strength, but string 5 under the barre has to be silent. Lift the barre slightly where it crosses string 5 so it only touches the string.
What goes wrong:

String 5 sounds.
String 1 rings.


Practice: play Cm7 alone, then add finger 3 for C7. Then try fingers 3 and 4 together for Cmaj7.
Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing; G-A11.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
section: G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings
text:
G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings



Cmaj7 xx2413 is fingered 2-4-1-3. That’s an order the hand hasn’t used before.

Easy because: only four strings, close together.
Hard because: the fingers come in unusual orders, and some shapes combine a small barre, a skipped string and a stretch of three or four frets.
What goes wrong:

Hand ache from long sessions.
Grabbing the wrong finger.
One note losing pressure in the stretch.


Practice: learn one ii–V–I in drop 2, saying the finger numbers out loud. Then move it up two frets.
Unlocks: the Drop 2 voicing, jazz comping, and the altered chords of G-A13.
crumbs: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

title: Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings
text:
Where the two sequences meet








Harmonic order
By hand





G-A1 Open triads
G-B1, G-B2, G-B3
The same chords, sorted by how many fingers they need and how far they reach.


G-A2 Fifths
G-B1
E5 is one of the first shapes.


G-A3 Barre chords
G-B8, G-B9, G-B10
The barre, then the slide.


G-A4 Sus and add9
G-B2, G-B3
One finger moved.


G-A5 Dominant 7th
G-B4, G-B5, G-B11
Open 7ths, then barre 7ths.


G-A6 m7 and maj7
G-B6, G-B11
Small barre, then full barre.


G-A8 Shells
G-B12
The first skipped strings.


G-A9 Top-string triads
G-B7
Physically easy, but they come later in the harmonic order.


G-A10 Drop 2
G-B14
The hardest fingerings.


G-A11 Drop 3
G-B13
A barre with a skipped string.



The orders differ most in the middle. In the harmonic order a shell (G-A8) is simpler than a full 7th chord. Physically it is harder, because the string between has to be muted. A player who knows G-B4 can try shells with the root on string 6 without learning the barre first.
