title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text: The quarter note gets one beat in common time. In a 4/4 measure you can fit four of them — one per beat. We count them simply: 1 – 2 – 3 – 4.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Hear it, then say it
Before reading a single quarter note, you should be able to audiate a steady beat — feel it internally — and chant a neutral syllable on each beat. Only after the sound is secure do we attach the symbol.

title: Lesson: The Quarter Note
text:
Practice steps

Tap a steady beat with your foot.
Chant “bah” on each tap for four beats.
Now look at four quarter notes and chant them while tapping.

When you’re ready, head to Practice → Rhythm Patterns and play a few quarter-note patterns. Your time on this page and your plays over there are both recorded automatically.






Tip



This page is being timed. Stay as long as you need; switch tabs and the timer pauses. Come back and it resumes.

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
So far every track has held MIDI notes. An audio track holds sound: what a microphone heard. Recording one is simple (pick the track, press record, play), but the microphone hears everything in the room, including the song you are playing along to. This lesson records twice, once with speakers and once with headphones, and measures the difference.
You need a microphone (the one in a laptop or a headset is fine), Chrome or Edge, and a pair of headphones.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
The setup
The Voice track below is an audio track; the band has 8 bars of drums, bass and keys to play along with. With the Voice track selected, the ● Rec button records from the microphone: a short sound check first (it tells speakers from headphones and asks for your loudest phrase), then one bar of count-in, then recording. The small meter by the buttons is the microphone’s input level: keep your loudest moments out of the red (Recording 1: Gain Staging).
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Experiment 1: speakers

Take off your headphones and play the band through your speakers at a normal listening level.
Select the Voice track, press ● Rec and stay silent for the whole 8 bars. Press Space to stop.
Under the tracks, This take gives the take’s average level. Write it down: everything in that take is bleed, the band and the click coming back into the microphone.
Click S on the Voice track to solo it and play. You hear the band, thin and roomy, and the click.
Now record yourself singing or clapping along. Solo it again: you, plus the band, plus the click.

Why it matters: that copy of the band is now part of your vocal for good. Turn the vocal up and the band comes up too. Change a chord in the keys part, and the old chord is still faintly in the vocal. Compress or EQ the vocal and you compress and EQ the band in it. And the click, which nobody is meant to hear, is in the song.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Experiment 2: headphones

Plug in headphones, put them on, and record 8 silent bars again.
Compare the average level with the speaker take. Closed headphones at a sensible level are usually 20 to 40 dB quieter in the microphone: almost nothing.
Now turn the headphones up loud, or take one side off, and record silence again. Headphones leak too: open-back ones, loud clicks and a mic close to the ear all bring bleed back.




Take (silent)
Average level




Speakers
______ dBFS


Headphones
______ dBFS


Headphones, loud / one side off
______ dBFS



Every studio records vocals and overdubs in headphones for this reason. More on headphones and the cue mix: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones; on bleed between instruments in one room: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Monitoring and latency
🎧 Monitor sends the microphone through the Voice track so you hear yourself in the headphones, as a DAW’s input monitoring does. Two things to notice:

Only with headphones. Monitoring through speakers sends the mic to the speakers, back into the mic, round and round: feedback, a howl.
You hear yourself a little late. Sound takes time to go through the computer and back out: latency, here shown in milliseconds. Over about 10 ms it starts to feel odd; over 30 ms it’s hard to sing with. Audio interfaces have direct monitoring (the mic straight to the headphones, before the computer) to get round it.

Latency also makes recordings land late on the timeline. The DAW moves each take earlier by the measured amount: the Latency fix box in the editor. Set it to 0 on a take and look at the waveform: everything has slid late against the grid.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
section: Why phone calls don’t sound like this
text:
Why phone calls don’t sound like this
Video-call apps and voice memos run echo cancellation: they subtract what the speakers played from what the mic heard. It’s good for calls and bad for music (it chews up singing and room sound), so this DAW, like every real one, switches it off and records exactly what the microphone hears.
crumbs: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones

title: DAW 6: Recording Audio: Bleed and Headphones
text:
Tips for a clean take

Headphones on, closed-back if you have them. The click quieter than you think.
Point the microphone away from the headphones and the speakers; get close to the mic.
Record a few seconds of the room in silence: you will hear what noise is there before it is under your voice.
Watch the input meter: peaks around −10 dBFS, never in the red.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text: Every song here stops two bars short. The chords for those bars are already written in: V, then I (or i in a minor key). That’s an authentic cadence, the strongest way to end. Your job is to write the melody that goes over it.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Pick a song
Loading the tune library...


  ▶ Hear it as written
  The last two bars are silent. Only the chords play there.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
section: What makes an ending sound finished
text:
What makes an ending sound finished

Land on the tonic. End on the home note (D in these songs) on a strong beat. Make it long.
Over V, sit on the leading tone or the 2nd. In D, that’s C♯ or E. Over A, both pull you home to D.
Step down into the last note. 3–2–1 (F♯–E–D) or 2–1 sounds settled. A leap up to the tonic sounds bolder.
Echo the opening. Bar 5 already repeats bar 1. Let your bars 7–8 answer bar 6 the way bars 3–4 answered bar 2.
Slow down. Use longer notes in the last bar than in the rest of the song.

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Write it
The chords are already in place. Choose rhythm patterns: they fill the empty bars in order, and once the last bar is full the song is complete (no bar is added). Then choose how to enter the notes (letters, the computer keys, or a MIDI keyboard) and enter them; they fill the rhythm from the first empty note. The score above the tools shows your ending as you go. Your work is saved for each song.

  ▶ Hear my ending
  Start this song over

title: Lesson: Write an Ending
text:
Compare
Write two different endings for the same song. Write one that steps down 3–2–1 and one that leaps up to the tonic. Then play them back to back. Which sounds more final? Which sounds more like this song?

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text: Mastering is the last step: the finished stereo mix is made to sound its best on every system and alongside other records, and turned into the files that get released. It works on the whole song at once, with small moves. If something in the mix is wrong (the vocal too quiet, the bass boomy on one note), go back and fix the mix; mastering can’t reach inside.

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Fresh ears
Mastering was traditionally a different engineer in a different room, for a reason: you’ve heard the mix a hundred times. Leave it a day. Listen to references. Listen on the speakers you know best.

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Tonal balance
A gentle EQ on the whole mix, compared with a reference:

Moves of 0.5 to 2 dB, wide curves. More than 3 dB means the mix needs work.
Too much low end (muddy, boomy on small speakers), too little (thin), harsh 2–5 kHz, dull top.
A high-pass below 20–30 Hz removes rumble nobody hears but that eats headroom.

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Glue compression
A slow, gentle compressor on the whole mix (ratio 1.5:1–2:1, 1–2 dB of gain reduction, slow attack, release timed to the beat) makes the parts move together. Often done in the mix already (“mix-bus compression”).

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Loudness and limiting
The limiter is the last plug-in: a very fast compressor with an infinite ratio that stops any peak crossing a ceiling, so the whole song can be turned up.

Set the ceiling at −1 dBTP (true peak: the level between the samples, which is what a converter or an MP3 encoder actually reaches). This keeps lossy streaming versions from clipping.
Raise the input until it’s loud enough, then back off: past a few dB of limiting the drums lose their punch and the sound gets flat and tiring.
Loudness is measured in LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale), averaged over the song, which follows how loud it sounds rather than its peaks.
Streaming services turn loud songs down to a target (Spotify, YouTube, Tidal about −14 LUFS; Apple Music −16). A master squashed to −8 LUFS is just turned down to −14, and now sounds smaller than a dynamic master at −14. For streaming, around −14 to −10 LUFS integrated is plenty; dynamic genres (jazz, classical, acoustic) often sit at −16 to −20.


Hear what over-limiting costs
A looping song through a limiter, measured the way streaming services measure it (LUFS, with a true-peak reading). Play it, then compare Dynamic with Crushed: the crushed one is louder, and has lost its punch. Now switch streaming normalisation on: both are turned to the same level, and the crushed one is simply smaller. Watch the peak-to-loudness figure shrink as the drive goes up.

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Stereo and mono
Check in mono (Sound 23: Stereo): the vocal and bass must stay solid. Keep the bass (below ~120 Hz) in the centre; wide bass cancels on mono systems and cuts badly on vinyl. More on mono playback, one earbud, live sound and subwoofers in Recording 7: Mono and Stereo.

title: Recording 6: Mastering
text:
Finishing

Sequence an album: the order, the gaps, matching levels so no song jumps out.
Fades at the start and end; trim silence.
Dither when reducing to 16-bit (CD, some distributors): a tiny noise that replaces the distortion of rounding. Only once, at the very end.
Files: a 24-bit WAV at the mix’s sample rate for streaming distributors, a 16-bit/44.1 kHz WAV for CD, and an MP3 for the band’s phones.
Metadata: title, artist, ISRC codes if you have them.

title: Recording 6: Mastering

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text: Scratching is playing the record as an instrument: moving it back and forth under the needle while the other hand opens and closes the sound with a fader. Grand Wizzard Theodore is credited with discovering it in the Bronx in the late 1970s; Grandmaster Flash, DJ Jazzy Jeff, Qbert and the turntablist crews made it an art.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Set up

A short sound at the start of a cue: “Ahh” or a horn stab. Put a cue point (or a sticker on the record) right at its start.
Record hand on the label; it pushes the record forward and pulls it back.
Fader hand on the crossfader or channel fader, with a sharp curve, so a tiny movement opens or closes the sound.
One revolution of the record at 33⅓ RPM is 1.8 seconds of sound. Short scratches move the record a quarter turn or less.

Below: one deck with the scratch sample, and a mixer with its fader. Click CUE (stopped) at the start of the “Ahh” to mark it. The platter’s label is the record: drag it forwards and backwards. Use your other hand (or a second finger on a touch screen) on the channel fader.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
The scratches
Learn each slowly, then in time with a beat (play a loop on your phone or the next widget’s deck at 90 BPM).

Baby scratch: record hand only, fader open. Push forward a quarter turn, pull back, in steady eighth notes. Forward is the sound played; back is it reversed. Even, smooth movements; the sound should be the same each time.
Forward scratch: push forward with the fader open, close the fader, pull back silently, open it again. Only the forward sound is heard. (The opposite, sound only on the pull, is a backward scratch.)
Chirp: push forward and close the fader during the push; open it as you pull back and close it again during the pull. Each movement gets cut off, making a short “chirp”. Record and fader hands move together.
Transformer: let the record move slowly (a slow push of a long “Ahh”), and tap the fader open and closed in rhythm, so the long sound is chopped into pulses (sixteenths, triplets). Named after the sound effects of the Transformers cartoon.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Back on the beat
Scratches sit on a beat played by the other deck. Here deck A plays a boom-bap loop at 90 BPM; deck B has the “Ahh”. With the crossfader curve sharp, cut B in and out from the crossfader while scratching it.

title: DJ 5: Scratching Basics
text:
Hamster switch, tips

Many scratch DJs reverse the crossfader direction (hamster style) so the fader hand pushes towards the deck being scratched.
Keep the needle (here, the platter) steady: small, precise movements sound better than big ones.
Practise slowly with a metronome; speed comes later.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text: A tuner is the right tool for a loud stage, a noisy room, or a quick check. It is the wrong tool for learning to play in tune, because it only answers one question (is this one note at this pitch?) and music asks many. This lesson is about what a tuner does well, where it misleads, and how to keep your ear in charge. Before this: Tuning 1 and Tuning 2.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
1. Kinds of tuner









Kind
How it hears
Strengths
Weaknesses




App, microphone
the air
free, always with you
hears the room too; low strings and noise confuse it


Clip-on
vibration of the headstock
works on a loud stage
a cheap one reads ±3 cents or worse; can be fooled by sympathetic strings


Pedal / cable
the pickup signal
very clean signal
electric only


Strobe
one stripe per harmonic, standing still in tune
about 0.1 cent; shows the harmonics
more to read; the precision often isn’t the problem



The site’s own strobe is in the top bar, and explained in How a strobe tuner works. Try it on a string here, or listen to the page’s own made-up string with demo:

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
2. Why the reading jumps
When you pick a string hard, it goes sharp for a moment: it’s stretched further than usual, and the attack is noisy. Then it settles, and slowly goes a little flat as it dies. So: pick at your normal strength, ignore the first half second, read the settled note. Many beginners chase the attack and end up flat.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
section: 3. In tune on the tuner, out of tune in the chord
text:
3. In tune on the tuner, out of tune in the chord
The tuner measured the open strings. You play fretted notes, and they can be off for reasons no tuner on an open string can see:

Finger pressure. Pressing hard stretches the string sharp, by 5–10 cents on a high fret. Fret just behind the fret wire, with only as much pressure as makes the note clean.
Intonation. If the bridge saddles are set wrong, fretted notes up the neck go sharp or flat. The Setup Check measures it: the 12th-fret harmonic against the 12th-fret note.
Old strings play sharp up the neck. Change them.
High action or a high nut stretches every fretted note sharp, most near the nut.
Equal temperament itself. A G chord’s major third (B) is 14 cents wider than a pure one. The tuner calls that in tune; your ear may hear it as a little bright. This is why a guitar tuned perfectly by a tuner can still sound “off” in one chord and fine in another.

title: Tuning 3: Tuners and Their Limits
text:
4. Using a tuner well

Ear first. Tune by ear, then look. In the tuning tool, tick Ear first: the reading stays blurred until you say flat, in tune or sharp. Keep score.
Listen, then stop listening. Turn the microphone off, play a chord, decide; turn it on to check.
End with a chord. If the chords you’re about to play sound wrong, trust that over the needle.
Check between songs. By ear: play the open strings against a chord, fix the one that’s moved.

The tuner is a ruler; your ear is the judge.

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text: An amplifier makes a small signal big enough to move a speaker. Instrument amps are part of the instrument’s sound; a PA (public address) should just make everything louder, faithfully.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Instrument amps

Combo (amp and speaker in one box) or head and cabinet.
The usual controls: Gain (or Drive) sets how hard the preamp is pushed: low is clean, high distorts. Volume / Master sets how loud. Bass, Mid, Treble shape it; Presence adds upper bite.
Guitar amps colour the sound heavily and are meant to. Bass amps need much more power for the same loudness (low notes take more energy), and are built to stay clean and reach low. Keyboard amps are flatter, more like a small PA. (More below: Guitar amps and bass amps.)
Start everything at noon (12 o’clock), gain low, then adjust. Small changes.
Valve (tube) amps need a minute to warm up and should go into standby for breaks. Never run one without a speaker connected: it can destroy the output transformer.
Impedance (ohms) of the cabinet must match what the head expects (printed by the speaker jack).


Gain (or Volume) and Master: two volume knobs
An amp is two amplifiers in a row. The preamp takes the tiny signal from the guitar and shapes it; the power amp makes it strong enough to drive the speaker. Each knob sits in front of one of them:

Gain, Drive, or on many amps a knob just called Volume (sometimes per channel), sets how hard the signal hits the preamp. That decides the sound: low is clean, higher breaks up, highest is full distortion. It changes loudness too, but only until the preamp is clipping; after that more gain means more distortion, not more level.
Master sits between the preamp and the power amp and decides how loud all of that is in the room. It doesn’t change the character, so you can have a fully distorted sound quietly at home, or a clean one loud.

Set them in that order: Master low, Gain for the sound you want, then Master up to the level the room needs. It’s the same idea as gain staging on a mixer: the first knob sets the sound, the last one the loudness.
An old-style amp with only one Volume (many vintage Fenders and Voxes) has no master: the one knob does both, so it is clean when quiet and only starts to break up when it is loud. That’s why those amps are “too loud” to get their overdrive at home. On a valve amp, turning the Master far up drives the power valves too, which adds a second, looser kind of distortion that a low-master setting can’t give you.


Treble and Presence
Both turn up the high end, and on a lot of amps they sit side by side, so they look like the same knob twice. They aren’t. Presence is a treble control, but not a second Treble knob. It works on a higher band (roughly 2–6 kHz: pick attack, string edge, the “cut” that lets a guitar be heard through a band), and it sits in a different place:

Treble is in the preamp’s tone stack, before or in the middle of the distortion. Turning it up also changes what gets distorted, and so how the distortion sounds.
Presence is in the power amp, after the distortion. On a valve amp it reduces the power amp’s negative feedback at high frequencies (the circuit that keeps the power amp flat), so those frequencies come through stronger. On a solid-state or modelling amp it’s a high-frequency boost placed at the same point. It adds clarity without changing how the drive feels.

Too little and the amp sounds woolly and lost in the mix, even when it’s loud. Too much sounds harsh and fizzy (the “ice pick”, worst with high gain and in small rooms). Start it at noon, set Treble first, then use Presence to make the guitar cut through the band. Some amps have a matching low control, Resonance or Depth, which does the same thing for the low end. On a bass amp the equivalent (sometimes Bright) helps slap and fingernoise speak.









Treble
Presence




Where
preamp tone stack, before the power amp
power amp, after the distortion


Range
a shelf from about 2.5 kHz up (everything above)
a broad bump around 2–6 kHz


With distortion
changes what gets distorted: more treble in, a buzzier, tighter drive
brightens the distortion that’s already there, like EQ after it


Too much
thin, spiky
harsh, fizzy, “ice pick”


Use it for
the basic colour of the sound
cutting through a band without more gain



To hear it, set High gain, quiet, then turn Treble from 3 to 8: the distortion itself changes, getting buzzier and tighter. Back to 5, and turn Presence from 3 to 8 instead: the same distortion, just brighter on top.


Middle and the Mid frequency
The Middle knob boosts or cuts one band, and where that band sits matters as much as how much. On most guitar amps it is fixed, somewhere around 500 Hz to 800 Hz. Many bass amps and some guitar amps (and almost every mixer channel, see the mixer) let you move it with a second knob, Mid frequency (a “sweepable” or semi-parametric mid):

200–400 Hz: body and boom. Cut here when the guitar is muddy or fights the bass; boost on a thin bass.
500 Hz–1 kHz: the honk and growl. A guitar’s mids live here; so does the “growl” of a bass that cuts through.
1.5–3 kHz: bite, pick and finger attack. Boost for a bass that has to be heard on small speakers.

To find a frequency: boost the Middle a lot (8 or 9), sweep the Mid frequency until it sounds worst (or best), then set the Middle back to the amount you want. The scooped sound (Middle at 2 or 3, bass and treble up) is big and exciting alone, and disappears as soon as the band plays, because the middle is where a guitar is heard.


Guitar amps and bass amps
A bass’s low E is 41 Hz; a guitar’s is 82 Hz. Most of the differences follow from that octave:

Power. Moving the air for low notes takes far more energy: a bass amp needs several times the watts of a guitar amp to keep up with it (300–500 W against a 30–50 W guitar valve amp in a band).
Clean on purpose. A guitar amp is designed to distort when pushed. A bass amp is designed to stay clean (more headroom, in the simulation: the same Gain distorts later); bass drive is something added on purpose, gently, usually keeping the clean lows underneath (Bass, growl).
The EQ sits lower. Bass at about 40–60 Hz instead of 100 Hz, a mid that is often sweepable, treble at 4–5 kHz and up for string and slap noise. Many bass amps add a graphic EQ.
The cabinet goes deeper and is closed, often with a horn tweeter for the top (see Cabinets below).
A DI out. Bass amps nearly always have an XLR DI output, so the PA gets the bass directly while the amp is only for the stage.

Playing bass through a guitar amp works quietly, but the amp throws away the bottom octave (the low-cut at the input and the cabinet’s roll-off), and loud low notes can tear a guitar speaker, which isn’t built to move that far. Try Bass through a guitar amp, then Bass amp. A guitar through a bass amp is safe, just clean and polite.


Cabinets
The speaker cabinet is the last, and largest, tone control. The amp’s raw output is harsh and fizzy (pick No cabinet to hear it); the speakers roll off almost everything above 5 kHz, and that roll-off is a large part of what “guitar tone” is. This is also why recording a guitar amp means a mic on a speaker, or a cabinet simulation (an IR, impulse response) when there is no speaker. What decides a cabinet’s sound:

Speaker size. A smaller cone moves faster and reaches higher but goes less deep: 10″ speakers sound quick, bright and punchy; 12″ is the usual guitar speaker, fuller, rolling off around 5 kHz; 15″ goes deep and round and has almost no top (old-school bass).
How many. More speakers move more air: louder, and fuller at the bottom, at the same amp power. They also interfere with each other a little (a dip in the upper mids, which changes where you stand) and spread the sound more narrowly. A 4×10 and a 2×12 have roughly the same cone area but sound different: the 4×10 tighter and brighter, the 2×12 warmer.
Open or closed back. An open-back combo also radiates from the back, and the back wave cancels the front’s lowest notes: airy, spread out, less bass, fills a room. A closed-back cabinet (most 4×12s and nearly all bass cabinets) traps that air: tight, punchy low end with a thump around 100 Hz, and more directional (beamy).
A horn tweeter (bass cabinets): a small extra speaker that adds back the top end that big cones can’t make, with a level knob or switch on the back. Turn it down for an old-school sound.
Impedance and power handling must match the amp (printed on the back, see above).

In the simulation, the cabinet changes the low end, the upper mids and the roll-off; switch between 2×12 open back and 4×10 open back on the same setting, or 4×12 closed back with high gain. It can’t model the real differences in loudness, spread and how a cab interacts with the room, but you can hear the colour.


Try it
Start with Clean, then Crunch: the Gain moved (and the cabinet is a 2×12). High gain, quiet is a full distortion at a low Master; Clean, loud is the opposite. Vintage, cranked greys out the Master: the one Volume knob makes it dirty and loud together. Then sweep Presence from 0 to 10 with the Treble left alone. Play your own notes from the keys at the foot of the page, or plug in a guitar (Source: Microphone, through an audio interface; headphones on). The guitar and bass riffs are the band’s own recorded samples, unamplified, as if the instrument were plugged straight into a desk. Bass amp, Bass, growl and Bass through a guitar amp switch the source to the bass riff. View switches the controls between sliders and knobs; click any number to type a value.









Modelling amps: the knobs may be lying



Many small practice amps are modelling amps: a computer that imitates many amps and stores presets. The Fender Mustang series, Boss Katana, Line 6 Spider, Positive Grid Spark and Yamaha THR are all like this. When you choose a preset (or switch the amp on, which loads one), the amp uses the preset’s stored Gain, Volume and EQ, not what the physical knobs point at. A Volume knob sitting at 2 can be playing a preset saved at 10. Turn a knob and the setting jumps to where the knob is.
So:

Before switching on and before changing presets, turn Master to 1 (on amps where Master is the one real, unstored knob, as on the Mustangs, it is the one control you can trust).
Choose the preset, play, and bring the Master up slowly to the level you want.
Then touch the other knobs one at a time to take control of them, and save if you want to keep the result.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Powered and passive speakers

Powered (active): the amplifier is inside. Plug in power and a line-level signal. Most small PAs and studio monitors.
Passive: needs a separate power amp and speaker cable. Never plug a passive speaker into a line output, or a speaker output into a line input.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
A small PA
A typical small rig: mics and instruments → mixer → two powered speakers on stands (the mains), plus monitor wedges for the players.
On each mixer channel, top to bottom:

Gain / Trim: set this first. Play or sing at full performance level and turn up until the peak light only just flickers, or the meter sits around 0 to −6. (Recording 1)
High-pass (low cut) on for vocals and anything without real bass.
EQ: small cuts, not big boosts.
Aux sends: the monitor mixes (pre-fader) and effects (post-fader).
Pan, Mute, and the fader, near 0 for the main sound.


Try it: one channel
Press Start here, then work down the strip in the lesson’s order. Bring the Gain up while the singer sings until the After-gain meter sits near the dashed line and PEAK only flickers, switch the High-pass on, then the Fader to about 0. Too hot shows what the fader can’t fix. Feedback turns the monitor up with the wedge in front of the mic (keep your volume low); the two Fixed presets show the two cures: the mic’s dead side toward the wedge, or a narrow cut at the frequency that rings.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Sound check

Everything on in the right order (Gear 1), master down.
One channel at a time: gain, then fader.
Monitors: ask each player what they need more of. Their voice/instrument first.
The whole band: balance from the audience, not from behind the mixer if you can help it.
Leave headroom. A crowd absorbs sound, and everyone plays louder at the gig.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Feedback
The howl or squeal when a mic hears a speaker that’s playing that mic.

Keep the mains in front of the mics, never behind.
Point the mic’s dead side at the monitor (the back of a cardioid; the sides at ~120° for a supercardioid).
Sing close to the mic: then the gain can stay lower.
Don’t cup the mic’s grille: it changes the pattern to omni and feeds back.
If it rings, pull the monitor or that channel down first, then find the ringing frequency with EQ.
crumbs: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA

title: Gear 3: Amps, Speakers and the PA
text:
Loudness and stage volume
The quietest stage that still works sounds best out front. Turn amps toward the players (tilt them back, or put them on a stand) rather than turning them up. See also Recording 7: Mono and Stereo for live speaker placement and subwoofers.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
One melody can sit on many sets of chords. A chord is right for a melody note if the note is in it (a chord tone) or if it passes quickly (a passing note). This lesson takes one tune, Ode to Joy, and puts four sets of chords under it.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it twice after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. The tune is written above the chart and its notes light up as they sound. ▶ Play with the band plays the melody on the piano with the chords under it.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
1. A plain setting
C and G, mostly. Two chords. Every note of the tune is a chord tone or a passing note on one of them. This is how the tune is usually harmonised in a school songbook.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
2. Sevenths on the dominants
G7 for G. The tune does not change. The chord under it does: G7 adds an F, and the F is a note the tune already passes through in bar 2. Now it is a chord tone.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
3. Secondary dominants
Am in bar 3, E7 in bar 4, and Am then D7 in bar 7. The notes of the tune are the same. Under bar 4, E7 has the tune’s E as its root and its D as the 7th. In bar 7, D7 holds the tune’s D, and the E after it is the 9th.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
section: 4. A chord for every pair of notes
text:
4. A chord for every pair of notes
C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 G7 | C F | C/E Dm7 | Am7 | Dm7 C. Now the chords change every two beats and the bass moves by step: C, F, E, D. It is the tune as a jazz pianist might play it, and it sounds quite different even though the tune has not changed a note.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Build your own
Choose one of the four settings for each pair of bars, and mix them. The tune is above the chart. All of the settings fit the tune, so there is no wrong combination.

title: Lesson: Reharmonizing a Melody
text:
Where to go next

Pick your own tune and try three sets of chords on it. Play the melody note by note against each chord.
The question to ask of every chord is: is this melody note a chord tone, or is it passing?

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text: Where the microphone goes changes the sound more than which microphone it is. Move it a few centimetres and the tone changes; move it a metre and the room becomes part of the recording.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Distance

Close (2–15 cm): big, intimate, dry. Lots of the source, little of the room. Every mouth noise, breath and pick scrape is there. Plosives (p, b) hit the diaphragm.
Medium (20–60 cm): the usual distance for a voice with a condenser or an acoustic guitar. More natural, the instrument has room to “bloom”.
Far (1 m and more): the room is part of the sound. Great in a good-sounding room, terrible in a small boxy one.

The level drops about 6 dB every time the distance doubles (the inverse-square law). So a singer moving from 5 cm to 10 cm changes the level as much as moving from 50 cm to a metre. Close up, small movements make big level changes; a little further back, the performer can move without the level jumping.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Proximity effect
Directional mics (cardioid, figure-8) boost the bass as the source gets close: below about 10 cm it can be +10 dB or more at 100 Hz. Radio voices use it on purpose. On an acoustic guitar it makes boom. Back off, or use a high-pass filter (a low cut around 80–100 Hz, often a switch on the mic or the interface). Omni mics have no proximity effect.



Bring the mic in and listen to the bass grow; then try omni:



Hear what a low cut and a bass boost do:

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Where on the instrument

Acoustic guitar: not at the soundhole (boomy). Start pointing at where the neck meets the body, about 20 cm away; move towards the soundhole for warmth, towards the neck for brightness.
Guitar amp: close on the speaker. At the centre of the cone, bright and aggressive; towards the edge, darker and rounder. Turn the amp down: it doesn’t need to be loud to sound good on a mic.
Voice: at mouth height or slightly above, pointing a little down; a pop filter 5–10 cm in front. Slightly off to the side cuts plosives and sibilance (s, sh).
Snare: 3–5 cm above the rim, angled at the centre of the head, the back of the mic towards the hi-hat.

Listen in headphones while someone else moves the mic, and choose by ear.

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Bleed
Bleed (spill) is one instrument getting into another’s microphone: the drums in the vocal mic, the guitar amp in the piano mics. It happens whenever more than one thing is recorded in one room.
Bleed isn’t always bad: a band playing together with some bleed sounds alive and glued together. But it takes away choices: you can’t re-record the vocal if the drums are in it, you can’t EQ one without the other, and Auto-Tune on a vocal with drums in it makes the drums warble.
To reduce it:

Get closer to the source you want. Each halving of the distance gains 6 dB over the bleed.
Aim the dead side of the mic (the back of a cardioid, the side of a figure-8) at the loud thing.
Separate players: across the room, behind gobos (movable baffles), amps in another room or a cupboard, bass and keys through DI.
Dynamic mics on loud close sources pick up less of the room.
Headphones for everyone, not speakers (see monitoring).
Try it: bring the singer close, then turn the mic so the drums sit at its quiet side.





After recording, a gate or careful editing can remove bleed between hits (tom mics, mostly):

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Phase
Two microphones on one source at different distances get the same sound at slightly different times. Added together, some frequencies cancel (a comb filter, as in Sound 18), and the sound goes thin and hollow. Bleed causes it too: the snare in the snare mic and in the overheads.

The 3:1 rule: the second mic at least three times as far from the first source as the first mic is. A singer 20 cm from one mic and a guitarist 20 cm from another: keep the two mics 60 cm or more apart.
Two mics on the same speaker or drum: put them at the same distance.
A mic above and a mic below a snare (or front and back of an open-back amp) face opposite ways: flip the polarity (Ø) of one.
Check by listening to both mics together and flipping polarity on one: choose whichever has more bass and body. Check the mix in mono.

Drag mic 2 away from mic 1 and watch the comb filter in the spectrum. Flip the polarity and compare the mono sum. Then switch to the 3:1 demo, where each mic has its own player:

title: Recording 3: Distance, Bleed and Phase
text:
Next

Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text: Monitoring is what you listen on: while recording, while performing, while mixing. The rule of thumb is simple: headphones while a microphone is open, speakers while mixing. But each has its reasons and its traps.

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
When to use headphones

Any time a mic is recording in the same room as the playback. Speakers playing the backing track, the click or the other parts will get into the mic (bleed). With the click, it can’t be removed.
Overdubbing: singing or playing to tracks already recorded.
Feedback: a mic, turned up, pointed near speakers playing that mic, howls. Headphones stop it.
Placing the mic: listen in headphones while the mic is moved.
Checking detail: clicks, edits, noise, breaths, distortion are easier to hear.
Late at night or in shared spaces.

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
Closed or open

Closed-back headphones seal round the ear. Little sound gets in or out. Use them for recording: a loud click in open-backs leaks into a sensitive condenser.
Open-back headphones are vented; they sound more natural and are more comfortable for hours, but leak both ways. Use them for mixing and listening, not next to an open mic.
In-ear monitors (IEMs): very good isolation; used live and by drummers.

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
When to use speakers

Mixing and mastering. In headphones, each ear hears only one side; on speakers, both ears hear both speakers, and the room, the way listeners will. Panning, reverb and bass sound very different. Headphone mixes often end up with too little reverb and wrong bass.
Tracking a band live in one room where everyone wants to hear each other and bleed is accepted.
Recording with no microphones: DI guitar, keyboards, drum machines, synths.
Set monitors in an equilateral triangle with your head, tweeters at ear height, away from the walls. Listen at a moderate level (around 75–85 dB SPL): ears hear less bass and treble when quiet, and tire when loud.

Do the mix on speakers, then check on headphones, earbuds, a phone and a car. Most people will hear it on one of those.

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
Latency and direct monitoring
Sound going into the computer and out again takes time: the buffer. At 256 samples and 48 kHz, each way is about 5 ms plus the converters; with a big buffer it can be 20–40 ms. A singer hearing their own voice that late sounds as if they’re singing in a tunnel, and timing suffers.

Direct monitoring (a knob or switch on the interface) sends the input straight to the headphones, with no delay, before the computer. Mute the track’s input monitoring in the DAW, or you hear yourself twice, slightly apart (a flanger, see Sound 18).
Or use a small buffer (64–128 samples) while recording, and a big one while mixing.
Under about 10 ms most players won’t notice. Drummers and singers notice soonest.


Try it: hear the delay
Press ▶ (headphones on), clap or speak along with the click, and try the buffer sizes. Then choose “Both on” to hear the flanging double.

title: Recording 4: Monitoring and Headphones
text:
The headphone mix
A performer plays better when the headphones sound good.

Hear yourself enough. Singers who can’t hear themselves sing sharp and push; too much and they sing flat.
Pulling one side off the ear helps some singers pitch; it also leaks the click into the mic: turn it down if they do.
A little reverb in the headphones (not recorded) helps singers.
Click: as quiet as still usable. A cowbell or rim click, not a high beep. Turn it off for the quiet ending, or it’ll be there in the mic.
Careful with level. Long sessions at high volume damage hearing for ever. If you need it very loud to hear yourself, turn the backing down instead.


Try it: build a cue mix
Set each fader, add the reverb, then switch to speakers to see how much click and backing would end up in the recording. Switch “Listen to” to the recorded track to hear it.

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
This lesson is about making up your own melody over a twelve-bar blues, using Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet as the model. It is for any instrument. You should already be able to play the tune (it is taught in Blues for Violin and Saxophone, section 7) and know what the chords are (Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues).
Choose your instrument first. The Instrument menu in the strip at the bottom sets up the page for you.
Where this page says “concert”, it means the note as the piano hears it.
How to use the page. Every line of notation has a ▶ Play button, and the note that is sounding lights up. The chord charts have ▶ Play with the band; the piano plays the written line unless you tick Leave out the melody. Under each note is its place in the chord (R = root) or its number in the scale.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
1. Start from the melody
The best first solo on any tune is the tune. It already fits the chords, it already has a rhythm, and the listener already knows it.



Three things about this melody are worth stealing.

It is a riff. One two-bar idea, played three times. A solo built from one idea that is repeated and changed a little sounds like it means something. A solo of new ideas in every bar does not.
It uses four notes: the root, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th below. You do not need many.
It leaves space. Each line ends on a long note. Half of each phrase is silence or holding.

Exercise. Play the tune. Then play it again and change one thing: leave a note out, repeat a note, or play the rhythm of the riff on a single pitch. Keep the long notes where they are. Do that for several choruses before you go on.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
2. Hitting the change
The most important moment in a blues is bar 5, where the home chord gives way to IV. In this tune the melody marks it with one note. In bars 1 to 4 the riff’s second note is the 3rd of the home chord (concert A when the tune is in F). In bars 5 and 6 that note drops a half step (concert A♭), and it is now the ♭7th of the IV chord. In bar 7 it goes back up.
A soloist who plays the higher note in bar 5 sounds lost: it is a half step away from a note the chord needs. A soloist who plays the lower one sounds like they know the tune. That is what players mean by hitting the change (or making the change).
Here is that move alone: one note per bar, the 3rd or 7th of each chord, taking the nearest one at every change.



Exercise. With Leave out the melody ticked, improvise using only the rhythm of the riff and the notes of this line: the upper note in bars 1 to 4, the lower one in bars 5 and 6, the upper again in bar 7. It is very little to play with. Hit the change every time, exactly on bar 5, before you add anything else.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
3. The minor blues scale
Six notes, and it can be played over the whole twelve bars without changing anything. That is why it is the first scale most improvisers learn.



Counted from the key note it is R, ♭3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭7. Two of those are blue notes:

The ♭3 is the same pitch as the note that hit the change in section 2 (concert A♭ in F). Over the IV chord it is a chord tone. Over the home chord it rubs against the chord’s major 3rd, and that rub is the sound of the blues.
The ♯4 is a passing note between 4 and 5. Slide through it; do not sit on it.

What this scale does not have is the major 3rd of the home chord. Played for a whole chorus it sounds dark and tough, and it never quite says which chord you are on.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
4. The major blues scale
The brighter one. Counted from the key note: R, 2, ♭3, 3, 5, 6.



It has both thirds: the ♭3 and the major 3rd, side by side. That is the same pair of notes the melody uses to hit the change. Sliding from the ♭3 up to the 3 is one of the most recognisable sounds in the music. This scale fits the home chord perfectly, because its 3, 5 and 6 belong to it.
It fits the IV chord less well. Its major 3rd is the note that section 2 told you to leave in bar 5.
Putting the two together. Use each scale where it is strongest:








Bars

either; the minor blues scale covers all four



That table is the melody’s own plan. Blues in the Closet uses the major 3rd on the home chord and the lowered one on IV.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
5. The pentatonic scales
Take the ♯4 out of the minor blues scale and five notes are left: the minor pentatonic.



Take the ♭3 out of the major blues scale and you have the major pentatonic.



Why bother with scales that have fewer notes?

Nothing in them clashes. Neither scale has a half step in it, so no two of its notes rub against each other, and any of them can be held. They are the safest notes there are.
They fall under the hand. On guitar and bass the minor pentatonic is the first position most players learn, two notes on every string. On a wind or string instrument it is five notes with no awkward corners.
The minor pentatonic covers the whole chorus, exactly as the minor blues scale does. Use it when you want to think about rhythm and phrasing and not about notes.
A major pentatonic built on a chord’s own root always fits that chord. It is the chord’s root, 3rd and 5th plus its 2nd and 6th: no 4th and no 7th, the two notes that cause trouble. So one more way through the form is three pentatonics: the home chord’s in bars 1 to 4, the IV chord’s in bars 5 and 6, and so on.
Two for the price of one. The major pentatonic of the key has the same five notes as the minor pentatonic that starts a minor 3rd below it. Compare the scale below with the major pentatonic above. If you know one shape, you know the other.




The blues scales are these two pentatonics with one extra note each: the ♯4 added to the minor, the ♭3 added to the major. Those added notes are the blue notes.
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
section: 6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
text:
6. A scale for each chord: Mixolydian
The blues scales treat the whole chorus as one sound. The other way to improvise is to give each chord its own scale. A dominant seventh chord takes the Mixolydian scale: a major scale with the 7th lowered. Its 1, 3, 5 and ♭7 are the chord, and the notes between join them up. (Where that lowered 7th comes from is explained in the “flat 7” panel of the instrument lessons.)
For the home chord:



For the IV chord:



Compare them note by note. They share every pitch but one. The home chord’s scale has its major 3rd; the IV chord’s scale has that note a half step lower, as its ♭7. It is the same half step as in section 2, the one the melody plays. Hitting the change and changing scale are the same act.
For the V chord:
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
7. The two-five: Dorian
Bars 9 and 10 are ii7 then V7. A minor seventh chord takes the Dorian scale: a major scale with the 3rd and the 7th lowered.



Now look back at the V chord’s Mixolydian scale above. It is the same seven notes, started from a different place. The ii chord and the V chord of a two-five share one scale, so bars 9 and 10 need only one set of notes, and the melody shows it: the riff passes over both chords unchanged.
That scale is also the plain major scale of the key. So the whole chorus comes down to three sets of notes, each one note different from the last:

Bars 9, 10 and 12 (ii7 and V7): the major scale of the key.
Bars 1 to 4, 7, 8 and 11 (I7): lower its 7th. That is the home chord’s Mixolydian.
Bars 5 and 6 (IV7): lower the 3rd as well. That is the IV chord’s Mixolydian.

To hear the notes that tell these scales apart, this line plays the ♭7, 6, 5 and 3 of every chord, one bar each:
crumbs: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet

title: Improvising on a Blues: Blues in the Closet
text:
8. Your chorus
Nothing is written here. The band plays the changes and the chorus is yours. Tick Loop in the strip at the bottom to keep it going.



A plan for practice, one item per session:

The melody, varied a little more each chorus (section 1).
Only the two notes of the change, in the riff’s rhythm (section 2).
Only the minor blues scale, in two-bar phrases with two bars of rest after each.
Major blues scale on the home chord, minor blues on IV, following the table.
Three major pentatonics: the root’s own, for whichever chord is sounding.
Chord scales: one chorus where every phrase ends on the 3rd or ♭7 of the chord of the moment.
Trade fours with the band: you play four bars, rest four, play four.

In every one of them, hit the change in bar 5.
To hear what the chords are doing under your solo, see guide tones and the changes lesson.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Clap in a cathedral and the sound goes on for seconds after your hands stop. It bounces off the walls, the floor and the ceiling, thousands of times, each echo a little quieter and a little duller, until they blur into a smooth wash. That wash is reverberation, and every room has its own. A reverb effect puts a dry recording into a room that isn’t there.
How to use the page. The source starts as single hits, so you can hear each hit’s tail die away. The strip under the controls is the room’s impulse response: what one instant click would sound like in this room.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
The room




Decay time (RT60): how long the tail takes to fall by 60 dB, which is about until you can’t hear it. A living room is about 0.5 s, a concert hall about 2 s, a cathedral 5 s or more.
Pre-delay: the gap before the reverb starts. In a big room the first reflection takes a while to come back. A little pre-delay keeps a voice clear in front of its reverb.
Damping: in real rooms the high frequencies die first, absorbed by air, carpet and people. Lower damping makes a darker, warmer tail.
Early reflections: the first few distinct echoes from the nearest walls. They tell your ear how big the room is before the tail arrives.
Mix: how far away the sound seems. More wet signal pushes it to the back of the room.

Try the presets: a small room, a hall, a cathedral, a plate (a big steel sheet with a pickup, used in studios since the 1950s: bright and dense, no early reflections) and reverse, the impulse response played backwards so each sound swells into itself.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
How it is made: convolution
This reverb is a convolution reverb. It needs one thing: the impulse response of the room. To capture a real room, engineers play a click (or a sweep) in it and record what comes back. The computer then replays that recording once for every sample of the input, scaled by that sample’s level, and adds them all up. That’s a lot of arithmetic, which the browser does for us.
The impulse responses here aren’t recordings. They are made from decaying noise that gets duller as it fades, plus a few early reflections. That’s close to what a real room does, and it means every control can change the room instantly.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Spring reverb
Before digital reverb, a guitar amp couldn’t carry a room around with it, so it carried a spring: a coil of wire with a small speaker-like driver at one end and a pickup at the other. The sound runs down the spring, bounces off the far end, runs back, and keeps bouncing.



Listen to a single snare hit. Instead of a smooth wash you hear a “drip” or “boing”: a quick falling whistle that repeats. A spring carries low frequencies faster than high ones, so each bounce arrives as a sweep from high to low (a chirp), and the bounces come back at a steady rate, which you can see as the evenly spaced bursts in the strip. Room size here sets how long the spring is, so how far apart the bounces are.

Surf guitar (Dick Dale, the Ventures) is a spring turned all the way up, with a clean, bright guitar hitting it hard.
Dub reggae engineers kicked their spring units to get a crash of thunder.
Most Fender amps since 1963 have one; pick a guitar amp up and shake it and you’ll hear it.

Compare it with Plate and Hall on the drum loop: the spring is the one that never quite sounds like a real place, and that’s why people like it.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
Shimmer and freeze
Two modern reverb tricks, both loved by ambient musicians and post-rock guitarists.




Shimmer: part of the reverb tail is pitch-shifted up an octave and fed back into the reverb. Every trip round, the tail climbs another octave, so a chord grows a halo of high notes that rises and glows above it. Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois made it in the 1980s with two machines; now pedals like the Strymon BigSky do it alone. Try the Fifths interval too.
❄ Freeze: press it while the chords play. The last second of sound is held forever (by reading it as overlapping grains) and the live input is shut off. Change the chord on your keys and the frozen one stays underneath. Press again to let go.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:
On music
Switch the source to the chords, the drum loop or your microphone (headphones on). Long reverb makes chords smooth and huge but turns drums to mush; fast music wants short reverb or a lot of pre-delay. Singing into the cathedral preset and listening to your own voice come back is the best way to learn what reverb does.

title: Sound 16: Reverb
text:

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Real rigs use several effects one after another: a guitarist’s pedalboard, the plug-ins on a channel in a DAW. The order matters, often a lot. And the level going from one to the next matters too: that’s gain staging.
How to use the page. Choose an effect for each of the three slots, or press a preset. The bars show the peak level after each stage. The dashed line is 0 dB, the ceiling.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Order



Compare each pair of presets on the Synth riff and the Drum loop:

Distortion → Delay: clean echoes of a distorted note. The usual order. Delay → Distortion: the echoes are distorted together with the new notes, so they pile into each other and turn to mush.
Distortion → Reverb: a distorted guitar in a room. Reverb → Distortion: a distorted room, a roaring wash.
Compressor → Wah: the compressor evens out the playing, then the wah sweeps it. Wah → Compressor: the compressor flattens the wah’s sweep back out.

A rough rule for a guitarist’s board: things that shape the note first (wah, compressor, overdrive, distortion), then things that change the sound (chorus, phaser, tremolo), then things that put it in a space (delay, reverb). Break the rule on purpose, not by accident.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Gain staging
In the computer, signals can get as loud as they like. Real equipment can’t: every pedal, preamp and converter has a ceiling, and above it the wave is chopped flat (hard clipping). The switch Clip above 0 dB at every stage makes this page behave like real gear.
Press Too hot: a big bass boost, then a compressor, then a delay, with the input turned up. Watch for a stage going red: everything after it carries that damage, and no amount of turning down later removes it. Now lower the Input gain until no bar goes red. The rule is simple: at every stage, loud enough to be well above the noise, never over the ceiling. Engineers aim for peaks around −18 to −6 dB at each stage, which leaves room for surprises.

title: Sound 24: The Signal Chain
text:
Your own rig
Choose Microphone (headphones on) and build a chain for your voice or instrument. Try the order you’d expect, then the opposite, and decide which you prefer.

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the bass player’s chair, starting from one note per chord. You need to know how to fret a note and pluck it. Everything else is built here, one step at a time. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button that starts the band. The diagrams read like a bass standing upright in front of you: the low E string is on the left, the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord’s name above a diagram to hear its notes. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff, and below the chord chart is the bass line the band is playing. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, the bar on the chart and the diagram of the chord being played both light up. Tick Leave out the bass and the band’s bass player stops so that you can take the part. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
1. The roots
The root is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. A blues has three chords, so it has three roots, and they sit close together. Find the key note on the E string. The root of the IV chord is at the same fret on the next string up. The root of the V chord is two frets higher on that same string. Your hand does not have to move.
In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of V is at the same fret on the lowest string and the root of IV is two frets below that.
Start with two notes in each bar, on beats 1 and 3.



Count the bars as you play: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I. When that is steady, play the root on every beat. Press Superimposed to see all three roots on one fretboard.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
2. Root, fifth and octave
The fifth of a chord is one string up and two frets up from its root. The octave (the root again, higher) is two strings up and two frets up. Index finger on the root, ring or little finger on the other two: the three notes make a box that has the same shape on every chord. Move the box to each root you learned in step 1.



The band’s bass plays root on beat 1 and fifth on beat 3. Play that first, then try root, fifth, octave, fifth, one note to a beat.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
3. The 3rd and the 7th
The root and fifth say which chord it is but not what kind of chord. Two other notes do that job.

The 3rd says major or minor. In a dominant seventh chord (G7) it is a major 3rd: one string up and one fret back from the root.
The 7th in a blues chord is a flat 7th (written ♭7), a whole step below the octave: two strings up at the same fret as the root.

Together they are called the guide tones, because they are the notes that change the most tellingly from one chord to the next. Root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7th are the four chord tones. Click each chord’s name to hear them climb.




Where the flat 7 comes from
Why is the 7th of these chords called flat? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the bottom.



The band’s bass plays exactly that: root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7th, one note on every beat, the same shape in every bar. The line is written out below the chord chart. It is not a walking line yet. It is the four chord tones in order, so that your hand learns each shape and your ear learns what each note sounds like against its chord.
Work up to it in three stages, each for a few choruses:

Root on beat 1, 3rd on beat 3. Two notes to a bar.
Root, 3rd, 5th, and rest on beat 4.
All four notes, as the band plays them.

Then switch to Superimposed and look at I and IV together. The 3rd of the I chord is one fret below the root of IV, and the ♭7th of I is one fret above the 3rd of IV. Those half steps are how the chords connect.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
4. Walking
In step 3 every bar went the same way: up the chord from the root. A walking line also has one note on every beat, but it chooses its notes so that each bar leads into the next. Three changes turn the step 3 line into a walking line: the notes after the root can come in any order, the octave joins them, and the last note of the bar points at the next root. A recipe that always works:

Beat 1: the root of the chord.
Beats 2 and 3: any two other chord tones (3rd, 5th, ♭7th, or the octave).
Beat 4: an approach note, one fret below or one fret above the root of the next bar’s chord.

When the next bar is the same chord, beat 4 can be any chord tone. The diagram shows the chord tones of all three chords at once. A split dot is a note two chords share.
Between the chord tones you can also step along the scale that goes with the chord. Over the I chord that is the scale from step 3, the major scale with its 7th lowered a half step (called Mixolydian). Here it is in one place on the neck, with the run written in tablature. Beats 2 and 3 can borrow its notes, so a bar can climb step by step instead of jumping.






Listen to the band’s bass player for a chorus, then tick Leave out the bass and walk it yourself. Slow the tempo down as far as you need. A plain line that lands on the root at every chord change is worth more than a busy one that does not.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
5. The jazz blues
The last line of a jazz blues is a two-five: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8 to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of the changes lesson). The ii chord is a minor seventh chord. Its 3rd is a minor 3rd, three frets above the root on the same string. Everything else about the shape stays the same.



In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Play the root on the beat each chord arrives and one other note after it: root and 3rd, or root and an approach note into the next root.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
section: 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
6. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford, who wrote this tune, was a bass player. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars 9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12 to turn it round. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, so the bass has room to be heard.



Play roots through the form first, two to a bar, and listen to how the riff sits against them. Then walk it. In bars 4 and 8 the melody holds one long note: that is the place for your line to lead clearly into the next chord. In bar 12, aim for the root of the V chord and then back to the top.
crumbs: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line

title: Blues for Bass: From Roots to a Walking Line
text:
Where to go next

Change the key in the strip at the bottom and find the same shapes in the new place. Start with F, B♭, A and E.
Loop a chorus with the bass left out and record yourself over the band.
Learn to improvise over the same tune in the improvising lesson.
Take any chorus from the changes lesson and walk through it with the recipe from step 4.
Next on bass: pop changes for bass, roots and the walking line.

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
A lead sheet writes swing eighths as plain eighth notes, and that is not an error. The way they are written is shorthand, the way a chord symbol is. It tells you which notes come where, and the style tells you how to play them. This lesson covers what the shorthand means, how much room it leaves you, and how to know when it does not mean swing. The two examples are Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet, which swings, and Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man, which does not.
How to use the page. Every example is written out and can be played. Press ▶ Play to hear it. Examples that have a Swing slider let you set how long the first eighth of each pair is held, from even (50%) up to a dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth (75%). The Tempo box sets the speed. Play each example at more than one setting before you read on.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 1. What the page says, and what it means
text:
1. What the page says, and what it means
Here is the first bar of Blues in the Closet exactly as a lead sheet writes it.


Played as written, the eighths are even: each beat is split exactly in half. No jazz player reads it that way. In a swing tune each pair of eighths is played long-short: the note on the beat is held longer and the note on the “and” comes late. The usual way to explain it is with a triplet: the beat is split into three, the first note gets two thirds and the second gets one.


Arrangers almost never write that, because it is hard to read and because, as the rest of this lesson shows, it is not quite right either. Instead they write plain eighths and put a word or a sign at the top of the chart:

Swing, Med. swing, Shuffle, Bluesy, or just a tempo and a style name.
The sign ♫ = ♩ ♪³: “a pair of eighths equals a quarter and an eighth under a triplet”.
Nothing at all. On a jazz lead sheet, swing is the default, and you are expected to know it.

The one way not to read swing eighths is as a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. That is a ratio of 3 to 1, and at most tempos it sounds stiff and jerky, like a march. Compare it with the triplet version above.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
text:
2. Swing is a range, not a ratio
The triplet is a useful first picture and a poor final answer. Measurements of recordings find that players swing anywhere from nearly even to a little past the triplet, and that the same player changes ratio with the tempo. The rough rule:




Tempo


Typical long:short


Slider


What it sounds like






Ballad, slow blues (under 80)


about 2:1, sometimes more


65–70%


Lazy, heavy triplet feel, often a 12/8 shuffle




Medium (100–160)


between 3:2 and 2:1


60–67%


The “standard” swing of a blues like Blues in the Closet




Up-tempo (over 220)


close to even


52–58%


Eighths almost straight; the swing is in the accents




The band on this site follows the same rule: its swing starts at 68% at 100 beats a minute and slides toward 60% as the tempo rises. Try it here. Set the slider to 66% and raise the tempo to 240: it becomes hard to play and starts to sound like a shuffle. Then lower the slider to 55% at the same tempo.



Everything else the shorthand leaves to you
The ratio is only one of the choices a plain line of eighths leaves open. Others matter at least as much, and the lead sheet says nothing about any of them.
Each choice below shows the line as written, two ways to play it that are both swing, and one way that is not. The played versions are written out more exactly than any chart would be: accent marks (>), staccato dots, and “ghost” over a note that is barely played.

Accents on the off-beats
Swing players lean on the “and”, not the beat. A line of eighths is usually played doo-BAH doo-BAH, with the beat note soft and the off-beat note pushed. This is why fast swing still swings at nearly even eighths.










Ghosted notes
A note in the middle of a run may be barely played at all, more felt than heard.










Length
A written quarter note is often played short (dit), especially on beats 2 and 4 and at the end of a phrase. A written eighth tied over the bar line is played long.










Where in the beat
Some players sit right on the beat, others play a fraction behind it (“laid back”) against a drummer who is on top of it. Neither is written; both are swing. Laid back is far smaller than any written note value; the sixteenth rest below is an exaggeration so it can be seen.








Small changes to the rhythm
Players anticipate a note by an eighth, delay one, or add a pickup. On a lead sheet, that is interpretation, not a wrong note.








What is not up to you: where the bar lines are, where the notes fall in the beat (on it or on the “and”), and the form. A swing eighth on the “and” of 2 is late, but it is still the “and” of 2.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
3. Blues in the Closet
Blues in the Closet is a medium-tempo jazz blues, usually played somewhere between 120 and 180 beats a minute. Here is the whole melody, in F, as it is written in the tune library.


There is no “Swing” marking on it, and none is needed: it is a bebop-era blues, every recording of it swings, and the eighth-note pairs are written the way every jazz player expects. Play it at 50% and then at 64% to hear what the marking would have told you.

The places that change when it swings

The pickup and the ties. The tune starts on the “and” of 4 and ties it into the bar. In swing, that pickup is late (it is the short note of a pair), so the first note of the tune arrives just before the bar line and pulls the band into it. The same figure ends bars 4 and 8. These anticipations are the strongest swing feature in the tune: give them a little accent.
The figure A F. In every bar the melody drops from the 3rd to the root in a pair of eighths. Swung, it is long-short, and the short F is the one to lean on.
The tied F in bar 2. A/F/- F/ C is four eighths, with the second tied to the third. Swung, the tied F lands on the late “and” of 2 and sustains through beat 3. Played even, the syncopation is weaker and the bar sounds square.
The long notes. The C in bars 4 and 8 is a dotted quarter tied to a quarter. It can be held full length or cut off early; both are common. The rest that follows is where the rhythm section, or another player, answers.



A range of good readings
Three players reading the same lead sheet would not play the same thing, and all three would be right. Try these settings and decide which one you like:




Setting


Tempo


Slider


Feel






Relaxed


120


66–68%


Close to the triplet, heavy, bluesy




Medium


150


60–64%


The usual jam-session reading




Up


200+


55–58%


Nearly even; put the swing in accents on the off-beats




What no setting allows is 50% at a medium tempo with every note accented equally. That is the one clear misreading.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
section: 4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
text:
4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing
Watermelon Man (from Takin’ Off, 1962) is also a blues, with 16 bars instead of 12, and it is written in exactly the same way: plain eighth notes, no triplets, no dots. Here are its first eight bars and the four-bar riff that follows.


On the page it looks like Blues in the Closet: eighth notes, ties over the bar line, anticipations. The difference is the style. This is a straight-eighth tune: the eighths are even, and they stay even when the tempo drops. It is often marked “Funky”, “Latin”, “Even 8ths” or “Straight 8ths”, but on many lead sheets it is not marked at all, and you are expected to know it from the record, the same as with a swing tune.
Now move the slider to 66% and play it again. Bars 9 to 12 suffer most: z2 cc g2 a2 starts on an off-beat pair, and swinging it turns a crisp, funky riff into something closer to a nursery rhyme. The off-beat F in bars 2 and 6, which should snap against the beat, goes soft.

“Somewhere between”
Even this tune is not perfectly even. Hancock said that Billy Higgins played it “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. That is a slider setting of perhaps 53 to 56%, which is not enough to sound like swing but is enough to keep the line from sounding mechanical. Mongo Santamaría’s hit version a year later is a cha-cha, and its eighths are straight. Both are good readings of the same lead sheet; a 66% swing is not.
So the range of acceptable readings exists for straight tunes too. It is just centred in a different place.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
5. The contrast, side by side






Blues in the Closet


Watermelon Man






Written as


Plain eighths


Plain eighths




Played as


Swing, long-short


Even, or very nearly




Slider


55–68%, by tempo


50–56%




Where the energy is


Accents on the off-beats, late pickups


Crisp, equal subdivisions locked to a backbeat or a Latin pattern




How you know


Jazz blues, bebop era, every recording


The record, the style (“funk”, “Latin”, “even 8ths”)




The point is that the notation is identical. Everything that separates these two tunes in performance comes from outside the notes: the style, the era, the recording and the band.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet
text:
6. Reading a new lead sheet
When you open a chart you have not played before, before you play a note:

Look at the top of the page for a style or feel word, a ♫ = ♩ ♪³ sign, or “even 8ths”.
Look at the tempo. The faster it is, the straighter the swing.
Know where the tune comes from. A jazz standard or a bebop blues swings unless told otherwise. A funk, Latin, rock, soul or bossa nova tune does not.
Listen to a recording. It is the only thing that settles the question, and it tells you about the accents and the note lengths too, which no lead sheet shows.
Listen to the band. If the drummer plays the swing ride pattern, match its ratio; if the drummer plays straight eighths on the hi-hat, play straight. The ratio is shared, not chosen alone.

Then practise both tunes in this lesson at three tempos each, and play the slider settings from the tables until you can hear the difference without looking.
crumbs: Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
This whole song is four chords, played over and over: G, D, Em, C. Many hit songs are built on this loop. Everyone in the class plays the same song at the same time. Each player picks a level.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Play and the band plays the loop. Under Who plays, switch your own instrument off and play its part yourself. The buttons under each example pick the level. The band plays exactly the part you choose, and it is written out underneath. Use the tempo control at the bottom of the window to slow it down.
Count it. Every chord lasts one bar: four beats. Count “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud. The chord changes on every “1”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Drums
You play with both feet and both hands. The bass drum (right foot) and the snare drum are the two most important sounds. The bass drum is low and goes on 1 and 3. The snare is sharp and goes on 2 and 4. Together they make the backbeat, the beat under nearly all rock.

Level 1: Bass drum and snare. Bass drum on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. Just “boom, crack, boom, crack”. (The band’s drummer also taps the hi-hat pedal on 2 and 4. Skip that at first.)
Level 2: Add the hi-hat in quarter notes. Your right hand plays the closed hi-hat on every beat. Your left hand plays the snare on 2 and 4. On 2 and 4, both hands hit at once.
Level 3: Hi-hat in eighth notes. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. The hi-hat plays on every number and every “and”.
Level 4: The rock beat. The bass drum moves around a little, and you play a fill at the end of each time through the loop. Next: Hi-hat Grooves.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Bass
The bass plays the lowest note of each chord. That note is the root, the letter name of the chord: G, D, E, C. On a bass in standard tuning (E A D G, lowest string first):



Chord
String
Fret




G
