Level 1: One note a bar. Play the root on “1” and let it ring for four beats.
Level 2: Two notes a bar. The root on 1 and on 3.
Level 3: Four notes a bar. The root on every beat.
Level 4: Eighth notes. The root eight times a bar: “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. This is the classic rock bass part. Lock in with the drummer’s bass drum.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Guitar
There are two things to learn: the chord shapes (left hand) and the strum (right hand). Pick a level of each. They do not have to match.
Chord shapes. Pick one row. The dots show where your fingers go; the number in each dot is the note’s place in the chord (1 = the root, 3, 5). An x above a string means don’t play it. Every shape opens in the Chord Library, with the other ways to play it.
Easy shapes (one or two fingers). The D is a D5: it has no F♯, but it fits the song.



Full open chords. More on these in Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand.



Power chords (for a louder, harder rock sound). Two fingers, the same shape every time; only E5 uses an open string.



Strum.

Level 1: One strum a bar. Strum down on “1” and let it ring. This gives you three beats to get to the next chord.
Level 2: Down on every beat. Four downstrokes a bar.
Level 3: Down, up. Eight strums a bar: down on the numbers, up on the “and”s. Keep your arm moving even when you miss a string.
Level 4: D, D-U, D, D-U. The folk-rock strum. Count “1, 2 and, 3, 4 and”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Keyboard
The notes below stay close together, so your right hand barely moves.
Level 1 plays only the root, the note marked 1 (G, D, E, C). Level 2 and up play all three notes.




Level 1: One note a bar. Play the root with your right thumb on “1” and hold it.
Level 2: The chord, once a bar. Three notes together on “1”, held for four beats.
Level 3: The chord on every beat, with your left hand playing the root on “1”.
Level 4: Driving eighths. The chord eight times a bar, left hand on the root. Keep it light so that it does not cover the guitar.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
section: Voice, and instruments that play one note at a time
text:
Voice, and instruments that play one note at a time
This is for singers, saxophone, violin, flute, trumpet and any other instrument that plays one note at a time. (Saxophone and trumpet players: these are concert pitches. Ask which notes to read on your instrument.)

Level 1: The roots. Sing or play G, D, E, C, one long note a bar. This is the bass part sung higher.
Level 2: A smooth line. B, A, B, C. Every note is in its chord, and each one is a step from the last. Sing it on “oo”, then make up words.
Level 3: Make up a riff. Use only the notes G A B D E (the G major pentatonic scale). They fit all four chords. Make a short rhythm, two beats long, and repeat it every bar.
Level 4: Make up a melody. Use the same five notes. Play a short idea, then answer it with a different one, like a question and an answer. See also Pop Singing.

Switch on all the players below and play along.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
The whole band
Everyone together. Turn off the players your class is covering. The buttons set every player in the band to the same level, so you can hear what level 1 and level 4 sound like as a band. They don’t have to match: a level 1 bass under a level 4 drummer sounds fine.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
Make it a song
A loop becomes a song when the parts change between sections.

Verse: quieter. Drums at level 1 or 2, guitars at level 1.
Chorus: everybody up a level. Louder.
Ending: play the G one last time on “1” and let it ring.

Try verse, chorus, verse, chorus, ending. Somebody counts it in: “1, 2, 3, 4”.
crumbs: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone

title: First Rock Song: One Loop, a Part for Everyone
text:
For the teacher

Grouping. A band of four to six covers drums, bass, one or two guitars, keys and a voice or melody player. Students who don’t play yet can start on drums level 1, bass level 1 or the voice level 1 line.
Tempo. 92 is a starting point. Slow the band to 70 for level 1 players. Speed it up for the final performance.
Checking progress. For each student, note the level they can play four times through without stopping, in time with the band. Four times through at a level is the goal before moving up.
Other loops. The same parts work over C, G, Am, F and the other loops in Four-Chord Loops. Change the chord names and the bass notes.



  Tempo 
  ■ Stop

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text: A violin is made of thin wood held under a lot of string tension. Looked after, it lasts centuries; a few minutes a week of care keeps yours sounding and playing well. (The same goes for viola, and mostly for cello and bass.)

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
section: Opening the case and holding it
text:
Opening the case and holding it

Lay the case flat, latches up, before opening. Close every latch and zip when you put it away; many violins are broken by falling out of a half-closed case.
Pick the violin up by the neck or the edges, not the bridge or strings.
Never leave it on a chair or the floor. In the case, or in your hands.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
The bow

Tighten the hair before playing by turning the screw at the frog: until there’s a gap about the width of a pencil between the hair and the stick at the middle. The stick should still curve toward the hair.
Loosen it completely every time you put it away. A bow left tight warps.
Rosin: a few strokes along the hair when the bow slides without gripping. New hair needs a lot; usually a few swipes per practice is plenty. Too much makes a scratchy sound and white dust.
Don’t touch the hair: skin oil stops the rosin working.
Hair breaks now and then: snip it close to the ends, don’t pull it out. When a lot is gone, it needs a rehair.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Wiping down
After every practice, with a soft dry cloth:

Wipe the rosin dust off the strings, the top under the strings, and the stick of the bow. Built-up rosin eats into the varnish.
Wipe the strings and fingerboard.
Never use furniture polish, alcohol or water on the varnish. Ask a luthier for proper cleaner.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Tuning

Use the fine tuners (small screws on the tailpiece) for small changes. Tighten = higher.
Pegs are for larger changes: push in slightly while turning, so they hold. If pegs slip or stick, a teacher or luthier can treat them (peg compound).
Tune A first, to A = 440 (the strobe tuner), then D, G and E.
When fine tuners are screwed all the way in, back them out and bring the string up with the peg instead.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
The bridge
The bridge isn’t glued; the strings hold it on. Tightening strings pulls its top toward the fingerboard.

Check it every week or two from the side: it should stand straight, at a right angle to the top (the back face, toward the tailpiece, perpendicular).
If it leans, a teacher can show you how to ease it back, holding it with both hands while the strings stay at pitch. If it falls, loosen all the strings and take it to your teacher: don’t play without it.
The sound post inside is wedged, not glued. If it falls (a rattle and a weak sound), loosen the strings and see a luthier.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Strings

Change a full set about every 6–12 months for regular players, sooner if they sound dull or won’t stay in tune, or one is fraying.
Change one at a time, so the bridge and sound post stay in place.
New strings stretch for a day or two: retune often.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
Temperature and humidity

Wood swells and shrinks with humidity. Dry air (winter heating) cracks violins and opens seams; very damp air makes pegs stick.
Keep it at room temperature: never in a car, in the sun, or by a radiator.
Aim for 40–60% humidity. In dry winters (north India), a case humidifier (such as a Dampit) helps.
In the monsoon and humid coastal cities the danger is the other way: swollen wood, sticking pegs, rising action, softened glue and mould in the case. Use silica gel or a two-way humidity pack in the case, open the case to air in a dry room now and then, and don’t keep it in a damp almirah or next to a wall.
Air conditioners dry the air fast: don’t leave the violin in the blast of an AC.
Coming in from the cold: leave it in the closed case 15–30 minutes before opening.

title: Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners
text:
When to see a luthier
Open seams (a buzz, a gap at the edge), cracks, a warped bridge, a fallen sound post, slipping pegs, a bow that won’t tighten, or rehairs. Don’t glue anything yourself.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
The harmonic series says a note is a stack of partials at 1, 2, 3, 4… times the fundamental. That is exactly true for an ideal vibrating string or an ideal pipe, and only roughly true for the real ones. Some instruments (a bowed violin, a clarinet, a singer) are harmonic almost to the cent. Others (a piano bass string, a marimba bar, a church bell, a timpani) have partials that are not whole-number multiples at all, and yet we hear a clear pitch. This lesson asks why, shows the numbers instrument by instrument, and asks who gets to change them: the player, or the maker. Click a section’s heading to fold it; the “On this page” bar at the right jumps to any section and opens it.
How to use the page. The tuner widgets are the strobe tuner of this site, listening to a made-up instrument instead of the microphone: press Start, pick a Practice instrument in the menu, and read the bands. Band k stands still when a partial is exactly k times the reference pitch; if it drifts right that partial is sharp of k, if left, flat, and the readout shows how many cents. The other widgets compute things (a ladder of partials, a string calculator, a pluck-position chart) and most have a ▶ button; the bar at the foot of the window sets the volume (start low). Nothing here needs a microphone. Numbers in square brackets, like [1], are the references at the end; where I could not find a source I say so.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 1. Harmonic, stretched, and not even close
text:
1. Harmonic, stretched, and not even close
Three different things get called “inharmonic”, and the rest of the lesson keeps them apart.

Slightly stretched. A stiff string. Partial k is a little sharp of k times the fundamental, more so for larger k. The ear still hears one note.
Clean but wrong for the key. A brass instrument’s partials are exact multiples, but the multiples themselves (the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics) fall between the notes of 12-tone equal temperament. UNSW’s page on string harmonics says the same of the 7th and 11th: they lie about halfway between equal-tempered notes [6].
Designed or accidental, far from harmonic. A free bar’s modes are at 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.93 times the first, a church bell’s at 0.5 : 1 : 1.18 : 1.51 : 2 and so on, a timpani’s at 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 : 2.65 before the air gets to it. We hear a pitch from these anyway, and makers go to great trouble to arrange it.

The widget below lays the partials of each practice instrument over the ideal harmonics, in cents off the nearest harmonic, and against the nearest note of 12-ET. It is the same table the tuner uses, so what you see here is what the strobe bands show below. (The ratios are in the source of synth-kit.js, each with its reference.)



For every instrument, “band 1” is the reference the tuner is set to. For the church bell it is the hum, the lowest partial, so the strike note you hear (the prime) is band 2. For the chime and the timpani it is the virtual pitch you hear, with nothing sounding there at all: the ear finds it from the spacing of the partials above (the “missing fundamental”, see [16] and [21]).
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
2. Strings: stiffness stretches the partials
An ideal string is pulled back only by its tension. A real one is also a springy rod, and bending it costs extra energy that rises with the shape’s curvature, so the more loops the string makes, the more extra restoring force there is, and the sharper the partial. For a plain round wire, with the partial numbers counted from 1:

fk = k f1 √(1 + B k²), where B = π³ E d⁴ / (64 T L²)

E is Young’s modulus of the wire, d its diameter, T the tension and L the vibrating length [2]. The sharpness of partial k, in cents, is 600 × log₂(1 + B k²), about 866 B k² for small B [3] (the strobe lesson uses the same formula for its test). For steel, E is about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; the only source I retrieved for the range, 200 to 207 GPa, is a forum post, so treat it as the handbook figure it is [3].
What the formula says, which sources agree on [4] [2]: thicker (the fourth power of d), shorter, and lower tension all make B larger. At a fixed pitch the three are tied together, because a fatter string needs less tension to make the same note, so a thick string is stretched on both counts. Making the string thinner, longer, more flexible or higher in tension reduces it. Wound strings do it from the other side: the winding adds mass without adding bending stiffness, so only the core resists bending [4] [6]. That is why the lowest strings on both guitar and piano are wound.
Fletcher, Blackham and Stratton built piano tones from measured partials and asked listeners to compare them with real ones. They found that the partials of notes below middle C had to be inharmonic to sound piano-like, and that some inharmonicity contributes to the “warmth” [1] [5].
Try the calculator. The six-string presets use typical electric-guitar gauges and a 648 mm scale; the gauges and the wound strings’ mass factors are my own typical values and estimates, not from one source. The tension is worked out from the string’s mass per length (steel, 7850 kg/m³) and the pitch, so changing the gauge or the length moves the tension too. Raise fret to see B at a shorter vibrating length: with the tension unchanged, shortening L by 2fret/12 multiplies B by 2fret/6 (four times at the 12th fret). That is straight from the formula, and it is why the same string is more stretched up the neck. UNSW adds that the high harmonics of thick strings drift out of tune after about the twelfth, and that the “touch at 1/n of the length” rule for harmonics fails above about the eighth [7] [6].



Piano stretch. A piano tuner hears an octave as in tune when the upper note’s fundamental matches the lower note’s second partial. If that partial is sharp because of B, the upper note has to be tuned sharp too, and the effect accumulates: bass notes are tuned flat, treble notes sharp, the Railsback curve [4] [10]. The curve is empirical, not an equation, and the sources I found for its size in cents were forum posts that disagree, so I give no figure. Giordano’s JASA paper explains the stretch as the tuning that minimises sensory dissonance among the stretched partials, in agreement with Railsback [10]. Small pianos suffer most in the bass: a short case forces thicker bass strings, which have a larger B [4] [7]; a longer string is the cure but needs room.
The guitar’s plain G. UNSW notes that the solid G string of a classical guitar tunes poorly at higher frets [6]. That the steel-string plain G is the notorious one (a thick plain string whose tension and stiffness make the 12th-fret harmonic, the open note and the fretted note disagree by a few cents) is widely repeated by guitarists; I found only an anecdotal forum post for it and no measurement, so call it practitioner lore. The calculator will tell you what B the physics predicts for it.



Press Start. With the string in tune on band 1, the upper bands drift right by 600 log₂(1 + B k²) cents: you can tune a stiff string so that its fundamental is right and its upper partials sharp, or the reverse. A tuner that listens to one partial has to choose, which is the next sections’ point about who chooses.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
3. Old strings versus new
Players say old strings are “dead” and hard to tune. What is established, and what is not:

Established. Strings that become inhomogeneous, for example from grease build-up, “tune successively worse”; dirty or worn strings are inharmonic and washing helps [6] [7]. Wikipedia adds that rust or dirt in the windings can raise the frequency of the higher modes [5]. UNSW’s demonstration is a small mass added at the middle of a string: it lowers the odd modes and leaves the even ones, so the tone becomes less pitched and more like a “bad quality bell” [7].
Not what I expected. Jont Allen measured B for new and old guitar strings, expecting B to change with age, and reported that what changed was the damping of the high partials, “the real source of the aging effect” (as he described it in a 1976 Catgut Acoustical Society Newsletter article, quoted second-hand on the AUDITORY list, which I could not retrieve itself) [8].
Practitioner lore, no source found. That the uneven mass of grime in the windings causes false beats (a note that wobbles) and split partials (two close frequencies where there should be one) is what players and luthiers say, and it is plausible from the mass-loading model above, but I found no measurement of it. The “old string” preset below is an illustration: every partial is stiff-sharp, scattered by a few cents and split into two components 4 to 14 cents apart, and the high ones die away faster. The sizes are made up.




Press Start and watch the rows that wobble rather than drift: a split partial is two stripes patterns slipping across each other, and that is a beat.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 4. Mode locking: why bowed and blown notes stay harmonic
text:
4. Mode locking: why bowed and blown notes stay harmonic
A plucked string is a free vibration: each mode rings at its own frequency, whatever that is, so the stretch of section 2 shows up in the sound. A bowed string, a reed, the lips of a trumpeter and the vocal folds are different. They are self-sustained oscillators: the string (or air column, or vocal tract) gets pushed by something nonlinear that is itself switched by the motion. Fletcher showed in 1978 that such an oscillator can lock its modes to exact whole-number multiples of one frequency even when the resonator’s own modes are not, provided they are not too far off, their amplitudes are large and the drive is strongly nonlinear [9]. Exactly periodic motion has an exactly harmonic spectrum, and UNSW says the near-harmonic spectra of bowed strings, winds and voice are because their sound production is nonlinear [7].
So the same stiff string gives a stretched spectrum when plucked and a (nearly) harmonic one when bowed: “bowing largely removes the inharmonicity through mode locking, which comes from the stick-slip action of the bow; plucked or struck strings keep it” [7]. The limit is that locking needs the resonator to be nearly harmonic to begin with (Fletcher’s condition); a bar or a bell cannot be locked by a mallet, because a mallet only starts it.
This is the single most important fact for the question in section 9: what a player can change on a locked tone is the level of each partial, never its pitch.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
5. Winds: bells, mouthpieces, tone holes
Brass. A trumpet’s air column is a long tube with a mouthpiece at one end and a flaring bell at the other, and neither is harmonic. HyperPhysics describes how the mouthpiece and bell shift the resonances toward a harmonic series: “the mouthpiece forces the upper resonances down (the mouthpiece effect) and the bell forces the lower resonances up (the bell effect)” [11]. The lowest note, the pedal note, is the fundamental of the series but “is not a resonant frequency of the air column”: players sound it by buzzing at that frequency so the harmonics above, which are resonances, produce it between them [11]. The same page says the upper harmonics are not exactly in tune with equal temperament and singles out the seventh [11].
How far off? The kth harmonic is 1200 log₂(k) cents above the first. The 7th is 3368.8¢ up, 31¢ below the equal-tempered minor seventh two octaves up; the 11th is 4151.3¢, 51¢ above one equal-tempered note and 49¢ below the next; the 13th is 4440.5¢, 41¢ sharp of A♭ and 59 flat of A. These are my arithmetic; the principle that the 7th and 11th fall “about halfway between” equal-tempered notes is in [6]. A trumpeter or horn player who needs these notes lips them into tune (see section 9) and a natural-horn player also puts a hand in the bell to change the resonances; I found no source for the hand-stopping on the pages I retrieved, so that part is general knowledge.
Clarinet. A cylinder closed at one end (the reed) and open at the other has resonances at the odd multiples only, so the clarinet’s tone has mostly odd harmonics; the register key kills the fundamental and the instrument jumps up a twelfth, the third harmonic [12]. Tone holes and the bell then bend the real resonances, and mode locking (section 4) puts the played partials back on exact multiples. I did not find a source for multiphonics, so I leave them out.



Start the Clarinet preset: bands 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 stand still and the even rows are empty. Switch to Brass and every band stands still, with a weak first: the weak pedal note. The tuner measures against exact multiples, so it cannot show you that the 7th is 31 cents from the piano; for that, set Target tuning to something else, or look at the ladder in section 1.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 6. Voice: harmonics are fixed, formants move
text:
6. Voice: harmonics are fixed, formants move
The vocal folds are a self-sustained oscillator, so a sung vowel on one pitch is exactly harmonic [9]. What the throat and mouth add is filtering: “A band of enhanced frequencies is called a formant”, and moving the tongue and lips moves the bands independently of the harmonic lines, which are a fixed comb [14]. The vowel is the formants; the pitch is the comb. The voice preset has exact harmonics whose levels follow two illustrative formants (F1 700 Hz and F2 1100 Hz, round numbers for an “ah”, not data) so every band stands still but their strengths ride a bump.



Change the Note to another octave while it plays: the rows that are strong change, because the same formants now sit over different harmonics. That is why a vowel changes colour as a singer goes up, and why sopranos do something about it (section 9). I did not find retrievable sources for vocal fry (subharmonics) or jitter in the pages I used, so they are not covered here.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
7. Bars: marimba, xylophone, vibraphone, glockenspiel
A free uniform bar is a beam, and the beam equation gives mode frequencies that grow roughly as the square of an odd-ish integer. With the standard free-free roots 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, 14.1372 (the solutions of cos x cosh x = 1), the modes are in the ratio 1 : 2.756 : 5.404 : 8.933 (my arithmetic from the roots). Stanford’s CCRMA notes give the glockenspiel’s bars as 1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.90 [16], and the overtones stay unrelated to the fundamental: you hear a bright, bell-like “ting” with a pitch that is clear only because the fundamental is loud.
Larger bars are given an arch, an undercut at the middle, which lowers the fundamental far more than the overtones. Yoo and Rossing: “the middle part of each bar is undercut and as a result the 1st mode frequency is lowered as the 2nd mode frequency becomes 4 times higher than the 1st” [18]. A plain bar’s first overtone is about 17.5 semitones above the fundamental (the 2.76 ratio is 1753 cents; MMDigest says about 18 semitones) and the undercut widens it toward two octaves [17].

Marimba: modes tuned 1 : 4 : 10 [18] (patent text; makers call tuning the third mode “triple tuning” [19]). CCRMA’s notes give the marimba’s second partial at 4 but the third near 9.2 [16]: so 10 is the target, and real bars can land near it. Vibraphone bars: CCRMA gives the first overtone at about 4 [16]; one European patent for vibraphone bars regulates to 1 : 4 : 8 [18], so vibraphones are not simply 1 : 4 : 10.
Xylophone: the first overtone tuned to a twelfth, 1 : 3 [16]. The sound is dry and short, and the third partial helps the ear hear one note.
Glockenspiel, raw bar: not tuned beyond the fundamental.

I did not retrieve Rossing’s own text; where I cite Rossing (The Science of Percussion Instruments, 2000) it is through the sources that cite him [20]. The finite-element and modal work on marimba bars (Bork and colleagues, 1999, with 25 modes found below 8 kHz on one bar) is the reference for why a bar is tuned by trial and measurement rather than by one equation [19].



Compare the presets Marimba bar, Xylophone bar and Raw bar: in the first two the bands for the overtones stand still; the raw bar’s overtones slide over every band, a bar’s version of “no harmonic relation”.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 8. Tubular chimes and church bells: pitch from partials that are not there
text:
8. Tubular chimes and church bells: pitch from partials that are not there
Chimes. For a tubular bell, modes 4, 5 and 6 “appear to determine the strike tone”, with frequencies in the ratios 9² : 11² : 13² (or 81 : 121 : 169), “close enough to the ratios 2 : 3 : 4 for the ear to consider them nearly harmonic”; the pitch you hear is an octave below mode 4, the missing “1” [21] (via Rossing 2000, pp. 67 to 69). That pitch is a virtual pitch: nothing sounds at that frequency. Mode 6 is 81 : 169 over mode 4, 4.17 against 4, so it is 72 cents sharp of the series, which the ear forgives.
Church bells. Each mode of a bell contributes one partial, with traditional names. For a well-tuned bell the table of ratios to the prime is [22] (as tabulated from Rossing 2000):

The strike note is the pitch heard when the bell is struck, “determined by three partials (the octave, upper fifth and upper octave)” and “generally close to the prime in a well-tuned bell”; it is a virtual pitch, a perceptual effect, not a radiated tone [22]. Hibbert’s study of the quantity measures it as a missing-fundamental effect and shows it can shift by fractions of a semitone, so the “an octave below the nominal” rule of Lord Rayleigh (1890) is not always exact [22].
Do bells sound minor? The research confirms the claim in the narrow sense: the tierce is a minor third above the prime, with a perfect fifth (quint) above it, so a struck bell contains a minor triad’s third; Starmer in 1902 already wrote “there are also present a minor third and perfect fifth in the first octave” [22]. A carillon page calls the tierce “somewhat melancholic” [24]. It is not that the tune is minor but that every note carries a minor third in its tone, which is why a carillon plays runs and arpeggios rather than thick chords [22]. A major-third bell has been made: after earlier failures, a Technical University of Eindhoven project and the Eijsbouts foundry produced one in 1985 (a secondary page; a 1987 paper by Lehr reports it) with an unusual shape with a bulge at the waist; carillonneurs were critical, other listeners generally positive [24].



Pick Church bell: band 1 is the hum, band 2 the prime and band 4 the nominal, all standing still. The tierce is at 2.366 times the hum, between bands, so it slides through rows 2 and 3, and the quint and upper octave sit a few cents off bands 3 and 8. Switch to Tubular chime: band 1 is the strike pitch with nothing sounding, band 2 stands still (mode 4), band 3 is 7 cents flat, and band 4 is 72 cents sharp.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 9. Timpani: a drum that has a pitch
text:
9. Timpani: a drum that has a pitch
An ideal circular membrane has modes at the zeros of Bessel functions: relative to the lowest mode (0,1), the (1,1), (2,1), (0,2), (3,1) modes are at 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653 times it (my arithmetic from the Bessel zeros 2.405, 3.832, 5.136, 5.520, 6.380), nowhere near a harmonic series. A timpani is different. The surrounding air loads the membrane, and Packer’s 1993 Durham thesis concluded that air loading moves the modes that have only radial nodes toward a harmonic series, “creating a distinct sensation of musical pitch”, while the fundamental (0,1) is damped out [25]. Mills’s 1980 NIU thesis found that the effective mass of the air is the dominant cause of the shift [25]. In Rossing’s description the (1,1) mode carries the note and the next three radiate a fifth, an octave and a tenth above it [25], which makes the frequency ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 of the modes (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (4,1), and the pitch you hear a virtual pitch an octave below the loudest mode. (I found the 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 target stated in a Purdue dissertation abstract and via Rossing’s ratios, though not in Rossing’s text itself [25].)
Where the drum is struck changes which modes start. A strike a quarter of the way in from the rim excites the preferred modes well; that is what drummers say and what a 2022 Emory thesis found when it modelled strike positions (0.75 of the radius from the centre fitted best) [25]. Rossing’s own statement of the quarter figure was not among the pages I retrieved.



Timpani preset: band 1 is silent (the virtual pitch), bands 2 to 5 stand still. The ratios 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 are the point: they are a harmonic series with the fundamental missing, which is how a drum, and a bell, can have a pitch at all.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
10. Gamelan and timbre-matched scales
If the instrument’s partials are not harmonic, which intervals sound smooth? William Sethares’s answer in Tuning, Timbre, Spectrum, Scale is that consonance depends on the spectrum, not only on the interval: a scale and a spectrum “are related” if the dissonance curve for the spectrum has its minima at the scale steps. The book’s gamelan chapter argues that the inharmonic spectra of gamelan instruments are related to the gamelan scales, and the preface says the same of the Thai renat [26]. The corollary for a maker: give an instrument a different set of partials and you get a different best scale. I read the book’s own pages and a secondary summary of the chapter, not the chapter itself, and I did not find the stretched-octave claim in them.
crumbs: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
section: 11. Can a player tune one overtone while performing?
text:
11. Can a player tune one overtone while performing?
Short answer: not its pitch. On a sustained, self-driven tone (a bowed string, a wind, a voice) mode locking (section 4) ties every partial to an exact multiple of the fundamental [9]. A player can change each partial’s level, not its pitch. On a plucked or struck instrument the partials can be out of tune with each other, but they were set before the performance. So a player chooses which partials are heard and lines the note up with other players’; tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench (section 12).

How players change the levels

Singers: formant tuning. The vocal-tract resonances R1, R2 are not harmonics, and a soprano whose pitch rises above her speaking R1 can tune R1 to the fundamental (and at the very top R2): louder, more even, easier, at some cost to the vowel (Joliveau, Smith & Wolfe 2004; Smith & Wolfe 2009; Henrich, Smith & Wolfe, who measured R1 and R2 of 22 singers across four vowels and found sopranos tuning R1 near f0 over part of their range) [13]. Vowels blur up high because the formants have been told to follow the pitch, not the vowel.
Overtone singers. A narrowed formant picks out one harmonic from a fixed drone. Bergevin and colleagues’ study of Tuvan throat singing reports singers shaping the tract to narrowly focus overtones near 1 to 3 kHz, by merging two formants, and argue that it is linear filtering, not a nonlinear source [15]. That the chosen harmonic is typically the 8th to 12th and the melody therefore in just intonation is the standard description of khoomei, but I did not find that figure in the paper’s pages; the melody is just because harmonics are exact multiples (section 4).
Winds and didgeridoo. Embouchure, air speed and the player’s vocal tract change which harmonics are strong. Wolfe’s didgeridoo page: the lips drive the tract “working backwards”, so the mouth shapes the output; a sung note adds more frequencies, and a fifth above the played note gives a Tartini tone an octave below [14]. I found nothing on the jaw harp in my sources.
Strings: where, how fast, how hard. Pluck or bow a string where a harmonic has a node and that harmonic is missing: touch at 1/4 of the length and you get 4f [7]; pluck at the 12th fret, the middle, and the even harmonics vanish. Bow position mostly changes the “node frequencies” in the spectrum, and bow force relative to the limits of the Schelleng diagram changes how much high partials are emphasised, with bow speed alone able to shift timbre [28]. Touched harmonics (flageolets) also work by killing the modes that have no node there. Sul ponticello and sul tasto are the same idea (bow near the bridge or over the fingerboard); I did not retrieve a source for them on their own.






What players tune instead
They tune the note, so that their partials line up with other players’.

Barbershop. The 7th of a dominant seventh is lowered to 7 : 4 (about 969¢, 31¢ under the piano’s), a harmonic seventh, so it continues the overtone series 4 : 5 : 6 : 7 of the chord. Barbershop quartets are generally expected to tune to it [27]. Hagerman and Sundberg (1980) measured singers’ accuracy in barbershop chords in STL-QPSR and found the choice of fundamental frequency extremely accurate and not dependent on vowel, but sources note their data challenge the accuracy of the 7 : 4 claim [27]; I could not confirm the “ring” or “expanded sound” explanation (partials coinciding) from a source and give it as the usual explanation, not a measurement.
Brass and string sections. In just intonation a 5 : 4 third is 13.7¢ below the piano’s, and a 3 : 2 fifth is 2.0¢ above, see tuning systems. Section players adjust until the beats between neighbouring parts’ partials stop: that is a listening procedure, not a measured result I can cite.
Natural horn and trumpet. Lipping the 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics and, on the horn, hand-stopping (section 5; no source retrieved for the hand).



Plucked and struck instruments

Guitar. Players pick which partial to tune by: the 12th-fret harmonic against the fretted 12th-fret note, the harmonic at the 5th fret against the 7th on the next string, or beats between partials. Stiffness (section 2) makes these disagree by a few cents, and UNSW notes that tuning the 4th harmonic of the E string to the 3rd of the A string gives a fourth wider than a true harmonic one, which partly offsets the equal-temperament error [6].
Piano and harp. The strings’ partials cannot be changed during a performance at all.
Timpani is the nearest to “yes”: the pedal and the strike point change the overall tuning and the balance of modes during the piece, but the modes move together [25] (a reading of the above, not a measurement).

Summary. A player chooses which partials are heard and lines them up with the other players. Tuning an individual partial is done at the workbench.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
12. Tuning overtones in the workshop
The player’s choices end where the instrument’s partials are fixed. Makers set them. The practice instruments above are the target of each trade.
Piano tuners choose which partials to match. For an octave they match the upper note’s fundamental to the lower note’s second partial, and because that partial is sharp, the tuned scale stretches from flat bass to sharp treble: the Railsback curve [4] [10]. Which pair of partials to match (the 4th of the lower note against the 2nd of the upper, the 6th against the 3rd, and so on) is the tuner’s choice, and different choices give different stretches; I found no source that lays the choices out, so I do not rank them. Stretching is “a comparative term”, so the first note tuned, usually in the middle, is not stretched [4]. Electronic tuning devices reproduce stretched octaves rather than a simple harmonic series [5]: aural tuners listen to beat rates, electronic ones measure the piano’s B and compute a stretch. I did not retrieve sources on the commercial products’ stretch profiles, so I name none. Designers reduce B with longer bass strings and winding (section 2); the limit is the case size [4].
Marimba, xylophone and vibraphone bars are tuned by removing wood: the undercut at the centre lowers mode 1 most, and cuts elsewhere move modes 2 and 3 [18] [19]. A Curtin University thesis describes a search algorithm that finds the undercut shape needed to tune the second and third bending modes to the fundamental, using Timoshenko beam receptances [19]. Marimba makers describe tuning each mode in turn and check with a strobe tuner or spectrum analyser [19]; I found no source on the best order of cuts, so I do not claim one. The result is the 1 : 4 : 10 or 1 : 3 of section 7: try the marimba and xylophone presets in the tuner.
Church bells are tuned in a lathe by shaving metal from the inside at chosen heights, so that hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal move separately. Hibbert’s history of Taylors: Canon Simpson wrote to the foundry in 1894 and published on true-harmonic tuning in 1895 and 1896; Taylors bought tuning forks in 1894 and installed a tuning machine in 1895, and by 1896 were making bells with hum, prime and nominal in octaves [23]. Cutting inside the shoulder can flatten a prime but cannot sharpen it much; hums could only be brought to the true octave by changing the shape, and tierces depend mainly on the soundbow shape [23]. That is why the major-third bell needed a new profile, not a new cut (section 8). Whitechapel’s practice I did not retrieve.
Tubular chimes. The pitch comes from modes 4 to 6 (section 8). I found no source for the roles of length, end plugs and caps, so I do not describe them.
Steel pans. Hansen and Rossing report the lowest three partials of a pan note usually tuned as an octave and a twelfth or double octave, with the (1,0) mode usually tuned to the octave and (0,1) to the twelfth; the fundamental is tuned by hammering from above and below, inside and outside the edge of the note area; hammering for the others is concentrated in the central and outer region; and since one note’s deformation changes the others, the tuner cycles through the notes repeatedly [29].
Gongs, gamelan and Thai instruments. Tuned by hammering or filing; gamelan sets are tuned as an ensemble (embat). I found no source for the filing or embat details here. For why a scale suits an instrument see Sethares [26].
Wind-instrument makers adjust the bore, tone-hole size, undercutting and bell flare to bring the resonances into alignment, so that the notes are in tune and mode locking is stable. HyperPhysics’ mouthpiece and bell effects (section 5) are the principle [11]; the maker-level detail (Benade, Fletcher & Rossing) was beyond what I could retrieve.
Guitar and string builders. Saddles are compensated: the string is made a little longer than the scale length, since fretting stretches it and raises the pitch; the sources I found disagree on how much is stiffness and how much stretch (one luthier’s tests showed bending stiffness had negligible effect on intonation; another source pointed to string stretch as the main factor) [30]. Gauge choice sets B and tension (calculator, section 2). Fanned frets: no source found.
What a tuner cannot fix. The strobe tuner shows you what each partial is doing, band by band. It cannot make a bell’s tierce major or a stiff string’s twelfth true: players set levels, makers set partials.

title: Out-of-Tune Overtones: Strings, Winds, Voice, Bars, Bells and Drums
text:
Things to try

In the calculator, load the plain G (196 Hz), then raise the fret from 0 to 12. By what factor does B grow? (4.) Then switch to the wound D and compare B with the plain G.
In the ladder, pick Marimba bar then Raw bar: which partial of the raw bar is closest to a harmonic? (The fourth, 8.933, is only 13 cents flat of the 9th harmonic, by coincidence; the second is 146 cents flat of the 3rd and the third 130 sharp of the 5th.)
In the tuner, Church bell: which bands stand still? Switch to Timpani: which row has nothing in it, and which pitch do you hear?
In the pluck chart, where must you pluck so that the 3rd harmonic vanishes? (A third of the way along; check the 6th, 9th too.) Which harmonics vanish at the 12th fret?
In the tuner, Brass: band 7 stands still. What does the piano say about that note? (31¢ off the minor seventh: see section 5.)
Run the Old, dirty string next to the stiff string and say which rows wobble.

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
The Timestamp Notes turns a recording into a map: where each section starts, where every bar falls, and how fast the band is really playing. With the map you can jump straight to the bridge, loop a verse until you have it, and see whether the drummer speeds up in the last chorus.
Keep the player open in a second tab and work through the steps with a song you know.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
1. Load a recording
Open the player. There are three ways in:

A file. Drop a video or audio file (MP3, M4A, WAV, MP4…) on the box that says Drop a video or audio file here, or press Choose file. A file is the best choice: it plays on this page, the timing is exact, and nothing can block it.
A YouTube link. Paste it into the box and press Load (or Return).
A link in the address. timestamp-player.html?v= followed by a YouTube link or id loads it straight away, which is handy for a link on a class page.

The big clock shows where the recording is. Space or Return plays and pauses from anywhere on the page; the arrows (or h / l) go 5 seconds back or on.
If YouTube says the video won’t play here, skip to When YouTube won’t play it.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: 2. Stamp the sections and the moments
text:
2. Stamp the sections and the moments
Listen through once. There are two keys, and both put a row in the Timestamps column, in time order:

S where a section starts (the next step).
C whenever anything else happens: a key change, a fill you want to learn, a wrong note in your own recording.

For a C note:

Press C. A row appears with the time.
The cursor jumps into the row’s note field. Type what happened (“Chorus”, “sax fill”, “key change”).
Leave the note with Esc, or type jk quickly. The letters are taken back out.
Keep listening and stamping.

Click any time in the list to jump there. Untick Jump to the note field after a stamp if you’d rather stamp everything first and write the notes afterwards.
Everything is saved in the browser as you go, so a reload doesn’t lose it. Copy all gives you a plain list (01:23  Chorus) and Paste… reads one back. Saving the whole song is covered in step 7.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
3. Name the sections
Press S where a section starts. The row is tinted blue and has a menu: Intro, Head, Verse, Pre-chorus, Chorus, Bridge, Interlude, a solo for each instrument, Shout, Outro, and the form letters (A, then A′ and B, and so on). Other… at the bottom lets you type a label of your own. A new stamp starts with the label of the one before it, so chorus after chorus is just S, S, S.

A label used more than once is numbered for you: two Heads become Head 1 and Head 2 everywhere.
Under the Timestamps, the page counts how many choruses each soloist takes (in a pop song, how many bars).
If you’ve pasted the words (step 6), S stamps their next section instead.

What each label means, and how the counting works: Section Labels.
A C note that names a section also counts as one (older song files work this way):







Write
For example




A section word first
Intro, Verse 1, Pre-chorus, Chorus 2, Bridge, Solo, Instrumental, Interlude, Break, Outro, Coda, Tag, Vamp, Head, Ending, Turnaround


A letter, with or without a number
A, B, A2


Anything after §
§ horns come in, § modulation



Any other note (“sax fill”, “check this bar”) stays a plain stamp.
Stamp each section on its first downbeat. You don’t have to be exact; the next step fixes that.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
4. Tap the bars
Now give the recording its bars.

Set Beats a bar: 4 for most pop and rock, 3 for a waltz, 6 for a slow 6/8 counted in six.
Go back to the start (click the first stamp, or drag the video’s own slider).
Press Return to play, and press B on beat 1 of every bar. Count “1 2 3 4” under your breath and press on each “1”.
Watch the line above the panels. It shows Bar 7 · Chorus and flashes on every tap.

Fixing mistakes:

Backspace takes back the last tap.
Tapping near a bar you already tapped (within about a sixth of a second) replaces it. So to fix one spot, go back a few bars before it and tap through it again.
Open the Bars panel. Any bar much longer or shorter than the others is highlighted yellow: that is almost always a missed or doubled tap. Click its time to jump there and tap it again.
Fill from the tempo: tap a stretch (the head), stamp where each later section starts (S), and it puts in the rest of the bars, each solo a whole number of choruses when it’s close. Tap B where a guessed bar drifts. See Section Labels.
Fill gaps puts in the bars of a stretch you missed. Halve bars / Double bars fix taps made every half bar or every other bar (Undo puts them back).
A bar really in another meter (a bar of 2 before a chorus)? Change its Beats in the Bars panel.
In the Sections panel, ⚠ beside two sections next to each other (9 bars then 7, say) means the stamp between them is probably a bar off.

Once the bars are in, every section moves onto the nearest tapped bar, so a stamp a little early or late lands on the right downbeat. The Sections panel now says Verse 1 · bars 9–16.
The summary line tells you the tempo: 64 bars · about 118 bpm (114–122). A narrow range means a steady band (or a click track); a range that climbs through the song means it speeds up.
Tip: listen to the first bars a couple of times before tapping. Tapping goes much better when you already know where “1” is. In a song with a pickup, start tapping at the first full bar.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
5. Use the map

Jump. Click a section’s time, or a bar’s time in the Bars panel.
Loop. Press Loop beside a section, or Shift+L while the playhead is in it. The recording goes back to the start of the section every time it reaches the next one. Press Shift+L again (or the button, now saying Looping) to stop.
Phrases. The Phrases panel cuts each section into 2-, 4- or 8-bar phrases, each looped from its lead-in. P loops the phrase under the playhead, , and . step to the one before or after, and T sends it to the Notation page to write down.
Without the audio. Once the timings are in, clicking a section (in the chord grid, the menu in Now playing, or the Sections panel) moves to it even with nothing loaded, so you can check and fix the map anywhere.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: 6. Words, chords and the chord grid
text:
6. Words, chords and the chord grid

Words and chords. Paste a song from Ultimate Guitar (chords above the words, [Verse 1] headings) and press Convert: it becomes ChordPro. No words yet? Sections from stamps puts your section labels in instead, so the chord grid shows each section’s bars anyway.
Chord timing. Press N as each chord starts (Shift+N takes the last one back); which chord it is comes from the words. Or play it all in from a MIDI keyboard: connect it in the box at the top of the right sidebar. The left hand plays a note on every barline (two together where a section starts), the right hand the chords.
The chord grid follows the section under the playhead. When a section’s chords are in the right places, press Timing is right to show them all.
Send on. Notation page (melody) sends the sections and chords for writing down the tune; Backing Track (style) sends the chart to play along with, at the tapped tempo.
crumbs: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
7. Save and start again

Save song file saves everything in one .json: the stamps, the bars, the words and chords, the chord timing, the phrases and the link. Open file reads one back (older .txt stamp lists and bar-map .json files open too).
The browser keeps one song at a time. Before you start on another, save the song file, then press Clear all data. It asks first (press it again within a few seconds), then empties everything kept for the song: stamps, bars, words and chords, chord timing, grids and phrases. The page reloads with nothing loaded. Your page settings (column widths, folded parts, the MIDI keyboard) stay.

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
text:
When YouTube won’t play it
Some videos show Video unavailable with a message like “…blocked it from display on this website or application”. The player shows the reason and YouTube’s error number in its own words:







Error
Means




101 or 150
The owner, or a rights holder such as a music publisher, blocks it from playing here


100
Removed, or private


2
Not a valid video link


153
YouTube couldn’t tell which page asked for it



First, try another browser window. These blocks depend on the browser as well as the website. The same video can play in one browser and be refused in another. Try a private window with extensions off, or another browser. If it plays there, use that.
If it still won’t play, follow along in a YouTube tab. The video plays on YouTube itself, and the player keeps its own clock in step with it.

Press Follow in a tab (next to Load, or on the error message). YouTube opens in a new tab.
Put the two windows side by side, so you can see YouTube and press keys on the player.
In YouTube, pause the video at a time you can read, for example 0:00 or 1:05.
On the player, type that time into Clock to and press Return. The big clock shows it.
Start the video in YouTube, click back onto the player straight away, and press Return as close to the same moment as you can. Or start the clock on a sound you can hear: pause at the start of a bar, set the clock to that time, then press Return here on the first note.
Check it after a few seconds. If the clock is ahead, press [** to pull it back 0.1 s; if it’s behind, press **].
If you slow YouTube down (its settings gear, Playback speed), choose the same Speed on the player.

Now C, B, section names and the bar map work as before.
What can’t work: the player can’t see or steer YouTube’s tab. YouTube’s tab cuts itself off from the page that opened it, so the player can’t pause it, move it, or close it.

Jumping (clicking a stamp, section or bar) opens a new YouTube tab at that time, and the clock stops there. Pause the old tab first, or you’ll hear two copies, then close it yourself. Press Return when the new tab starts playing.
Looping isn’t available. Loop in YouTube instead (right-click the video and choose Loop) or drag its slider back.
The clock drifts a little. Expect to nudge by a tenth of a second or two, and check it again when you jump.

The best fix is a file. If you have the recording (bought, from the band, from your own phone), drop it on the player instead. Everything works, exactly.

title: Mapping a Recording with the Timestamp Notes
section: Exercise: map a song in 15 minutes
text:
Exercise: map a song in 15 minutes
Choose a song you’re learning and do this in one sitting.

Load it (5 min). Play it through once, stamping and naming every section.
Bars (5 min). Set the beats, go back to the start, tap every bar. Fix the yellow bars.
Check (3 min). Click through the sections. Does each one start on a downbeat? Write down the tempo and whether it changes.
Practise (2 min, then as long as you like). Loop the hardest section and play or sing along.
Save the song file.

Questions to answer about your song:

How many bars is each section? Are the verses and choruses the same length every time?
Is the tempo steady? Where does it change?
Is there a bar of 2 or a bar of 6 anywhere? (A bar in the Bars panel whose length is half or one and a half times the others, that you tapped correctly, is one.)

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text: Skills mix two tracks. A set is an hour or more of them, chosen for these people at this moment. The best technical mix of the wrong record empties a floor; a rough mix of the right one fills it.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
The energy curve
A set usually builds: start below the room’s energy, raise it in steps, give it a peak, let it breathe, raise it again. Ways to raise energy: faster tempo (a few BPM at a time), busier drums, a brighter key step (+1 or +2 on the Camelot wheel), a familiar song. Ways to let it breathe: a breakdown, a vocal track, a lower tempo, a classic everyone sings.
Warm-up DJs keep the energy below the headliner’s, playing deeper, slower music. Playing your biggest tracks at 10 pm to an empty room is a classic beginner’s mistake.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Prepare

Crates / playlists by mood and energy, not only genre: “openers”, “builders”, “peak”, “breathers”, “closers”.
Know each track’s BPM, key, where its intro and outro are, and how long it takes to mix in. Set hot cues before the gig.
Plan the first three tracks and a few pairs that mix well. Then be ready to throw the plan away.
Gain: check levels so the meter peaks the same on every track; leave the master below the red (the venue’s sound system adds volume, not you).
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Read the room
Watch the floor, not the screen:

Are people dancing? Growing or shrinking? People leaving the floor after a track tells you something.
Who is dancing? Different crowds want different things; a room of friends of the birthday girl wants songs they know.
Energy: heads down and dancing hard, hands up at the drop, or talking at the bar?
Change direction one step at a time. A sudden switch of genre or tempo loses people; a bridge track (the same key, a shared rhythm) keeps them.
The request you get repeatedly tells you what the room wants, even if you don’t play it.
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
Practise a mini-set
Plan a four-track set from the loops (each listed with BPM and Camelot code), then play it with transitions from the earlier lessons.



One plan: Mirrorball 118 (9B) → Late Bus 120 (5A: a contrast, use a drum intro or a cut) → Warehouse 124 (8A) → Neon Floor 126 (9A) → Concrete 128 (4A, by a filter mix or a cut). Tempo rises 2–4 BPM each time. Where would the acapella go?

Write the order down with each track’s BPM and key before you play.
Mix each pair on a phrase, with an EQ bass swap or a filter.
Record yourself (your phone, or the navbar’s tools) and listen back: are the transitions even in level? Any clash of keys or phrases?
crumbs: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room

title: DJ 7: Building a Set and Reading a Room
text:
After the gig

Write down what worked and what emptied the floor.
Update your crates: tracks that worked well together become pairs.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text: A sample is a piece of a recording reused in a new piece of music. It can be one drum hit, a bar of a drum break, a chord from an old soul record, a word from a film, or a whole chorus. Hip-hop was built on samples; so were house, jungle, much of pop since the 1990s, and every DJ set ever played.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
Three sizes of sample

One-shot: a single sound (a kick, a snare, a horn stab, “Ahh”). You play it from a pad or key; it lasts as long as it lasts.
Loop: one, two or four bars that repeat seamlessly. A loop has a tempo (BPM) and usually a key.
Phrase: a longer piece (a sung line, a riff, a speech) placed once, not looped.

A break is a special loop: the moment in a funk or soul record when everything drops out but the drums. DJ Kool Herc played two copies of the same record in the Bronx in the 1970s and switched between them to stretch the break out for dancers: the “merry-go-round” that started hip-hop. The most sampled break is probably the Winstons’ “Amen, Brother” (1969), the basis of jungle and drum and bass.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
section: Two ways to use a sample
text:
Two ways to use a sample









The producer
The DJ




Where the sample lives
Inside a new track (a DAW, an MPC, an SP-404)
On a record, a USB stick or a laptop, played live


What changes it
Chopping, re-pitching, re-sequencing, effects
Mixing, EQ, loops, cue points, scratching


The result
A new recording
A performance (a set, a mix)


Typical material
Breaks, one-shots, chords, vocal phrases
Whole songs, acapellas (vocals only), instrumentals, edits



The two overlap more every year: DJ software can loop, slice and separate a song into stems live, and producers make “DJ tools” (intros, edits, loops) for other DJs to play.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
section: Hear a loop, then pieces of it
text:
Hear a loop, then pieces of it
The sampler below has a two-bar drum break loaded (made on this site, so it is free to use). Press ▶ Whole loop to hear it, then click the pads: each plays one of 16 equal slices. The waveform shows where each slice starts.




Find the pads that hold a kick, a snare and a hi-hat. Those are one-shots cut out of a loop.
Play the pads in order, 1 to 16, steadily. You have rebuilt the loop by hand.
Now play 1, 1, 5, 1, 1, 1, 5, 7. The same sounds, a new rhythm: that is sampling in one sentence.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
A loop on a deck
A DJ hears the same material as a whole. Press ▶ on the deck, then pull the pitch fader: the loop speeds up and its pitch rises, like a record on a faster turntable. Drag the label on the platter to move the record by hand.

title: Sampling 1: What a Sample Is
text:
What makes a good sample

Space: a few bars where one instrument plays alone, or the drums play alone, are easier to reuse than a full mix.
A clean start: a hit right on the beat makes a loop that lines up.
Character: tape hiss, room sound and a drummer’s swing are part of why producers sample old records rather than programming drums.

Every sample of someone else’s recording also raises a question of permission: Sampling 6 is about that.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
The tonewheel organ (the Hammond B-3 and its relatives) is in gospel, soul, blues, jazz and rock. It looks like a piano but behaves very differently: a key has no touch, a note sounds for as long as you hold it, and the sound is built by the player from nine pitches. Then it goes through a chorus, a volume pedal, and a speaker that spins.
The organ on this page is the band’s own: nothing is recorded, every note is built from the same parts as the real instrument. (How it’s built and where the numbers come from: apps/shared/band/ORGAN.md. It’s a model, so some of its levels are informed guesses.) Everything you set here is also what the organ plays in the band at the bottom of the page.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
1. The organ
Hold a key on the keyboard, or press Hold a chord, then work the controls while it sounds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
2. Tonebars (drawbars)
Each of the nine bars adds one pitch to every key you press. Each bar is named by the length of an organ pipe in feet: the 8′ is the note you play, 16′ is an octave below, 4′ an octave above, and so on. The white bars are octaves of the note. The black ones are the 5ths and 3rd above it, which give the sound its colour. The two brown bars are the sub-octave pitches.
Each bar has nine positions, 0 (in, silent) to 8 (all the way out, loudest). Each step is about 3 dB. A registration is written as the nine numbers in three groups: 88 8000 000 means the first three bars all the way out and the rest pushed in.
Try this:

Start from 00 8000 000: the note alone, nearly a pure tone. Pull out the 4′, then the 2′, and watch the pitches stack up on the right.
Pull out the 1⅗′ alone over the 8′. That’s the 3rd, two octaves up. The organ’s 3rd and 5ths are slightly out of tune with a pure harmonic, because they come from tonewheels tuned to the keyboard. That’s part of the sound.
Pick 88 8888 888: the whole organ.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
3. Chorus and vibrato
A scanner sweeps the sound through a very short delay, 6.9 times a second. On its own that wobbles the pitch: vibrato (V3). Mixed half and half with the plain sound the wobble becomes a shimmer: chorus (C3), the setting most players leave on for jazz, gospel and soul. Switch between Off and C3 chorus on a held chord to hear it.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
4. The swell pedal
Because a key sounds the same however hard you press it, the organist plays dynamics with the right foot. The swell pedal is a volume pedal that never quite closes: at its quietest the organ is 24 dB down and the bass is kept up so the sound doesn’t go thin. It sits before the amplifier, so opening it also makes the sound grittier.
Organists open the pedal through the end of a phrase into the next one, pull it back sharply after a big hit, and ride it the way a singer leans into a long note.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
5. The Leslie speaker
The organ’s sound goes into a cabinet where it is split: the high notes go into a horn and the low notes into a drum, and both spin. As each one turns toward you it gets a bit louder and higher; as it turns away it gets softer and lower. That’s the swirl.

Slow (“chorale”): about 48 turns a minute. A gentle movement.
Fast (“tremolo”): about 400 turns a minute. A shimmering, urgent sound.
Stop: the rotors stand still.

The best part is the change. The light horn reaches its new speed in about a second and a half; the heavy drum takes about five. Switch from Slow to Fast on a held chord and listen to it wind up, then switch back and hear it wind down. The picture spins at the model’s speeds.

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
6. The organ in the band
Here the organ comps in three styles. Unless you’ve taken them over above, the band’s organist works the pedal and switch by itself: the pedal follows how hard the band is playing and opens into each new phrase, and the Leslie goes fast at the end of a phrase that leads into a chorus. In swing, the speaker stays slow until the very end. Untick Let the band’s organist… above (or just move the control) to take them over.
Soul jazz, organ comping a boogaloo:



Swing, organ comping a jazz blues:



Ballad, long organ chords under a slow song (try 68 8600 000 and a low pedal):

title: Arranging 4: The Organ
text:
7. Try it

Set 00 8000 000, chorus Off, Leslie Stop. That’s a plain electronic tone. Now put back the chorus, then the Leslie on Slow, then pull out the 16′ and 5⅓′. Each step makes it more like the organ on a record.
In the boogaloo, take over the Leslie and switch it to Fast just before bar 9 each time round.
In the ballad, take the pedal and play the dynamics: low through the first two bars, opening through bar 4 into the top.



  Tempo 
  ■ Stop

text: Sing an ending for a song three times. The computer works out which of the site’s familiar rhythm patterns and familiar tonal patterns you sang. Then you write it into the song on the Notation page, and it tells you when the rhythm is right and when the pitches are right.

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it

The song

text:
Sing it three times
Press Play and sing once. The song plays three times in a row without stopping. Each time, sing your ending in its last two bars, where only the chords play. Only those two bars are recorded. Sing every note on a syllable (“da”, “la”), and separate repeated notes.

  
    Turn on the microphone
    ● Play and sing
    Clear the takes

text:
What I heard
Nothing yet.

  ▶ Hear what I understood
  Show the answer

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it
text:
Notate it
Write what you sang in the song’s two empty bars: choose the rhythm patterns, then enter the notes with letters, the computer keys or a MIDI keyboard. The rhythm and the pitches are checked separately, each confirmed once. Octave does not matter for the pitches.

Sing three takes first.

title: Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it
text:
How it works

Candidates. Rhythms come from the Rhythm Sequences bank (apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js), bars of the chosen meter only; any two bars together make a candidate. Tonal patterns come from the Tonal Patterns bank (apps/patterns/pattern-object.js), the chosen tonality only, as semitones above the tonic, so the key does not change the match.
Your three takes (the song’s last two bars, each time round) are put on a sixteenth-note grid. A note counts when two takes agree on it. Your tuning drift (up to about a third of a semitone, sharp or flat all the way through) is removed.
The match. Every rhythm is scored by how well its onsets fit yours; the pitches are covered with as few tonal patterns as possible, in whichever octave you used. It is lenient: onsets count up to about a third of a beat early or late, a repeated note counts as one pitch of a pattern, a pattern’s notes count in any octave (5 down to 1 is the pattern 5 1), and held notes over whole beats (half notes) are familiar rhythms. A fit needs rhythm 66%, pitches 66% and the takes mostly in agreement. A note a half step out of the key never counts. Otherwise you get a warning and a chance to sing again, never a guess.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
A wavetable is a list of different single-cycle wave shapes, one after another. The oscillator plays one shape, and a position control chooses which. Move the position while a note is playing and the sound morphs smoothly from one shape to the next. Wolfgang Palm’s PPG Wave (1981) made the idea famous; today it’s the heart of software synths like Serum and Vital.
How to use the page. Press ▶ Demo or play the keys or MIDI. Drag Position in the table while a note plays. The drawing shows every shape in the table, front to back, with the current one in red.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
The synth



This table has eight shapes: sine, triangle, sawtooth, square, a narrow pulse, a vowel (“ah”), a hollow wave and a sparse glassy one. Between two shapes the oscillator mixes them: halfway between sawtooth and square is half of each. Look at the spectrum as you drag: each shape is a different recipe of harmonics (see Sound 1), and the morph moves smoothly from one recipe to the next.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
Scanning the table
A wavetable is most interesting when the position moves by itself. Raise Scan LFO depth and the LFO sweeps the position back and forth through the table. A slow scan (0.1 Hz) gives a pad that slowly changes colour. A fast scan (4 Hz or more) gives a talking, rhythmic wobble.
In a full wavetable synth an envelope can also move the position, so that every note starts on one shape and ends on another. That’s the same idea as the filter envelope in subtractive synthesis, but the movement can be through any timbres at all, not just from bright to dark.

title: Sound 9: Wavetable Synthesis
text:
How it is built here
A full wavetable synth stores each shape as hundreds or thousands of samples and plays them back very fast. For a lesson that is more than we need. The browser can build an oscillator from a list of harmonic strengths (as in the additive widget in Sound 1), so each shape in this table is stored as 48 harmonic strengths, and the position mixes neighbouring lists about thirty times a second. Mixing harmonic recipes and mixing wave shapes give exactly the same result, so it sounds and looks the same as the real thing, just with a smaller table.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text: Short answer: yes, by its chords and its form. Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man (Takin’ Off, Blue Note, 1962) is a 16-bar blues in F: the first eight bars are an ordinary blues, then the V–IV pair (C7–B♭7) is played three times before two bars of F7. Every chord is a dominant seventh on I, IV or V, which is exactly what this site’s F Major (Blues) label means. By genre, though, critics file the record as hard bop, soul jazz or (in 1973) funk, and Hancock himself describes a street cry, not “a blues”. This page sets out the evidence and how sure we can be.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
The form, bar by bar

Set it beside the standard 12-bar blues (I for four bars, IV for two, I for two, then V, IV, I, I): bars 1–8 are identical, and the V–IV pair that ends a 12-bar blues is stated three times instead of once. 8 + 3 × 2 + 2 = 16. The analyst Ethan Hein puts it the same way: “essentially a twelve-bar blues in F, but with bars nine and ten repeated three times.” The original liner notes call it a “modified blues” and “a strongly gospel-infused 16-bar theme.”
There are two ways to read a 16-bar form like this:

A 12-bar blues with its ending stretched. This fits Watermelon Man closely, because the first eight bars are unchanged.
An 8 + 8 form, a verse and a refrain. Scholars who read 16-bar blues this way (for example Carter, Music Theory Online, 2025) still count them as blues: the blues is “inherently hybrid”, and blues that met the popular mainstream “did not cease to be blues”.

Either way it is a blues by form.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What makes something “a blues”?
“Blues” means at least three different things, and they give different answers:

A form and a set of chords. The textbook prototype is 12 bars, I–IV–V, every chord a dominant seventh, often with an AAB lyric. Watermelon Man: yes, with a stretched ending.
A genre or marketing category. The record industry of the 1920s named “blues” as a kind of record. Takin’ Off is filed as hard bop or soul jazz, and the 1973 Head Hunters version as jazz-funk. Watermelon Man: no.
An idiom or feeling. Albert Murray separated the blues as a mood from blues music; reviewers call this track “bluesy”. Watermelon Man: arguably.

Historians also warn that the 12-bar prototype is a later standardization: early blues used 8-bar, 16-bar and irregular forms (for example “Sitting on Top of the World”, nine bars), so counting only 12 bars as “a blues” would be arbitrary. 8-bar blues (“Key to the Highway”, “Trouble in Mind”) and 16-bar blues are treated as blues forms in the reference books and teaching sites we could reach.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What the published sources say
Every source that names the form calls it a blues of some kind:

AllSolos: “Blues – 16 bars”, “built on an extended blues structure”.
Standard Repertoire: an “Altered blues”, 16 bars.
Learn Jazz Standards: “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove.”
JazzFuel: “essentially a sixteen-bar blues: the first 8 bars mimic a classic blues exactly.”
FretDojo: “a 16 bar blues, rather than a 12 bar blues.”
Wikipedia: “written in a sixteen-bar blues form” (no source given).

No source we found says it is not a blues. These are mostly teaching and reference websites, and several probably repeat one another, so they are weaker evidence than they look. Critics and encyclopedias mostly use genre words instead: hard bop, soul jazz, R&B, funk, boogaloo, “bluesy”.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
What Hancock says
Hancock tells the story of the tune, not its form. In the 1962 liner notes he recalls “the cry of the watermelon man making his rounds through the back streets and alleys” of his Chicago childhood, and in his memoir Possibilities (2014) the “clackety-clack” of the horse-drawn wagon. He has said it “took 15 minutes to write” and that he wanted it to be “real”, not just commercial; he also says that growing up in Chicago he “heard the real blues, Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf”. In no source we found does he call Watermelon Man itself a blues. The groove is straight eighths over a gospel-style piano vamp, closer to soul jazz than to a shuffle.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
text:
The other famous versions

Mongo Santamaría (1963). A Latin version that reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998. It keeps the 16-bar form (with two extra groove bars on the second time through) over a slower guajira-based groove. Its chords match as far as we can tell, but we found no published chart.
Head Hunters (1973). A slow (about 75 beats per minute) funk re-composition with the hindewhu (whistle-and-voice) introduction, no solos, and a new section that leaves the I–IV–V frame. Sources disagree about the new chord (G♭7 or A♭7). This version should not be labelled “(Blues)” automatically.

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
section: So what does the site say?
text:
So what does the site say?
The tune is labelled F Major (Blues). On this site “(Blues)” describes the harmony: the chords on I and IV are dominant sevenths. Watermelon Man meets that test exactly. It is not a claim about genre, and it does not mean a shuffle feel.
We considered “(16-bar blues)” and decided against it: that puts a fact about the form into a label about the key, and would make a category with one tune in it. The 16-bar form is described in the lessons instead (see Watermelon Man for Congas, which uses the same form as the Backing Track’s “Watermelon Man (16 bars)” preset).

title: Is Watermelon Man a Blues?
section: How sure are we, and what would change it?
text:
How sure are we, and what would change it?

Not checked: the printed lead sheets (The Real Book, Sher’s New Real Book), Ted Gioia’s entry in The Jazz Standards (2012, p. 446), Grove Music Online, the Penguin Guide, Steven Pond’s book on Head Hunters, and Hancock’s memoir in his own words (quoted here second-hand). The bar-by-bar chart above comes from a teaching site and an independent analysis, not a published lead sheet.
Not analysed: the melody. Whether it uses blue notes or the blues scale was not checked; a transcription would settle it.
What would change the answer: only a printed chart in which the I or IV chord is not a dominant seventh, or a respected source arguing it is not a blues. A published chart with the same F7 / B♭7 / C7 changes would simply confirm it. A melody with no blues-scale notes would deserve a footnote, not a different label, because the label is about the chords.
