title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text: Before any microphone choice or plug-in, one thing decides whether a recording is usable: how loud the signal is at each step on the way in. Too quiet and the noise of the gear comes up with it; too loud and the top of the wave is cut off, for ever. Getting this right at every stage is gain staging.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: The chain on the way in
text:
The chain on the way in
A sound reaches the computer through a few stages, each with its own ceiling:

Source: the voice or instrument, and the room.
Microphone (or a DI box for a guitar or keyboard).
Preamp: the gain knob on the interface. A microphone puts out a tiny voltage (mic level, around −60 to −40 dBu); the preamp raises it by 30–60 dB to line level.
Converter (A/D): turns the voltage into numbers. Its ceiling is 0 dBFS (decibels relative to full scale): the largest number it can write. Nothing goes above it.
The DAW: tracks, plug-ins, buses, the master.

The gain knob is the one that matters most, and it is the one to set first, with the fader in the DAW left at 0. A fader turns down what was recorded; it cannot un-clip it.

Clipping at the converter is permanent. A clipped take sounds harsh and crackly on every peak, and nothing later removes it. When in doubt, record quieter.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
How loud to record
In 24-bit recording (the default in every DAW now) there is about 144 dB between the noise floor of the numbers and 0 dBFS, far more than any preamp or room can use. So there is no reason to record hot.

Aim for peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS and an average around −18 dBFS. That is where most analogue gear and plug-ins are designed to sit (−18 dBFS is about 0 VU, “line level”).
Set the gain while the player performs the loudest part of the song, not while they warm up. People play louder in the take than in the sound check; singers louder in the chorus than the verse.
If the meter touches red even once, turn the gain down a few dB and do it again.
16-bit recording (old gear, some phones) has 96 dB of range; there it is worth recording a bit hotter, but still never into the red.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Hear it go wrong
The signal chain from Sound 24, with every stage clipping above 0 dB like real gear. Press Too hot, watch a stage go red, then lower the Input gain until nothing does.



Notice that turning down the output after a clipped stage only makes the damage quieter.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: Try it: gain, clipping and hiss
text:
Try it: gain, clipping and hiss
A quiet microphone-level voice (or drum loop) goes through a preamp, a converter that cuts hard at 0 dBFS, and then the fader in the DAW. Press play, then the three Try buttons in turn.

Too hot, fader down: the track meter looks safe, the red light has latched, and it still sounds crunchy. The fader came after the damage.
Too quiet, fader up: nothing clips, but the signal-to-noise figure is poor and the hiss comes up with the voice.
Just right: peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS, hiss far below.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
section: Pads, DI and the gain knob
text:
Pads, DI and the gain knob

Pad (−10 or −20 dB switch on the interface or the mic): for very loud sources (kick drum, guitar amp, a belted high note close to a condenser) where even the lowest gain clips. It cuts before the preamp, so the preamp isn’t overloaded.
Instrument / Hi-Z input: an electric guitar or bass plugged straight in needs a high-impedance input (the “Inst” switch) or a DI box. On a mic input it sounds thin and dull.
Line input: keyboards, drum machines, the outputs of other gear. Already loud; little or no gain.
Too little gain then turning up in the DAW raises the preamp hiss with the signal. Too much is clipping. Somewhere between, the gain is right.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Inside the DAW
Floating-point DAWs (all modern ones) won’t clip inside a track; only the converter and the final file have a hard ceiling. But plug-ins that model analogue gear react to level: hit a vintage compressor or saturation plug-in at +6 dBFS and it distorts. Keep each track and bus around the same −18 dBFS average, use the clip gain or a trim plug-in at the start of a track rather than pushing faders far up, and leave the master peaking well below 0 before mastering.

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging
text:
Checklist

Faders at 0, gain at minimum, then bring gain up while they play the loudest part.
Peaks −12 to −6 dBFS. Never red.
Pad for loud sources, Inst/DI for guitar and bass.
Record 24-bit (48 kHz or 44.1 kHz).

title: Recording 1: Gain Staging

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text: The Akai MPC (1988 onwards) put a sampler and a sequencer in one box with 16 rubber pads. You chop a record onto the pads, tap out a pattern while the sequencer loops, and the box remembers it. The pads respond to how hard you hit them; the swing and quantize settings shape the timing. Much of 1990s and 2000s hip-hop was made this way; the Roland SP-404 carried it into lo-fi and beat scenes.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Pads and keys
The pads below follow the MPC layout: pad 1 is bottom left. With the sampler focused (click it), the keys play the pads:



1 = 13
2 = 14
3 = 15
4 = 16


Q = 9
W = 10
E = 11
R = 12


A = 5
S = 6
D = 7
F = 8


Z = 1
X = 2
C = 3
V = 4



A MIDI pad controller or keyboard works too (Connect MIDI): notes 36–51 (C1 up), the first bank on most controllers.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Make a beat




Find a kick, a snare and a hat among the pads (sliced at the hits). Note which keys they are on.
Press ● Rec. The click counts the beats; each pass round the pattern is two bars. Tap kicks only, on 1 and the and of 2.
Next pass, add snares on 2 and 4. Recording keeps going round and adds what you play (overdub). Made a mistake? Undo removes the last pass.
Stop recording, press ▶, and listen. Turn Quantize off and record a hat pass: the hits land exactly where you played them, human and uneven. With 1/16 they snap to the nearest sixteenth.
Change the Tempo from 100 to 88. The pattern slows down, but each chop still plays at its own speed: the beat now has gaps. Try Length ×1.15 on the snare pad (Repitch) to fill them, and hear it drop in pitch.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Chords over drums
A beat from one break is a start. Producers layer: drums from one record, a chord stab from another, a bass note from a third. Load Old Soul Record into a second sampler, slice it One a beat, and play chords over the pattern you recorded above.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
text:
Timing feel

Quantized to 1/16 sounds tight, machine-like: the house and trap way.
Unquantized keeps your timing. J Dilla famously turned quantize off on his MPC3000, so kicks fall slightly late and hats drag: the “drunk” feel.
Swing delays every second sixteenth. An MPC’s swing setting (50 % straight, 66 % triplet) is how many classic beats got their bounce.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops
section: The DJ’s version: finger drumming and the sampler
text:
The DJ’s version: finger drumming and the sampler
DJ software has a sampler too (slots you fire from pads on a controller), and the controllers’ performance pads fire hot cues, loops and samples. Setting hot cues on a break’s kick and snare and drumming a new pattern live is the DJ’s beat from chops.

title: Sampling 4: A Beat from Chops

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
A jazz singer is part of the band. The tone is conversational, the rhythm swings, and the melody is something to reshape rather than repeat. This lesson moves from tone and swing to scat, blue notes, singing the chords, and the back-phrasing of a ballad.
How to use the page. Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. Choose Your voice once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower. The playback is straight, but swing the eighth notes when you sing (see the next section). Click a heading to fold a section away.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Tone: talk the tune
Jazz singers from Billie Holiday to Shirley Horn sound like they are telling you something. Keep the tone close to your speaking voice, with clear words.
Vibrato is a natural, regular wobble in a held note’s pitch. Use it as a colour, not a constant. A common habit is to start a long note straight and let the vibrato bloom near the end.
Sing the note below, straight for two beats and then letting it relax into vibrato.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Swing eighths
In swing, a pair of eighth notes is played long–short, roughly like the first and last notes of a triplet: “doo-ba doo-ba”. Accent the off-beats (the “and”s) a little, and let some notes almost disappear. Those are ghost notes, shown in parentheses in the syllables under the staff.
The playback here is straight; sing it swung. For a swung band to sing with, try Reading swing or the Backing Track on a swing style.




Tap your foot on beats 2 and 4, not 1 and 3. That is where the drummer’s hi-hat closes in a swing feel, and it puts your body in the groove.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Scat syllables
Scat is improvising with syllables instead of words. The syllables work like articulation on a horn:

“doo” for a smooth, legato note.
“ba” and “da” for a note with an attack.
“dat” and “dot” for a short note at the end of a phrase.
“bee”, “bop”, “doo-dle” for quick runs.

Start by copying a horn line. Sing this phrase with the syllables written under it. Then make up your own syllables on the same notes.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Blue notes and the blues scale
text:
Blue notes and the blues scale
The blues scale adds the “blue notes” to a minor pentatonic: in C, that’s C, E♭, F, F♯ (the ♭5), G and B♭. The ♭3 and ♭7 sung over major chords give blues and jazz their bite. Slide into them, and bend them slightly sharp.



Practice: sing the scale over a 12-bar blues in C with the Backing Track, then improvise a two-bar phrase using only C, E♭, F and G.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Singing the changes: arpeggios
Improvisers outline the chords as they go by. Sing each chord’s tones from the root up: 1, 3, 5, 7. Here is a ii–V–I in C, the most common progression in jazz.



Then sing them going down, from the 7th of each chord, and you’ll see how the notes join up.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
section: Guide tones: the line inside the changes
text:
Guide tones: the line inside the changes
The 3rd and 7th of each chord are its guide tones. Sung in a row they make a smooth line that moves by a half step or not at all, and it outlines the harmony with only two notes per chord. Guide tones covers the idea in depth.



Practice: sing the guide tones while the Backing Track plays a ii–V–I. Then add one passing note between each pair.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Back-phrasing a ballad
On a ballad, jazz singers float the words over the beat. They start a phrase late and then catch up, stretch one word, and rush the next. This is back-phrasing. The band keeps strict time; the singer’s line is free on top of it.
Here is a phrase written plainly, then back-phrased, with each entry a beat or more late and some notes pulled together.






(The words are a stand-in to sing on, not a real tune.)
Practice: sing a ballad you know with a slow backing track. Say the words in rhythm first, as speech, then sing them with the same freedom.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Trading fours
In a jam the soloists trade fours: each takes four bars in turn, often answering what the last one played. Practise call and response: play the call, then sing a four-bar answer that starts with the same rhythm and ends somewhere new.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes
text:
Where to go next

Pop singing: mix, belt and runs.
Classical singing: breath, pure vowels and legato.
Improvising on a blues: the same ideas for any instrument.
crumbs: Jazz Singing: Swing, Scat and the Changes

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
A cadence is how a phrase ends. Every ending has a different feel, and the feel comes from the two chords that make it. This lesson plays the five you will meet most, each as a four-bar phrase, and then asks a harder question about one of them: is it a cadence at all?
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
text:
1. The authentic cadence: V7 to I
C, F, G7, C. The strongest ending there is. G7 contains the leading tone B and the note F, which are a tritone apart. Both are unstable: B wants to rise a half step to C and F wants to fall a half step to E. The tonic chord that follows is where they land. The bass falls a fifth, and everything leans the same way.



Learn this one first. Every other ending on the page is compared with it.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 2. The half cadence: ending on V
text:
2. The half cadence: ending on V
C, F, C, G. The phrase stops on the dominant, with the tension still in the air. It is a comma, not a full stop: the ear expects an answer, and the next phrase usually supplies it.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
text:
3. The deceptive cadence: V7 to vi
C, F, G7, Am. Everything points at C, and then the last chord is Am, which shares two notes with C (C and E). The leading tone still rises to C, but the chord on top of it is Am. The listener expects a full stop and gets a surprise.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
section: 4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
text:
4. The plagal cadence, and why it is the fake one
C, Am, F, C. IV to I, the “Amen”. Most books call this a cadence. This lesson does not, and here is the argument.

A cadence is made by the dominant. What ends a phrase in tonal music is the leading tone rising to the tonic and the tritone of V7 resolving inward. IV to I has neither. No note in F is pulled toward C, so nothing is resolved.
IV is a neighbour of I. I, IV, I leaves home and comes back, exactly as I, vi, I does. That is a prolongation of the tonic chord, not an arrival.
It comes after the real cadence. The “Amen” at the end of a hymn follows a V to I that has already closed the phrase. The plagal is tacked on afterwards, so it cannot be what made the ending.
Some theorists agree. William Caplin’s Classical Form counts only authentic and half cadences, and does not count IV to I as a cadence.




Here is the “Amen” in its usual place: an authentic cadence first, then the plagal after it. Listen to bars 1 and 2, which end the phrase, and then to bars 3 and 4, which only soften it.



There is a fair reply. In the blues, in gospel and in much rock, IV to I really is how a tune ends, because those styles never relied on a leading tone. So whether “fake” means “not a cadence” or “a different kind of ending” depends on the style. In the classical tradition the first reading is the one with the support.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
5. The backdoor: ♭VII to I
C, F, B♭, C. The chord on the flat seventh is B♭, and it falls a whole step to C. There is no leading tone here either. The ending sounds relaxed, a door left open instead of shut. Compare it with the plagal ending: both arrive without a dominant.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Build your own
Choose how the phrase opens and how it ends, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the plain authentic ending.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Test your ear
Two questions. The first asks which ending the band played. The second plays one of three endings and asks how the last chord feels, so you can decide for yourself whether the plagal is a cadence.
crumbs: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not

title: Lesson: Cadences, and the One That Is Not
text:
Where to go next

Play the five endings in a row at the same tempo and note which ones you could end a song on.
Take any of the phrases to Tools → Backing Track (Copy as ABC, then paste into Edit the changes (ABC)) to choose the bass line and drums.
The lesson on borrowed chords starts from the ♭VII to I ending.

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
This is the 12-bar blues from the drum chair, starting with nothing but the beat. You need to be able to hit the ride cymbal (or hi-hat), the snare and the bass drum, and to work the hi-hat pedal. For what the chords are and how the form gets varied, see Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues.
How to use the page. Every step has two bars of the beat written large, a chord chart, and the whole chorus written on a drum staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up on the chart. Tick Drums alone to hear the drummer without the bass and piano, and Leave out the drums to take over. Each step starts in its own feel and tempo; the strip at the bottom changes both.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Reading a drum part
Each line or space of the staff is one part of the kit. Cymbals and anything struck on the rim are written with an ✕. What the hands play has stems up; what the feet play has stems down. Click a piece to hear it: the picture shows where each one is written, and the line under it has the same notes in the same places, so you can click those too. Hover over any drum note on this page and it tells you which piece it is.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
1. The beat and the form
A drummer has two jobs on a blues: keep the time, and know where in the twelve bars the band is. Start with the plainest time there is. The ride cymbal (or the closed hi-hat) plays all four beats. The left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4. Nothing else.



Count the bars out loud while you play: four bars, then four more, then the last four. The chords change at bar 5, bar 7 and bar 9. Listen for the bass moving and learn to hear those moments coming.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
2. The ride pattern
Swing time on the ride cymbal is the four beats plus a skip note just before beats 3 and 1: ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a. It is written as two eighth notes, but the first is long and the second short, as if the beat were divided in three and you played the first and last parts. Keep the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.



Listen with Drums alone to hear how late the skip note sits. Slow the tempo down and it gets later still.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
3. Swing time
Now the other two limbs. In swing the bass drum is played very quietly on all four beats, felt more than heard (feathering), and it is not written. The snare does not keep time: it answers the band with a note here and there, often on the last part of a beat. The band’s drummer improvises this, so the notation changes every chorus.



Start with the ride pattern and the hi-hat foot. Add one snare note per bar, on the “a” of beat 4, and leave it at that until it is comfortable.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
4. Showing the form
A fill tells the band where it is. On a blues the places to mark are the ends of the three four-bar phrases: bar 4, which leads to the IV chord; bar 8, which leads to the last line; and bar 12, which leads back to the top. The small ones need only a beat or two. The one in bar 12 can be bigger, and the crash on beat 1 of the next chorus is its landing.



Keep the time going right up to the fill and come out of it on beat 1. A fill that loses the beat is worse than no fill.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
5. The shuffle
The beat of Chicago blues. The cymbal plays the swung eighths all the way through, long, short, long, short, with the bass drum on 1 and 3 and a full snare on 2 and 4. This is the first beat on this page with a backbeat.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
6. The slow blues in 12/8
At a slow tempo every beat divides in three, and the cymbal plays all three parts. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. It is written here in 4/4 with triplets; the same beat is often written in 12/8.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
7. Straight eighths
Not every blues swings. In a boogaloo or a rock blues the eighth notes are even. The cymbal plays eight to the bar, the bass drum is on 1 and 3, and the left hand plays a cross-stick on 2 and 4.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
8. Grabbing the crash
A crash cymbal rings for a long time. Sometimes you want the accent without the ring: hit the crash, then catch its edge with the other hand straight away, so that it stops. Drummers call this a choke. It is written as a short crash with choke over it.
Here the band plays the straight-eighths beat from step 7 with a small fill at the end of bars 4 and 8, and the crash is grabbed on beat 1 of bar 5 and bar 9, the first bar of the second and third lines. Hit the crash together with the bass drum, and have the hand on the cymbal before beat 2. Then go straight back to the time. When the band stops at the end, the last crash is grabbed too.



Try it with the loop on and listen to the gap the choke leaves. A grabbed crash says “here” louder than a ringing one, because of the silence after it.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
section: 9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
text:
9. A tune: Blues in the Closet
Oscar Pettiford’s riff blues, at a medium swing. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times, and each time it ends on a long note, in bars 4, 8 and 12. Those are the same three places step 4 marked with fills. The tune leaves the space; the drummer fills it and sets up the next phrase.



Play time through the riff and stay out of its way: no snare on top of the melody’s accents. Read the melody while you play. A drummer who knows the tune plays the form without counting.
crumbs: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle

title: Blues for Drums: From Quarter Notes to the Shuffle
text:
Where to go next

Loop each step with the drums left out and play it for ten choruses without losing the form.
Play the fills step with your own fills in bars 4, 8 and 12.
Take a chorus from the changes lesson: the busier the chords, the more the band needs the form marked clearly.
Tools → Backing Track has every groove on this page, and many others, under any tune.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text: Beatmatched tracks can still clash: if one reaches its drop while the other is halfway through a breakdown, the mix sounds wrong even with the beats together. Dance music is built in phrases, and a good mix lines phrases up.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Counting

A beat is one kick in four-on-the-floor music. A bar is four beats.
A phrase is usually 8 bars (32 beats). Changes (a new sound, a fill, a breakdown) arrive on the first beat of a phrase, and often bigger changes every 16 or 32 bars.
Many tracks start with a 16- or 32-bar intro of mostly drums (made for DJs to mix in) and end with a matching outro.

Count bars on your fingers: 1 2 3 4, 2 2 3 4, 3 2 3 4, …, 8 2 3 4. A drum fill or a cymbal crash in bar 8 tells you the next phrase is coming.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
The rule
Start the incoming track on the first beat of a phrase of the playing track. Then their phrases line up: when the outgoing track changes, so does the incoming one, and the switch sounds planned. A common plan: incoming intro (16 bars) under the outgoing outro (16 bars), then the outgoing track is gone exactly as the incoming one’s main part starts.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Practise
The decks have 8-bar loops, so each loop is one phrase (the long tick on the waveform marks each bar; the overview shows the whole phrase).




Start A. Watch the overview: the playhead goes round once per phrase. Count the bars aloud.
Match B to A (B needs about +1.6 %; use the readout to check).
Set a cue on B at its start: with B stopped at 0:00, press CUE.
Start B exactly when A’s playhead returns to the start of its loop (bar 1 of a phrase). Bring B’s fader up over the next 8 bars.
Now start B on bar 3 of A’s phrase instead. Listen for the chord change in B arriving at a different moment from A’s. That’s what phrasing avoids.

title: DJ 3: Phrasing and Counting Bars
text:
Reading a track’s structure
DJs learn their records. In software you see it: the waveform’s dense parts are full sections, the thin parts are breakdowns. Mark the phrases you’ll mix at with hot cues (the first beat of the intro, the drop, the outro), and colour them so you know at a glance.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text: A sample almost never arrives at the tempo and key of your track. There are two ways to change it.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Repitch: speed and pitch together
Play a record faster and it gets higher; slower and it gets lower. That is repitching. A turntable’s pitch fader does it, and so do the classic samplers (the E-mu SP-1200, the Akai MPC60, the SP-404’s pitch knob).

Twice as fast = one octave up (12 semitones). Half speed = an octave down.
One semitone is a speed change of about 5.95 % (the twelfth root of two is 1.0595).
So a turntable’s ±8 % pitch range is about ±1.3 semitones; ±16 % about ±2.6.

Repitching keeps transients sharp and sounds natural, because nothing is invented: it is the same sound, faster or slower. Pitching soul vocals up gave the “chipmunk soul” sound of early-2000s hip-hop; slowing whole songs down is the Houston “chopped and screwed” style.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Time-stretch: apart
Time-stretching changes the length without changing the pitch (and pitch-shifting the pitch without the length). The computer cuts the sound into tiny overlapping grains and spaces them further apart or closer together. Done simply, you hear it: drums smear, a “phasey” or metallic sound appears. Modern algorithms (Ableton Live’s Warp modes, élastique in many DAWs, DJ software’s key lock) hide it much better, but stretch anything far enough and it shows.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
text:
Hear the difference




Pick pad 1 (a chord). Set Pitch to +5 in Repitch mode. Shorter and higher, like a sped-up record.
Change Mode to Stretch. The same +5 semitones, but the chord keeps its length.
Leave pitch at 0 and set Length to ×2 in each mode. Repitch: an octave down and twice as long. Stretch: same pitch, twice as long, and listen to the attack: blurred. This sampler uses plain overlap-add on purpose, so the smear is easy to hear.
Load the Funky Break, slice At the hits, and stretch a snare to ×1.5 in each mode. Which would you put in a track?

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
section: Matching a sample to your track
text:
Matching a sample to your track
The arithmetic: the speed you need is your tempo ÷ the sample’s tempo. A 90 BPM break in a 100 BPM track: 100 ÷ 90 = 1.111, so 11.1 % faster, which repitched is about +1.8 semitones. If the key matters, choose:

Repitch to the nearest key and adjust the track’s tempo to fit (producers often build the track at the sample’s speed), or
Stretch to the exact tempo and pitch-shift separately, accepting some artefacts.

title: Sampling 3: Pitch and Time-Stretch
section: The DJ’s version: pitch fader and key lock
text:
The DJ’s version: pitch fader and key lock
On a turntable the pitch fader is repitch. Below, push deck A’s fader to +8 %: BPM and key both move; the readout shows the shift in semitones. DJ software and CDJs add key lock (Master Tempo on Pioneer gear): tempo changes, pitch stays, by time-stretching.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
A filter turns some frequencies down and lets others through. It is the most-used control on a synthesizer and on a mixing desk: the treble and bass knobs on a stereo, the “wah” in a wah-wah pedal and the “wow” in a synth bass are all filters.
How to use the page. Press ▶. The Source menu picks what goes into the filter: noise shows the filter’s shape most clearly; the riff and chords show what it does to music; Your keyboard plays the keys or MIDI; Microphone filters your own voice (wear headphones). The red line on the spectrum is the filter’s response: above the middle line it boosts, below it cuts. Bypass switches the filter out so you can compare.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Low-pass and high-pass



A low-pass filter lets the lows through and cuts the highs. The frequency where it starts cutting is the cutoff. Drag Cutoff down slowly with noise playing: the hiss becomes a rush and then a rumble. Switch the source to the synth riff and do the same: the sound goes from bright to muffled, as if behind a wall.
A high-pass does the opposite: it removes the lows. That’s how a sound is made thin, like a telephone or a small radio, and how mixing engineers clear rumble out of everything except the bass and kick drum.
The slope is how fast the filter cuts beyond the cutoff: 12 dB per octave is gentle, 24 dB per octave is the steep, classic “Moog” low-pass.

Why low-pass sounds “darker”. From the harmonic series lesson: brightness is the strength of the high harmonics. A low-pass removes those harmonics, starting from the top. On a sawtooth (all harmonics) you can hear them go one by one as the cutoff passes them.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Resonance
Resonance (or Q) boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff. With the riff playing and the cutoff around 800 Hz, turn Resonance up to 10 or more. A whistling peak appears on the red line and you can hear it ring. Now press Sweep: the cutoff moves up and down by itself, and the resonant peak sweeps through the harmonics. That’s the classic synth “wow”, and with a guitar it’s a wah pedal.
At very high resonance the filter rings at the cutoff frequency on its own, almost like a sine wave. Some synths let the filter self-oscillate and play it as an extra oscillator.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Band-pass, notch and EQ




Band-pass keeps a band around the cutoff and cuts both sides. Higher Q, narrower band. It’s the sound of a telephone or a megaphone, and it’s how a vocoder splits a voice into bands (Sound 22).
Notch is the opposite: it removes a narrow band and leaves everything else. Engineers use it to remove a hum. A phaser is several moving notches.
Peak (bell), low shelf and high shelf are the filters of an equaliser (EQ). They boost or cut (the Boost/cut slider) instead of removing. A shelf lifts or lowers everything above or below the cutoff, like the treble and bass knobs. A bell lifts or lowers a band in the middle.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Filters on your voice
Choose Microphone as the source (with headphones on), choose Band-pass and sweep the cutoff while you talk. The vowels in speech are themselves made by filters: your mouth and throat are resonant tubes, and moving your tongue and lips moves their resonances (the formants). Say “ee-ah-oo” slowly and watch the bumps in the spectrum move.

title: Sound 4: Filters
text:
Next

Sound 5: Envelopes

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
An LFO, or low-frequency oscillator, is an oscillator too slow to hear as a pitch, typically between a tenth of a beat and twenty times a second. Instead of being listened to, it moves a control: the pitch, the volume, a filter, the stereo position. Almost every effect that “moves” (vibrato, tremolo, wah, chorus, phaser, PWM) is an LFO turning a knob for you.
How to use the page. Press ▶ or play the keys. The strip above the scope draws the LFO itself over the last two seconds; the red dot is where it is now.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
What an LFO can move



Leave the shape on Sine and try each target with Rate about 5 Hz:

Pitch gives vibrato: the note bends slightly sharp and flat. Singers and string players use 5 to 7 cycles a second. Too deep and it sounds seasick; too fast and it sounds nervous.
Volume gives tremolo: the note gets louder and softer. The “tremolo” on a guitar amp is this, and so is a vibraphone with its motor on.
Filter cutoff gives an automatic wah. Slow it right down (0.2 Hz) for a slowly opening and closing sound; speed it up for a “wobble” bass.
Pan moves the sound between your left and right ear (auto-pan). Use headphones.

Depth is how far the LFO moves the control, and Rate is how fast. Those two plus the shape are all an LFO has.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
Shapes

Sine and triangle: smooth back-and-forth.
Square: jumps between two values. On pitch it’s a trill; on volume, a chopped “gate”.
Sawtooth (ramp): rises slowly, then drops. On pitch it sounds like a siren.
Random (sample & hold): jumps to a new random value every cycle. On the filter it’s the bubbling “computer” sound of 1970s science fiction.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
section: When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
text:
When an LFO gets fast enough to hear
Set the target to Volume, the shape to Sine and slowly push the rate past 20 Hz. The tremolo stops sounding like a pulse and becomes a rough, buzzy tone, and new pitches appear on the spectrum on both sides of the note. That is amplitude modulation. Do the same with Pitch and past about 30 Hz the vibrato becomes a metallic, bell-like timbre: that is frequency modulation, the subject of Sound 8. An LFO and an audible oscillator are the same thing at different speeds.

title: Sound 6: LFOs
text:
LFOs elsewhere on these pages

The PWM in Sound 2 is an LFO on the pulse width.
Chorus (Sound 18) is an LFO on a very short delay.
A phaser (Sound 19) is an LFO sweeping a chain of filters.
The Leslie speaker in the organ lesson is a mechanical LFO: a spinning horn moves pitch, volume and direction all at once.

title: Sound 6: LFOs

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text: Some effects change the pitch of a sound while it plays: an octave below to fatten a bass, a harmony above a voice, or a nudge to put a singer exactly in tune. All of them start from the same trick.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
section: How to change pitch without changing speed
text:
How to change pitch without changing speed
Play a tape faster and it gets higher, but it also gets shorter. A pitch shifter wants the pitch without the speed. It reads the sound through a short delay whose time keeps changing: a delay that keeps getting shorter plays the sound back faster (higher), one that keeps getting longer plays it slower (lower). That’s the Doppler effect again. Of course a delay can’t keep shrinking forever, so every few hundredths of a second it jumps back and starts again, and a second delay line, half a step behind, crossfades over the jump. Listen closely to big shifts and you can hear a faint flutter from the jumps: that’s the price.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
The octaver



The octaver adds the same notes an octave (or two) below, or above. Bass players use the octave down to sound like a synth bass; guitarists use the octave up to sound like a twelve-string.
Octave up made by: there’s an old analog trick. Fold the bottom half of the wave up so it’s all positive (a rectifier), and the wave now repeats twice as often: an octave up. It’s rough and buzzy, and it only works cleanly on one note at a time: Octave fuzz is the Jimi Hendrix “Purple Haze” solo sound. Switch between the two kinds and compare. Play the Chords through each: the digital shifter copes; the analog trick turns chords to mush.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
The harmonizer



A harmonizer adds one or two more voices at set intervals, so one singer becomes a trio.

Fixed intervals: always the same distance, say a major third and a fifth. Sing a scale and listen: some of the harmonies are out of the key, because the thirds in a major key are not all the same size.
In the key of C major: the harmonizer works out which note you’re singing and picks the third or fifth in the key, sometimes major, sometimes minor. This is how the “intelligent” harmonizers (Eventide, TC-Helicon, the ones built into vocal pedals) work. Try your Microphone and sing a C major scale slowly.

title: Sound 21: Pitch Effects
text:
Pitch correction (auto-tune)



The source is an out-of-tune singer: every note lands 20 to 50 cents sharp or flat. The graph shows the pitch as sung (grey) and after correction (pink), against the notes of the scale.

Key and Scale: which notes are “right”. Every sung note is pulled to the nearest one.
Retune speed: how quickly. At around 100 ms the correction is gentle: the slides and the vibrato survive, and you mostly can’t tell. This is what happens, invisibly, on most pop vocals today.
At 1 ms the pitch jumps instantly from note to note, with no slide at all. It sounds robotic, and that became a style of its own: Cher’s “Believe” (1998), T-Pain, Kanye West’s 808s & Heartbreak, much of trap and Afrobeats.
Wrong key: correct to the wrong scale and the singer is snapped confidently onto wrong notes.

Antares Auto-Tune came out in 1997, invented by an engineer who had used the same mathematics to look for oil underground. Try your own voice, on Hard and Natural.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text: Beatmatching is making two tracks play at the same tempo with their beats together, so you can blend them without a clatter. DJ software has a SYNC button for this; learn it by ear anyway. Sync needs a correct beatgrid and fails on live drummers, old records and tempo changes, and hearing two beats drift apart is the skill under every other one.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Two problems, two controls

Tempo (are they going at the same speed?): the pitch fader. A track at 120 BPM against one at 124 needs +3.3 % (124 ÷ 120 = 1.033).
Phase (are the beats on top of each other?): a nudge. Push the side of the platter, or the jog wheel, to speed it a moment (or hold it back) until the kicks line up.

Get the tempo close first; otherwise the beats line up for a moment and drift apart again.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
The routine

Deck A plays out loud. Cue deck B in the headphones (here: CUE on B, then Listen: phones).
Start B on a downbeat of A (the “1” of a bar): on a turntable, hold the record, let it go exactly on A’s kick.
Listen: do the kicks flam (two hits close together, “ka-tunk”)? Which is first?

If B’s kick comes before A’s, B is ahead: hold it back (drag the rim backwards, or the ‹ button) and, if it keeps getting ahead, pull B’s pitch slower.
If after, push it forward and make B faster.

Make small pitch corrections (0.1–0.3 %) and keep listening for a minute. When the beats stay together, the tempo is right.

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Practise
Deck A: Warehouse at 124 BPM. Deck B: Late Bus at 120. The Match line below the decks shows the tempo difference, and once both play, how far apart the beats are. Cover it with your hand (or a sticky note) once you’ve got the idea.




Start A. Press CUE on B and set Listen: phones, with the phones knob in the middle: you hear both.
Set B’s pitch fader to about +3.3 % (the shown number can be typed into: click it). Read B’s BPM: about 124.0.
Start B on one of A’s kicks. Hear the flam? Nudge with ‹ › (hold) until the kicks hit as one.
Now the hard way: reset B’s pitch to 0, start both, and find the tempo by ear: B’s kicks will drift behind A’s, slowly at first. Each time, push the fader a little faster and nudge back into place.
Swap: let B be the one playing out, and match A to it at 120 (pitch about −3.2 %).

title: DJ 2: Beatmatching by Ear
text:
Tips

Listen to the kick and the hats, not the melody. On a fast flam, the hats are easier to hear than the kick.
Count. If they drift apart within one bar, the tempo is far off; within 8 bars, close; staying together over 32 bars, done.
Tap: tap the TAP button on the beat to measure a track’s tempo when you don’t know it (records don’t print it).
A track’s tempo is a number you can read off a deck or software, but on a record you’re often matching by ear: that is the skill.

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Four chords, C, Am, F and G, are under more pop songs than any other progression: I, vi, IV, V. It can sound plain, and it can sound rich, depending on what the players do to it. Almost every move is one of four: add a note to each chord, walk the bass between chords, approach a chord with its own dominant, or split a bar into a two-five. This lesson adds those moves one at a time, on the same four bars. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four choruses after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. (The numerals only name the chord’s root, so a III7 in bar 1 is the dominant of Am, and a vii7 before it is its two.)
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
1. The basic changes
One bar each of I, vi, IV and V. Plain major and minor triads. The bass moves down a minor third, then down a third, then up a step, and the G at the end pulls back to the C.



Learn this version first. Every other version on the page is this one with something added, so you should be able to hear the plain one underneath.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
2. Add extensions
Extensions are notes added on top of the triad without changing what the chord is. Cadd9 adds a D. Am7 adds a G, and Fadd9 adds a G. Gsus2 takes out the B and puts in an A, so the chord has no third: it is neither major nor minor. It sounds suspended, and the ordinary G that follows it, or the C it leads to, feels like the answer.



Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ. Listen to bar 4: the leading tone B, which is what pulls G to C, is not there.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
3. Add passing chords
Two bars are split in half, so that the bass can walk instead of jump.

Bar 1: C, G/B. The bass steps down C, B and arrives on A in bar 2. The G/B is a G chord with its third in the bass.
Bar 2: Am, C/G. The bass keeps stepping down, A then G, to land on F in bar 3.
Bar 3: F, F♯dim. Now the bass goes up, F, F♯, and arrives on G in bar 4. The F♯dim is built from F♯, A and C, three of the four notes of D7, so it pulls up to G.




Listen to the bass. There is no jump anywhere in the line: every note is one step from the last. A slash chord such as C/G is the C chord with G as its lowest note.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
4. Secondary dominants
A dominant seventh chord pulls to the chord a fifth below it. The home key has one, G7, which pulls to C. A secondary dominant is the dominant of some other chord of the key, played just before that chord, so that chord gets to sound like home for a moment.

E7 goes to Am. It has a G♯, which is not in the key of C.
C7 goes to F. It has a B♭, which is not in the key of C either.
D7 goes to G. It has an F♯.
G7 goes to C: the usual dominant, now with its seventh.




Each bar now has a note from outside the key, and each of them leads by half step into the next bar’s chord (G♯ to A, B♭ to A, F♯ to G). That is why the progression sounds like it is travelling.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
5. ii-V-Is
A dominant can have a chord in front of it, the ii chord, a fifth above, so that the approach itself is a progression: ii, V, then I. Here each secondary dominant gets its own two.

Bar 1 keeps C for two beats, then Bm7 E7, a two-five into Am.
Bar 2 keeps Am for two beats, then Gm7 C7, a two-five into F.
Bar 3 is Fmaj7 for two beats, then Am7 D7, a two-five into G.
Bar 4 stays on G7.




Strictly, the two-five into a minor chord uses a half-diminished ii (Bm7♭5), but plain Bm7 is the common way to write it in pop and the band plays it as written. Compare the last chord of each of the first three bars with section 4: it is the same dominant, with a two in front.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Build your own chorus
Choose one option for each bar and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try a plain first bar with a busy last bar, or the reverse.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Test your ear
The band plays the plain four bars with one bar changed. The question tells you which bar to listen to. Pick what you heard.
crumbs: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

title: Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G
text:
Where to go next

Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and play or sing over each version in turn. The bars with new chords are the ones that ask for new notes.
Take a chorus you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove.
Learn each version in the keys you play most: C, G, D and A for guitar and voice.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
A great many songs are one loop of four chords, played round and round while the melody, the words and the arrangement change on top. The loops are not very different from each other: they are the same handful of chords (I, ii, IV, V, vi, and a few borrowed from the minor) in a different order, or with one of them swapped. This lesson goes through the loops one at a time. Each has the chords, the same four bars on a grand staff (block chords in the treble, the bass note below) and the site’s backing band, which plays it round and round so that you hear it as a loop.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four times round after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key: C G Am F in the key of C is the same loop as D A Bm G in the key of D. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the first loop.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
text:
1. The axis loop: I V vi IV
C, G, Am, F. The loop that is under Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry and the verse of Don’t Stop Believin’, among a great many others. The bass drops from C to G, rises a step to A and falls a third to F. Three major chords and one minor: the minor chord keeps it from sounding simply happy.



Play it until you can hum the bass note of each bar. Every other loop is compared with this one.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
text:
2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V
Am, F, C, G. The four chords are the same; the loop starts on the minor chord, so that it sounds like a minor song, and the major chord C arrives in the middle. Zombie by the Cranberries is this loop (in E minor), and so is the chorus of Despacito.



Compare the two charts: there is no new chord. Where a loop starts is what the ear takes for home. The other two starting points are IV I V vi (F, C, G, Am) and V vi IV I (G, Am, F, C).

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
text:
3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V
C, Am, F, G. The doo-wop loop. It has the chords of the axis loop, but with the minor chord second, so the bass steps down by thirds: C, A, F, and then the G climbs to C again. Stand by Me is built on it. Listen to bar 4: the V chord is the last bar and it leads straight back to C.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
text:
4. The turnaround: I vi ii V
C, Am, Dm, G. Replace the IV with its relative minor, ii. The bass now moves round the circle of fifths: C, A, D, G, and back to C. This is the turnaround of jazz, and the A section of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (the “rhythm changes”) begins this way. Put a seventh on each chord and it is the sound of a standard.



Bar 3 is the only difference from the fifties loop. The ii chord and the IV chord share two of their three notes (F and A), so one can stand in for the other.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 5. Out and back: I IV V IV
text:
5. Out and back: I IV V IV
C, F, G, F. The loop of Louie Louie and Wild Thing. There is no minor chord and no change of direction; the loop goes up to the dominant and back down by the same step. Because the bar-4 chord is IV, not I, it does not feel finished, and the loop goes round again and again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
section: 6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
text:
6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I
C, B♭, F, C. B♭ is not in the key of C. It is the chord on the flat seventh, borrowed from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat seventh) and the note that the blues calls the flat seven. Sweet Home Alabama goes I, ♭VII, IV this way. In C the bass goes down a step, then down a fourth, then down a fourth again.

title: Lesson: Four-Chord Loops
text:
7. The minor loops
Two loops in the minor, written here in C minor (three flats in the signature).

i ♭VII ♭VI V: Cm, B♭, A♭, G. The Andalusian loop. The bass falls by step, C, B♭, A♭, G, and the last chord is a major V, with the leading tone B, so that it pulls hard back to Cm. Hit the Road Jack is this loop.
i ♭VI ♭III ♭VII: Cm, A♭, E♭, B♭. The four chords of the axis loop in E♭ major, started on the vi chord: loop 2 in its minor key. It is the sound of much current pop.







Play the two minor loops and then loop 2. The notes are different, but the shape, down by steps then up by a third, is the same.

Build your own loop
Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the loops above, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. The numeral next to each chord is its place in the key of C.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text: To flip a sample is to make something new from it, so the listener hears your song, not the record you took it from. A loop of someone’s chorus with drums under it is not a flip. A chord chopped, re-pitched and played in a new order, under a new melody, is.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text:
The flipper’s moves

Reorder: play the chops in a sequence the original never had. Four chords become a new progression.
Re-pitch: move chops up or down until they make a new harmony (a minor chord pitched up 3 semitones sits on a new root).
Reverse: backwards attacks swell instead of hitting; reversed cymbals and vocals are a classic transition.
Filter: a low-pass filter removes the old record’s drums and top end and keeps the warm middle, so new drums fit on top.
Change the time: half-time (half the speed) or a different tempo turns a ballad into a club track, and the reverse.
Layer: add your own bass, drums and parts so the sample becomes one voice among several.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
text:
Flip it



The soul loop has one chord a beat in the first slices. A plan, one step at a time:

Play pads 1, 5, 9, 13 (the first beat of each bar): the original progression.
Re-pitch pad 9 by −2 and pad 13 by +3 (select a pad, then Pitch). Play 1, 5, 9, 13 again: a new progression from the same sound.
Reverse pad 16 (Reverse) and use it as a swell into bar 1.
Record a two-bar pattern with these pads (● Rec), with Quantize 1/8.
Then load the Funky Break on the next sampler and record drums at the same tempo (84) over a click. Two machines, one song.

title: Sampling 5: Flipping a Sample
section: The DJ’s flips: edits, acapellas, mashups
text:
The DJ’s flips: edits, acapellas, mashups
DJs flip whole songs, live or before the gig:

An edit (or re-edit) rearranges a song for the dance floor: a longer intro with just drums for mixing in, the best section repeated, the slow bridge cut. Disco DJs made them on tape with a razor blade; now they are made in a DAW.
An acapella is a vocal on its own; an instrumental is the song without it. Play one over another track and you have a mashup or a live remix. Matching key matters more here than anywhere: see DJ 6.
Stems: DJ software can now split a song into vocals, drums, bass and the rest as it plays, so any song becomes an acapella.

Try a live mashup: deck A has a house groove, deck B a vocal phrase in the same key and tempo. Start A, then start B on a downbeat; bring B’s channel up and cut A’s Mid EQ a little so the voice sits on top.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
Distortion changes the shape of a wave by squashing its loudest parts. A changed shape means a changed recipe of harmonics (Sound 1), so distortion adds harmonics that weren’t there. A little gives warmth; a lot gives the roar of a rock guitar.
How to use the page. Every effect on these pages has a Source menu (what goes in), a Mix (how much of the effect you hear), and Bypass to switch it out and back in. The square graph is the distortion curve: the input level runs across, the output level up. The dashed diagonal is “no change”.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
section: A sine wave in, harmonics out
text:
A sine wave in, harmonics out



The source starts as a pure sine tone: one spike on the spectrum. Raise Drive slowly.

The curve bends over at the ends: loud parts of the wave can’t get any louder.
The scope shows the sine’s peaks being flattened toward a square.
New spikes appear on the spectrum at 3, 5, 7… times the frequency: odd harmonics, because the top and bottom of the wave are squashed the same way. That’s the square-wave recipe.

Now try the other curves:








Curve
What it does
Sound




Soft clip
bends over gradually
overdrive: a warm, singing tone, like a valve amp turned up


Hard clip
flat-tops the wave at a fixed level
fuzz: buzzy and aggressive


Uneven (tube-like)
squashes the top and bottom differently
adds even harmonics (2, 4, 6) too, which sound sweeter and fuller


Wavefolder
folds the peaks back down instead of flattening them
the West-coast synth sound: glassy, metallic, changes wildly with drive


Bit crusher
rounds the wave to a few steps
the gritty sound of old computers and samplers



Tone is a low-pass after the distortion: almost every guitar amp has one, to tame the fizz that heavy distortion adds at the top.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
Overdrive, distortion or fuzz?
Guitarists use three words, and the pedals really are different. All three clip the wave; they differ in how hard they clip, what shape the clipping is, and what they do to the sound before and after.



Play the synth riff and step through the presets, with Bypass to compare with the clean sound. Watch the curve and the scope.










Overdrive
Distortion
Fuzz




Curve
soft clip: bends over gently
hard clip: flat tops
lopsided: one side clips much sooner, and a dead zone in the middle


Drive
low: clean when you play softly, gritty when you dig in
high: distorted however softly you play
extreme: nearly a square wave


Before
cuts the bass so the low notes don’t turn to mud (the “mid hump” of a Tube Screamer)
some bass cut
nothing: the full, fat low end goes in


After
a tone control
a darker tone control to tame the fizz
dark and woolly


Sound
a turned-up valve amp: warm, still sounds like the instrument
tight and aggressive: metal and hard rock
buzzy, spitting, raw: “Satisfaction”, Hendrix, the White Stripes


Inside
diodes in the op-amp’s feedback loop
diodes after the op-amp
two transistors pushed far past their limits



Two things to try:

On Overdrive, choose the Uneven riff source (loud and soft notes). The soft notes stay almost clean and the loud ones break up: overdrive responds to how hard you play. On Distortion every note is equally squashed.
On Fuzz, play a Sine tone and lower the Drive. The tone starts to sputter: quiet parts of the wave fall into the dead zone and vanish. Fuzz pedals with an old, dying battery do this on purpose, and the note cuts out raggedly as it fades.

title: Sound 12: Distortion
text:
On music
Switch the Source to Chords or the Synth riff. Distorting a chord sounds much messier than distorting one note: every note’s harmonics clash with the others’, and the curve also creates new frequencies at the differences between the notes (intermodulation). That’s why heavy rock guitar plays power chords (root and fifth only). The difference frequencies of a fifth are another octave of the root, so it stays clean.
Try your own voice or instrument through it with Microphone (and headphones).

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
The turnaround is a short chord pattern that sends a tune back to its beginning: I, vi, ii, V. Jazz players have been changing it for a century. This lesson starts with the plain one and adds the standard changes one at a time, and ends with the first four bars of I Got Rhythm.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
1. The plain turnaround
C, Am, Dm, G: I, vi, ii, V. The bass follows the circle of fifths: C, then A, D, G, and back to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
2. Sevenths
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Every chord gets its 7th. The 7th of one chord is often a step from the 3rd of the next, which is what makes the guide-tone line smooth (see the lesson on guide tones).

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
3. A dominant on the vi
Cmaj7, A7, Dm7, G7. Make the vi a dominant. A7 is the V of Dm7, and its C♯ pulls up to D.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
4. Start on the iii
Em7, A7, Dm7, G7. iii, VI, ii, V: the turnaround begun a step earlier. Em7 is a good stand-in for Cmaj7 (it has E, G and B, three of its four notes), and it makes a chain of fifths that is a link longer.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
5. Tritone substitution
Cmaj7, E♭7, Dm7, D♭7. Replace each dominant with the one a tritone away. A7 becomes E♭7 and G7 becomes D♭7. The bass line now falls by half step wherever a substitute is used: E♭ to D, D♭ to C.

title: Lesson: Turnarounds and Rhythm Changes
text:
6. Rhythm changes
C A7 | Dm7 G7 | Em7 A7 | Dm7 G7. The first four bars of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (in B♭ in the original, here in C). Two chords in every bar. Jazz players have written hundreds of tunes on these changes.

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A note played on a real instrument is never one frequency. It is a stack of frequencies, all at whole-number multiples of the lowest one. That stack is the harmonic series, and it explains why a violin and a flute playing the same A sound different, why the octave and the fifth sound “pure”, and how every synthesizer on the following pages works.
How to use the page. Every widget has a ▶ button, a picture of the wave’s shape (an oscilloscope) and a picture of its spectrum (how loud each frequency is, low on the left, high on the right). The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume. You can play the widgets from the computer keyboard (a w s e d f t g y h u j k is one octave, z and x move it), from the on-screen keyboard, or from a MIDI keyboard. Notes go to the widget you clicked last. Click a heading to fold a section away. Start with the volume low.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
A string vibrates in pieces
Pluck a string and it swings as a whole, but it also swings in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, all at once. Half the length vibrates twice as fast, a third of it three times as fast. If the whole string gives 100 Hz, the halves give 200 Hz, the thirds 300 Hz, and so on. The same happens in the air column of a trumpet or a clarinet, and in your voice.
Each of those frequencies is a harmonic. The first harmonic, the whole string, is the fundamental, and it’s the pitch you name. The others are overtones. You don’t hear them as separate notes. You hear them as the colour (the timbre) of the one note.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
The series, written out
Here are the first sixteen harmonics written as notes. The number under each note is the harmonic’s number: harmonic n vibrates n times as fast as the fundamental. The number above is how far the real harmonic is from the piano’s version of that note, in cents (100 cents = one half step). Choose a different fundamental and the whole series is transposed. The pattern of steps never changes.



Things to notice:

The octaves are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Doubling the frequency always gives an octave.
The gaps shrink as you go up. Octave, then a fifth (2 to 3), a fourth (3 to 4), a major third (4 to 5), a minor third (5 to 6), and then steps smaller than a minor third. The higher harmonics are close enough to make scales.
Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 are a major triad (C, E, G over a C fundamental). The major chord is built into every pitched sound.
Harmonic 7 is about a third of a half step flat of the piano’s B♭, harmonic 11 sits almost exactly between F and F♯, and harmonic 13 is well sharp of A♭. Press Harmonic, then tempered and listen at those three. Piano tuning (equal temperament) moves every note slightly so that all keys work. The pure intervals are the harmonics.
The 5th harmonic is 14 cents flat of the piano’s major third. Barbershop singers and string quartets lean their major thirds that way, toward the harmonic.

Press Build the tone to hear the harmonics enter one at a time, each a little quieter than the one before (harmonic n at strength 1/n). With all sixteen it no longer sounds like a chord. It sounds like one buzzy note: a sawtooth wave.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
section: Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
text:
Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves
The sine wave is the simplest sound there is: one frequency and nothing else. It sounds pure and a little dull, like a tuning fork or a whistle.
In 1807 Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating wave, whatever its shape, can be built by adding sine waves at whole-number multiples of its frequency. Each sine wave has its own strength (and it can be upside down). The recipe of strengths is the wave’s spectrum. Going from a wave to its recipe is the Fourier transform; going from the recipe back to the wave is Fourier synthesis.
You don’t need the maths to use the idea:

The shape of a wave (the oscilloscope) and its recipe (the spectrum) are two views of the same sound. Change one and the other changes.
Sharp corners and sudden jumps need lots of high harmonics. Smooth, rounded shapes need few. Bright sounds have strong high harmonics; dark, mellow sounds don’t.
The ear mostly hears the recipe, not the shape. Flip a harmonic upside down and the shape changes a lot while the sound hardly changes.

The spectrum display under every widget on these pages is a Fourier transform done about sixty times a second, by the browser.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
Build waves from harmonics
Each slider is one harmonic. Up is louder; below the middle line it is upside down. The numbers under the sliders play that harmonic alone. The drawing shows the harmonics faintly and their sum in bold. Press ▶ and move the sliders while it plays.



Try this:

Press Sine. One harmonic, one frequency. The spectrum shows a single spike.
Press Sawtooth: every harmonic, harmonic n at strength 1/n. Now turn Harmonics used down to 1 and slowly back up. Each added harmonic sharpens the ramp. With few harmonics the edge wobbles; the wobble (the Gibbs effect) gets narrower but never quite goes away.
Drag the slider for harmonic 2 to zero. The note now sounds hollow, a little like a clarinet.
Press Organ. Organ stops add harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and so on (see the organ lesson): the tonebars are an additive synthesizer.
crumbs: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier

title: Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier
text:
Square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse
These four shapes are the raw material of almost every synthesizer, because each has a simple, recognisable recipe.









Wave
Harmonics
Strength of harmonic n
Sound




Sine
1 only
—
Pure, flute-like, no edge


Sawtooth
all
1/n
Bright, buzzy, brassy and string-like


Square
odd only (1, 3, 5…)
1/n
Hollow, woody, clarinet-like


Triangle
odd only
1/n², alternating up and down
Soft, between sine and square


Pulse
depends on width
a pulse 1/k wide has no harmonics at multiples of k
Thin and nasal as it narrows



Press each preset above and compare the spectrum. A square is a pulse exactly half a cycle wide, so it’s missing every 2nd harmonic. Press Pulse 1/3 and harmonics 3, 6, 9 and 12 drop out. Pulse 25% loses 4, 8, 12 and 16. The next lesson makes the pulse width move, which is PWM.
The triangle’s harmonics fall away as 1/n², much faster than the square’s 1/n, which is why it sounds so much softer even though both have only odd harmonics.

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text: Ask ten drummers how to hold a stick and you’ll get several answers, and most of them are right. This lesson shows the common grips, why each exists, and then the other places where good kit players do things differently. Its aim is to tell a choice from a mistake: a choice suits a style or a body; a mistake causes pain or a choked sound in any style.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
What every grip shares

A fulcrum. The stick pivots at one point, held between the thumb and a finger (the first or middle finger). About a third of the way up from the butt end is a usual starting place; slide it until the stick bounces most freely off a pad.
Rebound. Let the stick come back up by itself. The hand guides it and doesn’t fight it. Gripping hard kills the rebound, dulls the sound and tires the forearm.
Back fingers loose. The other fingers wrap the stick lightly, never squeezing; there should be a little air between the palm and the stick.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Matched grip
Both hands hold the stick the same way, palm roughly down. Most kit players today use it. There are three named positions; they differ only in how far the hand is turned.









Grip
Palms
Moves mostly with
Good for




German
Flat, facing the floor; sticks about 90° apart
The wrist (up and down)
Volume, backbeats, big strokes


American
Turned about 45°
Wrist and fingers together
An all-round default, moving around the kit


French
Thumbs on top, palms facing each other
The fingers
Speed and finesse at low volume, cymbal work, jazz



Most players move between them in a single song: closer to German for a loud backbeat, closer to French for fast ride-cymbal patterns. Start with American.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Traditional grip
The left hand (for a right-handed player) holds the stick differently: it sits in the web between thumb and first finger, resting on the third finger, palm turned up; the hand turns like turning a doorknob. It comes from marching drums slung at an angle on a strap, where a matched left hand hit the tilted head awkwardly. It’s still common in jazz and drum corps for the light, controlled touch it gives the left hand, and many players simply like how it feels.
Choose traditional grip if you want it, not because a style requires it: plenty of jazz drummers play matched grip. It takes longer to learn, and the snare is usually tilted toward the player to suit it.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Stroke types
The grip matters less than the motion. Four strokes cover nearly everything:

Full stroke: start high, strike, let it rebound back to high. Loud notes in a row.
Down stroke: start high, strike, stop the stick low. An accent followed by a quiet note.
Tap: start low, strike, return low. Quiet notes.
Up stroke: start low, strike quietly, lift to high. A quiet note followed by an accent.

Moeller (after Sanford Moeller, a teacher of drum corps drummers) is a whipping motion of the forearm, wrist and stick that gets an accent and a tap or two out of one throw. Many drummers use something like it without the name.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Other places drummers differ



Choice
The options
What decides it




Which hand leads
Right-handed kit (hi-hat on the left, right hand crosses over to it), left-handed kit (a mirror image), or open-handed (right-handed kit, left hand plays the hi-hat, no crossing)
Comfort. Open-handed frees the right hand for the snare and toms; Billy Cobham and Simon Phillips play this way.


Leading foot
Bass drum on the right foot or the left
Usually the same side as the strong hand; a left-footed player often plays a left-handed kit.


Bass drum pedal
Heel up (on the ball of the foot, the leg does the work) or heel down (the ankle does it)
Heel up: power, rock. Heel down: control and quiet, jazz. Many players change in a song.


Burying the beater
Leave the beater against the head after a stroke, or let it bounce off
Buried: a short, punchy note. Off the head: a fuller, open note.


Hi-hat foot
Keep it closed, rock the foot heel-toe to keep time, or play it on 2 and 4
Style. Jazz drummers often play the foot on 2 and 4.


Throne height
Thighs level or sloping slightly down to the knee
Higher gives power; lower gives a stable seat. Too low hurts the hips and lower back.


Kit size
Four pieces (kick, snare, one rack tom, floor tom) up to large kits
The music and the room. Four or five pieces is enough for most styles.


Cymbal height and angle
Flat and low, or high and tilted
Reach without stretching; flat for jazz ride playing, angled so the stick hits with the side of the tip, not the edge with the shoulder of the stick (which cracks cymbals).


Sticks
7A (thin, light), 5A (the default), 5B and 2B (thick, heavy); wood or nylon tips
Volume and the hand. Nylon tips make a brighter cymbal sound.


Matched or traditional
See above
Taste.


Reading and counting
Read notation, count aloud, learn by ear
Most professionals do all three; the Drum Set page writes grooves in notation.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
section: Signs of a mistake, not a choice
text:
Signs of a mistake, not a choice

Pain in the wrist, forearm or lower back. Stop, rest, and look at your grip and throne height.
White knuckles, or the stick buzzing in a tight hand.
Hitting rim and cymbal edges with the shaft of the stick (chipped sticks, cracked cymbals).
Every stroke the same height: no accents and a flat sound.
Reaching or leaning to play anything you play often.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ
text:
Practice

On a practice pad, play 8 full strokes per hand at a slow tempo with a metronome. Watch that each stick comes back to the height it started at.
Play the same 8 strokes in German, then American, then French grip. Listen for the change in sound.
Accents: alternate a down stroke and three taps (R L L L, then L R R R), then put them in a groove.
Try one foot setting you don’t use: heel down if you play heel up, or the reverse.
crumbs: Stick Grips and Other Ways Drummers Differ

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
In a seventh chord the 3rd and the 7th say what the chord is. A line made of those notes, one for each chord, is called a guide-tone line, and it moves by step or by nothing at all. This lesson writes that line over four-chord loops, on a staff, so that you can hear what the chords are doing inside.
How to use the page. Press ▶ on a chart and the band plays it four times after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. Shaded bars are the ones that differ from the version named under the chart. Under each chart is a one-voice staff with the line, and the band’s piano plays the line over the chords.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
1. Just the 3rds
C, G, Am, F as plain triads, with the 3rd of each chord on the staff. The 3rd is the note that makes a chord major or minor. Listen to the line E, B, C, A: it is the loop with the chords taken away.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
2. Sevenths, and the 3rds again
Cmaj7, G7, Am7, Fmaj7. The same loop with a 7th on every chord. The 3rds are the same notes. The 7ths are new, and they are what the next step uses.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
3. Just the 7ths
The 7ths of those chords: B, F, G and E. The 7th of one chord is often the 3rd of the next, or a step from it: the B of Cmaj7 is the 3rd of G7, and the G of Am7 rises a step to the A that is the 3rd of Fmaj7.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
4. The guide-tone line
For each chord, take whichever of its 3rd and 7th is nearer the last note you played. The line now moves by a step or a skip, and it holds a note where it can.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
5. Over a two-five-one
Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. The most important use of the line. The F is the 3rd of Dm7 and the 7th of G7: it does not move at all. It then falls a half step to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7, which is the note that tells you the chord has changed to major.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
6. Over the turnaround
Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Four chords, and the line moves by half steps and whole steps through all of them. A bass player and a pianist who both play the guide tones will be in tune with each other without having said a word.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones
text:
Build your own
Choose a progression and what the staff shows: the chords, the 3rds, the 7ths or the guide-tone line. The band plays the line when the staff shows one.

title: Lesson: Guide Tones

Play each line on your instrument over the band, then try singing it.
The guitar and piano lessons on the blues use the same 3rd and 7th as their shell chords.
In turnarounds the line is the same, with a tritone substitution in the V.
