title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
A phaser sweeps a few notches up and down the spectrum, and the result is a soft, swirling “whoosh”. It’s the sound of the electric piano in a thousand 1970s records, and Eddie Van Halen’s guitar on the first Van Halen album.
How to use the page. The source starts as chords. The red line on the spectrum shows the notches moving. Turn Mix to 100% and the effect disappears (to the ear), which says something about how it works.

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text: The effect

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
How it works
A phaser passes the sound through a chain of all-pass filters. An all-pass filter is a strange kind of filter: it doesn’t change how loud any frequency is. It only delays some frequencies more than others, so it shifts their phase. On its own you can’t hear it.
But mix that phase-shifted copy back with the original, and wherever the copy has been shifted exactly half a cycle the two cancel. Those cancellations are the notches. The stages here are the browser’s all-pass filters, each of which makes one notch, so Stages = 4 gives four notches. (A guitar pedal uses simpler stages, and needs two of them per notch.) An LFO sweeps the all-pass filters up and down, and the notches sweep with them.
That’s why the wet sound alone (Mix at 100%) sounds plain. The notches only exist when the shifted copy meets the original. 50% gives the deepest notches.

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
The controls

Stages: more stages, more notches, a stronger effect. The MXR Phase 90 has two notches; 12 here is very dramatic.
Centre and Sweep: where the notches sit and how far up and down they move.
Rate: slow for a swirl, fast for a warble.
Width (Q): how sharp the phase change in each stage is, and so how narrow the notches are.
Feedback: feeds the output back to the input; the areas between the notches turn into resonant peaks and the effect becomes more vocal and whistling. (The red line doesn’t show the feedback.)

title: Sound 19: Phaser
text:
Phaser or flanger?
Both sweep notches. A flanger uses a short delay, which makes many evenly spaced notches, like the teeth of a comb, so it sounds metallic and jet-like. A phaser uses all-pass filters, which make a few notches that aren’t evenly spaced, so it sounds softer and more liquid. Switch the source to noise on both pages and compare the spectrum.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
For a Claude session asked to add a style (“add a samba”, “a second-line groove”, “a gospel 6/8”). Read this first, then the header comments of the files it names. NOTES.org beside this file is the history of the band and its open questions.


A style is a row in styles in catalog.js: a name, a group (the genre heading in the Style menu), and defaults that belong together.
{ id:"bossa", label:"Bossa nova", group:"Latin", genres:"Bossa nova, slow samba",
  feel:"straight", bass:"bossa", rhythm:"bossa", drums:"bossa", voicing:JAZZV,
  desc:"Root-and-fifth bass with pickups, a two-bar comping pattern and the bossa clave." }

bass, rhythm, drums are ids of entries in the bass, comp and drums lists of the same file. rhythm may be several joined by + (a blend).
voicing is { piano, guitar }: a voicing style id for each (PLAINV, STRUMV, JAZZV are ready-made).
Optional: sound ({ bass:"upright"|"electric", cymbal:"ride"|"hat"|"bell", piano, guitar, lead, kit }), where piano and guitar are sound ids from sounds.js (BandSounds.sounds("guitar") lists them: jazz, steel, nylon, clean and distorted electric), push (chords anticipate), full (the piano’s triads keep all three notes), bass and drums may each name several patterns joined by + (a blend: one of them per bar, planned four bars at a time by BandHarmony.blendOpts; shares in opts.bassMix / opts.grooveMix), calm (strike and hold the chords around cadences and in bars with more chords than usual: BandHarmony.calmAt; a chart marks phrase ends with "^phrase" and single bars with "^plain"), halfRhythm (comping rhythm ids, a+b: what the comping plays in bars of half time instead of its own rhythm), time ({ feel:"half", parts }), ext:true (unmarked extensions on offer). A style with no sound gets upright bass, ride, piano, jazz guitar.

A style made only of parts that already exist is one line in styles plus the fit lists (step 3). Most requests need at least one new part. Decide that first: listen in your head to what the bass, the chord instrument and the drums each play in that music, and check each against the existing entries before writing a new one.




Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Congas: PATTERNS in congas.js (see Congas below).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Write its pages. A style is taught as well as played:

Style Notes (history and listening): styles/<style id>.qmd, linked from the page by BandCatalog.article(id). Copy styles/swing.qmd: What it is, A little history, The band’s version (and what it leaves out), Listening, Sources. Add it to styles/index.qmd under its group, and end it with <script src="/apps/shared/lessons/sections.js?v=1"></script>.
Pattern lessons: every new bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove or conga part needs a PLAN entry (ladder, tips) in scripts/pattern-lessons.mjs, its style a STYLE chart, and any rhythm it shares a SAME group; then node scripts/pattern-lessons.mjs (it lists parts with no plan) and quarto render lessons/patterns.
A lesson when the style needs teaching beyond its patterns, or when two styles overlap (lessons/stride-boogie.qmd): .ar-demo examples from lessons/_arrange-kit.qmd, listed in lessons/index.qmd and the Lessons menu in _quarto.yml.
The pages that load a changed engine file include every lesson that has a band: bump ?v= in all of them (grep -rlE 'band/(bass|comp|catalog)\.js\?v=' --include='*.qmd' lessons tools) and render them.
Check: tests/band/lessons/patterns.cdp.js with PAGES= the new lessons (copy _site/lessons/patterns into tests/band/lead/site/lessons/).

Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.




The conga player (congas.js) is a part of its own beside bass, comping and drums: it has its own fader, staff and MIDI track, and any style may have it. Adding a pattern:

PATTERNS in congas.js: id: { bars: [...], three: [...], triplet: [...] }. bars is one or two 4/4 bars (a two-bar pattern follows the bar number); three is one bar of 3/4 and triplet one bar of 12/8, both optional. A bar is a list of rows [pos, drum, stroke, hand, vel]: drum is "c" (conga, the higher drum) or "t" (tumba); stroke is H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muffled, B bass; hand is "L" or "R". Positions are beats; 12/8 positions are thirds of a beat (x.333). A pattern with no bar for the meter plays the steady one, so it can stay short.
congas in catalog.js: { id, label, feel, group, tags, desc }; the desc says which stroke falls on which beat, with which hand.
FITS.congas: the style ids it belongs in (steady and none fit every style).
A style that should have them says congas:"id" on its row in styles. Left out, the style has none.
tests/band/congas/t_congas.js checks every pattern in every meter, and that the other players play the same notes with or without them.

Sounds: the congas are one sample set (congas in sounds.js) built from the soundfont’s three conga notes; a new stroke is a new piece name there, a trim, and its place in BandNotation.congaName and the GM table in midi.js.




The Style menu of the Backing Track page; ?style=id in its address.
A tune’s ABC: %%style bossa nova above the first P: line (the whole tune).
One section: %%style bossa nova on the line under its P: line, or "^style bossa nova" in a bar (from that bar to the next section; "^style none" ends it early). The form bar carries style, and BandCatalog.sectionOpts turns it into the options for those bars. Single parts can follow the name: %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two; drums funk; feel straight. The comping moves to the instrument the style is built around (sound.lead), if it has one. The page’s blend sliders and walk amount do not apply inside such a section. On the Backing Track page the Band menus change to a section’s settings as it starts, and a change made there stays with that section (opts.sectionOverrides, which the player puts before the section’s style).
A crash grabbed with the hand: "^choke" in a bar (the crash on its beat 1, stopped before beat 2), beside "^fill" and "^stop".
Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.





Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.
Write descriptions for a music teacher: beats and instruments, no code words.

Write the new parts, each in its own engine file. Copy the nearest existing pattern and read the comment block above the table you are adding to.

Bass line: LINES in bass.js (a fixed figure over the chord’s root, fifth, octave).
Comping rhythm: GRID in comp.js for a set pattern, FIG for a one-bar swing figure.
Drum groove: GROOVES in drums.js (bars for 4/4, threeBars for 3/4, triplet for 12/8 feels).
Congas: PATTERNS in congas.js (see Congas below).
Positions are beats from 0; x.5 is the off-beat eighth (swung by the player unless the event says straight:true). Velocities are 0..1 and the player scales them by the band’s intensity.
Use ctx.phrase.bar (0..3) to shape four-bar phrases and ctx.intensity for how hard the band is playing. phraseDyn, leanDyn and spread in comp.js are the shared dynamic shaping: use them rather than fixed velocities.
Every pattern must cope with 3/4 and with a bar holding two chords. The tests check both.

Describe each new part in catalog.js: an entry in bass, comp or drums with id, label, feel (swing, straight or any), group, tags and a desc that says what is played on which beats, in a musician’s words. The desc is shown on the page and on the Accompaniment Styles page.
Say where each part fits: add its id to FITS.bass, FITS.comp or FITS.drums with the style ids it belongs in (your new one, and any existing style it also suits). Locked, a menu lists only what fits the chosen style, so a part missing from FITS cannot be chosen. Add the new style id to the voicing lists it should offer (JAZZ, POP, PLAIN, or a VOICE row).
Add the style row to styles, in its group. The id is permanent: saved setups, links and song files name it. Never rename one.
Tests (plain node, run from the test’s own directory):

tests/band/pat/t_patterns.js runs every style and option against every meter. It has a want table of where chords must land for set patterns; add your rhythm there.
tests/band/pat/t_pop.js lists the style ids of some groups in order; update the list if you added to one.
tests/band/styles/t_sections.js, tests/band/fills/t_fills.js, tests/band/meter/t_change.js must still pass.

Publish it to the pages. In tools/_backing-track.qmd and tools/_accomp-styles.qmd, raise the ?v= number on every script you changed (browsers cache them). Then quarto render tools/backing-track.qmd and check that .gitignore did not change (Quarto appends to it). The lyrics site copies the engine: bash ~/Projects/carols/tools/build.sh.
Write its pages. A style is taught as well as played:

Style Notes (history and listening): styles/<style id>.qmd, linked from the page by BandCatalog.article(id). Copy styles/swing.qmd: What it is, A little history, The band’s version (and what it leaves out), Listening, Sources. Add it to styles/index.qmd under its group, and end it with <script src="/apps/shared/lessons/sections.js?v=1"></script>.
Pattern lessons: every new bass line, comping rhythm, drum groove or conga part needs a PLAN entry (ladder, tips) in scripts/pattern-lessons.mjs, its style a STYLE chart, and any rhythm it shares a SAME group; then node scripts/pattern-lessons.mjs (it lists parts with no plan) and quarto render lessons/patterns.
A lesson when the style needs teaching beyond its patterns, or when two styles overlap (lessons/stride-boogie.qmd): .ar-demo examples from lessons/_arrange-kit.qmd, listed in lessons/index.qmd and the Lessons menu in _quarto.yml.
The pages that load a changed engine file include every lesson that has a band: bump ?v= in all of them (grep -rlE 'band/(bass|comp|catalog)\.js\?v=' --include='*.qmd' lessons tools) and render them.
Check: tests/band/lessons/patterns.cdp.js with PAGES= the new lessons (copy _site/lessons/patterns into tests/band/lead/site/lessons/).

Say what was not verified. Nothing here can be listened to from a terminal. Report the pattern in beats, what the tests cover, and that it needs ears. Do not commit unless asked.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
The conga player (congas.js) is a part of its own beside bass, comping and drums: it has its own fader, staff and MIDI track, and any style may have it. Adding a pattern:

PATTERNS in congas.js: id: { bars: [...], three: [...], triplet: [...] }. bars is one or two 4/4 bars (a two-bar pattern follows the bar number); three is one bar of 3/4 and triplet one bar of 12/8, both optional. A bar is a list of rows [pos, drum, stroke, hand, vel]: drum is "c" (conga, the higher drum) or "t" (tumba); stroke is H heel, T toe, S slap, O open, M muffled, B bass; hand is "L" or "R". Positions are beats; 12/8 positions are thirds of a beat (x.333). A pattern with no bar for the meter plays the steady one, so it can stay short.
congas in catalog.js: { id, label, feel, group, tags, desc }; the desc says which stroke falls on which beat, with which hand.
FITS.congas: the style ids it belongs in (steady and none fit every style).
A style that should have them says congas:"id" on its row in styles. Left out, the style has none.
tests/band/congas/t_congas.js checks every pattern in every meter, and that the other players play the same notes with or without them.

Sounds: the congas are one sample set (congas in sounds.js) built from the soundfont’s three conga notes; a new stroke is a new piece name there, a trim, and its place in BandNotation.congaName and the GM table in midi.js.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
The Style menu of the Backing Track page; ?style=id in its address.
A tune’s ABC: %%style bossa nova above the first P: line (the whole tune).
One section: %%style bossa nova on the line under its P: line, or "^style bossa nova" in a bar (from that bar to the next section; "^style none" ends it early). The form bar carries style, and BandCatalog.sectionOpts turns it into the options for those bars. Single parts can follow the name: %%style Swing; voicing drop2; rhythm charleston; bass two; drums funk; feel straight. The comping moves to the instrument the style is built around (sound.lead), if it has one. The page’s blend sliders and walk amount do not apply inside such a section. On the Backing Track page the Band menus change to a section’s settings as it starts, and a change made there stays with that section (opts.sectionOverrides, which the player puts before the section’s style).
A crash grabbed with the hand: "^choke" in a bar (the crash on its beat 1, stopped before beat 2), beside "^fill" and "^stop".
Two built-in setups in presets.js (“Style demo: …”) tour the jazz and the pop, rock and country styles a section at a time. Add a new style to the one it belongs in.
A lyrics-site song file (~/Projects/carols/site/extra/*.cho): {style: carol} above the first heading for the song, or under a heading for that section. See the top of tools/chordpro.py there.
A name matches an id, a menu label, or part of a label, ignoring case.

title: Adding a style to the Backing Track band
text:
Plain JS globals, no build step, no dependencies. Match the comment density and voice of the file.
A new option is opt-in: an existing style must sound exactly as it did, and an option left unset must not draw from the random number generator (the tests compare runs).
Sample sets are named only in sounds.js. A new sound is one entry there (family, label, zones, and an optional amp chain); the Comping menu, the player and styleOpts pick it up from that entry. Add its General MIDI program to PROGRAM in midi.js, and its samples to tests/band/meter/fetch-samples.js.
Write descriptions for a music teacher: beats and instruments, no code words.

title: Lesson diagrams: the house style
text:
Lesson diagrams: the house style
Read from the drawings already on the site (diagrams.js, hands.js, drumkit.js, rec-kit-mic.js) and kept by every new one (gear-diagrams.js follows it).

Schematic, not photographic. Flat shapes, one ink stroke (--site-ink, 2 px, round joins), fills from --site-surface / --site-surface-2. No gradients, shadows or perspective; an end-on face or a side view, never 3/4.
Site tokens, not hex. Ink, surfaces, borders and accent come from custom.css (--site-*). A colour that means something gets a named token of its own (below), defined once.
Colour means one thing everywhere. Chord colours (LessonDiagrams.COLORS) mean “which chord”. For gear: | token | means | |————–|—————————————–| | --gd-hot | signal, hot (+), tip, left | | --gd-cold | cold (−, the flipped copy), ring, right | | --gd-gnd | ground, shield, sleeve, earth | | --gd-power | mains / DC power | | --gd-data | control data (MIDI, USB) | | --site-accent | “look here”: the one thing the caption is about | Anything without a role stays ink and surface.
Labels on the drawing, mono font (--font-mono), next to the part: pin numbers, T / R / S, piece names. No separate legend to look things up in.
Every part that has a name has a <title> (hover tooltip, read by screen readers), and the svg has role="img" and an aria-label saying what the whole picture shows.
Placed by a tag, drawn by a script. A page writes <div class="gear-fig" data-fig="..."> (or calls a LessonDiagrams.* function); no SVG is pasted into a .qmd. A fix in the script fixes every page.
One fact per drawing, with a one-line caption under it (data-caption overrides). Several facts → several figures in a row (.gear-row, .hand-row) that wrap on a phone.
Readable at phone width. Design in a viewBox about as wide as it will be shown (cards ~150-200, wide figures ≤ 480); text no smaller than 11 units. A wide chain wraps into rows rather than shrinking.
Doing something is a bonus. Click to play (drum kit), drag (bend), hover to name. A still picture that is right beats a moving one that is vague.
Facts checked. Pin numbers, wiring and orders come from a standard or a manual; say which in a comment beside the data.

title: Watermelon Man earns its “(Blues)” label
text:
Label it “F Major (Blues)”. By the site’s own definition (dominant-seventh chords on I and IV) the 1962 head qualifies exactly: every source that gives chords shows only F7, Bb7 and C7 in a 12-bar skeleton stretched to 16 bars. Every web form description found calls it a “16-bar blues”, or an “altered” or “extended” one, and none says it is not a blues. The evidence has three limits. Almost all of it is educational or encyclopedic, with no peer-reviewed or print authority confirmed. Critics classify the tune by genre as hard bop, soul jazz, funk or boogaloo, and Hancock never calls it a blues in any source reached. The melody’s blues content (blue notes, pentatonic basis) was not checked at all. “Blues” is therefore the right tonality tag on harmonic grounds. The “16-bar” detail belongs in a separate form field, not in the tonality label. Gioia (p. 446), the Real Book and Grove could shift the confidence but are unlikely to reverse the recommendation. The 1963 Mongo Santamaría version keeps the same form and harmony. The 1973 Head Hunters version is a rebuilt form and should not carry the label automatically.


The 1962 head is 16 bars in F. The best bar-by-bar chart found (a teaching site, not a published lead sheet) reads F7 for bars 1-4, Bb7 for 5-6, F7 for 7-8, then C7 / Bb7 / C7 / Bb7 / C7 / Bb7 in bars 9-14, and F7 for 15-16 (saxstation). Ethan Hein’s independent analysis agrees: “essentially a twelve-bar blues in F, but with bars nine and ten repeated three times” (Ethan Hein). Set against the standard 12-bar plan (I for four bars, IV for two, I for two, then V, IV and I), the first eight bars match exactly and the V-IV pair is simply stated three times before the tonic tag. That is 8 + 3×2 + 2 = 16.
The harmony is purely dominant sevenths on I, IV and V. No source shows an Eb7 or other flat-side chord in the 1962 head. A UVM blog mentions “four chords” (UVM blog), but that conflicts with the three-chord chart. Hooktheory lists I7, IV7 and V7 in F major (Hooktheory). Dominant-seventh chords on the tonic are the standard open-source description of blues harmony, and blues is commonly said to favour plagal motion (IV to I) over authentic cadences (Open Music Theory, via search summary). Watermelon Man fits both, and the V-IV alternation is a normal blues turnaround device, not a modal or functional departure.
Two readings of the form exist. The “variant” reading treats it as a 12-bar blues with the V-IV tail doubled, which keeps it inside the blues. Peer-reviewed work on 16-bar forms instead tends to describe an 8+8 hybrid with verse and chorus character, though it argues that “blues that connected with the popular mainstream formally and otherwise did not cease to be blues” and that the genre is “inherently hybrid” (Carter, Music Theory Online 2025). Either reading keeps the tune a blues. The “variant” reading fits this tune’s actual chords more closely, because bars 1-8 are an unaltered 12-bar opening.



Web databases and lesson sites converge. AllSolos lists the form as “Blues - 16 bars”, “built on an extended blues structure” (AllSolos). Standard Repertoire calls it an “Altered blues” of 16 bars (Standard Repertoire). Learn Jazz Standards says “This 16 bar blues is played in a straight eight groove” (learnjazzstandards.com). JazzFuel says “essentially a sixteen-bar blues: the first 8 bars mimic a classic blues exactly” (JazzFuel). FretDojo says “it’s a 16 bar blues, rather than a 12 bar blues” (FretDojo). Wikipedia states the tune “is written in a sixteen-bar blues form” (Wikipedia), and its Sixteen-bar blues page cites the tune as an example with no inline source. The three references on that page do not mention it (Wikipedia). The Herbie Hancock site quotes the 1962 liner notes calling it a “modified blues” and a “strongly gospel-infused 16-bar theme” (herbiehancock.com). Counting these as independent confirmations would overstate the evidence, since several sites likely echo one another.
The critical frame is different. Reviewers and encyclopedias use genre terms: hard bop and soul jazz for the album, and “bluesy” for the track (Wikipedia, Takin’ Off). Others cite R&B, soul jazz and bebop influences, and call the Head Hunters version a “radical jazz-funk makeover” (uDiscover). No dissenting source arguing “not a blues” was located, though the search for one was limited.



Hancock describes the origin as the cry and horse-drawn wagon of a Chicago watermelon seller, says “It took 15 minutes to write”, and says he wanted the tune to be “real” rather than merely commercial (MOJO). In the same interview he says he grew up in Chicago hearing “the real blues, Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf”. In no source reached does he call this tune a blues. Billy Higgins’ feel is described, via Hancock, as “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz” (uDiscover). The straight-eighths groove, gospel piano vamp and funk orientation place it in the soul-jazz and boogaloo idiom more than in a traditional shuffle blues.
This matters because “blues” has three meanings that give different answers. As a form or chord scheme it is a blues. As a marketing genre (blues as a category of 1920s recording) it is not. As an idiom in Albert Murray’s sense of stylised music of creative artists (Pistelli on Murray, secondary) it plausibly is. Scholars also caution that the 12-bar AAB I-IV-V prototype is a later standardisation, since early blues had many structures (Wikipedia, Blues, relaying Evans and Odum), so a strict 12-bar test would be historically arbitrary. The site’s tag measures harmony, so the first meaning is the relevant one.



Mongo Santamaría’s hit keeps the form per Hein, with two extra groove bars on the second head, and a slower guajira-based groove. It reached No. 10 on the Hot 100 (uDiscover says No. 11) and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998 (Wikipedia; JazzTimes). The claim that its harmony is unchanged rests only on Hein’s statement that the form matches, with no chart found. The 1973 Head Hunters track is about 75 BPM, has no solos, adds a chord (Hein hears a Gb7 and a new section a minor third up; UVM says Ab7) and replaces the final bars (Ethan Hein). The two accounts of the added chords conflict and no transcription resolves them. A tag on the composition would still be “F Major (Blues)”. A per-recording tonality tag for Head Hunters should not use “(Blues)” without a chart showing which chords sit where, since the new section leaves the I-IV-V frame.



“(Blues)” is the one the data supports. It matches the site’s definition, uses no unverified claim, and lets a student find the tune alongside other dominant-seventh pieces. “(16-bar blues)” is accurate to the web sources but defeats the tag’s purpose. It would create a new category for a single tune, misleads on 8-bar and 12-bar equivalence, and states a form fact inside a tonality field. If the site has a bar-count or form field, put “16 bars (12-bar blues with the V-IV pair repeated)” there. Not labelling would be defensible only if the site treated “Blues” as a genre judgement, which its own definition says it does not. The weakest honest objection is that “Blues” may suggest a shuffle feel and blue-note melody to a student. A short note on the tune page, that the groove is straight-eighths soul jazz, covers that.



Print authorities were not reachable: the Real Book and Sher charts, Gioia’s The Jazz Standards (the entry is on p. 446 per a catalogue listing; its wording was not obtained), Grove and New Grove Dictionary of Jazz, the Penguin Guide and AllMusic review text, Levine, Coker, Aebersold and Pond’s Head Hunters book. The chord chart rests on one teaching site plus Hein, not a published lead sheet. Key, chord extensions and any substitutions in the Real Book version are unchecked. The melody was not analysed: no source describes blue thirds, minor pentatonic or the blues scale, and an ABC transcription from the Jazz Day score would settle it. The Hancock quotes come from secondary pages, not the memoir or the NPR transcript. The Wikipedia entry for the tune cites Lyons 1989 and Santoro 2004 only second-hand.
Checking would change the following. A published chart with the same F7/Bb7/C7 changes would confirm the label with no edits. Gioia or a lead sheet calling it a “blues” would add a print authority for “16-bar blues” and could justify a form note quoting it. A chart with substituted chords (for example extended or altered dominants) would not alter the “dominant sevenths on I and IV” test unless the I or IV chord is not dominant. A melody showing no blues-scale content would argue for a footnote rather than removing the tag, because the site’s definition is harmonic. Only a respected source stating the tune is not a blues, or a chart where I and IV are not dominant sevenths, would justify dropping the label. The searches found neither, though the search for dissent was limited.



The question mixes form, harmony and genre, and the answer differs by lens: by harmony and form the 1962 head is a blues, by recording-industry genre it is soul jazz, and by Hancock’s own account it is a street-cry tune. The site’s tonality tag measures only the first, so “(Blues)” is correct and low-risk. The useful novel point is that the “16” only describes a stretched tail, with bars 1-8 identical to a standard blues. A form field can state this precisely without inventing a new tonality category, and the Head Hunters recording is the case that needs separate handling.
